## The Buddha Gem
## Chapter 38
## The Former Parents of the Blessed One
## The Story of the Brahmin and His Wife of Sāketa
On one occasion, after the Blessed One had completed his rains retreat (vassa) in the city of Sāvatthī, he reflected on several matters: the maintenance of his health, the prescription of training rules (sikkhāpada) that had not yet been established, the guidance of beings worthy of liberation, and the preaching of Jātakas and other discourses according to specific circumstances. Having considered these, he set out on a journey from Sāvatthī and in due course arrived at the city of Sāketa in the evening, where he entered the grove known as Añjana.
2:
2
The citizens of Sāketa, hearing the news of the Blessed One’s arrival, thought, “It is now night, and not the proper time to visit the Blessed One.” Thus, they did not go to him during the night. When morning dawned, they took flowers, perfumes, and other offerings and went to attend upon the Blessed One. They performed acts of worship, paid their respects, and engaged in pleasant conversation, remaining gathered around the Blessed One until it was time for him to enter the city for alms.

Then, when it was time for the alms round, the Blessed One, surrounded by a company of bhikkhus, entered the city of Sāketa for alms. At that time, a wealthy Brahmin of Sāketa was coming out of the city. Meeting the Blessed One face-to-face at the city gate, a powerful fatherly love arose in him. Crying out, “Dear son, it has been so long since I last saw you!” he rushed toward the Blessed One.

The Blessed One had already forewarned the bhikkhus, saying, “Bhikkhus, let this Brahmin do as he wishes; do not hinder him.” The Brahmin approached like a mother cow longing for her young calf. He moved around the Blessed One’s person from all four sides—front, back, left, and right—and embraced him, saying, “Dear son, it has been so long since I saw you; we have been separated for a very long time.” (Indeed, if that Brahmin had not been allowed to show such affection, his heart would have burst from grief.)
3:
3
The Brahmin of Sāketa addressed the Blessed One, saying, “Exalted Buddha, I am capable of offering alms-food to the bhikkhus who have come together with the Blessed One. Please show me compassion and favor.” The Blessed One accepted the Brahmin’s invitation by remaining silent. The Brahmin then took the Blessed One’s alms bowl and walked ahead, sending a messenger to his wife with the message, “Our eldest son has arrived; prepare the seats.” The Brahmin woman did as she was told. While she stood waiting for the Blessed One’s arrival, she saw him while he was still on the way. A powerful motherly love arose in her, and crying out, “Dear son, it has been a very long time since I saw you!” she embraced the Blessed One’s feet and wept. They then invited him into their home and respectfully offered alms-food. After the Blessed One had finished his meal, the Brahmin himself took the alms bowl and performed the task of washing it.

The Blessed One then preached a suitable Dhamma discourse to the Brahmin and his wife. At the conclusion of the sermon, the Brahmin and his wife became Stream-enterers (Sotāpannas). Thereafter, the couple pleaded with the Blessed One, saying, “Exalted Buddha, as long as the Blessed One resides in this city of Sāketa, please accept alms-food only at our home, together with your company of disciples.”
4:
4
Then the Blessed One said, “O Brahmin and wife, it is not the custom of Buddhas to always receive alms at only one place as you have requested.” When he declined in this way, the couple pleaded again, “Exalted Buddha, if that is the case, after you have gone on your alms round with the company of bhikkhus, please come and take your meal only at our home, and only after preaching the Dhamma, proceed back to the monastery.” The Blessed One, to show them favor, agreed to their request.

From that time on, the people called the Brahmin “The Father of the Blessed One” and the Brahmin woman “The Mother of the Blessed One.” The family of that Brahmin of Sāketa also came to be known as “The Family of the Blessed One.”

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One, “Exalted Buddha, I know the Mother and Father of the Blessed One (to be Queen Mahāmāyā and King Suddhodana). This being so, why do this Brahmin and his wife of Sāketa say, ‘I am the Buddha’s mother’ and ‘I am the Buddha’s father’?” The Blessed One then said to the Venerable Ānanda, “Ānanda, this Brahmin and his wife were my mother and father for five hundred consecutive births; they were my elder aunt and elder uncle for five hundred consecutive births; they were my younger aunt and younger uncle for five hundred consecutive births.”
5:
5
“They speak thus because of the exceptional love and affection that existed in the past,” the Blessed One said, and he preached this verse:

Pubbe va sannivāsena, paccuppannahitena vā.
Evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, uppalaṃva yathodake.

(Through past association or through present benefit, love is thus born, just as a lotus is born in water.)

By past association (pubbe sannivāsena): because of having lived together in previous lives with intertwined affection. Or by present benefit (paccuppannahitena): because of performing services for one’s welfare in this present life. In this way (evaṃ): through these two causes of connection. Love (pemaṃ): the two kinds of love, namely craving-based love and metta-based love. Is born (jāyate): arises and becomes manifest. (How is it so?) Just as a lotus (uppalaṃ va): or any other water-born flower. Depending on (nissāya): two causes, namely water and mud. Just as it is born (jāyate yathā): so it is.

After preaching this verse, the Blessed One resided in the city of Sāketa for as long as there were beings to be guided to liberation. When he set out on his journey again, he returned to Sāvatthī. The Brahmin and his wife of Sāketa, by attending upon the noble bhikkhus and hearing the appropriate Dhamma teachings, gradually attained the three higher paths and eventually entered Parinibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-parinibbāna).
6:
6
## At the Parinibbāna Ceremony of the Brahmin and His Wife
## Eighty-four Thousand Beings Attain Liberation
At that time, the Brahmins living in Sāketa thought, “We shall honor our relatives,” and they gathered together in unity. The laymen and laywomen who were Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners also thought, “We shall honor our fellow practitioners of the Dhamma,” and they gathered together in unity. Those Brahmins and Noble disciples placed the two physical remains (utujarūpa-kalāpa) of the Brahmin and his wife into a single gabled palanquin (pāsāda) and, honoring them with flowers and perfumes, carried them out of the city.

On that day, at dawn, the Blessed One surveyed the world of beings with his Buddha-eye (consisting of the knowledge of the latent tendencies of beings and the knowledge of the maturity of their faculties). Knowing that the Brahmin and his wife had entered Parinibbāna, he reflected, “If I go to the funeral ceremony of that Brahmin and his wife, many people will hear the Dhamma and realize the Four Noble Truths, entering the path of liberation.” Having understood this, he took his bowl and robes and traveled from Sāvatthī, arriving at the cemetery where the funeral was being held.

The people, seeing the Blessed One, said, “The Blessed One has come to perform the funeral rites for his mother and father,” and they stood respectfully paying homage. The citizens brought the palanquin carrying the remains to the cemetery.
7:
7
Having honored them and reached the cemetery, they asked the Blessed One, “Exalted Buddha, how should we honor this Brahmin and his wife who were Noble ones?”

The Blessed One, wishing to reveal that the Brahmin and his wife had attained the state of Arahantship, and intending that they should be honored just as Arahants are honored, preached this verse from the Dhammapada:

Ahiṃsakā ye munayo, niccaṃ kāyena saṃvutā.
Te yanti accutaṃ ဌānaṃ, yattha gantvā na socare.

(Those sages who are harmless and ever restrained in body, go to the deathless state where, having gone, they do not sorrow.)

Those sages (ye munayo): those Arahants. Are harmless (ahiṃsakā): they have no inclination whatsoever to harm or oppress others. By body (kāyena): or by the three doors of body, speech, and mind. Ever (niccaṃ): always. Restrained (saṃvutā): they practice restraint to avoid unwholesome deeds. Those sages (te munayo): those Arahants. To which Nibbāna (yattha): having reached that Nibbāna through penetrative knowledge. Do not sorrow (na socare): they do not grieve. To that state (taṃ ဌānaṃ): to that Nibbāna. Which is deathless (accutaṃ): where there is no falling away, vanishing, or death. They go (yanti): they arrive through the penetrative knowledge of the four paths and four fruits.

(At the conclusion of this Dhamma verse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other stages—according to the Dhammapada Commentary).

After the Blessed One had preached this Dhammapada verse, he addressed the great assembly of the citizens of Sāketa—
8:
Having observed them, and wishing to preach a discourse suitable for that moment, the Buddha preached the Jarā Sutta (Sutta Nipāta, Aṭṭhakavagga, Sutta 6). (That Jarā Sutta should be studied from the Myanmar translation of the Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi).

At the conclusion of the preaching of the Jarā Sutta, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.

This is the story of the elderly Brahmin couple of Sāketa.

## The Story of King Viṭaṭūbha (The Friend-Betrayer)

(1) Prince Pasenadi, the son of King Mahākosala, the ruler of Sāvatthī; (2) Prince Mahāli, a Licchavī prince from Vesālī; and (3) Prince Bandhula, the son of the Malla king of Kusinārā—these three princes went to the city of Takkasilā to study under a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha). They met at a rest house outside the city and, after inquiring about each other's purpose for coming, their lineage, and their names, they became close friends. Together, they approached the world-renowned teacher and studied their arts. Before long, they became proficient in their studies. After taking leave of their teacher, they departed from Takkasilā together and returned to their respective kingdoms.

Among those three princes, Prince Pasenadi demonstrated his skills to his father, King Mahākosala. The Great King was extremely pleased and satisfied,
9:
and having been consecrated in the kingship, he became King Pasenadi of Kosala, the ruler of Sāvatthī.

When Prince Mahāli demonstrated his skills to the Licchavī kings, he did so with such great effort that both of his eyes were destroyed and he became blind. The Licchavī kings said, "Alas! Our teacher, Prince Mahāli, has come to lose both his eyes. We shall not abandon Prince Mahāli, but shall care for and support him." Having consulted and agreed unanimously, they granted him ownership of a city gate that yielded a tax revenue of one hundred thousand. Relying on that gate, Prince Mahāli lived there, teaching the arts to five hundred Licchavī princes.

As for Prince Bandhula, the Malla kings (without Prince Bandhula's knowledge) placed an iron rod in the center of sixty bamboo stalks, making them into a single bundle. They set up sixty such bundles and, to test his skill, said, "Dear son, cut through these sixty bundles of bamboo." Bandhula leapt eighty cubits into the air and, with his sword, cut through the sixty bundles of bamboo in succession. Prince Bandhula heard the sound (kiri!) of the iron rod contained in the last bundle and asked, "What is this sound?" When he learned that iron rods had been secretly placed inside all sixty bundles, he threw down his sword and wept, saying, "Among so many of my relatives and friends, not a single one had a heart of affection to inform me of this."
10:
"If I had known this beforehand, I could have cut them without even making the sound of the iron rod." He then said to his parents, his benefactors, "I shall kill all these Malla kings and take the kingship myself." His mother and father restrained him in various ways, saying, "Dear son, this system of reigning by turn is an arrangement descended through the lineage of the Malla kings. You cannot act according to your current plan." When they said this, Prince Bandhula said, "If that is the case, I shall go to my friend, King Pasenadi of Kosala," and he went to live in Sāvatthī.

King Pasenadi of Kosala, hearing that Prince Bandhula had arrived in his kingdom, went out to welcome him. With great honor and ceremony, he brought Prince Bandhula into the city and appointed him to the position of Commander-in-Chief (Senāpati). Commander Bandhula sent for his mother and father and had them live in Sāvatthī as well. This is the account of the three princes: Prince Kosala, Prince Mahāli the Licchavī, and Prince Bandhula the Malla.

## King Pasenadi of Kosala

## Planning to Become Familiar with the Sāsana

One day, while King Pasenadi of Kosala was standing on his golden palace and looking out at the city streets, he saw thousands of monks heading to the houses of Anāthapiṇḍika the Treasurer, Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika the Treasurer, Visākhā the Great Lay-Supporter, and the Treasurer's wife Suppavāsā for their daily alms. He asked his attendants, "Where are the venerable ones going?"
11:
The attendants replied, "Great King, every day two thousand monks go to the house of Anāthapiṇḍika the Treasurer for daily alms, alms by lottery (salāka-bhatta), alms for the sick, and so on. Five hundred monks go to the house of Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika. Similarly, five hundred go to the house of Visākhā the Great Lay-Supporter, and five hundred monks go to the house of the Treasurer's wife Suppavāsā."

When they reported this, the King also wished to serve and support the Saṅgha with alms. He went to the Jetavana Monastery and invited the Buddha along with one thousand monks. For seven days, he personally offered alms with his own hands (sāhattika-dāna). On the seventh day, he paid homage to the Buddha with great respect and requested, "Exalted Buddha, may the Blessed One, together with five hundred monks, always accept alms from me."

Then the Buddha said, "Great King, it is not the custom of the Buddhas to always receive alms in a single place. Many people long for the arrival of the Buddhas." The King then requested, "If that is the case, then please send one permanent monk along with five hundred others, O Buddha." The Buddha assigned this responsibility to the Venerable Ānanda Thera.

When the monks arrived, the King did not make arrangements such as, "When the Saṅgha arrives, receive their bowls, and such-and-such persons must serve them." For seven days, he himself
12:
served them. However, on the eighth day, his mind was distracted by various state affairs, and he forgot to serve alms to the Saṅgha.

In the King's palace, if no orders are given, people do not have the opportunity to arrange seats and serve the monks alms. (Consequently, not a single person paid attention to or served the monks). Many monks thought, "We cannot stay here," and they departed. The King forgot again the next day, and on that day too, many monks departed. The King forgot for a third day as well. At that time, all the remaining monks departed, except for the Venerable Ānanda Thera. Only the Venerable Ānanda Thera remained.

Those who are possessed of glory and merit (the Great Disciples) are accustomed to remaining after considering various reasons; they are accustomed to protecting the faith of the lay devotees. To continue—the Buddha's two Chief Disciples, (1) Venerable Sāriputta and (2) Venerable Mahāmoggallāna; the two Chief Female Disciples, (1) Khemā Therī and (2) Uppalavaṇṇā Therī; among the male lay devotees, (1) Citta the Householder and (2) Hatthaka Āḷavaka; and among the female lay devotees, (1) the Treasurer's wife Nandamātā of Veḷukaṇḍaka and (2) Khujjuttarā—starting with these eight, all the disciples who attained the rank of Etadagga (pre-eminence) were,
13:
in a partial sense, those who had fulfilled the ten perfections (pāramīs) and were thus individuals possessed of glory, merit, and the fulfillment of past aspirations. The Venerable Ānanda Thera had also fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and was a person of glory and merit who had fulfilled past aspirations. Because he was accustomed to remaining after considering various reasons, he stayed behind alone to protect the faith of the lay devotees.

The attendants had to provide a seat and serve alms to the Venerable Ānanda Thera, who remained alone. King Pasenadi of Kosala arrived only after the monks had departed. When he saw the various kinds of food remaining as they were originally prepared, he asked, "Did the venerable ones not come?" When he heard the attendants' reply, "Great King, only the Venerable Ānanda Thera came," he became angry with the monks, thinking, "Surely, the monks have caused the waste of so much of my food!" He went to the Buddha and asked, "Exalted Buddha, I prepared alms for five hundred monks. I am told that only the Venerable Ānanda Thera came. The prepared alms remain exactly as they were. The five hundred monks did not even take notice that they were invited to my palace. What is the reason for this?"

Then the Buddha, without mentioning any fault of the monks, said, "Great King, for my disciples,
14:
the monks, there is no familiarity or intimacy with you. That is likely why they did not come." Having said this, and wishing to preach in detail the nine reasons why one should not approach or visit the houses of the four classes of devotees, and the nine reasons why one should approach and visit them, the Buddha addressed the monks and preached the Kula Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Navaka Nipāta, 1-Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka, 2-Sīhanādavagga, Sutta 7) as follows:

## The Kula Sutta Discourse

## (Houses of Devotees That Should Be Visited and

## Houses of Devotees That Should Not Be Visited)

Monks, it is not proper to visit the house of a devotee who possesses nine characteristics if one has not yet gone there; and if one has already gone there, it is not proper to sit down. What are the nine? They are:

(1) They do not welcome one with respect,
(2) They do not bow with respect,
(3) They do not offer a seat with respect,
(4) They hide their existing possessions from the monks,
(5) Although they have many things to give, they give only a little,
(6) Although they have excellent things to give, they give only coarse things,
16:
Monks, if a lay devotee's house is endowed with these nine factors, it is proper to visit if one has not yet gone, and if one has already gone, it is proper to sit down.
This is the Kula Sutta.

"Great King, in this way, my disciples, the monks, may depart because they do not find intimacy or familiarity in your presence. Indeed, even in the past, wise men, though treated with great respect in a place where there was no intimacy, would go to a place where intimacy existed when they were afflicted by a terminal illness." Having said this, at the request and inquiry of King Pasenadi of Kosala, the Buddha preached the Kesava Jātaka from the Catukka Nipāta. (This Kesava Jātaka was already described in the section on the conversion of Baka Brahmā in Volume 6, Page 441).

After hearing the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One, King Pasenadi of Kosala reflected, "I should act so as to establish intimacy and familiarity with the Order of Monks. How should I do this?" He then considered, "It would be appropriate to elevate a Sakyan princess, a relative of the Blessed One, to the position of Chief Queen in my golden palace. If I do so, all monks, including the young monks and novices, will think, 'The King is a relative of the Blessed One,' and they will come to me frequently with intimacy and affection." Thinking thus, he sent a royal message to the Sakyan kings, saying, "Please present a Sakyan princess to me." The messengers who were to deliver the royal message asked, "The daughter of which Sakyan king..."
17:
...should we bring?" King Pasenadi of Kosala replied, "Bring any daughter of a Sakyan king, as long as you ensure she is truly a Sakyan princess," and sent the messengers on their way.

The messengers went to the city of Kapilavatthu and requested a daughter from the Sakyan kings. The Sakyans held a meeting and discussed, "King Kosala is a rival king of equal power. If we do not give him a daughter, he will surely act as an enemy and destroy us. However, King Pasenadi of Kosala is not of the same lineage or caste as us. What should we do?"

Then, Mahānāma the Sakyan said, "I have a daughter named Vāsabhakhattiyā, born of my slave woman (named Nāgamuṇḍā), who is endowed with great beauty. Let us give this daughter of the slave woman, Vāsabhakhattiyā." After consulting, they told the messengers, "Very well, messengers, we shall give a noble maiden to your master, King Kosala."

When the messengers asked, "Whose daughter is this maiden you are giving?", the Sakyans replied, "Messengers, she is the daughter of Mahānāma the Sakyan, who is the son of the Blessed One's paternal uncle (Amitodana the Sakyan) and thus a cousin of the Blessed One. Her name is Vāsabhakhattiyā." The messengers returned to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to King Pasenadi.
18:
King Pasenadi said, "If that is so, it is very good. Bring her quickly. However, kings are very deceitful; they might send a daughter of a slave woman claiming she is a princess. Therefore, bring the maiden who eats from the same plate as her father."

The messengers went back to Kapilavatthu and informed the Sakyan kings, "Our master, the great King Kosala, desires only the princess who eats from the same plate as the noble Sakyan kings."

Mahānāma the Sakyan said, "Very well, young men." He had Vāsabhakhattiyā adorned with all kinds of ornaments. When it was time for his meal, he had Vāsabhakhattiyā called and, showing the messengers the act of eating together with her, he handed her over to them.

(In this matter, the way Mahānāma the Sakyan deceived them was: when the messengers demanded, "We can only take the princess who eats together with the noble Sakyans," the Sakyans gave the messengers a place to stay and consulted among themselves. Mahānāma the Sakyan said, "Do not worry too much. I will use a stratagem. When I am eating, you all adorn Vāsabhakhattiyā and bring her to me. When we appear to be eating together, just as I take a handful of rice, you must say, 'Great Lord, such-and-such a king has sent a royal letter; please listen to this letter first,' and show the letter to me." He thus explained his stratagem.)
19:
All the Sakyan kings agreed to this stratagem and acted accordingly.

The messengers took Vāsabhakhattiyā and returned to Sāvatthī, where they reported the matter to King Pasenadi of Kosala. The King was greatly pleased and, making Vāsabhakhattiyā the head of five hundred concubines, he consecrated her as the Chief Queen and cherished her. Before long, Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā gave birth to a son with a golden complexion.

On the day the prince was to be named, King Pasenadi sent a message to the prince's grandfather, Mahānāma the Sakyan, saying, "Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā, the Sakyan princess, has given birth to a son. What name should be given to this son?" The messenger who carried this message happened to be slightly hard of hearing. He went to Kapilavatthu and reported the matter to the prince's grandfather, Mahānāma the Sakyan.

When Mahānāma the Sakyan heard the news, he remarked, "Even before she gave birth to a son, Vāsabhakhattiyā was one who won over everyone. Now, because she has given birth to a son, she will be extremely intimate (vallabhā) with King Kosala."

The hard-of-hearing messenger misheard the word "vallabhā" (meaning intimate/beloved) as "Viḍūḍabha." He returned to King Pasenadi and reported, "Great King, they have named the prince Viḍūḍabha."
20:
King Pasenadi thought, "This name Viḍūḍabha must be an old family name passed down through our lineage," and thus named the prince "Viḍūḍabha." Later, with the intention of pleasing the Buddha, King Pasenadi appointed Prince Viḍūḍabha to the position of General even while he was still young.

Prince Viḍūḍabha grew up with royal honors. When he was seven years old, he saw other princes receiving gifts such as toy elephants and horses from their maternal grandparents. He asked his mother, Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā, "O Mother, other princes receive gifts like toy elephants and horses from their maternal grandparents, but for me, not a single grandparent sends any gift. Why is this? Do you have no parents, Mother?"

Then, Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā deceived Prince Viḍūḍabha, saying, "Dear son, the Sakyan kings are your maternal grandparents. However, because your grandfather and grandmother live in a very distant place, they are unable to send any gifts."

When Prince Viḍūḍabha was sixteen years old, he said, "O Mother, I wish to see the palace of my maternal grandparents." His mother replied, "Dear son, it is not appropriate to go. What would you do at the palace of your maternal grandparents?"
21:
Despite her prohibition, Prince Viḍūḍabha repeatedly pleaded to go. Finally, unable to stop him, his mother relented and said, "If that is so, then go."

Prince Viḍūḍabha informed his father, the King, and departed from Sāvatthī with a large retinue of troops. Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā sent a secret message ahead, saying, "I am living happily as the Chief Queen here in Sāvatthī. Please, noble Sakyans, do not show any sign of distinction or difference to Prince Viḍūḍabha."

When the Sakyans learned of Viḍūḍabha's coming, their pride of birth was so fierce that they thought, "We cannot pay homage to Viḍūḍabha, the son of a slave woman." They sent all the princes who were younger than Viḍūḍabha away to the countryside beforehand. When Prince Viḍūḍabha arrived at Kapilavatthu, the Sakyans assembled at the royal assembly hall.

Prince Viḍūḍabha went and stood at that assembly hall. Then the Sakyans said to him, "Dear son, this person is your grandfather (mother's father); this person is your uncle (mother's brother)," and had him pay homage to them. Prince Viḍūḍabha went around paying homage to all the Sakyan kings, but he did not see a single Sakyan who would pay homage to him. He asked, "Are there no Sakyan kings who should pay homage to me?" The Sakyans replied, "Dear son, your younger brothers, the princes, have gone to the countryside for a visit."
22:
After speaking thus, they provided Prince Viḍūḍabha with great hospitality and entertainment. Prince Viḍūḍabha stayed in Kapilavatthu for two or three days and then departed with a large retinue of troops. At that time, a slave woman was washing the plank where Prince Viḍūḍabha had sat in the pavilion, saying and cursing, "This is the plank where Viḍūḍabha, the son of the slave woman named Vāsabhakhattiyā, sat," while washing it with milk-water (water mixed with milk). One of Viḍūḍabha's men, having forgotten his weapon and returning to retrieve it, heard the sound of her cursing Viḍūḍabha. Upon inquiring about the matter, he learned that "the maiden Vāsabhakhattiyā was born of a slave woman named Nāgamuṇḍā through a union with Mahānāma the Sakyan." He then informed his fellow soldiers of this fact. Consequently, the news spread among the people, and a great rumor arose, saying, "Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā is the daughter of a slave."

When Prince Viḍūḍabha heard of this, he harbored a great grudge, saying, "Let these Sakyans wash the plank where I sat with milk-water for now. When I become king, I shall take the blood from the throats of those Sakyans and wash the plank where I sit with their throat-blood."

When Prince Viḍūḍabha arrived back at Sāvatthī, the ministers reported the matter to King Pasenadi of Kosala. The King, thinking, "They have given a slave woman to a great king like me," became angry with the Sakyans.
23:
Being enraged, the King stripped Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā and her son Viḍūḍabha of their royal titles, honors, and the rank and regalia of Commander-in-Chief, granting them only the provisions suitable for male and female slaves.

Two or three days later, the Buddha went to the golden palace of King Pasenadi of Kosala and sat upon the prepared Buddha-seat. The King arrived, paid respectful homage to the Buddha, and reported, "Venerable Sir, your relatives have given me a slave's daughter (passing her off as a princess). Therefore, I have stripped that slave's daughter Vāsabhakhattiyā and her son Viḍūḍabha of the royal honors of a Queen and the honors of a Commander-in-Chief that were previously conferred, and have allowed them only the provisions suitable for slaves."

The Buddha said, "Great King, the Sakyans have indeed done what is improper. When giving, they should only give a maiden of equal lineage. However, Great King, I wish to specifically tell you this: the maiden Vāsabhakhattiyā is not only a daughter of the noble Mahānāma the Sakyan, but she was also consecrated as the Chief Queen in the palace of you, a noble King of the Khattiya caste. Prince Viḍūḍabha is also a son born of you, a noble King of the Khattiya caste."
24:
"What can the mother's lineage do? Only the father's lineage is the standard to be respected." Having gained this right understanding, the Buddha continued, "In the past, wise men gave the position of Chief Queen to a poor wood-gathering woman. The child born from the womb of that poor wood-gatherer became the king of the twelve-yojana-wide city of Bārāṇasī, known as King Kaṭṭhavāhana." He then preached the Kaṭṭhavāhana Jātaka from the Ekanipāta.

Upon hearing the Buddha's discourse, King Pasenadi of Kosala was pleased and satisfied, thinking, "Indeed, only the father's lineage is the standard to be respected." He then restored to Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā and Prince Viḍūḍabha their original honors of Chief Queen and Commander-in-Chief as they were before.

## The Story of Commander Bandhula and his wife Mallikā
Mallikā, the wife of Bandhula (the Malla prince) who was the Commander-in-Chief for King Pasenadi of Kosala, was the daughter of the Malla King of Kusināra. Although Mallikā had lived with Commander Bandhula for a long time, she had no children. Then, Bandhula sent her away, saying, "Return to your parents' home."

Mallikā thought, "I shall return to my parents' home only after seeing the Buddha." She entered the Jetavana monastery and paid homage to the Buddha. The Buddha asked, "Where are you going?" She replied, "Venerable Sir,
25:
"My lord and husband, Commander Bandhula, is sending me back to my parents' home, Venerable Sir." When the Buddha asked, "For what reason?", she replied, "I am a woman who has no children. Therefore, the Commander is sending me back to my parents' home, Venerable Sir." Then the Buddha said, "If that is the case, there is no need to go back to your parents' home. Return to the Commander's house."

Mallikā was filled with joy, paid respectful homage to the Buddha, and returned home. When she arrived, Commander Bandhula asked, "Why have you come back?" She answered, "I have returned because the Buddha told me to return home." Commander Bandhula reflected, "The Buddha, who sees far, must have seen a reason for the birth of children," and he accepted her as his wife as before.

Before long, Mallikā became pregnant and developed a pregnancy craving. She said to General Bandhula, "O Lord, I have developed a craving." When the Commander asked, "What kind of craving?", Mallikā replied, "O Lord, I wish to descend into and bathe in the ceremonial pool used for the consecration of the Licchavī princes in the city of Vesālī, and to drink that water."

Then Commander Bandhula said, "Very well." Taking his thousand-strength bow and placing Mallikā in the chariot, he departed from Sāvatthī. Driving the chariot, he entered the city of Vesālī through the gate assigned to
26:
Mahāli the Licchavī. Mahāli the Licchavī's house was situated near that very gate.

As soon as Mahāli the Licchavī heard the sound of the chariot driven by Bandhula striking the threshold of the gate, he said, "This is the sound of Bandhula's chariot. Today, a great danger will befall the Licchavī princes." There were many guards both inside and outside the ceremonial pool. An iron net was spread over the pool so that even birds could not enter.

Commander Bandhula descended from the chariot, struck the guards with a cane, making them flee, and broke the iron net with his sword. He then let his wife Mallikā bathe in the pool. After he himself had bathed, he calmly placed Mallikā back in the chariot and drove out of Vesālī, returning by the same path he had come.

The guards reported the matter to the Licchavī princes. The Licchavī princes became very angry, and five hundred of them mounted their respective chariots, setting out for battle, saying, "We shall capture Bandhula, the Malla prince and Commander-in-Chief." When the attendants reported this to Mahāli the Licchavī, he warned them, "O Licchavī princes, do not pursue him. Indeed, that Commander Bandhula will kill all of you Licchavī princes." The Licchavī princes replied, "We cannot tolerate this in any way; we will surely pursue him."
27:
At that time, Mahāli the Licchavī, being a former schoolmate who knew Bandhula's strength well, said to the Licchavī princes:

"O Licchavī princes, if that is the case (if you cannot help but pursue), when you see a place where the hubs of Bandhula's chariot wheels have sunk into the ground, turn back from that very spot.

If you do not turn back from there, and as you continue to pursue, you hear a sound like thunder, turn back from that spot.

If you do not turn back from there, you will see holes in the fronts of your chariots. Turn back from that spot where you see them; do not continue to pursue further."

The Licchavī princes did not turn back according to Mahāli's words but continued to pursue Commander Bandhula.

Mallikā, the Commander's wife, saw the chariots of the Licchavī princes approaching and said, "O Lord, I see enemy chariots pursuing us." Bandhula said, "My lady, if that is so, tell me when all five hundred chariots appear as if they were a single chariot."

When all the chariots appeared as one, Mallikā said, "O Lord, they appear as if there were only a single chariot front." Then Commander Bandhula said, "If so, you hold these reins," and giving the reins to Mallikā, he stood in the chariot and prepared his thousand-strength bow.
28:
The chariot wheels sank into the ground up to their hubs. Although the Licchavī princes saw this, they did not turn back and continued their pursuit. Commander Bandhula went a little further and twanged the bowstring. The sound of twanging the bowstring was like a clap of thunder. The Licchavī princes did not turn back from that spot either and continued to advance. Commander Bandhula, while standing in the chariot, shot a single arrow. That arrow pierced the fronts of all five hundred chariots and passed through the five hundred Licchavī princes at the point where their armor was fastened (the chest area) and entered the ground.

The five hundred Licchavī princes, not realizing they had been hit by the arrow, shouted, "Hey Bandhula, stop!" and continued their pursuit. Commander Bandhula stopped the chariot for a moment and said, "You Licchavī princes are already dead men. I have no reason to fight with the dead." When the Licchavī princes said, "Dead men are not like us," Commander Bandhula replied, "If that is so, loosen the armor of the last Licchavī prince and see."

The Licchavī princes, following Bandhula's words, loosened the armor of the last Licchavī prince. As soon as the armor was loosened, that last Licchavī prince passed away and fell. Then Commander Bandhula said to the remaining Licchavī princes, "All of you are dead men in the same manner. Return quickly to your own homes, settle your affairs, and give your final instructions to your wives and children."
29:
"Take off your armor," he gave the final warning. The Licchavī princes did as Bandhula said and all of them met their end.

General Bandhula safely brought Mallikā to the city of Sāvatthī. Mallikā gave birth to sixteen pairs of twin sons. All thirty-two sons were extremely brave and endowed with great strength. They became masters of all branches of knowledge. Each son had a retinue of one thousand heroic men. When they went to the royal palace together with their father, General Bandhula, the entire palace courtyard was filled with Bandhula, his thirty-two sons, and their thirty-two thousand heroic followers.

## General Bandhula Judging in the Court

One day, people who had been unfairly judged and lost their cases at the court saw General Bandhula arriving and cried out loudly, reporting the unfair decisions of the court judges to him. General Bandhula went to the court, re-examined the cases, and made a just decision, ensuring that the rightful owner remained the owner. The people shouted "Sādhu" in loud acclaim.

King Pasenadi Kosala heard the sound of the "Sādhu" acclaim and asked, "What is this sound?"
30:
Upon hearing the reason, the King was greatly pleased and satisfied. He dismissed all those court judges and handed over the court to General Bandhula. From that time on, Bandhula made decisions in accordance with the law.

Then, the former judges who had been dismissed, no longer receiving even small bribes and thus losing their source of income, spoke divisive words at the royal palace to cause a rift, saying, "General Bandhula is aspiring for the kingship." King Pasenadi Kosala, hearing the slander of those former judges, believed them and could not restrain his mind. He thought, "If I have this Bandhula killed within this city of Sāvatthī, the people will blame and condemn me." Planning again, he used a deceptive tactic by having his own men stage a rebellion at the border. He then summoned General Bandhula and ordered, "Friend General, my border regions are on the verge of ruin due to the danger of rebels. You must go with your sons and capture the rebel villains."

He sent him off with a secret order: "You must cut off the heads of Bandhula and his thirty-two sons right outside the city and bring them back." He also sent other brave military commanders along with Bandhula and his sons.

When General Bandhula reached the border region, the men who were pretending to be rebels fled as soon as they heard, "The Great General has arrived." General Bandhula then organized the border region to make it populous and prosperous.
31:
After making the arrangements, he returned. Then, at a place not far from the city (Sāvatthī), the brave military commanders to whom the King had given secret orders cut off the heads of General Bandhula and his thirty-two sons.

On that day, Mallikā, the General's wife, had invited the two Chief Disciples (Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna) along with five hundred monks for a meal. At that time, early in the morning, a message was delivered to Mallikā: "The heads of your husband, General Bandhula, and your thirty-two sons have been cut off." Upon hearing this news, Mallikā did not tell anyone. She kept the message in her bodice and continued to serve the Sangha led by the two Chief Disciples.

Then, while Mallikā's maidservants were serving the monks and bringing a jar of ghee, the large ghee jar accidentally broke in front of the Great Elders. The Elder Sāriputta, the Marshal of the Dhamma, addressed Mallikā, saying, "It is the nature of things that are breakable to break; do not let your mind be troubled by various thoughts."

Mallikā took the message out from her bodice and replied, "Venerable Sir, this message has been delivered to me stating that the heads of the father, General Bandhula, and his thirty-two sons have been cut off. Even upon hearing this news, I was not troubled by various thoughts. Why then should I be troubled
32:
by the breaking of a ghee jar, Venerable Sir?" Venerable Sāriputta then preached the Dhamma discourse starting with "Animittamaññātaṃ, maccānaṃ idha jီvitaṃ—" (Sutta Nipāta, Mahāvagga, Salla Sutta), rose from his seat, and returned to the Jetavana Monastery.

After serving the Sangha, Mallikā called her thirty-two daughters-in-law and advised them, "Daughters-in-law, your husbands, who were without fault, have received the results of their past kamma. Do not worry, do not grieve, and do not weep. Do not harbor ill will toward King Kosala."

King Kosala's spies heard these words, went to the King, and reported the innocence of Bandhula and his sons. King Pasenadi Kosala was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He went to Mallikā's house and apologized to Mallikā and her thirty-two daughters-in-law, asking for their forgiveness. He then told Mallikā to take any boon she desired.

Mallikā replied, "Great King, let it be that I have already received the boon." After the King had left, she performed a meal offering (Kupphī-bhatta), bathed, and then went before the King. She bowed and said, "Great King, you have already granted me a boon. For my part, I have no need for other boons. Please grant permission for my thirty-two daughters-in-law and me to return to our parents' home."
33:
King Pasenadi Kosala satisfactorily accepted Mallikā's request. After sending each of the thirty-two daughters-in-law back to their respective parents' homes, Mallikā herself returned to her parents' home in the city of Kusinārā.

(Continuation of Mallikā's story: Mallikā lived in her parents' home in Kusinārā for a long time. Later, when the Buddha attained Parinibbāna and she heard the news that the Malla princes were carrying the Buddha's body into the city of Kusinārā, she thought, "I will honor the Buddha with this Mahālatā ornament." She took out the Mahālatā ornament, which she had kept without wearing since the death of her husband, General Bandhula. She polished it, washed it with scented water, and waited at her doorway.

According to the Mahā-parinibbāna Sutta Commentary, this Mahālatā ornament existed only in the houses of three people: 1. Visākhā, 2. Mallikā, the wife of General Bandhula, and 3. the thief Devadāniya. According to the Dhammapada Commentary, only three women in the world obtained the Mahālatā ornament: 1. Visākhā, 2. Mallikā, the wife of General Bandhula, and 3. the daughter of a treasurer in Bārāṇasī.)

When the Buddha's physical remains reached her doorway, Mallikā said, "Friends, please set down the Buddha's remains for a moment." She then draped her Mahālatā ornament over the Buddha's body. The ornament, draped from the head, covered him down to the soles of his feet. The golden body of the Buddha appeared exceedingly beautiful when adorned with the Mahālatā ornament made of the seven kinds of jewels.
34:
Seeing how beautiful it was, Mallikā felt great devotion and made an aspiration: "Venerable Blessed One, for as long as I wander in the cycle of Saṃsāra, may I never have the need to wear separate ornaments. May my body always appear as if it were already adorned with ornaments."

(From the Mahā-parinibbāna Sutta Commentary, page 189).

Later, Mallikā passed away and was reborn as a goddess in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. According to her prayer, she became the mistress of a mansion, possessing a unique and radiant golden complexion unlike other deities, and was adorned with clothes and ornaments made of the seven kinds of jewels. (The detailed account should be noted from the Vimānavatthu Commentary, 3. Parittakavagga, 8. Mallikā-vimānavatthu).

King Pasenadi Kosala appointed General Bandhula's nephew, named Dīgha Kārāyana, to the position of General. Even though he was given the position, Dīgha Kārāyana lived seeking an opportunity for revenge against King Kosala, thinking, "This King killed my uncle who was innocent."

King Kosala, ever since he had Bandhula killed without fault, felt intense remorse and found no peace of mind. He could not enjoy his royal luxury. At that time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Medāḷupa in the territory of the Sakyans. King Kosala went to Medāḷupa and stayed in a temporary leaf-palace not far from the monastery where the Buddha resided. Then, with a small retinue, he went to the monastery to pay respects to the Buddha, carrying the five royal regalia.
35:
35
Having handed them over to General Dīghakārāyana, the King entered the Gandhakuti alone.

(In this matter, King Kosala handed over the five royal regalia into the hands of Dīghakārāyana for two reasons: (1) with the intention that "it is not proper to go in the form of a king with a distracted nature into the presence of the most venerable and respected Buddha," and (2) with the intention that "I shall attend upon the Buddha alone and speak words of joy according to my own heart." Indeed, when the five royal regalia are returned, there is no need to tell anyone, "You may return"; all the royal attendants return of their own accord.

When King Kosala entered the monastery alone, a thought arose in the mind of Dīghakārāyana through the power of resentment: "Previously, this King, after holding a private consultation with the monk Gotama, had my uncle, General Bandhula, together with his thirty-two sons, arrested and executed. Now he wishes to hold another private consultation. What is this? Will he have me arrested and executed as well?")

Then, as soon as the King entered the Gandhakuti, General Dīghakārāyana took the five royal regalia, spoke forcefully to Prince Viṭaṭūbha, and consecrated him as king right there. He left behind only one horse, one sword, and one female servant for King Kosala, and after leaving instructions saying, "If the King wishes to live, let him not follow," he took Prince Viṭaṭūbha under the white parasol and returned to Sāvatthī.

King Kosala, after speaking pleasant words with the Buddha and paying homage to Him, departed from the monastery and, no longer seeing his army,
36:
36
questioned the young female servant and learned of the situation. With the thought, "I will go to the city of Rājagaha, call upon my nephew King Ajātasattu for military aid, and then go to Sāvatthī to capture and execute Viṭaṭūbha," he set out for Rājagaha. Along the way, he had to eat broken rice and drink muddy water. Being a person of naturally delicate and refined constitution, that coarse food and water did not digest well for King Kosala. Although the King reached Rājagaha, he arrived at an untimely hour when the city gates were already closed. Thinking, "I will sleep in a rest-house outside the city for tonight and meet my nephew King Ajātasattu tomorrow," he slept in a rest-house outside the city.

During the night, the three humors (phlegm, bile, and wind) became agitated within King Kosala, and he was oppressed by the disease of indigestion. The King was able to go outside only two or three times. From then on, unable to walk on foot, he lay in the lap of the young female servant and passed away at the time when the night was turning into dawn. (At the time King Kosala passed away, he was eighty years of age. At that time, the Buddha was also eighty years of age. From the Dhammacetiya Sutta, Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, page 320.)

When the young female servant realized the King had passed away, she lamented loudly, saying, "My master, King Kosala, having ruled over the two kingdoms of Kāsi and Kosala, has now passed away helplessly in an old rest-house, a place for the destitute, outside another's city." Many people heard this and reported the matter to King Ajātasattu.
37:
37
When King Ajātasattu was informed, he came and looked, and upon recognizing his uncle and learning the reason for his coming, he performed the funeral rites with great ceremony. He then had drums beaten throughout the city to gather his troops, saying, "I shall capture Viṭaṭūbha."

The ministers of King Ajātasattu bowed at his feet and advised him, saying, "Great King, if your uncle (King Kosala) were still alive and healthy, it would be proper for you to go. But now, your younger brother Prince Viṭaṭūbha is also worthy of attaining kingship under the white parasol by relying on you." Thus they restrained him with words of wisdom.

Prince Viṭaṭūbha, after attaining kingship, remembered the old grudge he had formed and planned, "I will kill all the Sakyans." He then set out from Sāvatthī with a large army. On that day, at dawn, the Buddha surveyed the world of beings and saw the impending destruction of His relatives. Thinking, "I should perform an act of assistance for my relatives," He went on His alms round in the morning, and after returning, He lay down on His right side like a lion king in the Gandhakuti. In the evening, He traveled through the air to the territory of Kapilavatthu and sat at the foot of a tree that provided sparse shade near the city.

Not far from that tree, within the territory of King Viṭaṭūbha, there was a banyan tree that provided thick shade. King Viṭaṭūbha saw the Buddha, approached Him, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Buddha, why
38:
38
do You sit at the foot of this tree with sparse shade during such heat? Venerable Sir, please sit at the foot of that banyan tree with thick shade located within my territory."

When he said this, the Buddha replied, "Let it be, Great King. The shade of relatives is indeed cool." At that time, King Viṭaṭūbha thought, "The Buddha must have come to protect His relatives," and after paying respectful homage to the Buddha, he withdrew his army and returned to Sāvatthī. The Buddha also flew into the sky and returned to the Jetavana monastery.

King Viṭaṭūbha again remembered the offense the Sakyans had previously committed against him and set out for a second time in the same manner. He saw the Buddha as before and returned again. For the third time, he set out with a great army, and seeing the Buddha as before, he returned again.

When King Viṭaṭūbha set out for the fourth time, the Buddha surveyed the past kamma of the Sakyans. He saw that the opportunity for the unwholesome kamma of the Sakyans—who had once poured poison into a river in the past—to bear fruit had arrived and could not be averted. Therefore, He did not go on that fourth occasion.

King Viṭaṭūbha set out with a large army, thinking, "I will kill the Sakyans." The Sakyans, who were the Buddha's relatives,
39:
39
were not people who would kill other living beings. Even if they themselves had to die, they would not kill others. Thus, the Sakyan relatives thought, "We are masters of the art of archery. However, we have no custom of killing others. We shall only show our skill in archery to make the enemies flee." Having planned thus, they put on their armor, departed from Kapilavatthu, and made a show of engaging in battle. The arrows shot by those Sakyans passed through the gaps between King Viṭaṭūbha's soldiers; they passed through gaps in armor, ear-holes, and so on.

King Viṭaṭūbha, seeing this and thinking they were truly shooting at them, said, "Friends, did the Sakyans not say, 'We are those who do not kill other beings'? Despite saying so, they are now shooting, destroying, and killing my soldiers with arrows."

Then a royal attendant asked King Viṭaṭūbha, "Sire, have you looked back at your own army?" King Viṭaṭūbha replied, "Friend, the Sakyans are shooting, destroying, and killing my soldiers with arrows." The attendant then boldly addressed him, "Great King, not a single soldier from your side has fallen. I wish to urge you to have your soldiers counted right now." When the soldiers were counted, not a single one was found to have fallen.
40:
40
King Viṭaṭūbha retreated slightly from that place and issued a royal command: "Friends, kill everyone who claims to be a Sakyan. However, grant life to those Sakyans who stand near my grandfather, Mahānāma the Sakyan."

When King Viṭaṭūbha's soldiers advanced and began the slaughter with great intensity, the Sakyans, seeing nothing to hold onto or cling to, some stood biting grass, while others stood holding onto reeds. When asked, "Are you not Sakyans?", because it was not the custom of Sakyans to tell lies even if they were to die, those Sakyans standing and biting grass said, "No Sāko, tiṇaṃ" (Not a Sāka tree, but grass). Those Sakyans standing and holding onto reeds said, "No Sāko, naḷo" (Not a Sāka tree, but a reed). Only those Sakyans and the Sakyans standing near King Mahānāma were spared their lives.

Among those Sakyans, those who stood biting grass became known as the Tiṇa-Sākiyans, and those who stood holding onto reeds became known as the Naḷa-Sākiyans.

King Viṭaṭūbha had the remaining Sakyans slaughtered, not even sparing nursing infants, causing a river of blood to flow, and he had his seat washed with the blood from the throats of those Sakyans. In this way, the lineage of the Sakyans was severed because of Viṭaṭūbha.
41:
King Viṭaṭūbha had his grandfather, Mahānāma the Sakyan, captured alive. While returning, at the time of the morning meal, he thought, "I shall have my breakfast," and descended at a certain place. When the morning meal was served, he said, "I will eat with my grandfather," and sent for Mahānāma the Sakyan. Generally, those of the royal caste would not eat with the sons of slave women even at the cost of their lives. Therefore, King Mahānāma, looking at a pond, said, "My grandson, my body is soiled. I shall bathe first." King Viṭaṭūbha, in a gentle and compliant manner, gave permission, saying, "Very well, grandfather, please bathe."

Mahānāma thought, "If I do not eat with this Viṭaṭūbha, he will surely kill me. It is better that I die by my own hand." Reflecting thus, he untied his hair, made a knot at the ends, inserted his two big toes into that knot, and submerged himself in the water. Due to the power of Mahānāma's virtues, the Naga realm showed signs of heat. The Naga king, investigating the cause and realizing the situation, came to Mahānāma the Sakyan, placed the king on his hood, and took him to the Naga realm. Mahānāma the Sakyan stayed in that Naga realm for twelve years.

## The Destruction of King Viṭaṭūbha and His Retinue

King Viṭaṭūbha sat waiting, thinking, "My grandfather will come any moment, he will come any moment." After a long time had passed and Mahānāma the Sakyan did not return, he had the entire pond...
42:
...stirred and searched. When he was not found in the pond, thinking he might be hiding, the king had the area searched with torches between the men, but he was still not found. Thinking, "My grandfather must have fled," he departed with his army.

King Viṭaṭūbha reached the Aciravatī River at nightfall. Unable to enter the city, he set up a temporary camp on the riverbank. Some people lay down on the sandbank within the river, while others lay on the high ground of the bank. Among those lying on the sandbank were those who had not committed bad kamma in the past. Among those lying on the high ground were those who had committed bad kamma in the past. In the places where both groups lay, bedbugs and insects swarmed uncontrollably. Both groups complained, "Bedbugs are swarming where I lie! Bedbugs are swarming where I lie!" They got up from their places; those who had not committed bad kamma moved from the sandbank to sleep on the high ground, while those who had committed bad kamma moved from the high ground to sleep on the sandbank in the river.

At that moment, a great cloud arose and a heavy downpour of rain and hail fell violently. A flash flood, filling the Aciravatī River to its banks, came forcefully and swept King Viṭaṭūbha and his retinue away into the ocean. Every single one of them became food for fish and turtles.
43:
## The Past Bad Kamma of the Sakyan Kings

At that time, the multitude of people said, "Friends, the death of the Sakyan kings was not fitting. This event, where the Sakyan kings were hacked and slaughtered without even sparing the children, is most inappropriate." The Blessed One, hearing the words of those people, said, "Monks, although such a death for the Sakyan kings in this existence is unfitting, if one looks at it in connection with the evil kamma they committed in the past, these Sakyan kings have met a death that is appropriate to its cause." When the monks asked, "Venerable Sir, what evil deed did those Sakyan kings commit in the past?", the Blessed One briefly preached their past kamma: "Monks, all those deceased Sakyans, in a certain past life, being of one mind and one purpose, threw poison into a river."

Again, on another day in the Dhamma Hall, the monks discussed, "Friends, King Viṭaṭūbha, after killing so many Sakyan kings, has himself become food for fish and turtles in the great ocean along with his vast retinue, even before his heart's desire was fully accomplished." The Blessed One came to the Dhamma Hall and asked, "Monks, for what purpose are you gathered here now?" When the monks replied, "We are gathered for this purpose," the Blessed One said:
44:
"Monks, just as a great flood sweeps away all the sleeping villagers and drowns them in the ocean before their heart's desire is fulfilled, so too does Death cut short the lives of those who are heedless and asleep, drowning them in the ocean of the four woeful states (apāya)." Having said this, he preached the following verse of Dhamma:

Pupphāni heva pacinantaṃ, byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ.
Suttaṃ gāmaṃ mahogho va, maccu ādāya gacchati.

(Monks, just like a person who greedily plucks various fragrant flowers, Death carries away the man whose mind is deeply attached to the five cords of sensual pleasure—longing for what he has not yet obtained and clinging to what he has—and sweeps him away to the ocean of the four woeful states, just as a great flood carries away all the people of a village while they are fast asleep.)

At the conclusion of the teaching, many beings attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The teaching was highly beneficial to the multitude.

The story of King Viṭaṭūbha (who was a betrayer of friends) ends here.
45:
## The Story of Kosala Mallikā and Bandhula Mallikā

In the city of Sāvatthī, there were two Mallikās: (1) Mallikā, the Queen of King Pasenadi of Kosala, and (2) Mallikā, the wife of General Bandhula. Among them, it has already been described in detail (starting from page 24) that Mallikā, the wife of General Bandhula, was the daughter of a Mallian king of Kusināra. Here, I shall describe the story of Queen Mallikā, the consort of King Pasenadi, for general knowledge.

Mallikā, who was to become the Queen of King Pasenadi, was the daughter of a master flower-seller in Sāvatthī. She was endowed with beauty and exceptional past merit. When she reached the age of sixteen, one day, while going to the flower garden with her friends to pick flowers, she carried three balls of barley cake in her flower basket.

As she left the city, she saw the Blessed One entering the city, surrounded by a company of monks and emitting the six-colored rays. With a heart overflowing with faith and devotion, she offered the three balls of barley cake to the Blessed One. The Blessed One accepted the three barley cakes offered by the maiden Mallikā in the alms-bowl offered by the four Great Kings (Cātumahārājā).

Mallikā prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and taking joy (pīti) in the Buddha's virtues, she stood in a suitable place. The Blessed One looked at Mallikā and smiled. Venerable Ānanda...
46:

Mallikā, hearing these words and being filled with joy, went to the flower garden with her friends. On that same day, King Pasenadi had been defeated in battle by his nephew, King Ajātasattu. While fleeing on horseback, he heard the sound of Mallikā singing. With a heart full of attraction, he steered his horse toward the flower garden. While her friends were frightened and hid upon seeing the King, Mallikā, possessing the merit to become a Queen, did not hide but came forward boldly and took hold of the horse's bridle.

While still on the horse's back, King Pasenadi asked, "Do you have a husband or master?" Upon learning that she had no husband, he dismounted. Being exhausted from the wind and sun, he rested for a moment with his head in Mallikā's lap. Then, he placed Mallikā on the horse's back and, surrounded by his army, entered the city and had Mallikā sent to her parents' house. In the evening, he sent the royal carriage used by queens and brought her from her parents' house with great ceremony and honor.

This is the story of Kosala Mallikā and Bandhula Mallikā.

## The Preaching of the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta

At one time, the Blessed One was staying at the Vulture’s Peak (Gijjhakūṭa) monastery near the city of Rājagaha. Then, the Four Great Kings—Dhataraṭṭha, Virūḷhaka, Virūpakkha, and Kuvera—having stationed a vast number of Yakkha, Gandhabba, Kumbhaṇḍa, and Nāga troops at the four quarters to provide sufficient protection (to prevent attacks from the Asuras), met at Āṭānāṭā, the city of King Kuvera. Their magnificent forms illuminated the entire Vulture’s Peak with their radiance. They paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at a respectful distance, avoiding the six faults of sitting.

(Note: It is rare for devas to sit when approaching the Blessed One; they usually remain standing. In this Sutta, however, they sat down out of deep respect for the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta. — Commentary).

## Instructions for Chanting the Paritta
The person who is to chant the Paritta must have learned the relevant Paritta perfectly and purely in both meaning and sound. They must have learned it completely without omitting any words or syllables. Indeed, if one chants while corrupting the meaning and the Pāḷi, or without complete mastery, the Paritta of that person cannot have great power. Only when chanted with complete mastery can it have great and noble power.

The Paritta of a person who learns and chants it out of a desire for gain, honor, and offerings also cannot fulfill the desired benefit. Only when chanted with a mind of loving-kindness (mettā), focusing primarily on the desire for liberation from the round of rebirths (saṃsāra), can it fulfill the desired benefit. (From the Pāthikavagga Commentary, page 150).

The person chanting the Paritta should not chant the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta first. They should first chant the Mettā Sutta, Dhajagga Sutta, and Ratana Sutta for seven days. If the possessing Yakkhas leave because of such chanting, it is well. Only if they do not leave should the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta be chanted.

A monk who chants the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should not eat cakes made of flour, meat, fish, or other such savory foods. He should not stay in a cemetery. This is because those foods and places are the favorites of Yakkhas (ogres),
59:
and because those Yakkhas (ogres) can easily find an opportunity to possess them.

The place for chanting the Paritta should be smeared with fresh cow dung, and a clean seat should be spread there before the chanting monk sits. That chanting monk must also be a pure person.

Those who escort the chanting monk from the monastery to the house should surround him with shields and weapons. He should not chant the Paritta while sitting in an open space. He should sit inside the house with the main doors and windows closed, and for the sake of protection both inside and out, people holding weapons should surround him, and he should chant with a mind of loving-kindness as the forerunner. Only when chanting is arranged with such external protection of armed guards and internal protection of loving-kindness will the Yakkhas (ogres) be unable to cause harm to the chanting of the Paritta.

First, the patient should be made to undertake the precepts, and the Paritta protection should be performed for the patient established in virtue (sīla). (If the Paritta protection is performed according to this arrangement, the possession by Yakkhas can be pacified).

If the possession by Yakkhas is not pacified by this method, the patient should be taken to the monastery and laid down on the stupa platform (cetiya-yangaṇa). After making offerings to the Blessed One at his seat, lighting lamps, and sweeping the stupa platform, the Mangala verses should be chanted as a preliminary arrangement. To assemble all the monks residing in that monastery (or that village area), one should
60:

A messenger should be sent to those tree-deities to say: "The Saṅgha of monks expects and desires your presence." A possessing Yakkha will not be able to stay away from the place where all the monks are assembled, out of fear of the authority of the Blessed One and the Four Great Kings.

Then, the person possessed by the ogre should be asked, "What is your name?" (In this context, by addressing the patient possessed by the ogre, the possessing Yakkha himself is being questioned). If the possessing Yakkha reveals his name, the monks should address him by that name as follows:

"Friend Yakkha named [Name], we share with you the portion of merit from the offerings of flowers and scents, the merit from the offerings at the Buddha's seat, and the merit from the offerings of alms-food. For your sake, the Saṅgha of monks has chanted and preached the Great Mangala verses as a gift. Out of respect for the Saṅgha of monks, friend, please release this patient."

Thus, he should be asked to release the patient with words of loving-kindness. If he does not release the patient even after such words of loving-kindness, one should report to the thirty-eight great celestial generals such as Inda, Soma, and Varuṇa, saying: "You great generals are aware of this; this Yakkha does not follow our request made with loving-kindness. ## Preaching the Sakkapañha Sutta
At one time, the Blessed One was staying in the "Indasāla" Cave where Sal trees grew, on the slopes of Mount Vediyaka, north of the brahmin village named Ambasanda, to the east of the city of Rājagaha in the Magadha country.

(Because it was a village situated near a mango grove, the name of that brahmin village was Ambasanda. Because it was surrounded by a forest of trees that grew in rows like polished blue gems around the foot of the mountain, the name of that mountain was Vediyaka.

Regarding the distinction between a cave (guhā) and a grotto (leṇa): a natural mountain cavity is called a 'guhā' in Pāḷi (Burmese: gu), and such a mountain cavity that has been decorated and prepared with walls, doorways, and floral carvings using plaster, bricks, stones, or wood is called a 'leṇa' in Pāḷi (Burmese: loin).

The grotto where the Blessed One was now staying was originally a natural mountain cavity that had formed between two mountains in ancient times, and because a Sal tree grew at the mouth of that cave, it was known as Indasālaguhā in Pāḷi (Burmese: Indasāla Cave). Only later—"

They installed entrance doors and windows, and decorated it with exquisite plaster carvings of floral and vine patterns. Thus, although the place where the Buddha was currently residing had become a large grotto and should be called the Indasāla Grotto (Indasāla-leṇa), the public continued to recognize it by its ancient name, the Indasāla Cave (Indasāla-guhā).

## To the King of Devas
## The Appearance of the Five Omens of Death

While the Buddha was residing in the Indasāla Cave on the slopes of Mount Vediyaka near Rājagaha, where the Nampai (Kutaja) trees grew, the lifespan of Sakka, King of Devas, was nearing its end. He clearly perceived the five omens of death: (1) his flowers withered, (2) his garments became soiled, (3) sweat trickled from his armpits, (4) his physical appearance faded and became unsightly, and (5) he felt dissatisfied with his own seat. Seeing these, he reflected and realized, "Now, my lifespan has indeed come to an end."

When the five omens of death appear, devas who were born in the celestial realms due to weak wholesome kamma become fearful and trembling, reflecting, "Where will we be reborn now?" However, devas born in the celestial realms due to powerful and abundant wholesome kamma do not fear or tremble. Relying on the merit of the charity (dāna) they gave, the virtue (sīla) they observed, and the meditation (bhāvanā) they practiced, they reflect, "We shall now enjoy the bliss of the higher celestial realms."
63:
63
When Sakka, King of Devas, saw the aforementioned five omens of his impending death, he looked upon all his celestial glory: the Tāvatiṃsa realm spanning ten thousand yojanas, the Vejayanta Palace a thousand yojanas high, the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall spanning three hundred yojanas, the celestial Pāricchattaka tree a hundred yojanas high, the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone seat sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas thick, the twenty-five million celestial dancers, his vast retinue of devas in the two realms of Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa, and the great celestial gardens—Nandavana, Cittalatā, Missaka, and Phārusaka. Looking at all this splendor, he was overwhelmed by the fear of death and filled with grief, thinking, "Alas, this magnificent celestial glory of mine is about to perish and be lost!"

Then Sakka considered, "Is there any recluse, brahmin, or Brahma outside this Dispensation who can pull out this arrow of sorrow piercing my heart and make this celestial glory stable and firm?" Looking around, he saw no one. Reflecting further, he saw the Buddha, thinking, "The Blessed One is indeed capable of pulling out the arrow of sorrow that arises in the hearts of hundreds of thousands of Sakkas like me." Upon this reflection and seeing the Buddha in his mind, a fervent and intense desire to visit the Buddha arose within Sakka.

Then Sakka looked to see, "Where is the Blessed One residing at this time?"
64:
64
Upon reflection, he clearly saw that the Buddha was residing in the Indasāla Cave on the slopes of Mount Vediyaka near Rājagaha. He then addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas, saying, "Friends, the Blessed One is currently staying in the Indasāla Cave on Mount Vediyaka near Rājagaha. Friends, it would be good if we were to approach the Blessed One to pay our respects." The Tāvatiṃsa devas replied, "Very well, Lord Sakka."

(Note: Two or three days prior, while the Buddha was staying in the Pine-wood Fragrant Chamber (the monastery donated by King Kosala) within the Jetavana Monastery, Sakka had gone to visit the Buddha accompanied only by his attendant Mātali and others, without a large celestial retinue. The Buddha, reflecting that Sakka's wisdom was not yet mature, knew: "In two or three days, after seeing the five omens and becoming terrified of death, Sakka will approach me together with the devas of the two realms, Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa, and ask fourteen questions. At that time, upon the conclusion of the answer to the question regarding neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā), this Sakka, along with eighty thousand devas, will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala)." Knowing this, the Buddha remained in the bliss of the Attainment of Fruition (Phala-samāpatti) so that Sakka would not have the opportunity to have an audience at that time.

On this occasion, Sakka thought: "Three days ago, I went to see the Buddha alone without a celestial retinue, and the Buddha did not grant me an audience. Surely, I must lack the supporting merit (upanissaya) for attaining the Paths and Fruits. If someone possesses the supporting merit for the Paths and Fruits, the Buddha usually teaches the Dhamma to the assembly even as far as the edge of the universe."

"Surely, if I go taking many devas from the two celestial realms, among them there might be one who possesses the supporting merit (upanissaya) for the Paths and Fruits. The Buddha will teach the Dhamma with reference to that deva who has the merit. By hearing that Dhamma, I too may be able to appease the dissatisfaction in my heart." Thinking thus, he invited the Tāvatiṃsa devas to accompany him. This should be specifically noted from the Commentary.

Then Sakka thought, "It is not appropriate for me to approach the Buddha by bringing all the devas of the two realms, Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa, as if striking him with the front of a chariot. This celestial youth Pañcasikha is an attendant of the Buddha and is also familiar with him; he goes to the Buddha at any time he wishes to ask questions and listen to the Dhamma. I shall send Pañcasikha ahead to arrange an audience. Once he has secured permission, I shall then approach the Buddha and ask my questions." Having planned this, he said to Pañcasikha, "Dear Pañcasikha, the Blessed One is currently residing in the Indasāla Cave on Mount Vediyaka near Rājagaha. (Sakka arrived at Mount Vediyaka just after the people had finished their evening meal and while children were still playing in the middle of the village. Thus, many people saw it and spoke as mentioned before. Although it is the custom for devas and Brahmas to visit the Buddha at midnight, Sakka came during the early part of the first watch (pathama-yāma) because he was so terrified of the danger of death.)

Then Sakka said to Pañcasikha, "Dear Pañcasikha, Buddhas are often absorbed in jhāna and delight in jhāna. At such times, they dwell in solitude. Therefore, it is not easy for someone like me, who is not free from greed, hatred, and delusion, to approach."
67:
67
"Dear Pañcasikha, you should first ask permission from the Blessed One. Only after you have obtained permission would it be good for us to approach the Blessed One to pay our respects." Pañcasikha replied, "Very well, Lord Sakka." Taking the Beluvapaṇḍu celestial lute which he had carried on his shoulder during the journey, he held it in his left hand to play and approached the Indasāla Cave. Thinking, "At this distance, I am neither too far nor too close to the Blessed One, and he will be able to hear the sound of my lute," he stood in a certain spot.

## Pañcasikha's Verses on the Lute

Standing there, Pañcasikha played the Beluvapaṇḍu lute and sang verses (to be mentioned) related to the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the Arahants, and sensual desire (kāma-guṇa).

(Note: The meaning of these verses by Pañcasikha is presented in this work as extracted from the Kavi-maṇḍana-medanī treatise, written by the Seeban-ni Sayadaw, the leader of the Fifth Council, who received three royal titles: (1) Narindābhisiri-saddhammadhaja-mahādhammarājādhirājaguru, (2) Narindābhisiri-saddhammajotipāladhaja-mahādhammarājādhirājaguru (two titles from King Mindon), and (3) Narindābhidhaja-atulādhipati-siripavara-mahādhammarājādhirājaguru (from King Thibaw).)

(1) Vande te pitaraṃ bhadde, timbarū sūriyavacchase.
Yena jātāsi kalyāṇī, ānandajananī mama.

Sūriyavacchase = O you who possess a radiance like the rising sun. Bhadde = O auspicious lady...
68:
Because of that King of Devas named Timbaru, you, my dear sister, are endowed with the fivefold beauty (kalyāṇī). To me, the player of the Beluva lute, you are the one who generates delight and intimacy. Because I desire you, I pay homage to your father, the Gandhabba King Timbaru.

(2) Like the wind to those who sweat, like water to those who thirst, you are dear to me, O Angīrasī, like the Dhamma is to the Arahants.

(3) Like medicine to the sick, like food to the hungry, extinguish my fever, O blessed one, as if with water on a blazing fire.

O Angīrasī, you who are radiant and beautiful... Just as those dripping with sweat desire a gentle breeze; just as a person parched with thirst desires cool and sweet water; just as an Arahant, who has broken the cycle of rebirth, desires the ninefold Supramundane Dhamma;

Just as a sick person, weary and weak, desires excellent medicine; just as a person who is extremely hungry, with the digestive fire burning within, desires the five kinds of food.
69:
...desires food; so I, Pañcasikha, desire you, Suriyavacchasā, with eternal love. O blessed one, whose body is tender and youthful... just as a great blazing fire is extinguished with cool water, please extinguish the fever of sensual lust (kāmarāgapariḷāha) that has arisen because of your smiles and charms.

(4) Like an elephant oppressed by the heat of the sun descending into a cool lotus pond filled with pollen, so would I descend into your bosom, O Suriyavacchasā.

Like an elephant oppressed by the heat of the sun... descending into a square pond of clear, cool water filled with lotus pollen... so I long to enter your bosom, which is fragrant with the scent of divine flowers.

(5) Like an elephant that has gone beyond the hook, or one that cannot be restrained by the goad, I do not know what is right or wrong, being intoxicated by your beautiful thighs.

O blessed Suriyavacchasā... Like a great elephant that has surpassed the hook, or cannot be subdued by it, being intoxicated by the rut flowing from its ears and eyes, ignoring the goad and spear...
70:
...ignoring the spear and the hook, and not knowing what is right or wrong; so I, the master of the lute, do not know right from wrong, being intoxicated by your shapely thighs.

(6) My mind is obsessed with you; my thoughts are transformed. I cannot turn back, like a fish that has swallowed a hook.

O Suriyavacchasā, radiant as the sun... I, the master of the lute, have a mind filled with longing and attachment for you. Just as a fish that swallows a hook in search of bait cannot spit it out or dive back, so my mind, the master of the Beluva lute, is spinning and cannot retreat.

(7) O lady of lovely thighs (Vāmūru), embrace me, O blessed Suriyavacchasā. O soft-eyed one (Mandalocane), embrace me. O beautiful one (Kalyāṇī), embrace me completely. This is what I have long desired.

O Suriyavacchasā, who has golden thighs as soft as a bundle of cotton... embrace me, the five-crested deva.
71:
Embrace me, O blessed one, with your soft-eyed gaze and gentle embrace. O Suriyavacchasā, endowed with the sixty-four qualities... embrace me completely. This embrace is what I, Pañcasikha, have many times yearned for.

(8) My desire was small indeed, but because of you with your wavy hair, it has grown manifold, like a gift (dakkhiṇā) given to an Arahant.

Before meeting you, my sensual desire was slight, but now, because of you with your long, curling hair, it has become unstable and overwhelming, like the merit of a great gift given with faith to an Arahant.

(9) Whatever merit (puñña) I have gained by making offerings to such Arahants, may it ripen together with you, O lady of perfect limbs.

O Suriyavacchasā, endowed with the fivefold beauty... I, the master of the seven-stringed golden lute, have performed merit by offering the four requisites to the Arahants who are steadfast in the eight worldly conditions.
72:
Whatever pure merit I have performed, may it ripen for me to enjoy together with you, my divine lady. 

(10) Whatever merit I have gained on this earth, may it ripen together with you, O lady of perfect limbs.

O Suriyavacchasā, endowed with all beauty... I, the master of the lute, have performed merit on this earth by offering the four requisites. May that pure merit, as clear as a polished shell, ripen for me to enjoy in union with you.

(11) Like the Sakyan Son (the Buddha) who, through Jhana, is unified, wise, and mindful, seeking the Deathless (Amata), so do I seek you, O Suriyavacchasā.

O Suriyavacchasā, radiant as the sun... Like the Sage, the King of Dhamma, the son of the Sakyan King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, who dwells alone and serene through the noble Jhanas...
73:
...who is wise and mindful, seeking the state of Nibbāna (Arimadda) free from aging, sickness, and death, so I, the Gandhabba god, search for you, the beloved of Timbaru, every day.
