(12) Just as the Sage rejoices upon reaching Supreme Enlightenment (Sambodhi), so would I rejoice, O beautiful one, in union with you.

O Suriyavacchasā, endowed with the fivefold beauty... Just as the Sage, the highest of monks, rejoices after reaching the Diamond-like Knowledge through the seven stages of purification, so would I be a hundred times more joyful if I were united with you.

(13) If Sakka, the Lord of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, were to grant me a boon, I would choose you, O blessed one; such is the strength of my desire.

O Suriyavacchasā... If the King of Devas, Sakka, who rules over the Tāvatiṃsa gods and has the power to grant prosperity, were to offer me a choice between his divine sovereignty and you, and say, 'Take whichever you desire'...
74:
I, the five-crested deva, would choose you, the goddess I never tire of looking at, as my supreme boon. (I would not choose the status of the King of Devas). O Suriyavacchasā, radiant as sunlight, my intense longing and attachment for you is so firm that it cannot be broken by anyone, like a fixed iron nail.

(14) Like a Sal tree in full bloom, I pay homage to your father, O wise one, he who has such a daughter.

O Suriyavacchasā of vast and wondrous wisdom... I, the master of the seven-stringed lute, pay homage to your father Timbaru, because he is the father of such a beautiful daughter as you. (These are the 14 verses of Pañcasikha's song).

When the deva Pañcasikha had thus played his lute and sung, the Blessed One praised him, saying: "Pañcasikha, the sound of your lute harmonizes with your song, and your song harmonizes with the sound of your lute. The sound of your lute does not exceed the song, nor does the song exceed the sound of your lute."
75:
75
(In this regard, it might be asked: Why did the Blessed One praise the sound of the song and the lute? Did the Blessed One have any delight or attachment to that sound of song and lute? The answer is: There was no delight or attachment at all. The Blessed One, who remains indifferent to both like and dislike through chaḷaṅgupekkhā (six-factored equanimity), perceives such things only as desirable or undesirable objects. He has no attachment whatsoever to those objects. [This can be understood by referring to the Koṭṭhika Sutta of the Saḷāyatana Vagga Saṃyutta, Saṃ 2, page 372].

If the Blessed One had not praised the song and the lute, the deva Pañcasikha would not have known, "The Blessed One has given me permission." If that were the case, Sakka, the King of Devas, thinking, "The Blessed One has not given permission to Pañcasikha," would have taken the devas and returned from that very spot. Had they returned, it would have been a great loss. However, because the words of praise were spoken, Sakka, thinking, "The Blessed One has given permission to Pañcasikha," approached the Blessed One together with the devas. The Blessed One praised the song and the lute because He clearly foresaw that after asking his questions and receiving the answers, Sakka, along with eighty thousand devas, would be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala)).

After praising him in this way, the Blessed One further asked the deva Pañcasikha, "Pañcasikha, when did you compose these verses for the lute, which are connected with the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the Arahants, and sensual pleasure?" Then, the deva Pañcasikha replied to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, once, when the Blessed One had recently attained Enlightenment and was dwelling near the banks of the Nerañjarā River in the Uruvelā forest,
76:
76
at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree (during the eighth week after Enlightenment), enjoying the bliss of liberation. Venerable Sir, at that time, I was in love with Bhaddā Suriyavacchasā, the daughter of the Great Deva King Timbaru. But, Venerable Sir, that maiden was in love with another, named Sikhaṇḍī, the son of Mātali the charioteer.

Venerable Sir, when I could not win Suriyavacchasā by any means, I took my Beluvapaṇḍu lute, approached the mansion of the Great Deva King Timbaru, and played the Beluvapaṇḍu lute. I also sang these verses connected with the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the Arahants, and sensual pleasure:

(1) I pay homage to your father, O Bhaddā, Timbaru, O Suriyavacchasā,
By whom you were sired, O beautiful one, the source of my joy... (etc.)

(14) Like a Sal tree in full bloom for a long time, your father, O wise one,
I pay homage to him with respect, he who has such offspring.

(The meaning of these 14 verses has been written previously).

Venerable Sir, when I sang in this manner, the goddess Bhaddā Suriyavacchasā said to me:

'Lord, I have not seen that Blessed One face to face. However, I have heard about that Blessed One while I was at the Sudhammā Hall of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Lord, because you spoke and praised that Blessed One,
77:
77
let this be our meeting today.'

Thus she spoke. Venerable Sir, I met with that maiden only that much, and from then until now, we have not met again."

## Sakka's Approach to the Blessed One

Then, the thought occurred to Sakka, the King of Devas: "The deva Pañcasikha is conversing joyfully with the Blessed One, and the Blessed One is also conversing joyfully with the deva Pañcasikha." Sakka then said to the deva Pañcasikha, "Dear Pañcasikha, please pay homage to the Blessed One on my behalf, saying: 'Venerable Sir, Sakka, the King of Devas, together with his ministers and his retinue, pays homage with his head at the feet of the Blessed One.'" The deva Pañcasikha replied, "Very well, Lord Sakka," and after accepting Sakka's request, he said to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, Sakka, the King of Devas, together with his ministers and his retinue, pays homage with his head at the feet of the Blessed One."

Then the Blessed One said, "May Sakka, the King of Devas, together with his ministers and his retinue, be happy, Pañcasikha. For indeed, devas, humans, asuras, nagas, gandhabbas, and many other beings all desire happiness." (Blessed Ones usually address powerful devas in this manner).
78:
78
When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Sakka, the King of Devas, entered the Indasāla Cave, paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, and stood at a respectful distance. The deva Pañcasikha and the other Tāvatiṃsa devas also entered the Indasāla Cave, paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, and stood at a respectful distance.

At that time, although the Indasāla Cave was naturally uneven, it became level. Although it was narrow, it became spacious. By the radiance of the devas, the darkness within the cave (outside the eighty-cubit radius around the Blessed One) vanished, and light appeared. (Within the eighty-cubit radius around the Blessed One, the darkness vanished due to the Blessed One's own radiance. The radiance of the devas could not outshine the radiance of the Blessed One).

Then the Blessed One said to Sakka, the King of Devas, "It is wonderful that you, Kosiya, have been able to come here, despite having so many duties. it is extraordinary, something that has not happened before." Sakka, the King of Devas, replied to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, I have long wished to come and see the Blessed One, but I have been occupied with various duties* of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, and so I was unable to come to see the Blessed One." (The speech continues).

(In this context, "various duties of the Tāvatiṃsa devas" means: For the devas, sons and daughters appear spontaneously (upapāta) in their laps; celestial maidens who serve as queens appear on their beds; attendant celestial maidens who will dress and adorn those queens appear surrounding the bed; and servant devas who will perform various services appear within the mansion. Regarding these devas, there is no dispute at all as to who owns whom. Only regarding devas who appear on the boundary between the mansions of two deva kings does a dispute arise as to who owns whom, and they go to Sakka for a decision.
79:
79
Sakka gives the decision that the new deva belongs to the owner of the nearest mansion. If the new deva is equidistant from both mansions, he decides, "Let it belong to the deva king towards whose mansion it was looking when it appeared." If the new deva is equidistant and was not looking at either mansion when it appeared, Sakka decides it belongs to himself in order to end the quarrel between the two mansion-owners. This is one type of duty; besides this, activities such as merry-making and playing are also duties of the devas. Sakka's statement refers to these duties. —From the Commentary).

Continuing his speech, Sakka said, "Venerable Sir, on another occasion (= about three days ago), the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, in the Salala-gandhakuṭi (a dwelling built of salala wood, a gift from King Pasenadi Kosala) within the Jetavana Monastery. Venerable Sir, at that time, I went to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One. Venerable Sir, at that time, the Blessed One was absorbed in a certain concentration (phalasamāpatti). A celestial maiden named Bhūjati, the queen of the Great King Vessavaṇa, was standing with palms joined, paying homage and attending to the Blessed One. Venerable Sir, at that time, I said to the maiden Bhūjati, 'Sister, please pay homage to the Blessed One on my behalf, saying:
80:
80
"Venerable Sir, Sakka, the King of Devas, together with his ministers and his retinue, pays homage with his head at the feet of the Blessed One."' Venerable Sir, when I said this, the maiden Bhūjati said to me, 'Lord Sakka, it is not the time to see the Blessed One; the Blessed One is in solitary seclusion.' Then I said, 'Sister, if that is so, when the Blessed One emerges from that concentration (phalasamāpatti), please pay homage to the Blessed One in my words, saying: "Venerable Sir, Sakka, the King of Devas, together with his ministers and his retinue, pays homage with his head at the feet of the Blessed One."' Venerable Sir, did that maiden Bhūjati pay homage to the Blessed One on my behalf? Does the Blessed One remember the words of that maiden?"

Then the Blessed One said to Sakka, "Sakka, King of Devas, that maiden did speak to me. I remember the words of that maiden. Indeed, I emerged from that attainment just as the sound of your chariot wheels was heard."

(A special note here: Within the Jetavana Monastery, there were (1) the Karerikuṭi dwelling (at the entrance of which Kareri trees stood with branches intertwined like a pavilion), (2) the Kosambakuṭi dwelling (at the entrance of which stood a large Kosamba tree), (3) the Gandhakuṭi dwelling (built of fragrant wood), and (4) the Salalāgāra dwelling (built of salala wood).
81:
There are four great monasteries where the Blessed One resided; each monastery was worth one hundred thousand. Among these four great monasteries, the Salalāgāra monastery was built and offered by King Pasenadi of Kosala, while the remaining three monasteries were the meritorious deeds of Anāthapiṇḍika. (From Dī-ṭṭha 2, page 1).

About three days before the Sakkapañha Sutta was preached, while the Blessed One was residing at the Salalāgāra monastery, Sakka, the King of Devas, came to pay his respects to the Blessed One. At that time, as Sakka's faculties (indriya) were not yet mature, the Blessed One did not grant him an audience but remained in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) for a predetermined duration.

The deity Bhūjatī was one of the queens of the Great King Vessavaṇa. Since this deity Bhūjatī was a noble female disciple (ariyasāvikā) who had attained the two lower noble fruitions, namely the fruition of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and the fruition of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala), she found no delight in the celestial realm. For this reason, she constantly attended upon the Blessed One, standing with her hands joined in reverence above her head, paying homage and serving the Blessed One.

After giving instructions to the deity Bhūjatī, Sakka thought, "At this time, the Blessed One does not grant me the opportunity to pay respects," and after paying homage to the Salalāgāra monastery, he turned his chariot back and drove toward the celestial realm. The sound of the chariot filled the entire monastery precinct, sounding like the five kinds of musical instruments. The time when the Blessed One emerged from the attainment of fruition, having completed the predetermined duration, coincided with the time when Sakka turned his chariot and drove toward the celestial realm. Thus, in the Blessed One's mental process, upon emerging from the attainment of fruition, the advertence (āvajjana) mind that took the sound of Sakka's chariot wheels as its object occurred first. It was not that he emerged from the attainment of fruition because of the sound of the chariot, but rather because the predetermined
82:
82
It was only because the time was right that He emerged from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). The moment of emerging from the attainment of fruition coincided with the sound of the chariot wheels. Therefore, it should be specifically noted that upon emerging from the attainment of fruition, the adverting consciousness (āvajjana) that reflected on the sound of the chariot wheels arose first in the Blessed One’s mental continuum. (From Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 298).
## The Prosperity of the Celestial Realms when a Buddha Arises
Sakka, the King of Devas, further addressed the Blessed One (regarding the prosperity of the celestial realms when a Buddha arises):
“Venerable Sir, I have heard and learned this from the Devas who were born in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven before us: ‘When the Blessed Ones, the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas arise, the hosts of Asuras decline and the hosts of Devas fill and prosper.’ Venerable Sir, I am now seeing with my own eyes that since the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened Buddha has arisen in the world, the hosts of Asuras are declining and the hosts of Devas are filling and prospering.”
## The Story of Gopaka Devaputta
In the city of Kapilavatthu itself, there was a Sakyan princess named Gopikā who had confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and who habitually observed the five precepts. She felt loathing for being a woman and cultivated the practice to become a man.
83:
after the breaking up of the body and death, was reborn in a good destination in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as our son. In that Tāvatiṃsa heaven, they call that deva 'Gopaka Deva, Gopaka Deva.'

"Venerable Sir, three other monks, although they practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, were reborn in the lowly class of Gandhabba devas (celestial musicians). Those devas, fully endowed with and enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure, came to the Sudhammā assembly hall to attend upon and entertain us. To those devas who came to attend upon and entertain us, Gopaka Deva said:

'Sirs, where was your wisdom directed when you heard the Dhamma of that Blessed One? Even though I was a young woman who had confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha and habitually observed the five precepts, I loathed the state of being a woman and cultivated the state of being a man. After the breaking up of the body and death, I was reborn in a good destination in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as the son of Sakka, the lord of devas. In this Tāvatiṃsa heaven, they call me "Gopaka Deva, Gopaka Deva."

'Sirs, you, however, although you practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, have been reborn in the lowly class of Gandhabba devas. Sirs, for us who see fellow practitioners of the Dhamma
84:
reborn in the lowly class of Gandhabba devas, we are indeed seeing a sight that should not be seen.'

Thus he spoke words of admonition. Venerable Sir, among those three devas who were admonished by Gopaka Deva, two devas regained mindfulness of the first jhāna (paṭhama jhāna) in that very life and reached the Brahmapurohita realm. One deva, however, remained enjoying the sensual realm."

Thus Sakka reported. (Sakka's report is not yet finished).

(This is the story of Gopaka Deva. A special point to note in this story of Gopaka Deva is: why were these three monk-devas, who had pure virtue during their lives as monks in the human world, reborn in the lowly class of Gandhabba devas? It should be answered that it was due to their previous attachment to that existence (bhavanikanti). To clarify further—those three monk-devas had been reborn in that Gandhabba class many times before. Therefore, by the power of craving and greed (bhavanikanti taṇhā lobha) that was attached to that life of a celestial musician, they were reborn in that Gandhabba life (the Cātumahārājika deva realm).

In the section where Gopaka Deva gave the admonition: When Gopaka Deva saw those three monk-turned-Gandhabba devas, he reflected, "These Gandhabba devas are very beautiful and handsome. What meritorious karma did they perform to come here?" Upon considering, he saw that they had been monks in their previous lives. Then he further investigated, "Even if they were monks, did they fulfill their virtues (sīla)?" and he saw that "they were those who had fully practiced their virtues." "Even if they were those who had fully practiced their virtues,
85:
did they have other higher qualities or not?" Upon reflecting again, he saw that "they were attainers of jhāna." "Even if they were attainers of jhāna, where did they live?" Upon further investigation and reflection, he saw that "they were the venerable ones who came for alms at my house." Those with pure virtue can be reborn in any of the six deva realms they desire; however, these monks were not reborn in the higher deva realms. Those who attain jhāna are usually reborn in the Brahma realm; however, these monks were not reborn in the Brahma realm. As for me, because I stood in the advice and exhortation of those monks, I have become a true son in the lap of Sakka, the lord of devas. These monks, however, are reborn in the lowly class of Gandhabba devas. Since these devas are 'aṭṭhivedha' persons (those who need to be pierced to the bone), they are persons who should be spoken to as if being rolled over and over and intensely prodded and beaten." Thinking and reflecting thus, he gave a sharp and intense admonition with the words, "Sirs, where was your wisdom directed when you heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One?" and so on.

In this passage, regarding the term "aṭṭhivedha persons," one should briefly note the four types of excellent horses and the four types of excellent men mentioned in the Patoda Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Catukka Nipāta, Tatiya Paṇṇāsaka, 2-Kesivagga, 3-Patoda Sutta, Aṅguttara 1, page 429):

The four types of excellent horses are: (1) the Chāyāditta excellent horse, which is disciplined just by seeing the shadow of the whip; (2) the Lomavedha excellent horse, which is not yet disciplined by seeing the shadow of the whip but becomes disciplined and alarmed only when struck until the hair falls off; (3) the Cammavedha excellent horse, which is not yet disciplined by the previous two methods but becomes disciplined and alarmed only when struck and prodded until the skin is torn; (4) the Aṭṭhivedha excellent horse, which is not yet disciplined by the previous three methods but becomes disciplined and alarmed only when struck, beaten, and prodded until it reaches the bone. Just as there are these four types of excellent horses—

There are also four types of excellent men. The four types are: (1) "In such and such a town or village, such and such a woman or man
86:
is suffering, (or) has passed away and died." Just by hearing such news, an excellent man who is alarmed and gains a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and strives to attain insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) and the wisdom of the path (magga-paññā) is a Chāyāditta person (similar to the first excellent horse). (2) An excellent man who does not yet gain alarm and spiritual urgency by the first method, but only when he personally sees a woman or man suffering (or) passing away and dying, then gains alarm and spiritual urgency and strives to attain insight-wisdom and the wisdom of the path is a Lomavedha person (similar to the second excellent horse). (3) An excellent man who does not yet gain alarm and spiritual urgency by the previous two methods, but only when he sees one of his own relatives suffering (or) passing away and dying, then gains alarm and spiritual urgency and strives to attain insight-wisdom and the wisdom of the path is a Cammavedha person (similar to the third excellent horse). (4) An excellent man who does not yet gain alarm and spiritual urgency by the previous three methods, but only when he himself experiences suffering such as a major disease or ailment, then gains alarm and spiritual urgency and strives to attain insight-wisdom and the wisdom of the path is an Aṭṭhivedha person (similar to the fourth excellent horse). Thus there are four types of excellent men. (The details should be taken and noted from the Burmese translation of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Volume 1, page 442). Referring to the fourth type of excellent man among these four, Gopaka Deva thought and reflected, "Since these devas are aṭṭhivedha persons," and so on.

In the words reported by Sakka, "Among those three devas, two devas regained mindfulness of the first jhāna in that very life and reached the Brahmapurohita realm," the details to be noted are: When Gopaka Deva spoke the words of admonition, among the three Gandhabba devas, two devas reflected, "Those Gandhabba who dance, sing, and play music should only receive rewards; however, this Gopaka Deva, from the time he saw us, has been speaking only words of blame that crackle like salt thrown into a brazier. Why is this?" When they reflected thus,
87:
87
They clearly remembered that in their previous human lives, they had been monks, possessed pure virtue, were attainers of Jhana, and had been alms-collectors at the home of the princess Gopikā of the Sakyan clan, who was the former life of this deva son Gopaka. They reflected, "Those with pure virtue are reborn in whichever of the six sensual deva realms they desire; those who attain Jhana are reborn in the Brahma realm. We, however, were unable to be reborn in the higher deva realms or the Brahma realm. Because she established herself in our instructions and advice, this young woman has been reborn in a higher deva realm. As for us, although we were monks and practiced the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One, we have been reborn in the lowly class of Gandhabba devas (due to attachment to our previous existence). Therefore, the deva son Gopaka rebukes us with such words."

While listening to the admonishing words of the deva son Gopaka, two of the devas (among the three) regained mindfulness of the first Jhana (i.e., they attained the first Jhana). Using that first Jhana as a basis (pādaka), they contemplated the conditioned phenomena of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa saṅkhāra) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and thereby attained the Fruit of Anāgāmī (Non-returner) right then and there.

At that moment, their current sensual-sphere Gandhabba bodies, which possessed little power, were unable to sustain the supramundane quality of the Fruit of Anāgāmī. Consequently, they passed away (cuti) at that very instant and, being attainers of the intermediate first Jhana, were reborn in the Brahmapurohita realm among the three realms of the first Jhana of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). Specifically, although it is said they were "reborn in the Brahmapurohita realm," the bodies of those two Brahmas did not appear in the higher Brahmapurohita realm [immediately]; rather, while they were still standing in that very Tāvatiṃsa deva realm (the Sudhammā assembly hall), their Gandhabba bodies vanished and their Brahmapurohita Brahma bodies became manifest.

As for the other Gandhabba (Samana) deva son, he was unable to cut off the craving and greed (taṇhā-lobha) attached to that Gandhabba life.
88:
88
Because he could not abandon his attachment, he remained in that Cātumahārājika sensual-sphere Gandhabba life. (This concludes the detailed extract from the Commentary regarding the story of the deva son Gopaka).

Sakka, the Lord of Devas, having related the story of the deva son Gopaka to the Blessed One in prose (cuṇṇiya) as previously mentioned, recounted the matter again in fifteen great verses (gāthā). He then continued with three more verses, praising the Dispensation (Sāsana) and the virtues of the Blessed One, and stating that they had now come before the Blessed One to attain the supramundane Path and Fruit (Magga-Phala) which those two Brahmas had attained. He further requested permission to ask questions if the Blessed One would allow it. (The Pali of those verses and their meanings should be noted from the Pali Text and the Myanmar Pitaka Translation; here, only the final verse of his request will be presented):

Tassa dhammassa pattiyā, āgatamhāsi mārisa.
Katāvakāsā bhagavatā, pañhaṃ pucchemu mārisa.

"Mārisa (O Blessed One, who has stilled all suffering), we have now come before the Teacher for the sake of attaining (pattiyā) that supramundane Dhamma (tassa dhammassa) which those two Brahmas attained. (The word 'āsi' is merely an ornament of speech). Mārisa (O Blessed One, who has stilled all suffering), if we are granted the opportunity (katāvakāsā) by the Blessed One (bhagavatā) out of His compassion, we wish to ask (pucchemu) questions (pañhaṃ)..."
89:
89
"...We wish to ask questions with the desire to know and to be free from doubt, O Lord." Thus he requested permission to ask questions.

At that time, the thought arose in the mind of the Blessed One: "This Sakka has possessed pure conduct for a long night (a long time). Whatever question he asks, he will ask only a question connected with a cause (a question that will be fruitful); he will not ask a question unconnected with a cause (a question that will be fruitless). When he asks and I answer, he will understand that answer very quickly."

## The Story of Magha the Youth
(In this context, regarding the statement "This Sakka has possessed pure conduct for a long night," I shall briefly present the "Story of Magha the Youth" as explained in the Commentary to show how Sakka had pure conduct since the long past):

This Sakka had been a person of pure conduct since the time he was Magha the youth in Macala village in the kingdom of Magadha, before the Buddha appeared. To elaborate: When this Sakka was Magha the youth in that Macala village, he rose early one day and went to the place in the center of the village where people gathered for village affairs. Using his feet, he cleared away the dust and rubbish from the spot where he stood, making it clean and pleasant. Another man, liking that spot, came and stood in the place Magha had cleared.

Magha, mindful of this, then cleared an area as large as a threshing floor in the center of the village, spread white sand, brought firewood, and made a fire when it was cold.
90:
90
The villagers, both old and young, would come to that place, joyfully warm themselves by the fire, and sit comfortably.

Then one day, a thought arose in Magha's mind: "When we go to the city, we see those who possess great wealth, such as kings and royal ministers. People say that in the celestial mansions wandering in the sky above, the Moon deva and the Sun deva clearly exist. By performing what deeds did those kings, ministers, and the Moon and Sun devas obtain such wealth and status?" He then reflected correctly: "They would not have obtained them by any other means; they must have obtained such wealth only by performing pure wholesome deeds (kusala). I, too, should perform only such pure wholesome deeds that can provide such wealth."

After reflecting thus, Magha rose early, drank his gruel, and taking tools such as a billhook, an axe, a hoe, and a sledgehammer, he went to the four-way crossroads. With the sledgehammer, he broke and removed stones, rolling them away from the roadside. He cut down and cleared trees that might strike the axles of carts and carriages. He leveled the uneven ground of the road. He built a rest house and pavilion at the crossroads for people to stay. He dug a square pond. He laid bridges and planks on difficult paths. In this way, he spent his days performing wholesome deeds and returned home only at sunset.

Another man asked Magha, "Friend Magha, you leave the village early in the morning and return from the forest only in the evening. What work do you do?" Magha replied, "O friend, I am performing pure wholesome deeds. I am clearing the good path leading to the deva realm."
91:
91
Then that friend and Magha questioned and answered each other further as follows:

Friend: "O friend Magha, what is called 'pure wholesome deed'?"

Magha: "Friend, do you not know what a pure wholesome deed is?"

Friend: "No, I do not know."

Magha: "When you go to the city, have you not seen those with great wealth, such as the king and his great ministers?"

Friend: "Yes, I have seen them."

Magha: "Those people, such as the king and his great ministers, performed pure wholesome deeds and thus obtained those positions of kingship and high office. I, too, am performing the kind of wholesome deeds that can yield such results as royal wealth and ministerial wealth. Have you heard of the Moon deva and the Sun deva?"

Friend: "Yes, I have heard of them."

Magha: "I am clearing the path to that deva realm."

Friend: "Friend Magha, is this wholesome deed you speak of only for you to perform? Can no one else perform it?"

Magha: "O friend, there is no prohibition against anyone else performing this wholesome deed."

Friend: "Friend Magha, if that is so, when you go to the forest tomorrow, please give me a call."

In this way, they questioned, answered, and exchanged words. The next day, Magha took that man and went to the forest. In this manner, thirty-three strong young men of Macala village...
92:
92
...became Magha's companions and fellow-workers in performing wholesome deeds, following his example.

Those thirty-three men, sharing the same wholesome intention, went about performing wholesome deeds. Their way of working was such that wherever they went, if they were making a road pleasant and level, they would work with all their might to finish it in a single day. Whether they were digging a pond, building a rest house, or constructing a bridge, they would exert their full effort to complete it in a single day.

## The Evil Plan of the Macala Village Headman
At that time, a thought arose in the mind of the Macala village headman: "In the past, when these men used to drink liquor or commit crimes such as fighting and killing one another, I obtained much wealth through fines and taxes (such as one or two coins from liquor sales and fines from their criminal cases). Now, since these men started performing wholesome deeds, I no longer have such income. Well then, I shall speak slanderous words to cause misunderstanding and discord at the King's palace."

The wicked village headman, having planned thus, went to the King of Magadha and reported, "Great King, I am seeing many robbers and bad people."

When the King asked, "Friend headman, where do you see them?", the wicked headman replied, "Great King, I see them in my village of Macala."

"Friend headman, what kind of robbers and bad people are they?" the King asked. The wicked headman replied, "Your Majesty..."
93:
"They are criminals who commit crimes," he slandered. Then the King asked, "What is the lineage of these criminals who are committing crimes?" The wicked village headman replied, "Your Majesty, they are of the householder class." The King then asked, "What could those of the householder class do? Why did you not inform me sooner if you knew?" "Great King, I did not report earlier because I was afraid those criminals would harm me; please do not punish me now," the wicked headman said convincingly. The King, thinking, "This headman speaks to me firmly and boldly," trusted him and said, "If that is the case, go now. You yourself must arrest and bring those criminals here." He then provided him with soldiers and sent him off.

## The Arrest of Magha and His Group
The wicked village headman returned to Macala village. After Magha and the thirty-three men had performed meritorious deeds in the forest all day and finished their evening meal, they sat together in the middle of the village. While they were discussing, "What good deed shall we do tomorrow? Shall we level the roads? Shall we dig a pond? Or shall we build a bridge?" the headman surrounded them and the thirty-three men led by Magha. Shouting, "Do not move! This is the King's command!" he arrested and bound them, then led them to the King.

At that time, the wives of those young men heard the news: "Your masters and husbands have been arrested and bound as criminals who committed crimes." They said, "They have been deceitful and crooked for a long time. Those men
94:
claimed, 'We are performing meritorious deeds,' and lived in the forest every day while deceiving us. All household affairs have been ruined and declined; there has been no progress or benefit at home. Therefore, it is very good that they are bound; it is very good that they are arrested. (It is better that they are bound and taken away)," they said, speaking words of blame.

## Planning to Kill by Elephant Trampling
The wicked village headman brought Magha and his group and presented them to the King. Without investigation or reflection, the King ordered, "Have an elephant trample and kill these men." When Magha and his group were led to the place where they were to be trampled by the elephant, Magha asked the other young men, "Friends, will you be able to follow my words?" The others replied, "Friend Magha, even while following your words, we have now reached this danger of death. Even so, we will continue to follow your words. O friend Magha, please speak; what should we do?" Magha then said, "O friends, for those wandering in this cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra), it is natural to encounter such dangers. Friends, are you truly thieves (as the wicked headman said)?" The others replied, "We are not thieves." Magha then advised, "Friends, the Act of Truth (Saccakiriya) is the great refuge of this world. Therefore, all of you should perform an Act of Truth, saying: 'If we are truly thieves (as the village headman said), let the state elephant trample us. If it is true that we are not thieves, let the state elephant not trample us.'"

When those thirty-three young men performed the Act of Truth as Magha had instructed, the state elephant, far from trampling them,
95:
95
The elephant was unable even to approach Magha and his group; it fled, trumpeting in fear. Although the royal mahouts again tried to control and drive the elephant forward using spiked goads, harpoons, and hooks, they were unable to make it approach Magha’s group.
When the attendants reported to the King, “We are unable to make the elephant approach Magha’s group,” the King ordered, “If that is the case, cover those men with mats and have the elephant trample them.” When they were covered with mats according to the King’s command, the elephant trumpeted in fear twice as much as before and fled.
## The King Gains Right Understanding and Appoints Magha’s Group as Village Headmen with Many Rewards
The King, hearing of this, summoned the wicked village headman who had slandered them and said, “Master Headman, it seems the elephant does not wish to trample those men.” The wicked slanderer replied, “It is true, Your Majesty. The leader among them, the youth Magha, is one who knows a mantra that prevents elephants from trampling. This refusal of the elephant to trample is the power of that mantra.” The King then summoned Magha and asked, “Is it true that you have a mantra that prevents elephants from trampling?”
Then Magha replied, “Your Majesty, I have no such mantra. In truth, we made an Act of Truth (Sacca), saying: ‘If we are indeed wicked enemies of the King, let the elephant trample us. If it is true that we are not wicked enemies of the King, let the elephant not trample us.’ This refusal of the elephant to trample is the power of that Act of Truth.” Then the King asked, “Master Magha, what work do you all perform?”
96:
Magha replied in detail, "Your Majesty, we make uneven roads level. We build rest houses at four-way intersections for people to rest and relax. We dig ponds. We build bridges. We spend our lives performing such meritorious deeds."

When the King asked, "Friend Magha, why did this village headman slander you?" Magha replied, "Your Majesty, when we used to live in intoxication and negligence, this headman received such and such wealth from us. Now that we are no longer negligent, he no longer receives that wealth at all. For this reason, he slandered us."

Then the King said to Magha, "Friend Magha, even this elephant, though an animal, knows your virtues. I, however, though a human being, did not know your virtues. I grant you the village of Macala where you live, without ever taking it back. Let this elephant also be your elephant, and let the former wicked village headman be your slave. From now on, perform meritorious deeds for my sake as well." After saying this, he gave them much wealth as a reward and released the entire group of Magha.

Magha and his group took the wealth given by the King. While they were traveling, taking turns riding the elephant, they discussed, "Friends, meritorious deeds should be performed for the future life. For us, however, it has given benefits in this very life, like a blue lotus blooming in the water. Now, let us perform meritorious deeds even more than before." They continued to discuss,
97:
"What kind of meritorious deed shall we perform?" They decided, "Let us build a large, strong, and permanent rest house at the four-way intersection for the public to relax. Specifically, let us build it without including our wives in the merit. Indeed, when we were unjustly arrested as 'criminals,' not one of our wives even thought of a way for us to be released. Instead, they spoke joyfully and excitedly, saying, 'It is good that they are well-bound; it is good that they are well-captured.' Therefore, let us not give a share of this merit to those wives."

## Building the Great Rest House
When those thirty-four members of Magha's group (including the elephant) reached their homes, they gave the elephant a morsel of rice and a handful of grass every day. That morsel of rice and handful of grass were sufficient to fill the elephant's stomach. The members of Magha's group went into the forest and felled trees. After each tree was cut, the elephant dragged it and placed it near the cart track. The members of Magha's group then planed the timber and began the effort of building the great rest house.

In Magha's house, there were four wives: Sujātā, Sudhammā, Cittā, and Nandā. Among the four, Sudhammā asked the master carpenter, "O father, Magha and his thirty-four friends go to the forest early in the morning and return home only in the evening. What work are they doing?" The master carpenter replied, "My daughter, Magha and his thirty-four friends are building a great rest house." Sudhammā then said, "O father, I too wish to perform merit for the rest house."
98:
“Please make me a sharer in this merit,” she pleaded. The head carpenter replied, “O lady, the members of Magha’s group have said, ‘We shall build this without any share of merit for women.’” Sudhammā then gave the head carpenter a bribe of eight pieces of money and pleaded, “O father, please find a way for me to have a share of merit in this deed.”

The head carpenter said, “Very well, lady.” He then took his adzes and axes, stood in the middle of the village, and shouted loudly to alert them, “Friends, what is this? Have you not left the village even at this hour?” Knowing that all the members of the group had set out on their journey, he said, “Friends, you go ahead; I have a matter that needs to be delayed for a while.” Having sent the thirty-three members ahead, he went another way, felled a tree suitable for making a pinnacle (the pinnacle-post), planed it smooth, and brought it back to the village. He left it at Sudhammā’s house with the instruction, “On the day I ask for it, please bring it out and give it to me.”

Later, when the collection of timber was complete, and the tasks from clearing the ground to laying the foundation, erecting the pillars, placing the beams, and setting up the scaffolding (for the mounting of the pinnacle) were finished, the head carpenter sat on the scaffolding for the pinnacle. Lifting the rafters from the four directions, he started the conversation, saying, “Friends, we have forgotten one thing.” The members of the group blamed him, saying, “O head carpenter, what have we forgotten? You, teacher, have forgotten everything!”
99:
When they spoke thus, the head carpenter (ignoring their blame) said, “Friends, where will these rafters meet and be joined? We must have a pinnacle-post for the rafters to join.” When they asked, “O head carpenter, where can we get one at this time?” the head carpenter replied, “It might be found in the houses of the noble families. Go around to every house and ask.”

The members of Magha’s group entered the village to inquire. Standing at the door of the lady Sudhammā, they asked, “Is there any wood in this house to make a pinnacle?” Sudhammā replied, “There is.” The members of Magha’s group said, “Take the price for it now.” She replied, “I do not wish to take the price. If you give me a share of the merit, I will give you this wood for the pinnacle.” The members of Magha’s group said, “Friends, come away; we cannot give a share of merit to a woman in any way. Let us go to the forest and fell a tree suitable for a pinnacle.” Saying this, they left the village.

Then the head carpenter asked, “Friends, what happened? Did you not get the wood for the pinnacle?” The members of Magha’s group told him the reason. While still sitting on the scaffolding for the pinnacle, the head carpenter looked up at the sky and said, “O friends, the astrological timing of the stars is very good today. Such a constellation can only be found after another year. You have also brought these timbers with great hardship. If these timbers are left for a whole year, they will rot and decay right here. When reborn in the celestial realm, let there be a hall for that lady Sudhammā as well. Bring that pinnacle-wood from the lady Sudhammā’s house.”
100:
Even before the members of Magha’s group returned, the lady Sudhammā had the inscription “This rest house is named Sudhammā” carved on the lower surface of the pinnacle, and she had wrapped and covered that area with a new cloth. The builders came and said, “O Sudhammā, give us the pinnacle. Let happen what may; we shall let you have a share of the merit.” Sudhammā brought the pinnacle-wood out of the house and gave it to them, instructing, “Friends, do not remove this cloth until you have finished mounting the eight or sixteen rafters.”

The builders agreed, saying, “Very well,” and took it away. After mounting the rafters, they removed the covering cloth. A sharp-eyed villager looked up and, seeing the inscription, said, “Friends, what is this?” and called someone who could read to show him. That person read it out, “This rest house is named Sudhammā.”

Then the members of Magha’s group shouted loudly, “Friends, remove that pinnacle! Although we built this rest house from the very beginning, we do not even have our names on it. This lady Sudhammā, with just a cubit’s length of pinnacle-wood, has made the whole rest house called by her name.” While those men were shouting loudly, the head carpenter inserted the rafters, drove in the pins, and completed the construction of the great rest house.

The members of Magha’s group divided the completed rest house into three sections: (1) one section was made as a place for government officials to stay;
101:
(2) one section was made as a place for the poor to stay; (3) one section was made as a place for the sick to stay.

## Division of Duties in the Rest House
The thirty-three members laid out thirty-three wooden planks (seats). They trained the elephant given by the king, instructing it: “O noble elephant, when a guest arrives and sits on a certain person’s plank, take that guest and lead him only to the house of the owner of that plank. All hospitality, such as massaging the feet and hands, providing food and snacks, and providing a bed and place to stay, shall be the responsibility of the owner of that plank.” Whenever a guest arrived, the elephant would lead the guest to the house of the owner of the plank. The owner of the plank would then fully perform the duties of hospitality for that guest for the day.

## Merits of Magha’s Household
(1) Magha had a Kovilāra tree (celestial coral tree) planted not far from the great rest house, and he also had a large stone slab laid at the foot of that tree. (2) Magha’s wife named Nandā had a large lake dug not far from the rest house. (3) The wife named Cittā had a flower garden planted not far from the rest house.

(4) Sujātā, the eldest wife, held a mirror and adorned her body, wandering about in vanity without performing any merit. Magha encouraged his eldest wife Sujātā, saying, “Lady Sujātā, the lady Sudhammā has become a sharer in the merit of the great rest house. The lady Nandā has had a large lake dug. The lady Cittā has had a flower garden planted. But you have not a single deed of merit. Perform some kind of merit, Lady Sujātā.” The eldest wife Sujātā replied, “Lord, for whom
102:
do you perform merit? Is not the merit you perform also my merit?” Saying this, she continued to prioritize the task of adorning herself.

## The Afterlife of Magha and His Group
Magha lived out his lifespan and, upon passing away from that life, became Sakka, the King of Gods, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Those thirty-three villagers also passed away and became thirty-three gods, arising in the presence of Sakka. (Among Magha’s four wives, the three wives named Sudhammā, Cittā, and Nandā also passed away from that life and became the three chief queens of Sakka. However, Sujātā, the eldest wife, because she did not listen to Magha’s words and remained negligent, only adorning herself, passed away from that life and was reborn as a crane in a mountain valley.)

## Sakka’s Possessions
Sakka’s celestial palace, the Vejayanta Palace, is seven hundred leagues high. The victory banner is three hundred leagues high. Due to the merit of planting the Kovilāra tree, the great Pāricchattaka tree appeared, which is three hundred leagues in circumference, fifteen leagues in girth, and one hundred leagues high. Due to the merit of laying the stone slab at the foot of the tree while a human, the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone throne appeared at the foot of the celestial Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, being sixty leagues long, fifty leagues wide, and fifteen leagues thick.

Due to the merit of donating the wood for the lady Sudhammā, the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall (the great Dhamma hall) of three hundred leagues appeared. Due to the merit of the lady Nandā digging and donating the lake, the great lake named Nandā, fifty leagues wide, appeared.
103:
Due to the merit of the lady Cittā, who had planted and offered a flower garden, a great celestial garden named Cittalatā, sixty leagues in extent, appeared in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Sakka, the King of Gods, was seated on a golden throne of one league in the Sudhammā Hall (the celestial assembly hall), sheltered by a great white celestial umbrella of three leagues. He was surrounded by the thirty-three celestial lords, three celestial queens, twenty-five million celestial dancers, and the entire host of gods from the two realms of Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa. As he looked upon his great majesty as Sakka, he saw the three great queens Sudhammā, Nandā, and Cittā. Seeing them, he thought, “These three great queens are well-known; but in which realm has Sujātā been reborn?” Looking further, he saw clearly, “Because this Sujātā did not follow my words, she has become a little crane in a mountain valley.” He then descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and went to the presence of that little crane Sujātā.

As soon as the crane Sujātā saw Sakka, she recognized him and stood with her head bowed. Sakka said, “O foolish Sujātā, why do you not dare to lift your head now? You did not follow my words and spent your time only adorning your physical body. The ladies Sudhammā, Nandā, and Cittā have attained the great glory of celestial queens. Come, follow me; look at our splendor.” Having said this, he took her to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, left her at the great Nandā celestial lake, and returned to sit on his original golden throne within the Vejayantā Palace.

## The Celestial Dancers

## Mocking the Sujātā Crane

The celestial dancers asked Sakka, “O Lord Sakka, where did you go?” Sakka—
104:
—did not wish to tell them the reason, but since the celestial dancers questioned him persistently, he replied, “I have been to see Sujātā.” When the celestial dancers asked again, “O Lord Sakka, where is the lady Sujātā reborn now?” Sakka replied, “She is reborn in a mountain valley.” When the celestial dancers asked, “Where is she now?” Sakka replied, “I have left her in the great Nandā celestial lake.”

The celestial dancers consulted one another, saying, “Friends, come, let us go and see our lady Sujātā.” Then all the celestial dancers went to that great Nandā lake. In her previous life as a human, Sujātā had been the eldest among them and had treated them with contempt. Now, when those celestial dancers saw the crane Sujātā, they mocked and ridiculed her, saying, “O friends, look at the beak of our mistress Sujātā, which is like a needle used for piercing crabs!” and so on.

Sujātā felt extremely ashamed and hurt, and she said to Sakka, “O Lord Sakka, what use are these golden mansions, silver mansions, ruby mansions, and the great Nandā lake to me? O Lord Sakka, for every being, only one's birthplace is pleasant. Therefore, please release me back into that mountain valley (my place of birth).” Sakka released the crane Sujātā in that mountain valley and asked, “Will you follow my words?” The crane Sujātā replied, “I will follow them, Lord Sakka.” Sakka said, “Take and observe the Five Precepts, and guard them so they do not break or become flawed. In just two or three days, I will raise you to be the chief of these celestial dancers.” Following Sakka’s words, the crane Sujātā took and practiced the Five Precepts.
105:
After two or three days had passed, Sakka, wondering, “Is the crane Sujātā able to guard her precepts?” went to that place, disguised himself as a fish, and floated on his back downstream in front of the crane Sujātā. Thinking, “It must be a dead fish,” the crane Sujātā went to where the fish was and bit its head. The fish wiggled its tail. Thinking, “I think the fish is alive,” the crane Sujātā released it back into the water. Sakka, standing in the sky, gave her words of encouragement, saying, “Sādhu! Sādhu! You guard the training rules well. For you, who guard the training rules so they do not break or become flawed, I shall make you the chief of the celestial dancers in just two or three days.” He then returned to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

## Sujātā Becoming a Potter’s Daughter

The lifespan of the crane Sujātā was five hundred years. She did not get enough food to fill her stomach even for a single day. Day by day, her flesh and skin became thin and dry, and she withered; however, she guarded the Five Precepts without flaw. When she passed away from that life, she became the daughter of a potter in a potter’s house in the city of Vārāṇasī.

Sakka looked to see, “Where has Sujātā been reborn?” and seeing that she had become a potter’s daughter, he thought, “It is not proper to bring her from that potter’s house to this Tāvatiṃsa heaven yet. I shall give her wealth for her livelihood.” He then loaded a cart full of golden cucumbers, and in the guise of an old man, he sat in the middle of the potter’s village and cried out, “Buy my cucumbers!”

The villagers from all four directions came to the old man and said, “Grandfather, give us cucumbers,” speaking to buy them. The old man asked, “O sons and daughters, I can only give these cucumbers to those who guard the precepts. Do you, sons and daughters, guard the precepts?”
106:
The villagers replied, “Grandfather, we do not even know what the precepts are. Please just give us the cucumbers for a fair price.” The old man spoke firmly, “I can only give them to those who guard the precepts.” Then all the villagers said, “Friends, come, let us go. We do not know what kind of old man this cucumber-selling grandfather is,” and grumbling, they went away.

Seeing the villagers return, the potter’s daughter met them and asked, “Mother and father, did you go to buy cucumbers and return empty-handed without any?” The villagers replied to the potter’s daughter, “Dear daughter, we do not know what kind of old man that cucumber-selling grandfather is. He keeps saying, ‘I will only give cucumbers to those who guard the precepts.’ We think this old man’s daughters must have grown up and thrived by eating precepts. As for us, we do not even know what the precepts are.” When they said this, the potter’s daughter reflected, “This must have been brought for me,” and she went to that place and said, “O father, please give me the cucumbers.” The old man Sakka asked, “Dear daughter, do you guard the precepts?” The potter’s daughter replied, “O father, I guard the precepts without flaw.” Then the old man Sakka said, “I have brought these golden cucumbers specifically for you,” and having left them along with the cart at the door of the potter’s daughter’s house, he departed for the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

## Sujātā Becoming the Daughter of the Asura King

That potter’s daughter also guarded the Five Precepts without flaw until the end of her life. When she passed away from that life—
107:
—she became the daughter of the Asura King Vepacitti. Due to the result of the precepts she had guarded in her lives as a crane and a potter’s daughter, she became a person of exceedingly beautiful and inspiring appearance. The Asura King Vepacitti, thinking, “I shall celebrate a marriage festival for my daughter,” summoned the Asuras to assemble.

Sakka looked to see, “Where has Sujātā been reborn now?” and realized, “She is now in the Asura realm. Today, they will celebrate a marriage festival for that Asura princess Sujātā.” He then thought, “I should now take the Asura princess Sujātā by some means.” He disguised himself as an Asura, went to the marriage festival, and stood mixed among the Asuras.

The father, Asura King Vepacitti, said, “Dear daughter, name your lord and husband,” and handing a garland to the princess Sujātā, he said, “Dear daughter, throw it upon the one you desire.” As the Asura princess Sujātā looked here and there, she saw Sakka (disguised as an Asura). Because of their past association and living together in previous lives, a strong feeling of love arose in her, and she said, “This person is my lord and husband,” and threw the garland upon Sakka.

Sakka firmly grasped the Asura princess Sujātā by the arm and flew up into the sky. At that moment, the Asuras realized he was Sakka and shouted, “Friends, catch the old Sakka! This old Sakka is our enemy. We cannot by any means give the Asura maiden Sujātā to this old Sakka!” and they pursued Sakka.

The Asura King Vepacitti asked the Asuras, “Who has taken my daughter?” The Asuras—
108:
108
When it was said, “Great King, Sakka the Elder has taken the Asura maiden Sujā,” the Asura King Vepacitti said, “Among all the gods except me, this Sakka is indeed the most noble. Move aside, brothers,” thus speaking words of restraint. Sakka took the Asura maiden Sujā to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and appointed her as the chief queen over twenty-five million celestial dancers.

The Asura maiden Sujā made a request to Sakka, saying, “Lord Sakka, I have no mother, father, brother, or sister in this Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Wherever you go, Lord Sakka, please take me with you.” Sakka gave his promise, saying, “Very well.” (This is the story of the youth Magha).

In this way, the Blessed One, having clearly seen the purity of Sakka’s conduct since he was the youth Magha in the village of Macala, reflected: “This Sakka has had pure conduct for a long time. Whatever question he asks, he will ask only a question connected with a cause (a question that will lead to benefit), and he will not ask a question not connected with a cause (a question that will not lead to benefit). When I answer his question, he will understand that answer quickly.”

Then the Blessed One addressed Sakka:

“Puccha vāsava maṃ pañhaṃ, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.
Tassa tasseva pañhassa, ahaṃ antaṃ karomi te.”

“O Vāsava, King of Gods, whatever question you desire in your mind...
109:
109
“icchasī = You desire to ask; taṃ pañhaṃ = that question you wish to ask; maṃ = of Me, the Teacher of the three worlds; puccha = ask, to clear your doubts. ahaṃ = I, the Teacher of the three worlds; te = to you, Sakka, the Lord of Devas; tassa tassava pañhassa = for each and every question you ask; antaṃ karomi = shall provide an end, clearing and resolving the doubts (vicikicchā) that repeatedly arise in your mind.”
With this verse, the Fully Enlightened One issued the invitation.
## Sakka Asks Questions and the Blessed One Answers
(1) Having received the Blessed One’s permission, Sakka, the King of Devas, asked the Blessed One:
“Venerable Sir, many beings—Devas, humans, Asuras, Nagas, and Gandhabbas—possess the strong desire: ‘May we live without enmity, without violence, without foes, without sorrow, and without anger.’ Yet, despite such desires, these beings live with enmity, with violence, with foes, with sorrow, and with anger. By what fetter (saṃyojana), Venerable Sir, are they bound that they must live in this way?”
110:
110
This was the first question he asked. When Sakka had thus asked, the Blessed One answered:

“O Sakka, King of Gods, gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, gandhabbas, and many other beings have a strong desire in their hearts, thinking: ‘May we live without enmity, without violence, without foes, without sorrow, and without anger.’ Yet, despite having such a desire, they live with enmity, with violence, with foes, with sorrow, and with anger. This is because of the two fetters of Envy (issā) and Stinginess (macchariya).”

Thus He answered this first question.

(Here, I shall first explain the noteworthy points regarding Envy and Stinginess:

The nature of resenting and not tolerating the prosperity of others is called Envy (issā). This Envy (1) has the characteristic of resenting and not tolerating the prosperity that others have already gained or will gain. (When one sees or hears that someone has gained or will gain wealth and prosperity, the unwholesome mental factor of envy arises in those who do not wish to see or hear it. If one observes this characteristic of the evil state of envy, one should know it through the wisdom of Abhidhamma as the unwholesome mental factor of envy arising in that person). (2) It has the function of being unable to delight in or being unable to endure the prosperity of others. (Being unable to rejoice, or being unable to bear it when seeing or hearing others gain wealth and prosperity, is the function of the evil state of envy). (3) It has the manifestation of turning away from the prosperity of others...
111:
111
...as it appears to the wisdom of the yogi. (A person overwhelmed and oppressed by this evil state of envy cannot look with joy when seeing others endowed with wealth and prosperity, but only turns their face away. Because of the cause of envy, the effect of turning away from others' prosperity arises. Therefore, when noble yogis deeply contemplate envy with wisdom, it appears to their knowledge as ‘the state that turns away from others' prosperity.’ Among the four types of manifestation, this is the manifestation as an effect). (4) Envy has the prosperity of others as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). (Envy arises only when seeing or hearing of others' prosperity; if not seen or heard, envy does not arise. Thus, the prosperity of others is the closest cause for the arising of the evil state of envy). (From Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā 1, page 299).

This characteristic of resenting and not tolerating, which is the evil state of envy, should be illustrated with both laypeople and monks. To elaborate: some layperson, through one of the livelihoods such as farming or trade, depending on their own manly effort and ability, may obtain inanimate vehicles like carts, carriages, or motor cars, or animate vehicles like elephants, horses, buffaloes, or oxen, or fine jewels like diamonds, gold, and rubies. Another person, an envious one who resents that person’s gain, cannot be pleased in any way by that person’s good fortune. Furthermore, they always think and plan for that person’s ruin, wondering, “When will this person fall from this prosperity, become a destitute pauper, and wander in misery?” If, for some reason, that owner of wealth falls from their prosperity, the envious person becomes greatly satisfied and delighted.

A monk whose mind is associated with envy and resentment, upon seeing another monk who is endowed with learning and great knowledge, or who is successful in teaching the scriptures and thus endowed with gains, honor, and respect, cannot be happy. He thinks only of that monk’s ruin, wondering, “When will this monk fall from these gains, honors, and respect?” Whenever he sees that monk fall from those gains and honors for some reason, that evil monk overwhelmed by envy becomes delighted. In this way, the evil state of envy has the characteristic of resenting and not tolerating the prosperity of others. (From Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā 1, page 405).

The evil state of envy cannot endure seeing or hearing of the prosperity naturally obtained by others; it only desires and wishes for the destruction of that prosperity. Even upon hearing the news that “Such and such a person will receive such and such prosperity,” it cannot bear it and only desires and wishes for that person not to receive the gain. (From Ledi Sayadaw’s Paramatthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Cetasika section, page 99). This is what should be noted regarding Envy.

The nature of being miserly and stingy with one’s own prosperity is called Stinginess (macchariya). This Stinginess (1) has the characteristic of hiding one’s own prosperity, whether already gained or yet to be gained. (A person overwhelmed and oppressed by the evil state of stinginess does not want to let others know of their gained or future prosperity and miserly hides it). (2) It has the function of being unable to endure sharing one’s prosperity with others. (A person overwhelmed and oppressed by the evil state of stinginess feels unbearable when they have to share their prosperity with others; this is the function of stinginess). (3) It has the manifestation of shrinking from giving...
112:
...seeing another monk endowed with gains, offerings, and honor due to his great learning, teaching of scriptures, etc., one is unable to be happy and dwells thinking only of that monk's ruin: “When will this monk fall away from these gains and honors?” When, for some reason, that monk is seen falling away from those gains and honors, the wicked monk overwhelmed by envy (issā) becomes delighted. Thus, the evil state of envy has the characteristic of being jealous and resentful of the prosperity of others. (From Abhi-ṭṭha 1, p. 405).

The evil state of envy cannot endure seeing or hearing about the prosperity naturally obtained by others; it only desires and wishes for the destruction of that prosperity. Even upon hearing the news that “such and such a person will receive such and such prosperity,” one cannot bear it and only desires that person not to receive the gain. (From Ledi Sayadaw’s Paramatthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Cetasika Section, p. 99). This is what should be noted regarding envy.

Stinginess (macchariya) is the nature of being miserly and protective of one's own prosperity. That stinginess has (1) the characteristic of hiding one's own prosperity, whether already obtained or yet to be obtained. (A person overwhelmed by the evil state of stinginess does not want others to know about their gains and tends to hide them). (2) It has the function (rasa) of not being able to endure sharing one's prosperity with others. (A person overwhelmed by stinginess cannot bear it if they have to share their possessions with others; this is the function of stinginess). (3) It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of shrinking from giving. (Alternatively) It has the manifestation of harsh anger, like being placed in a hot fire, if one cannot prevent others from taking by force. (Alternatively) It has the manifestation of giving or offering very little, as if using the tip of a ladle. (When noble practitioners contemplate the nature of stinginess, it appears as...)
113:
...the mental state that shrinks from giving; this is the natural manifestation (sabhāva-paccupaṭṭhāna). (Alternatively) It appears to the wisdom as the state of intense anger when others forcibly take one's possessions; this is the functional manifestation (kicca-paccupaṭṭhāna). (Alternatively) It appears to the wisdom as the state of giving only a tiny amount, just enough to say one has given, as if with the tip of a ladle or spoon, when one cannot avoid giving; this is the result manifestation (phala-paccupaṭṭhāna). (4) It has one's own prosperity as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). (From Abhi-ṭṭha 1, p. 299).

## The 5 Types of Stinginess (Macchariya)
That stinginess is of five kinds: (1) Āvāsa-macchariya: stinginess regarding dwellings such as monasteries, buildings, parks, rooms, day-places, and night-places; (2) Kula-macchariya: stinginess regarding families and supporters, not wanting them to associate with others; (3) Lābha-macchariya: stinginess regarding the four requisites and gains; (4) Vaṇṇa-macchariya: stinginess regarding physical appearance or reputation; (5) Dhamma-macchariya: stinginess regarding the Dhamma (scriptural knowledge).

(1) Among these five, the entire monastery, a compound, a room, a day-place, or a night-place is called āvāsa. Those living in such dwellings live comfortably and receive the four requisites. A monk with stinginess does not want another virtuous monk, who is endowed with duties and conduct, to come and stay in that dwelling. Even if that virtuous monk comes to stay, he wishes for him to leave quickly. Such stinginess is called āvāsa-macchariya. However, it is not āvāsa-macchariya for a monk who does not want a quarrelsome monk to stay in that dwelling.

(2) Supporters and relatives who provide service are called kula. Not wanting another monk to approach or associate with one's own supporters or relatives is called kula-macchariya. Especially, regarding wicked and immoral persons...
114:
Not desiring association [with an immoral person] is not kula-macchariya (stinginess regarding families). Indeed, such a person of immoral conduct behaves in a way that destroys the faith of lay devotees; therefore, not desiring their association is not kula-macchariya. It is only when one does not desire the association of a virtuous monk, who can protect the faith of those lay devotees, that it is called kula-macchariya.

(3) Robes, alms-food, dwellings, and medicine are called the four requisites or gains (lābha). For a monk who thinks, "May another virtuous monk not receive these four requisites," it is lābha-macchariya (stinginess regarding gains). In particular, there are monks who misuse the four requisites donated out of faith by lay devotees, those who destroy the faithful offerings of devotees by not using them at all or by using them improperly, and those who are so stingy they will not give to others even until the items rot or decay. Seeing such a monk and thinking, "If another virtuous monk received these four requisites instead of this monk, they would be put to use; it would be better," does not constitute lābha-macchariya.

(4) Physical appearance and qualities of merit are called vaṇṇa. Among these two types of vaṇṇa, a person with stinginess regarding physical appearance, when told, "Another person has a beautiful appearance; they are inspiring," does not want to speak of it at all and wishes only to be beautiful and attractive themselves. A person with stinginess regarding the vaṇṇa of qualities of merit does not wish to speak at all of another's qualities of virtue (sīla), ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), or practice (paṭipatti).

(5) Dhamma is of two types: pariyatti-dhamma (scriptural learning) and paṭivedha-dhamma (attainment of the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna). Among these two, regarding paṭivedha-dhamma, Noble Ones (ariyas) are not stingy. They desire all beings—humans, devas, and brahmās—to attain and know the paṭivedha-dhamma they have attained. They wish and aspire, "May others know this extraordinary paṭivedha-dhamma of the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna that I have realized." Regarding pariyatti...
115:
...it is only in pariyatti-dhamma that what is called dhamma-macchariya (stinginess regarding the Dhamma) can occur. A person with this dhamma-macchariya does not want others to know the profound and difficult Pāḷi and Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) that they themselves know; they wish to be the only one who knows. In particular, if a person does not give the profound and difficult Pāḷi and Commentary texts they know to another, either by considering the person to protect the Dhamma, or by considering the Dhamma to protect the person, that withholding is not dhamma-macchariya.

In this context, there are some people in the world who are fickle and unstable, sometimes becoming a monk, sometimes a brahmin, and sometimes an ascetic. If a monk reflects deeply, "This fickle and unstable person might take the subtle Pāḷi handed down through generations and turn wholesome states into unwholesome ones, or because they are fickle themselves, they might turn the Dhamma taught by the Buddha into the kind of teachings taught by heretics (titthiyas), causing confusion and entanglement," and thus does not give the profound pariyatti-dhamma they know to that person, this monk is said to be one who withholds by considering the person to protect the Dhamma. If a monk reflects, "This Dhamma is very subtle. If this person learns it, they might claim to be an Arahant when they are not, telling laypeople and monks, and thus ruin themselves," and thus does not give the profound pariyatti-dhamma they know to that person, this monk is said to be one who withholds by considering the Dhamma to protect the person. For both these types of monks, dhamma-macchariya does not occur. However, if one does not give the pariyatti-dhamma they know to another, thinking, "If this person learns this Dhamma, they will be able to destroy our views; they will become superior to us," only such withholding is dhamma-macchariya.
116:
## The Faults of the Five Types of Macchariya

Among these five types of macchariya: (1) Due to āvāsa-macchariya (stinginess regarding dwellings), after death, one may become a yakkha (demon) or a peta (hungry ghost) and (due to the attachment and base desire for the dwelling) may have to wander around carrying the rubbish of that dwelling, which they were stingy about, on their head.

(2) Due to kula-macchariya, when a monk sees others giving gifts or showing respect in the homes of their own relatives or lay supporters of the four requisites, and thinks with anxiety, "These lay devotees have become estranged from me," (having a heart that is very hot with mental distress), they may vomit blood, or suffer from diarrhea, or their intestines may break into pieces and come out.

(3) Due to lābha-macchariya, by being stingy regarding the gains of the Saṅgha or the gains of a group, and using them as if they were personal belongings for oneself alone, after death, one may become a yakkha, a peta, or a great python.

(4) Due to vaṇṇa-macchariya, which is stinginess regarding physical appearance and reputation, one praises only one's own appearance and reputation. Regarding the appearance and reputation of others, one speaks of various faults, saying, "What kind of appearance or reputation does this person have?" and so on, and is likely to become an ugly person in the next life.

(5) (Paṭivedha-dhamma, which is the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna, is a state that occurs only in the continuum of Noble Ones and is attainable only by those Noble Ones. Since those Noble Ones have completely eradicated the unwholesome state of macchariya with the Path, they are not stingy regarding the paṭivedha-dhamma they have attained and realized. Thus, in the matter of dhamma-macchariya, only the stinginess of worldlings (puthujjanas) regarding the pariyatti-dhamma they know is found). Due to this pariyatti-dhamma-macchariya...
117:
...because of being stingy regarding the pariyatti-dhamma one knows and not giving any pariyatti-dhamma to anyone, one is likely to become a dull-witted and ignorant person (duppañña) in the next life.

Alternatively: (1) Due to āvāsa-macchariya, one may be cooked in the hot iron hell (because one obstructed the welfare and happiness others would have received from the dwelling). (2) Due to kula-macchariya, one may become a person completely devoid of gains (because one obstructed the gains others would have received in the homes of lay devotees). (3) Due to lābha-macchariya, one is reborn in the Gūtha-niraya (Dung Hell). (The Dung Hell is a hell completely devoid of anything pleasant. The monk with lābha-macchariya was one who obstructed the pleasant things others would have received due to gains. Therefore, because that monk with lābha-macchariya obstructed the pleasant things others would have received based on gains, he is reborn in the Dung Hell, which is completely devoid of anything pleasant). (4) Due to vaṇṇa-macchariya, in every life throughout saṃsāra, the two types of vaṇṇa—physical appearance and reputation—will not even exist in name for that person. That person with vaṇṇa-macchariya will only be ugly in the lives throughout saṃsāra. In a physical form that is deformed and ugly, usually, good reputations such as virtue (sīla) cannot find a footing. Even the qualities that should find a footing do not appear or increase in that person's continuum, like an arrow shot in the night. (5) Due to dhamma-macchariya, one is likely to be reborn in the Kukkula-niraya (Hot Ash Hell). (From Abhi-A. 1, pages 405-6).

Envy (issā) arises with the wealth of others as its object; stinginess (macchariya) arises with one's own wealth as its object. Because their objects are different in this way, envy and stinginess cannot occur together.

In the world, the formation of grudges, the use of force, and acts of hostility between one another occur because of these two evil fetters of envy and stinginess. These two fetters of envy and stinginess can only be completely eradicated by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga).
118:
As long as these two fetters of envy and stinginess have not been completely eradicated by the Path of Stream-entry, even though devas and humans may desire to be free from grudges and so on, they cannot be free from the formation of grudges and must live in suffering and exhaustion. Therefore, to the question of Sakka, King of Devas, "Why is it that many devas and humans, while wishing to live happily without suffering and free from grudges, etc., are not free from grudges and live only in suffering and exhaustion?" the Blessed One replied, "Because of the two bonds of the fetters of envy and stinginess."

When the Blessed One replied in this way, Sakka, King of Devas, joyfully accepted the Blessed One's teaching:

"O Blessed One of great glory... it is just as You have said. O Blessed One who is skilled in speaking good words... it is just as You have said. Because of hearing the Blessed One's answer, I have overcome doubt in this problem; my uncertainty has vanished."

Thus ended the first question and answer.
