## (2) The Second Question and Answer

In this way, after Sakka, King of Devas, had joyfully accepted the Blessed One's teaching, he asked the Blessed One again:

"Venerable Sir, what state is the foundational cause (nidāna),
119:
the cause of increase (samudaya), the cause of manifestation (jāti), and the cause of origin (pabhava) for envy and stinginess? (=The main point of the question is: Because of what state do envy and stinginess arise?) When what state exists do envy and stinginess occur, and when what state does not exist do envy and stinginess not occur?"

When Sakka asked in this way, the Blessed One replied:

"O Sakka, Lord of Devas, the two states of envy and stinginess have dear beings and formations (saṅkhāra), and undear beings and formations as their foundational cause (nidāna), their cause of increase (samudaya), their cause of manifestation (jāti), and their cause of origin (pabhava). (=The main point of the answer is: Envy and stinginess arise because of these two: dear beings and formations, and undear beings and formations.) When dear beings and formations, and undear beings and formations exist, envy and stinginess occur; when dear beings and formations, and undear beings and formations do not exist, envy and stinginess do not occur."

(In this context: If it is a being or formation that one owns and possesses, even if that object is an unpleasant one, because of the perverted arising of defilements, it becomes a dear and pleasant being or formation. If it is a being or formation owned and possessed by another, even if that object is a good and noble one, for a person who is angry...)
120:
120
...for him, they become beings and formations that are not dear and not pleasing. This is an excerpt from the Mahāvagga Commentary and Sub-commentary.

Avarice (macchariya) has its root in beings and formations that are dear and pleasing. (This means that avarice arises because of beings and formations that are dear and pleasing). Envy (issā) has its root in beings and formations that are not dear and not pleasing. (This means that envy arises because of beings and formations that are not dear and not pleasing).

Alternatively, both envy and avarice have their basic root in both beings and formations that are dear and pleasing, and those that are not dear and not pleasing. (This means that both envy and avarice arise because of both dear and pleasing beings and formations, as well as those that are not dear and not pleasing).

To elaborate: For a monk, there are beings who are dear, desired, and cherished, such as his pupils (saddhivihārika). For a layperson, there are beings who are dear, desired, and cherished, such as children, elephants, and horses. If they do not see these dear beings even for a moment, it becomes unbearable. When that monk or layperson sees another monk or layperson obtaining such dear beings—like pupils, children, elephants, or horses—he feels envy, resentment, and jealousy (issā). If others ask for those dear beings, saying, "We have some work for your pupil, child, elephant, or horse; please give them to us for a moment," he acts with stinginess, saying, "I cannot give them; my dear pupil, child, elephant, or horse will be tired or lazy," and so on. This is how avarice (macchariya) arises. This is how both envy and avarice arise because of dear beings.

For monks, there are types of dear requisites such as alms-bowls and robes. For laypeople, there are types of dear utensils and ornaments. These are dear
121:
121
pleasing formations (saṅkhāra). When that monk or layperson sees another monk or layperson possessing such dear requisites or utensils, he gives rise to envy (issā), thinking, "It would be good if this monk or person did not have such requisites or utensils." If others ask to borrow those dear requisites or utensils for a moment, they act with stinginess (macchariya), saying, "Even we do not dare to use these things because we cherish them so much; we cannot give them to you." This is how both envy and avarice arise because of dear formations.

Furthermore, whether it be a monk or a layperson, after obtaining beings they do not love or like—such as bad pupils, bad sons, bad daughters, bad elephants, or bad horses—or formations such as bad alms-bowls, robes, requisites, utensils, or ornaments, even though these beings and formations are not dear and not pleasing to them, because of the perverted nature of the defilements, greed associated with self-exaltation (attukkaṃsana-lobha) arises, thinking, "Who else but me can obtain such beings and formations?" Based on that greed, he feels envy (issā) that others might obtain such beings and formations. (This type of envy is directed towards the prosperity others might obtain). Alternatively, after the greed of self-exaltation arises as mentioned before, based on that same greed, when he sees others possessing such unpleasant (apiya) beings and formations, he feels envy, intolerance, and resentment, thinking, "It would be good if that person did not have such beings and formations." (This type of envy is directed towards the prosperity others already have or are obtaining. This latter method is not shown here as it is already mentioned in the Commentary; only the former method is expressed through circumlocution (vaṅkavutti). That
122:
122
circumlocution from the Commentary has been written clearly in this text based on the Sub-commentary and the Mūla-ṭīkā of the Atthasālinī). When others ask for those unpleasant beings and formations, he cannot give them even for a moment and acts with stinginess (macchariya). This is how envy and avarice arise because of beings and formations that are not dear and not pleasing.

The second question and answer is concluded.

## (3) The Third Question and Answer
Then, Sakka, the King of Devas, having delighted in and welcomed the Buddha's words as before, asked the Buddha again:

"Venerable Sir, what is the source (nidāna), what is the origin (samudaya), what is the birth (jāti), what is the cause (pabhava) of 'dear and not-dear' (piya-appiya)? (=The main point is: because of what do love and hatred arise?) When what exists do 'dear and not-dear' come to be, and when what does not exist do they not come to be?"

Thus he asked the question again. When Sakka had thus asked, the Buddha replied:

"Sakka, King of Devas, 'dear and not-dear' have desire (chanda-taṇhā) as their source, desire as their origin, desire as their birth, and desire as their cause. (The main point of the answer is that love and hatred arise because of desire).
123:
123
When desire exists, 'dear and not-dear' come to be; when desire does not exist, 'dear and not-dear' do not come to be."

(In this context: There are two kinds of desire (chanda): (1) the desire to see, hear, smell, taste, touch, or know various objects, which is the mental factor of desire as the 'desire to act' (kattukamyatā-chanda); and (2) the desire that craves and delights in various objects, which is the 'desire of craving' (taṇhā-chanda), the mental factor of greed (lobha). Here, 'desire of craving' (taṇhā-chanda), which takes the mental factor of greed as its essence, is intended.

## Five Kinds of Craving-Desire
That craving-desire (taṇhā-chanda) is of five kinds: (1) desire as seeking (pariyesana-chanda), which is the craving-desire that occurs when searching for sensual objects; (2) desire as obtaining (paṭilābha-chanda), which is the craving-desire that occurs because of obtaining sensual objects; (3) desire as consuming (paribhoga-chanda), which is the craving-desire that occurs when using or consuming those sensual objects; (4) desire as hoarding (sannidhi-chanda), which is the craving-desire that occurs when storing, keeping, and guarding those obtained sensual objects for security; and (5) desire as relinquishing (vissajjana-chanda), which is the craving-desire that occurs when giving or distributing to royal servants, thinking, "These servants will guard and protect me," thus giving with the expectation of benefits such as protection in the present life.

Regarding the statement "Love and hatred arise because of craving-desire," it means that if one obtains the sensual objects one desires, love (piya) arises. If one does not obtain them despite desiring them, hatred (appiya) arises).

The third question and answer is concluded.

## (4) The Fourth Question and Answer
Then, Sakka, the King of Devas, having delighted in and welcomed the Buddha's words as before, asked the Buddha again:

"Venerable Sir, what is the source (nidāna), what is the origin (samudaya), what is the birth (jāti), what is the cause (pabhava) of desire (taṇhā-chanda)? (=The main point is: because of what does craving-desire arise?) When what exists does desire come to be, and when what does not exist does desire not come to be?"

Thus he asked the question again. When Sakka, the King of Devas, had thus asked, the Buddha replied:

"Sakka, King of Devas, desire has decisive thought (vinicchaya-vitakka) as its source, decisive thought as its origin, decisive thought as its birth, and decisive thought as its cause. (=The main point of the answer is that craving-desire arises because of decisive thought). When decisive thought exists, desire comes to be; when decisive thought does not exist, desire does not come to be."
125:
125
(In this context: Regarding 'thought' (vitakka), one should not take it as casual thought, but only as thought that thinks decisively. The Buddha taught that there are two kinds of decision: (1) decision through craving (taṇhā-vinicchaya), which consists of the 108 modes of craving; and (2) decision through wrong view (diṭṭhi-vinicchaya), which consists of the 62 types of wrong views. Through such taṇhā-vinicchaya, one cannot decisively conclude what is good or bad, or what is pleasing or not. Indeed, the same object may be a desirable object (iṭṭha-vatthu) for one person and an undesirable object (aniṭṭha-vatthu) for another. For example, earthworms are highly desirable objects for kings of the border regions (paccantajanapada), but for kings of the middle country (majjhimadesa), they are extremely loathsome and undesirable objects. Similarly, venison is a highly desirable object for kings of the middle country, but for kings of the border regions, it is an undesirable object. However, the ability to decisively determine regarding an obtained object that has not been decided by taṇhā-vinicchaya—thinking, "This much will be for the sense of sight, this much for sound, smell, taste, and touch; this much will be for me, and let this much be for others; I will keep this much and give this much to others"—is due to decisive thought (vitakka-vinicchaya).

The point is: one decisively determines with thought (vitakka) regarding the objects one has obtained as mentioned. Then, one delights in and craves those decided objects with craving-desire (taṇhā-chanda). Therefore, the Buddha answered, "Craving-desire arises because of decisive thought (vinicchaya-vitakka)."

The fourth question and answer is concluded.

## (5) The Fifth Question and Answer
Then, Sakka, the king of devas, having rejoiced and welcomed the words of the Blessed One as before, asked the Blessed One a further question:
"Venerable Sir, what is the source (nidāna), what is the origin (samudaya), what is the birth (jāti), and what is the cause (pabhava) of decisive thinking (vinicchaya-vitakka)? (The intended meaning is: Due to what does decisive thinking arise?) When what exists does decisive thinking arise, and when what does not exist does decisive thinking not arise?"
When Sakka, the king of devas, had asked thus, the Blessed One replied:
"O Sakka, king of devas, decisive thinking (vinicchaya-vitakka) has the group of perceptions associated with proliferation (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā) as its source, its origin, its birth, and its cause. (The intended meaning is: Decisive thinking arises because of the group of perceptions associated with proliferation.) When the group of perceptions associated with proliferation exists, decisive thinking arises; when the group of perceptions associated with proliferation does not exist, decisive thinking does not arise."
Thus did the Blessed One answer.
127:
(In this context: The three factors—craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi)—are called 'papañca' because they proliferate in saṃsāra; or because they clearly manifest a person as 'one who is greedy, one who is conceited, or one who has wrong views'; or because they lead to states of intoxication and heedlessness. Here, craving-proliferation (taṇhā-papañca) is intended. The perceptions (saññā) associated with that papañca are of six groups according to the objects: visual perception, auditory perception, olfactory perception, etc. Because of this group of perceptions, decisive thinking (vinicchaya-vitakka) arises.)
The Fifth Question and Answer is finished.

## (6-7-8) The Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Questions and Answers
Then, Sakka, the king of devas, having rejoiced and welcomed the words of the Blessed One as before, asked the Blessed One a further question:
"Venerable Sir, how should a monk practice so that he follows the path leading to the cessation of the group of perceptions associated with proliferation (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā) and reaches Nibbāna, the state of that cessation?"
## Meditation on Feelings (Vedanā-kammaṭṭhāna)
"(a) O Sakka, king of devas, I declare that joy (somanassa) is of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued.
128:
(b) O Sakka, king of devas, I declare that grief (domanassa) is also of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued.
(c) O Sakka, king of devas, I declare that equanimity (upekkhā) is also of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued. (In brief).
(a) O Sakka, king of devas, I have said this: 'Joy (somanassa) is of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued.' For what reason did I say this? Among these two kinds of joy, if one knows of a certain joy: 'While I pursue this joy, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease,' then such joy is not to be pursued. (The meaning is: The kind of joy where unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease is called 'joy not to be pursued'; the same logic applies to the next two types of feeling).
Among these two kinds of joy, if one knows of a certain joy: 'While I pursue this joy, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase,' then such joy is to be pursued. (The meaning is: The kind of joy where unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase...
129:
...is called 'joy to be pursued'; the same logic applies to grief and equanimity hereafter).
Among those joys to be pursued (somanassa-vedanā), there is joy that is accompanied by initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) (called savitakka savicāra somanassa). There is also joy that is without initial thought and without sustained thought (called avitakka avicāra somanassa). Of these two, the joy that is without initial thought and without sustained thought (avitakka avicāra somanassa) is superior and more sublime. (Detailed explanation of section a).
O Sakka, king of devas, it was for this reason that I said: 'Joy (somanassa) is of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued.' (Conclusion of section a).
(b) O Sakka, king of devas, I have said this: 'Grief (domanassa) is of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued.' For what reason did I say this? Among these two kinds of grief, if one knows of a certain grief: 'While I pursue this grief, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states...

...decrease,' then such grief is not to be pursued.
Among these two kinds of grief, if one knows of a certain grief: 'While I pursue this grief, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase,' then such grief is to be pursued.
Among those griefs to be pursued (domanassa-vedanā), there is grief that is accompanied by initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) (called savitakka savicāra domanassa). There is also grief that is without initial thought and without sustained thought (called avitakka avicāra domanassa). Of these two, the grief that is without initial thought and without sustained thought (avitakka avicāra domanassa) is superior and more sublime. (Detailed explanation of section b).
O Sakka, king of devas, it was for this reason that I said: 'Grief (domanassa) is of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued.' (Conclusion of section b).
(c) O Sakka, king of devas, I have said this: 'Equanimity (upekkhā) is of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued.'
131:
For what reason did I say this? Among these two kinds of equanimity, if one knows of a certain equanimity: 'While I pursue this equanimity, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease,' then such equanimity is not to be pursued.
Among these two kinds of equanimity, if one knows of a certain equanimity: 'While I pursue this equanimity, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase,' then such equanimity is to be pursued.
Among those equanimities to be pursued (upekkhā-vedanā), there is equanimity that is accompanied by initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) (called savitakka savicāra upekkhā). There is also equanimity that is without initial thought and without sustained thought (called avitakka avicāra upekkhā). Of these two, the equanimity that is without initial thought and without sustained thought (avitakka avicāra) is superior and more sublime. (Detailed explanation of section c).
O Sakka, king of devas, it was for this reason that I said: 'Equanimity (upekkhā) is of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued.' (Conclusion of section c).
132:
O Sakka, king of devas, a monk who practices in this way is said to be practicing the path that leads to the cessation of the group of perceptions associated with proliferation (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā) and to Nibbāna, the state of that cessation."
Thus the Blessed One taught by analyzing the meditation on feelings (vedanā-kammaṭṭhāna). When the Blessed One had thus answered the question, Sakka, the king of devas, joyfully accepted the Blessed One's teaching, saying:
"It is so, O Blessed One! It is so, O Sugata! Having heard the Blessed One's answer, I have overcome my doubt; my uncertainty has vanished."
(Here, I shall further present a special note from the Commentary:
In this current question, Sakka asked about the practice leading to Nibbāna (using the method of personification - puggalādhiṭṭhāna). The Blessed One answered using the three types of feelings (meditation on feelings) (using the method of phenomena - dhammādhiṭṭhāna). In this answer, because three points were given—meditation on joy, meditation on grief, and meditation on equanimity—the Commentary counts these as three questions: the question on joy (somanassa-pañha), the question on grief (domanassa-pañha), and the question on equanimity (upekkhā-pañha).
Here, Sakka asked: "How should a monk practice so that he is said to be practicing the path leading to Nibbāna?"...)
133:
133
The Buddha did not answer by saying, "A monk practicing in such a way is said to be practicing the path leading to Nibbāna." Instead, he replied, "Sakka, I declare that joy (somanassa-vedanā) is of two kinds: that which is to be pursued and that which is not to be pursued," and so forth. To those unskilled in the Buddha's method of teaching the Dhamma, this might seem as if the answer is different from the question. Therefore, for their sake, the Commentary presents the challenger's doubt as follows:

"In this sixth question, did the Buddha answer what was asked by Sakka, or what was not asked? Is there a connection (anusandhi) in the speech, or is there no connection? (Alternatively) Is the Buddha's answer consistent with Sakka's inquiry, or is it inconsistent?"

The answer is: In this question, Sakka asked about the practice leading to Nibbāna using the person-centric method (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), focusing on the person who practices. Among the many practices leading to Nibbāna, the Buddha wished to teach the meditation on mentality (nāma-kammaṭṭhāna) starting with the phenomenon of feeling (vedanā), in accordance with Sakka's disposition (ajjhāsaya). Therefore, he began the teaching by taking up the three kinds of feelings. Thus, because the Buddha answered the "practice leading to Nibbāna" asked by Sakka by teaching the path of mentality-meditation starting with the three feelings, the Buddha's answer is indeed consistent with Sakka's inquiry. (This is the brief answer).

The detailed answer is: For devas, mental phenomena (nāma) are more prominent than material phenomena (rūpa). Among mental phenomena, feeling (vedanā) is particularly prominent. This is because for devas, the physical body known as the karaja-kāya—
134:
134
—is many times more delicate and subtle than that of humans. Because it is produced by superior wholesome kamma, and because the digestive fire (kammaja-tejo) is very strong, being able to digest even the extremely heavy, sweet, and subtle divine ambrosia (sudhā). Because the physical body (karaja-kāya) is so delicate and subtle, and because the digestive fire is so strong, they cannot survive if they miss even a single meal. If they do not consume a single meal's worth of divine ambrosia, intense painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) arises, and their physical bodies crumble and perish like a lump of butter placed on a red-hot stone.

Considering this point, painful feeling is very prominent in the continuity of devas. Likewise, pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) which arises without interruption in superior and excellent sense objects, and neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) which is peaceful and sublime, are also very prominent. Therefore, for Sakka's sake, the Buddha encouraged and taught the meditation on the three feelings: somanassa-vedanā, domanassa-vedanā, and upekkhā-vedanā.

To expand further—the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) is of two kinds: 1. Materiality-meditation (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), which involves grasping material phenomena and practicing insight (vipassanā) by focusing on materiality; 2. Mentality-meditation (nāma-kammaṭṭhāna), which involves grasping mental phenomena and practicing insight by focusing on mentality. Between these two, the Buddha (generally) teaches materiality-meditation by explaining the meditation on the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna) in detail to those beings (veneyya-satta) for whom materiality is prominent, using either brief or detailed methods of reflection. To those for whom mentality is prominent, he teaches mentality-meditation. When teaching mentality-meditation, he first mentions the materiality which is the basis for that mentality before teaching it. (Thus, when teaching mentality-meditation to Sakka—
135:
135
—he first partially explained materiality-meditation and only then taught mentality-meditation in detail. In the Pali text, however, it should be understood that only the teaching on mentality-meditation is recorded in the sequence of the discourse).

Since mental phenomena are prominent for devas, he began the teaching with the three feelings as a form of mentality-meditation. To expand further—in the context of mentality-meditation, the initial practice of reflection is of three types: 1. Reflection by way of contact (phassa), 2. Reflection by way of feeling (vedanā), and 3. Reflection by way of consciousness (citta). (This classification applies only to the beginning of the practice and study. After starting the practice and gaining mastery over mental phenomena, the work of comprehension knowledge (sammasana-ñāṇa)—which reflects on all things as impermanent, suffering, and non-self—encompasses all phenomena).

To expand further: (1) For some individuals, after materiality has been grasped either briefly or in detail, the mental phenomenon of contact (phassa), which occurs by touching the object and is the first to fall upon that object of materiality-meditation, becomes prominent. (2) For some, the mental phenomenon of feeling (vedanā), which occurs by experiencing the flavor of that object, becomes prominent. (3) For some, consciousness (viññāṇa), which knows the object distinctly, becomes prominent.

## Comprehending the Five Factors Beginning with Contact
Among these three types of individuals, (1) the person for whom the mental phenomenon of contact is prominent in their knowledge (should not grasp only that single prominent phenomenon of contact, but rather) should grasp with knowledge the group of five factors beginning with contact (phassa-pañcamaka)—namely contact, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness—reflecting: "Oh, it is not just contact that occurs in this object of materiality-meditation; along with that contact, there is also feeling which thoroughly experiences the flavor of the object. There is also perception (saññā) which marks the object. There is also volition (cetanā) which coordinates the associated phenomena toward the object.
136:
136
There is also consciousness (viññāṇa) which knows the object distinctly. (Or) Indeed, they occur!" Thus, one must grasp with knowledge the group of five factors beginning with contact (counting backward from consciousness, contact is the fifth).

(2) The person for whom the mental phenomenon of feeling is prominent in their knowledge (should not grasp only that single prominent phenomenon of feeling, but rather) should grasp with knowledge the five factors beginning with contact, reflecting: "Oh, it is not just feeling that occurs in this object of materiality-meditation; along with that feeling, there is also contact which touches the object. There is also perception which marks it. There is also volition which coordinates it. There is also consciousness which knows the object distinctly. (Or) Indeed, they occur!"

(3) The person for whom the mental phenomenon of consciousness is prominent in their knowledge (should not grasp only that single prominent phenomenon of consciousness, but rather) should grasp with knowledge the five factors beginning with contact, reflecting: "Oh, it is not just consciousness that occurs in the object of materiality-meditation; along with that consciousness, there is also contact which touches the object. There is also feeling which experiences it. There is also perception which marks it. There is also volition which coordinates it. (Or) Indeed, they occur!"

Having thus grasped and studied the five factors beginning with contact, the noble yogi further investigates: "On what do these five factors beginning with contact depend?" Upon such investigation, they clearly see: "These five factors beginning with contact depend on this physical body (karaja-kāya) called the base (vatthu)." This physical body called the base is, in its ultimate sense, only primary materiality (bhūta-rūpa) and derived materiality (upādā-rūpa). Thus, between these two—the five factors beginning with contact which are the dependents, and the physical body called the base which is the support—the yogi clearly perceives with knowledge:
137:
137
"The physical body which is the support is indeed materiality (rūpa); the group of five factors beginning with contact which are the dependents is indeed mentality (nāma)." Thus, only mentality and materiality appear clearly to the knowledge. Among these two, materiality is the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha), and mentality is the four [mental] aggregates; thus, there are only the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha). Truly, there is no aggregate apart from mentality and materiality, and there is no mentality and materiality apart from the five aggregates.

That noble yogi again reflects: "What is the cause of these five aggregates?" Upon such reflection, they see according to reality: "These five aggregates have ignorance (avijjā), craving (taṇhā), kamma, etc., as their cause. (Or) These five aggregates arise because of ignorance, craving, kamma, and so forth." Thereafter, that noble yogi, having thoroughly grasped with knowledge mentality and materiality along with their causes, realizes: "This continuity of aggregates is indeed only cause and effect. Apart from cause and effect, there is no other person or being; it is merely a heap of conditioned formations (saṅkhāra)." Then, by the power of those grasped mentality and materiality along with their causes, the yogi applies the three characteristics and lives contemplating repeatedly as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, according to the stages of insight knowledge. (By this passage, powerful insight (balava-vipassanā) is shown).

The noble yogi who has reached such powerful insight continues to strive in the work of insight with a longing for the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, thinking, "I shall attain the Path and Fruition this very day; I shall attain the Path and Fruition this very day." On a day suitable for attaining the Path and Fruition, having obtained the four suitable factors (sappāya)—suitable weather, suitable person, suitable food, and hearing the suitable Dhamma—while sitting in a single session with legs crossed, the yogi brings their insight work to its climax (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) and becomes established in the fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala).

In this way, for the person for whom contact is prominent, the person for whom feeling is prominent, and the person for whom consciousness is prominent—these individuals—
138:
For three types of individuals, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) leading up to the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) has already been taught by the Buddha.

In this present Sakkapañha Sutta, however, when the Buddha taught the meditation on mental phenomena (nāma-kammaṭṭhāna), he did so by focusing on the three types of feelings (vedanā). Indeed, for the assembly of devas led by Sakka, if the meditation on mental phenomena were taught by focusing on contact (phassa) or consciousness (viññāṇa), it would not be clear (as it is with the meditation on feeling). It would appear only as darkness. Since the arising of feelings is clear to the devas, the meditation on mental phenomena can only become clear if it is taught by focusing on feeling.

To elaborate: the manner in which pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) and painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) arise is very distinct. When pleasant feeling arises, it disturbs, overwhelms, pervades, and flows through the entire body, just like being made to eat butter that has been refined a hundred times, or being anointed with oil that has been cooked a hundred times, or like quenching heat with a thousand jars of clear water; it arises making the one experiencing the feeling utter words of joy: "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!"

When painful feeling arises, it also disturbs, overwhelms, pervades, and flows through the entire body, just like thrusting a red-hot iron ball into the body, or pouring molten iron into the body, or throwing a large bundle of firewood into a forest filled with dry grass and dry trees; it arises making the one experiencing the feeling cry out in delirium: "Oh, what suffering! Oh, what suffering!" Thus, the manner in which these two feelings—pleasant feeling and painful feeling—arise is very distinct.

Equanimous feeling (upekkhā-vedanā), however, is difficult to demonstrate; it is as if it were covered by darkness. That equanimous feeling becomes clear to a meditator (yogī) who notes it by way of inference (anumāna), thinking: "When pleasant and painful feelings are absent, that neutral, indistinct, and indifferent mode of experiencing, which is neither comfort nor discomfort, is called equanimous feeling." For example, as if on a stone slab...
139:
...a hunter closely following the footprints of a deer running across a stone slab sees the footprints going up on this side of the slab and the footprints descending on that side. Although he does not see the footprints in the middle of the stone slab, he notes the path the deer took across the middle of the slab by way of inference, thinking: "It ascended from this spot and descended from that spot; therefore, it must have traveled across the middle of the stone slab by this path."

In the same way, the arising of pleasant feeling is distinct, like the footprints at the place of ascent on the stone slab. The arising of painful feeling is distinct, like the footprints at the place of descent from the stone slab. Just as one notes by inference, "It ascended from here and descended from there, and thus traveled in the middle in this way," equanimous feeling becomes clear to a meditator who notes and grasps it by way of inference, thinking: "When pleasant and painful feelings are absent, that neutral, indistinct, and indifferent mode of experiencing, which is neither comfort nor discomfort, is called equanimous feeling."

In this manner, the Buddha first taught the meditation on material phenomena (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) to Sakka, and then taught the meditation on mental phenomena (nāma-kammaṭṭhāna) by analyzing it through the power of the three feelings. This method of first teaching rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna and then teaching nāma-kammaṭṭhāna through the power of the three feelings according to the disposition of the individuals to be guided (veneyya) is not found in the Sakkapañha Sutta alone. It is taught in the same way in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, the Mahāvedalla Sutta, the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, the Āneñjasappāya Sutta, and throughout the entire Vedanā Saṃyutta. Thus, in many Suttas, the Buddha first taught rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna and then analyzed and taught nāma-kammaṭṭhāna through the power of the three feelings. Just as in those various Suttas, in this Sakkapañha Sutta as well, the Buddha first taught rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna and then analyzed and taught nāma-kammaṭṭhāna through the power of the three feelings, according to the inclination (āsaya) of the individuals to be guided, namely the assembly of devas led by Sakka.
140:
"In this Sakkapañha Sutta, the meditation on material phenomena (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) has been condensed as merely the object of feeling; therefore, it may be that it was not included in the Pāḷi text." This is a specific explanation in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). This explanation in the Commentary has a profound and subtle meaning. Therefore, the intended meaning of the Teacher of the Commentary should be understood as follows:

Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "To the assembly of devas led by Sakka, according to their inclination, the Buddha first taught rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna and then analyzed and taught nāma-kammaṭṭhāna through the power of the three feelings," an objector might ask: "How did the Buddha teach rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna in this Sakkapañha Sutta? It is not found in the Pāḷi text; it is not apparent."

The answer is: The assembly of devas led by Sakka are individuals to be guided (veneyya) for whom mental phenomena (nāma) are prominent. Among those mental phenomena, they are individuals for whom the phenomenon of feeling (vedanā) is particularly prominent. The Buddha usually teaches material phenomena (rūpa)—that is, rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna—only briefly to make it known first for beings for whom mental phenomena are prominent, and then teaches mental phenomena—that is, nāma-kammaṭṭhāna—in detail. Thus, in this present Sakkapañha Sutta, because the assembly of devas led by Sakka are individuals for whom mental phenomena are prominent, the Buddha, when teaching them rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna first, did not teach it in detail. He taught only those material phenomena that are the objects of feeling, condensing them to the simplest level, saying, "This group of phenomena are material phenomena," and then taught the three feelings related to nāma-kammaṭṭhāna in detail. Thus, in this Sakkapañha Sutta, because the Buddha taught the section on rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna by condensing it to only the material phenomena that are the objects of feeling, "it remains unrecorded in the Pāḷi text." This is the intended meaning.

Now, regarding the previously mentioned sections (a), (b), and (c) which show the meditation on the three feelings in detail:
141:
I shall now write and present the special instructions and explanations from the Commentary and Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā), condensing them as much as possible:

Section (a): Regarding the first heading, "Joy (to be avoided) through which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease," this refers to joy based on sensual pleasures = somanassa-vedanā. This somanassa-vedanā is called household-based joy (gehasita-somanassa-vedanā). (The group of six sensual objects—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and mental objects—are called 'geha' because they are like the great house of craving for sensuality (kāma-taṇhā). The joy (somanassa-vedanā) that arises in association with craving based on that group of sensual objects called 'geha' is known as gehasita-somanassa-vedanā). If one indulges in this gehasita-somanassa-vedanā (i.e., causes it to arise repeatedly), unwholesome states will increase and wholesome states will decrease day by day. Therefore, the Buddha taught that this gehasita-somanassa-vedanā should not be indulged in = it is not fit to be indulged in.

Section (a): Regarding the second heading, "Joy (to be pursued) through which unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase," this refers to joy based on renunciation (nekkhammasita-somanassa-vedanā). Here, all wholesome states, including ordination, the first jhāna, Nibbāna, and Vipassanā, are called 'nekkhamma' because they are free from the bonds of the household and from opposing states such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). To make it clearer: the practices of one who intends to escape the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa-dukkha), who goes to the monks to ordain, who ordains after arriving, who remains firm in the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) after ordaining, who practices that virtue purely, who undertakes and practices the dhutaṅga observances, who prepares and develops the preliminary work for kasina meditation, who attains the first rūpāvacara jhāna etc. through such development, and who develops Vipassanā based on that jhāna—these are called 'nekkhamma'. The joy arising based on such nekkhamma practices...
142:
...is called renunciation-based joy (nekkhammasita-somanassa-vedanā). If one pursues this nekkhammasita-somanassa-vedanā (i.e., causes it to arise repeatedly), unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase. Therefore, the Buddha taught that this nekkhammasita-somanassa-vedanā should be pursued = it is fit to be pursued.

(Note: The gehasita-somanassa-vedanā that should not be pursued is the somanassa-vedanā that arises in association with craving and greed (taṇhā-lobha) which delights in the six desirable objects appearing at the six sense-doors; it has six varieties according to the different objects. The nekkhammasita-somanassa-vedanā that should be pursued is the somanassa-vedanā associated with the mental states that develop the practices of renunciation, taking the six desirable objects as a basis, from the time of going to the monks for ordination until the attainment of the mundane and supramundane first, second, and third jhānas; it also has six varieties according to the different objects. Therefore, in the field of scriptural Dhamma, the terms "six types of gehasita-somanassa-vedanā" and "six types of nekkhammasita-somanassa-vedanā" are widely used. In the descriptions of domanassa-vedanā and upekkhā-vedanā that follow, one should be skilled in Dhamma terminology to understand that they are also called six gehasita and six nekkhammasita types according to the six objects.)

Section (a): In the third heading, it is meant that "Among the nekkhammasita-somanassa-vedanā to be pursued, there are two types: (1) Savitakka-savicāra somanassa = joy accompanied by initial and sustained thought (the nekkhammasita-somanassa that arises from the time of going to the monks for ordination until the attainment of the first jhāna), and (2) Avitakka-avicāra somanassa = joy unaccompanied by initial and sustained thought (the nekkhammasita-somanassa present in the second and third jhānas). Between these, the second type, avitakka-avicāra somanassa-vedanā, is superior and more noble."

What did the Buddha teach with this group of statements in the third heading? He taught the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) of two monks. To elaborate: (a) One monk [attained] savitakka-savicāra somanassa-vedanā...
143:
143
(= Pleasant feeling of the sense-sphere and pleasant feeling of the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere). When practicing insight meditation (vipassanā) on these, one contemplates: "Upon what does this pleasant feeling (somanassa-vedanā) depend?" While contemplating thus, one clearly perceives that it depends on this physical body (karajakāya), the individual self. Thereafter, by continuing to develop and practice the Dhamma according to the method described starting from page 135, one gradually established oneself in the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala).

(b) Another monk, while practicing insight meditation on pleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra somanassa-vedanā, which is the pleasant feeling associated with the second and third jhānas of the fine-material sphere), established himself in the fruition of Arahantship according to the aforementioned method. Among the pleasant feelings attended to, grasped, and contemplated by these two monks, the pleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought (the object) attended to by the second monk is superior to the pleasant feeling with initial and sustained thought (the object) attended to by the first monk. In the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that views these two feelings as impermanent, suffering, and non-self through insight, the insight without initial and sustained thought (the subjective observer) in the second monk's continuum is superior to the insight with initial and sustained thought (the subjective observer) in the first monk's continuum. The fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti) of pleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought attained by the second monk is far superior to the fruition attainment of pleasant feeling with initial and sustained thought attained by the first monk. Therefore, the Buddha taught: "Pleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought is superior."

This is the special note regarding section (a).

Regarding section (b): The "unpleasant feeling (domanassa-vedanā) that should not be cultivated, which causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline," mentioned in the first heading, refers to household-related grief (gehasita-domanassa). Household-related grief is the mental distress of one who, through the six doors of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, does not obtain the desired and longed-for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and
144:
144
mental objects—this collection of six types of sensual objects—and laments, "I do not obtain these sensual things," or the mental distress of one who, when the already obtained collection of sensual objects perishes and disappears, laments, "The collection of sensual things I possessed has perished and disappeared." This is the unpleasant feeling (domanassa-vedanā) that arises depending on (taking as object) the collection of sensual objects.

If one cultivates this household-related grief (gehasita-domanassa) (i.e., allows it to occur repeatedly), unwholesome states alone increase, and wholesome states decline day by day. Therefore, the Buddha taught that this household-related grief should not be cultivated.

Regarding section (b): The "unpleasant feeling (domanassa-vedanā) that should be cultivated, which causes unwholesome states to decline and wholesome states to increase," mentioned in the second heading, refers to renunciation-related grief (nekkhammasita-domanassa). Renunciation-related grief arises in the continuum of a noble practitioner (yogī) who exerts effort in the work of renunciation, such as going to monks to enter the monkhood as previously mentioned, or in the practice of insight meditation (vipassanā-bhāvanā) and recollection (anussati-bhāvanā). After clearly perceiving the impermanent nature, the nature of change, and the nature of cessation of the six objects—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and mental objects—when one sees with insight-wisdom according to reality that all these objects of the past and the present are indeed impermanent, indeed suffering, and indeed subject to change and destruction, there arises a subtle greed called longing (pihā) for the supramundane noble fruitions (lokuttara-ariya-phala) which take Nibbāna as their object, the state of liberation from the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha) of these six objects and the two-fold mind and matter.

(In this context: Regarding the statement "there arises a subtle greed called longing (pihā) for the supramundane noble fruitions," it does not mean that
145:
145
unwholesome greed (lobha) definitely and directly takes the noble fruition (ariya-phala) as its object. Indeed, let alone unwholesome states like greed, even wholesome states dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta kusala) cannot directly take supramundane states as an object at all. In truth, they long for the supramundane noble fruitions by way of inference (anumāna), either by hearing from others that "the noble fruitions possess such and such extraordinary power and attributes," or by standing upon the wisdom that notes the mode and nature of supramundane states which become apparent through the power of studying the scriptures and developing tranquility and insight meditation. To state it directly, the concepts (paññatti) of the very noble and subtle states of jhāna, path (magga), fruition (phala), and Nibbāna also possess a noble and subtle nature like those states themselves. Thus, worldlings (puthujjana) like us cannot directly objectify and long for the jhāna, path, fruition, and Nibbāna that we have not yet attained or known; we can only long for them by way of inference, taking as objects the concepts of jhāna, path, fruition, and Nibbāna (very subtle concepts). Therefore, in this instance, when worldling practitioners long for the supramundane noble fruitions known through learning (suta-pariyatti) by way of inference, taking only the concept "supramundane noble fruition" as an object, the arising of that subtle greed called longing (pihā) is described as "there arises a subtle greed called longing (pihā) for the supramundane noble fruitions." Understand this subtly.)

After such subtle greed called longing (pihā) for the supramundane noble fruitions has arisen, when a practitioner who, while striving and exerting effort in the practice of insight meditation without rest to attain those supramundane noble fruitions, is unable to reach the noble fruition, and repeatedly worries, "Alas, though I have striven and exerted effort in insight meditation without rest for this fortnight, this month, this whole year, I am unable to reach the noble fruition I long for," the unpleasant feeling (domanassa-vedanā) that occurs is called renunciation-related grief (nekkhammasita-domanassa). If one cultivates this renunciation-related grief (i.e., allows it to occur repeatedly), one gains the strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya) from that grief, unwholesome states decline, and wholesome states increase day by day. Therefore, the Buddha taught that this renunciation-related grief should be cultivated.
146:
146
Regarding section (b): In the third heading, concerning "unpleasant feeling with initial and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra domanassa) and unpleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra domanassa)," although unpleasant feeling (domanassa-vedanā) is strictly of only one type—with initial and sustained thought—the Buddha taught them as distinct categories based on the practitioner's perception: household-related grief as unpleasant feeling with initial and sustained thought, and renunciation-related grief as unpleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought.

To elaborate further: In this Dispensation, a practitioner develops insight meditation, striving to attain the paths and fruitions, using access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) or the first jhāna, etc., as a basis. If he is unable to attain those paths and fruitions, unpleasant feelings (domanassa) may arise. When such unpleasant feelings arise, the base states of access concentration or the first jhāna, etc., are called "unpleasant feeling" by way of metaphorical designation of the result (phalūpacāra). However, that practitioner, even though such unpleasant feeling arises, does not slacken his energy and continues to strive in the work of insight meditation until he attains the paths and fruitions. Those attained paths and fruitions are called "unpleasant feeling" by way of metaphorical designation of the cause (kāraṇūpacāra).

The practitioner, having noted the states with initial and sustained thought and the states without initial and sustained thought—which are the causes of unpleasant feeling—as "unpleasant feeling with initial and sustained thought" and "unpleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought," contemplates: "When shall I be able to practice insight meditation on the states of unpleasant feeling with initial and sustained thought and the states of unpleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought?" Furthermore, noting the fruitions obtained based on the states of unpleasant feeling with initial and sustained thought as "fruition attainment of unpleasant feeling with initial and sustained thought," and the fruitions obtained based on the states of unpleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought as "fruition attainment of unpleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought," he considers: "When shall I be able to produce the fruition attainment of unpleasant feeling with initial and sustained thought and the fruition attainment of unpleasant feeling without initial and sustained thought?" Having so considered, he gradually undertakes and practices the three types of practice: the three-month practice (temāsika-paṭipadā),
147:
147
the six-month practice (chamāsika-paṭipadā), and the nine-month practice (navamāsika-paṭipadā).

First, having undertaken the three-month practice (temāsika-paṭipadā), during the first month, he exerts effort in insight meditation for one watch out of the three watches of the night and allows himself two watches for sleep. During the middle month, he exerts effort in insight meditation for two watches and allows himself one watch for sleep. During the final month, he no longer allows any sleep at all, but practices the monk's Dhamma throughout all three watches of the night, sustaining himself only through walking and sitting. If he attains the fruition of Arahantship by this method, it is well. If he cannot attain the fruition of Arahantship by this method, he does not slacken his effort and undertakes the six-month practice (chamāsika-paṭipadā) again.

Having undertaken the six-month practice (chamāsika-paṭipadā) (dividing the time into three parts: the first two months, the middle two months, and the final two months), he practices as before. If he still cannot attain the fruition of Arahantship, he does not slacken his effort and undertakes the nine-month practice (navamāsika-paṭipadā) again.

Having undertaken the nine-month practice (navamāsika-paṭipadā) (dividing the time into three parts: the first three months, the middle three months, and the final three months), during the first three months, he exerts effort in insight meditation for one watch out of the three watches of the night and allows himself two watches for sleep. During the middle three months, he exerts effort in insight meditation for two watches and allows himself only one watch for sleep. During the final three months, he no longer allows any sleep at all, but practices the monk's Dhamma throughout all three watches of the night, sustaining the body only through walking and sitting. In the continuum of a practitioner who, even after practicing in this way, is unable to attain the fruition of Arahantship, when he reflects, "Alas, I am not worthy to invite the Purification Pavāraṇā (visuddhi-pavāraṇā) together with my fellow monks," as occurred in the continuum of the Venerable Mahāsīva Thera who resided in the village-boundary cave (gāmanta-pabbhāra)—
148:
Unhappiness = the feeling of mental grief (domanassa-vedanā) arises; a stream of tears flows continuously.

## The Story of the Elder Mahāsīva

In the island of Sri Lanka, there was a great elder named Mahāsīva who resided there teaching the scriptures to eighteen great groups—eighteen assemblies of monks. Established in the advice and instruction of this great elder, thirty thousand monks had already attained the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). At that time, among those thirty thousand Arahant disciples, one Arahant reflected: "In my own continuity, the qualities such as virtue (sīla) are indeed incomparably great. What are the qualities such as virtue of my teacher, the great elder Mahāsīva?" When he reflected thus, he saw that the teacher was still a worldling (puthujjana). He thought, "Alas! Our teacher, the great elder Mahāsīva, is only a refuge and reliance for others, but he is unable to be a refuge for himself. I shall give advice and instruction to our teacher, the great elder Mahāsīva."

Having planned this, he traveled through the air by means of his meditative absorption (jhāna), descended near the monastery, and approached his teacher, the great elder Mahāsīva, who was sitting in his place of daytime rest. After paying respects and performing his duties, he sat in a suitable place.

Then, the teacher and disciple engaged in conversation as follows:

(Teacher)
"Friend Piṇḍapātika (alms-food collector), for what reason have you come?" (The elders of old used to affectionately call disciples who practiced insight meditation 'Friend Piṇḍapātika').

(Disciple)
"I have come to learn a single verse of appreciation (anumodanā), venerable sir."

(Teacher)
"There will be no opportunity, friend."
149:
(Disciple)
"Venerable sir, when you are standing in the pavilion circle, considering 'Where shall I go for alms today?', let me ask then."

(Teacher)
"At that place, other monks ask questions, friend."

(Disciple)
"Let me ask on the road while going for alms, venerable sir."

(Teacher)
"At that place too, other monks ask questions, friend."

(Disciple)
"Let me ask at the place where you double the robe to wear it, where you wrap it, at the place where you take the bowl out of its bag (before the alms round), or when you have finished the alms round in the village and are drinking rice gruel in the refectory (within the city or village), venerable sir."

(Teacher)
"At those places too, elders who ask about the meaning of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) dispel their doubts, friend."

(Disciple)
"Let me ask when you have finished the alms round and are departing from the city or village, venerable sir."

(Teacher)
"At that time too, other monks ask questions, friend."

(Disciple)
"Let me ask on the way back from the village to the monastery after the alms round, venerable sir."

(Teacher)
"At that time too, other monks ask questions, friend."

(Disciple)
"Let me ask when you have reached the monastery and the business of eating is finished in the refectory, venerable sir... (etc.). Let me ask when you are washing your feet at the place of daytime rest, venerable sir. Let me ask when you are washing your face, venerable sir."
150:
(Teacher)
"At those times too, other monks ask questions, friend. From that time until the dawn of the next day, other various monks ask questions without any interval, friend."

(Disciple)
"When the dawn has broken and you have used the tooth-stick and are going to wash your face, let me ask then, venerable sir."

(Teacher)
"At that time too, other monks ask questions (there is no opportunity), friend."

(Disciple)
"When you have finished washing your face and are returning to the monastery, let me ask then, venerable sir."

(Teacher)
"At that time too, other monks ask questions (there is no opportunity), friend."

(Disciple)
"When you have entered the monastery and are sitting down, let me ask then, venerable sir."

(Teacher)
"At that time too, other monks ask questions (there is no opportunity), friend."

(Disciple)
"Venerable sir, truly, for those like you who, after washing the face and entering the monastery, sit cross-legged, changing positions three or four times to gain bodily warmth and then practice meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), there should be an available time. If it is like this, will you not even have time to die? Venerable sir, you are like a leaning board (nissayaphalaka); you are only a support for others, but you cannot be a support for yourself. I truly have no desire to learn a verse of appreciation from you, venerable sir."

Having spoken these words of warning, the Arahant disciple flew up into the air and departed.
151:
## The Great Elder Mahāsīva Goes Forth into the Forest

The great elder Mahāsīva reflected correctly, thinking: "For this monk, there is no task to be done regarding the scriptures (pariyatti). Indeed, this monk came with the intention of being like a goad (ankusa) to admonish and subdue me." He then thought, "Now is not yet the time to go to the forest. I shall go to the forest at the time of dawn." Having placed his bowl and robes nearby in readiness, he taught the scriptures throughout the day and during the first and middle watches of the night. When the dawn watch arrived, as another monk finished learning a Pali text and departed, he took his prepared bowl and robes and left together with that monk (in the guise of a student monk).

The disciple monks who were sitting ready to learn thought only, "Our teacher, the great elder Mahāsīva, has gone out for a moment for some personal business." The monk who was learning the Pali text and left with him also thought, "He is just a fellow monk" (he did not know it was his teacher Mahāsīva).

The great elder Mahāsīva reflected, "How could the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) be difficult to attain for a person like me? In just two or three days, I shall return after practicing and striving to reach the fruit of Arahantship." Without informing his disciples, he went to the forest on the thirteenth day of the waxing moon of Āsāḷha. He went to the Gāmantapabbhāra (Village-border Cave), and while practicing meditation on the walkway, he was unable to attain the fruit of Arahantship on that day. When the full moon Uposatha day arrived, he thought, "I came thinking I would attain Arahantship in two or three days, but I have not been able to. (Thinking of the three months of the rains retreat as if they were only three days), I will know it by the full moon of Assayuja = the Great Pavāraṇā day." Encouraging himself thus, he spent the rains retreat (vassa) in that very monastery, but although he practiced the monk's Dhamma with great effort, he was still unable to attain the fruit of Arahantship.
152:
When the full moon of Assayuja, the Great Pavāraṇā day, arrived, he reflected: "Alas! I came thinking I would attain it in two or three days. Even in the three months of the rains retreat, I have not been able to attain the fruit of Arahantship. My fellow monks are performing the Visuddhipavāraṇā (the invitation of Arahants whose taints are exhausted)." When he reflected thus, a stream of tears flowed continuously from the great elder.

Then he thought, "For me, who lives alternating between the four postures of lying, sitting, standing, and walking on a couch, the paths and fruits will not arise. As long as I have not reached the fruit of Arahantship, I shall no longer stretch my back on a couch, nor shall I wash my feet." Having thought this, he leaned the couch against a suitable place. Another rains retreat arrived, but the great elder Mahāsīva was still unable to attain the fruit of Arahantship. For twenty-nine years (according to the number of Pavāraṇā ceremonies performed), his tears flowed continuously.

The village children used to stitch the cracks in the great elder Mahāsīva's feet with thorns. When they joked and mocked one another, they would say, "May our feet also be cracked like the feet of the venerable great elder Mahāsīva."

## Becoming an Arahant through a Goddess's Warning

On the Great Pavāraṇā day of the full moon of Assayuja in the thirtieth year, the great elder Mahāsīva stood leaning against a support board and reflected: "It has now been thirty years that I have practiced the monk's Dhamma, yet I have not been able to reach the fruit of Arahantship. The paths and fruits will certainly not arise for me in this life. Alas! I no longer have the opportunity to perform the Visuddhipavāraṇā together with my fellow
153:
venerable monks." Even as he was reflecting thus, the feeling of mental grief (domanassa-vedanā) arose repeatedly within the elder. A stream of tears flowed continuously.

At that time, a goddess stood not far from the elder, weeping loudly. When the elder asked, "Who is it that comes and weeps in this place?", the goddess replied, "Venerable sir, I am a goddess." When the elder asked again, "Why are you weeping so loudly?", the goddess spoke mockingly, "Venerable sir, I am weeping with the thought, 'Will a person who weeps be able to cause the paths and fruits to arise?' (imitating you), I too shall weep so as to bring about the first path and fruit, and the second path and fruit."

Then the great elder thought, "O Mahāsīva! Even young goddesses are mocking you as an equal. Is it proper for you to be mocked by young goddesses in this way? (Is it not shameful?)" Feeling a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he made his right effort (sammapadhāna) more intense than before. Practicing insight meditation with great striving, he attained the fruit of Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). (This means he became an Arahant who has attained the analytical insights).

The great elder Mahāsīva thought, "Well then, now I shall stretch my back and rest for a moment just to balance the postures." After cleaning the sleeping place in the monastery, he spread out the couch he had leaned up, set out drinking and washing water, and thought, "Only now shall I wash my feet, which have not been washed for thirty years." He then sat down on the board at the head of the stairs.
154:
## Sakka Coming to Wash the Feet

The disciples of the Great Elder also reflected: "It has been exactly thirty years since our teacher, the Great Elder Mahāsīva, departed to diligently practice the Dhamma of a recluse. Is he now able to attain the noble Paths and Fruits, or is he not?" Upon reflecting, they realized, "He has now reached the Fruit of Arahantship and is sitting on a wooden plank at the head of the stairs to wash his feet." They thought, "It is not fitting that our teacher should wash his own feet while disciples like us are present. I shall wash them! I shall wash them!" Thus, all thirty thousand Arahant disciples traveled through the air, paid respectful homage, and requested, "Venerable Sir, let us wash your feet."

Then, the Great Elder Mahāsīva said to his disciples, "Friends, it has been exactly thirty years that I have left my feet unwashed. I myself shall wash them."

Sakka, the king of devas, also reflected and thought, "My master, the Great Elder Mahāsīva, has reached the Fruit of Arahantship and has not given permission to the thirty thousand Arahant disciples who came to wash his feet. It is not fitting that my master should wash his own feet while a supporter and attendant like me is present. I myself shall go and wash them." Having made this decision, he appeared near the thirty thousand monks together with Queen Sujā. Sakka, placing the Asura maiden Sujā in front, requested, "Please move aside, Venerable Sirs; a woman (mātugāma) has come." Having obtained permission, he approached and paid homage to the Great Elder Mahāsīva, squatted in front of him, and requested, "Please let me wash your feet, Venerable Sir."
155:
The Great Elder Mahāsīva said, "Sakka, the donor of the Kosiya lineage, it has been exactly thirty years that I have left my feet unwashed. For devas, the natural scent of humans is repulsive. Even to devas standing a hundred yojanas away, it is like a rotting carcass tied around the neck. I myself shall wash them."

Sakka, the king of devas, replied, "Venerable Sir, the natural body scent you mentioned is not apparent to us. The fragrant scent of your virtue (sīla) surpasses the six heavens of the sense sphere and reaches up to the Highest Plane (Bhavagga). Venerable Sir, there is no other fragrance superior to the scent of virtue. Because of the scent of your virtue, we could not stay away and had to come." He then firmly grasped the Elder's ankle with his left hand and rubbed, washed, and cleansed the sole of the foot with his right hand. At that time, the Elder's feet became tender and rosy like those of a young child. Thus, after washing the Elder's feet, Sakka paid respectful homage and returned to the celestial realm. This is the story of the Great Elder Mahāsīva.

In this way, it should be well understood that the Buddha taught the unhappiness (domanassa-vedanā) that arises in a yogi monk who reflects, "Alas, I have no opportunity to perform the Visuddhi Pavāraṇā together with my fellow practitioners of the holy life." Based on the power of that yogi's perception, the Buddha taught the objects of insight—such as access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), the first jhāna, etc., as well as insight (vipassanā), the Path (magga), and the Fruit (phala)—as 'domanassa with initial and sustained thought' or 'domanassa without initial and sustained thought' (by way of metonymy of cause and metonymy of effect as appropriate).

In that context, when a yogi monk develops insight by contemplating impermanence, suffering, and non-self in the access concentration or the first jhāna, which is called 'domanassa with initial and sustained thought' (savitakka-savicāra domanassa):
156:
If he investigates where this group of domanassa states depends, he realizes that it depends on this physical body (karajakāya) called the 'basis' (vatthu). In this manner, he gradually establishes himself in the Fruit of Arahantship according to the method described in the section on the 'Five Factors Beginning with Contact' (Phassapañcamaka) on page 136.

When another yogi monk develops insight by contemplating impermanence, suffering, and non-self in the group of states such as the second jhāna, third jhāna, etc., which is called 'domanassa without initial and sustained thought' (avitakka-avicāra domanassa), he establishes himself in the Fruit of Arahantship according to the method previously described.

While those two yogi monks were practicing diligently to reach the Fruit of Arahantship, among the states called domanassa (which were the objects of their insight) that they attended to, domanassa without initial and sustained thought is superior and more noble than domanassa with initial and sustained thought. The insight (vipassanā) on domanassa without initial and sustained thought is also superior and more noble than the insight on domanassa with initial and sustained thought. The fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti) of domanassa without initial and sustained thought is also superior and more noble than the fruition attainment of domanassa with initial and sustained thought. Therefore, the Blessed One taught (on page 130): "Between those two types of unhappiness, the unhappiness that is without initial thought (vitakka) and without sustained thought (vicāra) is superior and more noble."

This is the special note on section (B).

Section (C): The "equanimity (upekkhā) that should not be cultivated, which increases unwholesome states and decreases wholesome states" mentioned in the first heading refers to household-based equanimity (gehasita-upekkhā). Household-based equanimity is the equanimity that arises when the six desirable and longed-for objects—visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects—appear at the six sense doors. Like a fly caught in a lump of molasses (palm sugar), one cannot overcome the defilements regarding these objects.
157:
It is the equanimity that arises by depending on and taking as an object the group of sensual things (kāmavatthu) that one is attached to and entangled with, making it difficult to loosen or separate from those objects (as one views them as pleasant). If one cultivates this gehasita-upekkhā (i.e., allows it to occur repeatedly), unwholesome states only increase, and wholesome states decrease day by day. Therefore, the Blessed One taught that this gehasita-upekkhā should not be cultivated.

Section (C): The "equanimity (upekkhā) that should be cultivated, which decreases unwholesome states and increases wholesome states" mentioned in the second heading refers to renunciation-based equanimity (nekkhamma-sita-upekkhā). Renunciation-based equanimity is the equanimity associated with knowledge that arises in a yogi who truly contemplates the six types of objects—pleasant or unpleasant (iṭṭha/aniṭṭha), desired or undesired—as they appear at the six sense doors. He does not allow greed (lobha) to arise toward pleasant objects, nor does he allow hatred (dosa) to arise toward unpleasant objects, nor does he allow delusion (moha)—which is an unbalanced way of looking—to arise toward both types of objects. Instead, he contemplates all six types of objects as they appear, realizing, "These are indeed a group of states that are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change (anicca, dukkha, vipariṇāma)." (Alternatively) Tatramajjhattatā-upekkhā, which has the nature of feeling, is also called upekkhā in this context. (This means that both equanimity as feeling, vedanā-upekkhā, and equanimity as mental neutrality toward various pleasant and unpleasant objects, tatramajjhattatā-upekkhā, should be taken as 'upekkhā' here.)

Thus, if one cultivates the six types of renunciation-based equanimity—which occur from the moment of going to the monks to ordain, during the practice of insight, during the development of mindfulness (anussati), and upon attaining the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas—unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase.
158:
Therefore, the Blessed One taught that this renunciation-based equanimity (nekkhamma-sita-upekkhā) should be cultivated.

Section (C): In the third heading, it means: "There are two types of renunciation-based equanimity that should be cultivated: (1) equanimity with initial and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra upekkhā), which arises from the time of going to the monks to ordain, during the development of insight and mindfulness, and upon attaining the first jhāna; and (2) equanimity without initial and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra upekkhā), which arises upon attaining the second jhāna and so forth. Between these, the second type, avitakka-avicāra upekkhā, is superior and more noble."

By this statement, the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship by two types of yogi monks is taught. To elaborate: (A) When one monk practices insight on equanimity with initial and sustained thought and investigates, "On what does this equanimity depend?", he clearly perceives, "It depends on the individual existence of the five aggregates, namely the physical body (karajakāya)." In this manner, as he continues to develop and practice the Dhamma according to the method described starting from page 135, he gradually establishes himself in the Fruit of Arahantship.

(B) When another monk practices insight on equanimity without initial and sustained thought (the equanimity associated with the second, third, and fourth jhānas), he establishes himself in the Fruit of Arahantship according to the method previously described.

Among the types of equanimity attended to, grasped, and contemplated by those two monks, the equanimity without initial and sustained thought (which is the object) attended to by the second monk is superior and more noble than the equanimity with initial and sustained thought (which is the object) attended to by the first monk. Also, among the states of consciousness that practice insight on those two types of equanimity as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, the insight on equanimity without initial and sustained thought (as the subject/observer) in the second monk is superior and more noble than the insight on equanimity with initial and sustained thought (as the subject/observer) in the first monk. The equanimity with initial and sustained thought obtained by the first monk...
159:
The attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) of equanimity without initial and sustained application (avitakka-avicāra upekkhā) achieved by the second monk is far more noble than the previous phalasamāpatti. Therefore, the Buddha preached: "Equanimity without initial and sustained application is superior."
This is the special point to be noted regarding the phrase (c).

## Sakka's Attainment of Stream-entry
The Buddha, following the aforementioned method, preached in detail, culminating in the fruition of Arahatship (arahattaphala) regarding all three types of feelings: pleasant feeling (somanassa-vedanā), painful feeling (domanassa-vedanā), and neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā).
"O Sakka, Lord of Devas, a monk who practices in this way is said to be practicing the path leading to the cessation of the group of perceptions associated with conceptual proliferation (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā) that tends to expand the cycle of rebirth, and thus reaches Nibbāna, the state of cessation."
Thus, the Buddha concluded the noble discourse. Sakka, the King of Devas, attained the fruition of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

## The Exalted Intent of the Buddhas
Indeed, the intent of the Buddhas is never inferior; it is always an exalted and noble intent. Whether preaching the Dhamma to one being or many, they always preach by highlighting the practice that culminates in the fruition of Arahatship. However, the beings who are to be disciplined (veneyya) remain established in their own respective sufficing conditions (upanissaya)—the past meritorious deeds that lead to the attainment of the paths and fruits. Thus, some become Stream-winners (sotāpanna), some Once-returners (sakadāgāmi), some Non-returners (anāgāmi), and some become Arahats.
For example, the Buddha is like a Great King, and the beings to be disciplined are like young princes. To make it clearer: when a Great King partakes in a royal feast, he takes a morsel of rice according to his usual portion and feeds it to the princes.
160:
Just as the princes eat only as much of the rice morsel fed by the King as their mouths can hold, so too does the Great King, the Buddha, out of His great and exalted intent, feed the morsel of Dhamma-teaching, culminating in Arahatship, to the princes who are the beings to be disciplined. These beings, however, can only accept and consume as much of the great morsel of Dhamma-teaching as the capacity of their 'mouths'—their sufficing conditions (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits—allows. Some can only accept and consume the fruition of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), some the fruition of Once-returning, some the fruition of Non-returning, and some consume up to the fruition of Arahatship. Sakka became a Stream-winner according to the capacity of his own sufficing conditions.

## Sakka Obtaining a New Life as Sakka
After Sakka became a noble disciple (ariya) as a Stream-winner, he passed away (cuti) right in the presence of the Buddha and was immediately reborn into a new life as the King of Devas (Sakka).
It should be specially noted that for devas who pass away, there is no need to carry and cremate the physical body (as is done for humans). When these devas pass away, their physical bodies vanish and disappear like the flame of a lamp being extinguished. Indeed, for humans who are conceived in a mother's womb, when they pass away, the karma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) ceases first. About seventeen thought-moments after the death-consciousness (cuti-citta), where the final karma-born matter ceases, the mind-born matter (cittaja-rūpa) also ceases. Nutriment-born matter (āhāraraja-rūpa) also ceases within a short time as it no longer receives support from external essence (bahidda-ojā). However, the succession of temperature-born matter (utuja-rūpa) continues to exist for a long time. For devas, it is not so. Indeed, since devas are beings of spontaneous birth (upapāta), as soon as the karma-born matter ceases, the remaining mind-born, temperature-born, and nutriment-born matters cease simultaneously with that karma-born matter.
161:
Therefore, when those devas pass away, there is absolutely no need to carry and cremate the physical body as is done for humans in the human world. At the very place where they pass away, they vanish and cease entirely, like a lamp flame being extinguished.
In this matter, the fact that a large corpse of temperature-born matter (utuja-rūpa) remains for a long time after humans pass away, while no such corpse remains for devas, can be understood and satisfied only by deeply contemplating the way the human body and the deva body are formed at the time of rebirth. The points for contemplation are:
(I) For humans, at the moment of conception, the house of life is built starting from about three atoms of karma-born material clusters (kammaja-rūpa-kalāpa), namely: the body-decad (kāya-dasaka), the sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka), and the base-decad (vatthu-dasaka). Whenever the karma-born clusters, mind-born clusters, temperature-born clusters, and nutriment-born clusters (which arise at their respective times) reach their static phase (ṭhī-khaṇa), the temperature (tejo-dhātu) within each of those clusters produces a new temperature-born cluster. Thus, as the body grows over time, the temperature-born clusters take up space first throughout the body, acting like the permanent resident (āvāsika) of the house. The remaining karma-born, mind-born, and nutriment-born matters act like visiting guests (āgantuku). Therefore, for humans and other womb-born beings, when they pass away, although the guest-like karma-born, mind-born, and nutriment-born matters vanish, the resident-like temperature-born matters continue in succession for a long time, leaving behind a large corpse of temperature-born matter that remains for a long duration.
(II) For devas, however, at the very moment of spontaneous rebirth (upapāta), the karma-born clusters that they are to receive arise simultaneously and extensively to form a physical body as large as three gāvutas. These karma-born matters occupy the entire body and act as the permanent resident (āvāsika) of the house. The remaining mind-born,
162:
temperature-born, and nutriment-born matters arise as visiting guests (āgantuku) occupying the spaces between the resident karma-born matters.
