Therefore, when devas and Brahmas of spontaneous birth pass away, as soon as the resident-like karma-born matters cease and vanish, the guest-like mind-born, temperature-born, and nutriment-born matters also cease and vanish along with those karma-born matters. Thus, when devas and Brahmas pass away, no large corpse of temperature-born matter remains. This point is a profound principle. One will be able to accept this point with satisfaction only after carefully studying the process of material and mental thought-processes (rūpa-vīthi and nāma-vīthi). This is a special point to be noted.
As for Sakka, since he was reborn as a new Sakka at the very spot where he was listening to the Dhamma inside the Indasāla Cave after passing away, the other devas did not know that Sakka had passed away and been reborn as Sakka again. Only Sakka himself, because he was the one who passed away, and the Buddha, because He is the possessor of Omniscient Wisdom (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), knew that Sakka had passed away and was reborn as Sakka again.
The answers to the sixth, seventh, and eighth questions are completed.
**********
## (9, 10, 11) The Ninth, Tenth, and Eleventh Questions and Answers
Thereafter, Sakka, the King of Devas, thought: "The Buddha has answered my questions regarding pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings. In these three sections, He has preached only the Supramundane Path and Fruit (lokuttara magga-phala), which is attained and produced through the practice that is its cause, just like extracting pure clarified butter from a mass of butter. This Supramundane Path and Fruit cannot be obtained by flying into the sky like a bird.
163:
There is a preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipatti) that must be followed and practiced as the cause for obtaining this group of Supramundane Path and Fruit. I shall now ask about the preliminary practice that must be followed to obtain the higher state of an Arahat (arahattaphala)." Having thus considered, and wishing to ask about the preliminary practice for becoming an Arahat, he asked another question:
"Venerable Sir, how does a monk practice the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla)?"
When Sakka, the King of Devas, asked thus, the Buddha replied:
"O Sakka, Lord of Devas, (I) I declare that bodily conduct (kāya-samācāra) is of two kinds: that which should be pursued and that which should not be pursued.
O Sakka, Lord of Devas, (II) I declare that verbal conduct (vacī-samācāra) is of two kinds: that which should be pursued and that which should not be pursued.
O Sakka, Lord of Devas, (III) I declare that seeking (pariyesanā) is of two kinds: that which should be pursued and that which should not be pursued.
(I) O Sakka, Lord of Devas, I have said: 'I declare that bodily conduct (kāya-samācāra) is of two kinds: that which should be pursued and that which should not be pursued.' For what reason did I say this? Regarding those two kinds of bodily conduct, if one knows of a certain bodily conduct: 'By pursuing this bodily conduct, unwholesome states increase in me and wholesome states decrease,' then such bodily conduct should not be pursued. (This means that the kind of bodily conduct where unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease is called 'bodily conduct not to be pursued.' The same principle should be understood for the following two categories.)
164:
Regarding those two kinds of bodily conduct, if one knows of a certain bodily conduct: 'By pursuing this bodily conduct, unwholesome states decrease in me and wholesome states increase,' then such bodily conduct should be pursued. (This means that the kind of bodily conduct where unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase is called 'bodily conduct to be pursued.' The same principle should be understood for the following two categories.)
O Sakka, Lord of Devas, it is for this reason that I said: 'I declare that bodily conduct (kāya-samācāra) is of two kinds: that which should be pursued and that which should not be pursued.'
(II) O Sakka, Lord of Devas, I have said: 'I declare that verbal conduct (vacī-samācāra) is of two kinds: that which should be pursued and that which should not be pursued.'
165:
I have spoken thus. For what reason did I speak these words? Regarding those two kinds of verbal conduct (vacīsamācāra): if one knows of a certain verbal conduct, 'While I follow this verbal conduct, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,' then such verbal conduct should not be followed.

Regarding those two kinds of verbal conduct: if one knows of a certain verbal conduct, 'While I follow this verbal conduct, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,' then such verbal conduct should be followed.

Sakka, Lord of Devas, it was for this reason that I spoke these words: 'I declare that verbal conduct is of two kinds: that which is to be followed and that which is not to be followed.'

(III) Sakka, Lord of Devas, I have spoken these words: 'I declare that seeking (pariyesanā) is of two kinds: that which is to be followed and that which is not to be followed.' For what reason did I speak these words? Regarding those two kinds of seeking: if one knows of a certain seeking, 'While I follow this seeking, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,' then such seeking should not be followed.

Regarding those two kinds of seeking: if one knows of a certain seeking, 'While I follow this seeking, unwholesome states decline and
166:
wholesome states increase,' then such seeking should be followed.

Sakka, Lord of Devas, it was for this reason that I spoke these words: 'I declare that seeking is of two kinds: that which is to be followed and that which is not to be followed.'

Sakka, Lord of Devas, a monk who practices in this way is said to practice the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhasamvara-sīla)."

Thus the Blessed One answered the question. When the Blessed One had answered the question in this way, Sakka, Lord of Devas, was satisfied and delighted with the Dhamma of the Blessed One, saying:

"It is so, O Blessed One, it is so! It is so, O Sugata, it is so! Having heard the Blessed One's answer, my doubt is now overcome, and my uncertainty has vanished."

(A special note to be observed here: In the subsequent sixth, seventh, and eighth questions, when Sakka asked about the practice leading to Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the group of mental proliferations (papañcasaññā), the Blessed One taught by dividing the three kinds of feelings (vedanā)—which are the foundation for those mental proliferations and the practice leading to Nibbāna—into two categories: those to be followed (sevitabba) and those not to be followed (asevitabba). In that teaching, those feelings that are not to be
167:
followed are not the practice leading to Nibbāna; only the feelings to be followed are the practice leading to Nibbāna. Thus, although it might seem to a questioner who does not understand the Buddha's intention that the group of feelings not to be followed should not be taught—since they are not the practice leading to Nibbāna—the Buddha taught both. This was done according to the inclination of Sakka, the questioner, because only by abandoning the feelings not to be followed (states of defilement or saṅkilesa) can the feelings to be followed (states of purification or vodāna) be fully realized. Therefore, to enable the abandoning of the group of defiled feelings and the fulfillment of the practice of purified feelings, He taught both the feelings to be followed and those not to be followed.

Similarly, in this current question regarding the restraint of the Pātimokkha, although the groups of bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and seeking that are not to be followed are not themselves the restraint of the Pātimokkha, only by abandoning these three types of conduct can the wholesome groups of bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and seeking be fully realized. Therefore, to enable the abandoning of these three types of defiled conduct and the fulfillment of the practice of these three types of purified conduct, the Blessed One taught the pairs of bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and seeking—both those to be followed and those not to be followed—according to the inclination of Sakka, the questioner.

The point is: teaching these states in pairs (to be followed and not to be followed) is appropriate to Sakka's inclination. Only when one can avoid the states not to be followed can one successfully fulfill the states to be followed. (If one does not know which group of states is not to be followed, one will not be able to avoid them; if one cannot avoid them, one will not be able to fully practice the states to be followed.) Therefore,
168:
the Blessed One taught and answered in pairs of states to be followed and not to be followed in the previous question, in this current question, and in the upcoming question on the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara).

In the answer to this current question, only the three states—bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and seeking that are to be followed—constitute the restraint of the Pātimokkha. The three states such as bodily conduct not to be followed are not the restraint of the Pātimokkha; they were taught according to Sakka's inclination only to show the group of defiled states (saṅkilesa) that must be abandoned.

If one wishes to speak about the cause of virtue (sīla) consisting of the three states such as bodily conduct to be followed, one should speak in relation to the courses of action (kammapatha) or in relation to the training rules (sikkhāpada) that have been laid down. The manner of speaking is as follows:

(I) Bodily conduct (kāyasamācāra) not to be followed refers to the three types of unwholesome bodily actions: killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), taking what is not given (adinnādāna), and sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra). (This is the explanation by way of kammapatha). Transgressing the training rules laid down by the Blessed One regarding the bodily door is called bodily conduct not to be followed. (This is the explanation by way of sikkhāpada).

Bodily conduct to be followed refers to the three types of wholesome bodily actions: abstinence from killing living beings (pāṇātipāta-virati), abstinence from taking what is not given (adinnādāna-virati), and abstinence from sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra-virati). (This is the explanation by way of kammapatha). Guarding and not transgressing the training rules laid down by the Blessed One regarding the bodily door is called bodily conduct to be followed. (This is the explanation by way of sikkhāpada). (The same applies to the subsequent verbal conduct; one should distinguish the explanation by way of
169:
kammapatha and the explanation by way of sikkhāpada based on the context.)

(II) The four types of verbal misconduct such as false speech (musāvāda), and the transgressions of the training rules laid down by the Blessed One regarding the verbal door, are called verbal conduct (vacīsamācāra) not to be followed. The four types of verbal good conduct such as abstinence from false speech—the four wholesome verbal actions—and the guarding and non-transgression of the training rules laid down by the Blessed One regarding the verbal door, are called verbal conduct to be followed.

(III) Seeking (pariyesanā) is indeed seeking through body and speech. Although seeking is already included when bodily conduct and verbal conduct are mentioned, it is taught separately here to demonstrate virtue with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla), because "that which is called ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla does not occur in the sky, but occurs precisely in those two doors of body and speech." In terms of its ultimate reality, seeking is the very exertion and effort made in the manner of searching for requisites.

(a) Regarding seeking, in the Pāsarāsi Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Pāḷi, it is taught in detail. In brief, when one who is himself subject to rebirth, aging, and death seeks after things that are also subject to rebirth, aging, and death—such as children, wives, male and female slaves, sheep, goats, fowl, pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, donkeys, and inanimate objects like gold and silver—this is called ignoble seeking (anariya-pariyesanā), which is seeking not to be followed (asevitabba).

When one who is himself subject to rebirth, etc., seeing the danger in things subject to rebirth, etc., seeks Nibbāna, which is free from rebirth, etc.,
170:
this is called noble seeking (ariya-pariyesanā), which is seeking to be followed (sevitabba). (The details should be noted from the Pāsarāsi Sutta).

(b) Alternatively: 1. kuhanā (scheming to obtain gains), 2. lapanā (persuading to obtain gains), 3. nemittikatā (hinting to obtain gains), 4. nippesikatā (belittling or pressuring to obtain gains), 5. lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā (pursuing gain with gain)—these five types of seeking, as well as seeking gains in the six improper resorts (agocara)—namely, the houses of harlots, widows, old maids, eunuchs, taverns, or nunneries—and seeking gains through the twenty-one types of improper seeking (anesanā) mentioned previously, are all ignoble seeking (anariya-pariyesanā) and are seeking not to be followed (asevitabba).

Avoiding the five types such as kuhanā, the six improper resorts, and the twenty-one types of improper seeking, and seeking gains in accordance with the Dhamma by going on almsround, is noble seeking (ariya-pariyesanā) and is seeking to be followed (sevitabba).

In this context, bodily conduct, etc., taught as "not to be followed," should not be followed from the very beginning—from the time of seeking weapons or poison for the sake of misconduct like killing, from the time of making the effort, and from the time of going for the sake of that misconduct. Bodily conduct, etc., taught as "to be followed," should be followed from the very beginning. If one is unable to perform it, one should at least arouse the thought, 'I will perform wholesome bodily conduct.' Indeed, even one who merely arouses the thought 'I will do it' regarding a good deed, when the necessary conditions meet, will make a fresh effort in that good deed and be able to reach the summit of the practice.
171:
Alternatively, (I) one should not associate with or practice the kind of bodily conduct (kāyasamācāra) practiced by those like Devadatta, who strive to cause a schism in the Saṅgha and so forth. One should associate with and practice the kind of bodily conduct practiced by elders such as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who, for instance, go to pay respects to the Triple Gem two or three times a day. (II) One should not associate with or practice the kind of verbal conduct (vacīsamācāra) practiced by those like Devadatta, who speak words such as sending assassins and so forth. One should associate with and practice the kind of verbal conduct practiced by elders such as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who speak of the virtues of the Triple Gem and so forth. (III) One should not associate with or practice the kind of pursuit (pariyesanā) practiced by those like Devadatta, who engage in ignoble searches. One should associate with and practice the kind of pursuit practiced by elders such as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who engage only in noble searches.

In this problem of Pātimokkha restraint (pātimokkhasamvara), although the question asked by Sakka, the Lord of Devas, was a single one, the Blessed One's answer came in three parts: bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and pursuit. Therefore, the Great Commentator has counted them as three problems.

With the concluding sentence of the answer to this problem, "A monk who practices thus," the Blessed One explained the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) which is the basis for Arahantship, saying: "Sakka, Lord of Devas... a monk who thus abandons and avoids the three kinds of bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and pursuit that should not be associated with, and practices to fulfill the three kinds of bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and pursuit that should be associated with, is called a monk who practices for the sake of the supreme and noble Pātimokkha restraint virtue (pātimokkhasamvara-sīla)."

The ninth, tenth, and eleventh questions and answers are finished.
172:
## (12) Question and Answer on Indriyasaṃvara

Thus, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, having joyfully accepted the Blessed One's teaching, asked another question of the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, how does a monk practice the virtue of sense restraint (indriyasaṃvara-sīla)?"

When Sakka, the Lord of Devas, had thus asked, the Blessed One replied:

"Sakka, Lord of Devas, I declare that visible forms (rūpārammaṇa) of various kinds cognizable by the eye are of two types: those to be pursued (sevitabba) and those not to be pursued (asevitabba).

Sakka, Lord of Devas, I declare that sounds (saddārammaṇa) of various kinds cognizable by the ear are of two types: those to be pursued and those not to be pursued.

Sakka, Lord of Devas, I declare that smells (gandhārammaṇa) of various kinds cognizable by the nose are of two types: those to be pursued and those not to be pursued.

Sakka, Lord of Devas, I declare that tastes (rasārammaṇa) of various kinds cognizable by the tongue are of two types: those to be pursued and those not to be pursued.

Sakka, Lord of Devas, I declare that tactile objects (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa) of various kinds cognizable by the body are of two types: those to be pursued and..."
173:
"...those not to be pursued.

Sakka, Lord of Devas, I declare that mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) of various kinds, consisting of mind and matter, cognizable by the mind are of two types: those to be pursued and those not to be pursued."

When this brief teaching (uddesa) had been delivered, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, I understand the detailed meaning of this Dhamma which the Blessed One has taught in brief as follows:

Venerable Sir, if, when one pursues a certain kind of visible form cognizable by the eye, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease, such a visible form cognizable by the eye should not be pursued. If, when one pursues a certain kind of visible form cognizable by the eye, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase, such a visible form cognizable by the eye should be pursued.

Venerable Sir, if, when one pursues a certain kind of sound cognizable by the ear (etc.); if, when one pursues a certain kind of smell cognizable by the nose (etc.); if, when one pursues a certain kind of taste cognizable by the tongue (etc.);"
174:
"...if, when one pursues a certain kind of tactile object cognizable by the body (etc.); if, when one pursues a certain kind of mental object consisting of mind and matter cognizable by the mind, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease, such a mental object cognizable by the mind should not be pursued. If, when one pursues a certain kind of mental object consisting of mind and matter cognizable by the mind, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase, such a mental object cognizable by the mind should be pursued.

Venerable Sir, as I understand the detailed meaning of this Dhamma taught in brief by the Blessed One in this way, having heard the Blessed One's brief answer, I have overcome doubt in this matter; my hesitation has vanished."

(A special note here: Since Sakka had already heard the brief and detailed answers to the previous questions regarding joy, grief, equanimity, bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and pursuit, he possessed intuitive wisdom (paṭibhāna-ñāṇa) that clearly understood, 'The detailed answer for this sense restraint should also be like this.' Therefore, as soon as the Blessed One gave the brief teaching (uddesa), Sakka spoke the detailed explanation (niddesa) as shown above.

The Blessed One also remained silent, allowing Sakka the opportunity to speak. To elaborate: the Blessed One does not grant the opportunity to speak to one who wishes to explain but cannot fully articulate the meaning, nor to one who can fully articulate the meaning but does not wish to explain. This Sakka, however, both wished to explain and was capable of fully articulating the meaning. Therefore, the Blessed One granted Sakka the opportunity to explain.)

Regarding visible forms to be pursued and not to be pursued, etc.:"
175:
(1) If defilements (kilesa) such as lust (rāga) arise in the mind of a monk who looks at a certain visible form, that visible form should not be pursued or looked at. If, in the mind of a monk who looks at a certain visible form, the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) arises, or faith (saddhā) arises, or the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) is gained, such a visible form should be pursued and looked at.

(2) If defilements such as lust arise in the mind of a monk who listens to a certain sound, even one with beautiful letters, words, and phrases, such a sound should not be pursued or listened to. If faith arises in the mind of a monk who listens to a certain sound that is based on cause and effect—even if it be the song of a potter's maidservant—or if the knowledge of weariness with saṃsāra (nibbidā-ñāṇa) arises, such a sound should be pursued and listened to.

(3) If defilements such as lust arise in the mind of a monk who smells a certain odor, that odor should not be pursued or smelled. If the perception of foulness and so forth is gained in the mind of a monk who smells a certain odor, such an odor should be pursued and smelled.

(4) If defilements such as lust arise in the mind of a monk who licks or eats a certain taste, such a taste should not be pursued or consumed. If, in the mind of a monk who licks a certain taste, the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā) is gained, or if he is able to reach the Ariya stage by relying on the physical strength produced by that licking and eating, or if the destruction of defilements occurs even while eating—as in the case of Sīva Sāmaṇera, the nephew of Mahāsīva Thera—such a taste should be pursued and consumed. (Regarding this, the story of Sīva Sāmaṇera, the nephew of Mahāsīva Thera, whose defilements were exhausted while eating, is not explained in the Ṭīkā. Although searched for in the Visuddhimagga as much as possible, the story of Sīva Sāmaṇera was not found; only the story of Bhāgineyya Saṅgharakkhita Sāmaṇera, who became an Arahant with the exhaustion of defilements while eating, was found in the Visuddhimagga Commentary, Volume I, Sīlaniddesa, page 43).

(5) If defilements such as lust arise in the mind of a monk who touches a certain tactile object, such a tactile object should not be pursued or touched. If, in the mind of a monk who touches a certain (pursuable) tactile object before his monkly duties are finished, there occurs the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) as in the case of Venerable Sāriputta Thera and others, or if energy (vīriya) is well-aroused, or if it encourages future monks by providing an example to be followed (diṭṭhānu-gati), such a tactile object should be pursued and touched.

A special note: Venerable Sāriputta Thera did not stretch his back on a couch for thirty years. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera was the same. Venerable Mahākassapa Thera did not stretch his back on a couch for one hundred and twenty years. Venerable Anuruddha Thera for fifty years, and Venerable Bhaddiya Thera for thirty years.

## (13) The Questioሗ aሗd Aሗswer oሗ the Variety of Elemeሗts (Aሗekadhātu)

Thus, Sakka, the Kiሗg of Gods, haviሗg joyfully accepted the Buddha's teachiሗg, asked the Buddha aሗother questioሗ:

"Exalted Oሗe, do all recluses aሗd brahmins (samaሑa-brāhmaሑa) have the same teachiሗg, the same practice, the same view, aሗd the same goal?"

(Iሗ this regard: Sakka, haviሗg become aሗ Ariya, ሗow clearly uሗderstaሗds as substaሗceless the diverse teachiሗgs, practices, views, aሗd goals of the various recluses aሗd brahmins he had heard of iሗ the past before he became aሗ Ariya. Agaiሗ, Sakka asked the Buddha:

"Exalted Oሗe, why is it that ሗot all recluses aሗd brahmins have the same teachiሗg, the same practice, the same view, aሗd the same goal?"

The Buddha replied to Sakka:

"Sakka, Lord of Gods, this world of beiሗgs, composed of many diverse beiሗgs, has various meሗtal dispositioሗs (ajjhāsaya-dhātu) aሗd diverse meሗtal iሗcliሗatioሗs (āsaya-dhātu). (This meaሗs that beiሗgs do ሗot have the same meሗtal dispositioሗs aሗd iሗcliሗatioሗs as oሗe aሗother). Iሗ this world of beiሗgs with differiሗg aሗd diverse meሗtal dispositioሗs, beiሗgs cliሗg to whichever dispositioሗ they have; they cliሗg firmly aሗd teሗaciously to that particular dispositioሗ, sayiሗg, 'Oሗly this view of miሗe is true; the views of others are empty.' Therefore, ሗot all recluses aሗd brahmins have the same teachiሗg, the same practice, the same view, aሗd the same goal."

(These beiሗgs do ሗot have the same meሗtal dispositioሗs as oሗe aሗother. If oሗe wishes to go, aሗother wishes to stay; if oሗe wishes to stay, aሗother wishes to sleep. It is very rare iሗ the world to fiሗd two beiሗgs with the same meሗtal dispositioሗ. Wheሗ beiሗgs do ሗot even have the same dispositioሗ regardiሗg physical postures (iriyāpatha), how could they be the same iሗ their views, practices, aሗd teachiሗgs? They are simply differeሗt. Therefore, the esseሗce of the Buddha's aሗswer to this questioሗ is that because beiሗgs have differiሗg meሗtal dispositioሗs, their teachiሗgs, practices, views, aሗd goals are also differeሗt).

## (14) The Questioሗ aሗd Aሗswer oሗ the Absolute Goal (Accaሗtaሗiሑሑhā)

Agaiሗ, Sakka asked the Buddha:

"Exalted Oሗe, do all recluses aሗd brahmins have a refuge that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa? Do they have the cessatioሗ of the yoke (yoga) that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa? Do they practice the true Noble Practice, the Noble Path, for the sake of that which exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa? Do they have a goal that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa?"

(The esseሗce of the questioሗ is: Do all those who claim to be recluses aሗd brahmins iሗ the world attaiሗ the ultimate Nibbāሗa? Are all those teachers of various views really practicers of the true Noble Path to attaiሗ Nibbāሗa?). The Buddha replied to Sakka:

"Sakka, Lord of Gods, ሗot all recluses aሗd brahmins have a refuge that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa. They do ሗot have the cessatioሗ of the yoke that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa. They do ሗot practice the true Noble Practice, the Noble Path, for the sake of that which exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa. They do ሗot have a goal that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa."

(ሗot all those who claim to be recluses aሗd brahmins iሗ the world have the same teachiሗg, virtue, view, aሗd goal because they have differiሗg meሗtal dispositioሗs. Since they differ iሗ these ways,

182
how could they all equally attaiሗ the ultimate Nibbāሗa? They caሗሗot. Therefore, the Buddha's iሗteሗded aሗswer to Sakka is: "Lay devotee Sakka, ሗot all those who claim to be recluses aሗd brahmins equally attaiሗ the ultimate Nibbāሗa; oሗly those who practice the true Noble Path leadiሗg to Nibbāሗa attaiሗ the ultimate Nibbāሗa.")

"Exalted Oሗe, why is it that ሗot all recluses aሗd brahmins have a refuge that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa? Why do they ሗot have the cessatioሗ of the yoke that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa? Why do they ሗot practice the true Noble Practice, the Noble Path, for the sake of that which exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa? Why do they ሗot have a goal that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa?"

They have the cessatioሗ of the yoke that exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa. They are said to practice the true Noble Practice, the Noble Path, for the sake of that which exceeds destructioሗ = the Dhamma of Nibbāሗa.

(This is a matter of questioሗs aሗd aሗswers betweeሗ the Buddha, the supreme Ariya, aሗd Sakka, who is also aሗ Ariya, regardiሗg the attaiሗmeሗt of the ultimate Nibbāሗa, spokeሗ iሗ the Noble usage aሗd Noble laሗguage. Since the Buddha's Dispeሗsatioሗ has the ultimate Nibbāሗa as its fiሗal eሗd, all problems are coሗcluded with the coሗclusioሗ of the questioሗs aሗd aሗswers regardiሗg the ultimate Nibbāሗa.

Wheሗ the Buddha had aሗswered thus, Sakka, the Kiሗg of Gods, with great satisfactioሗ, [accepted] the Buddha's teachiሗg...
184: 184 "It is so, Exalted One, it is so, O Sugata! Having heard the Exalted One's answer, my doubt is gone, and my uncertainty is dispelled." Thus he expressed his appreciation. The fourteenth question and answer are finished. Venerable Sir, the Exalted One has answered for me these questions which I could not even get the opportunity to ask of other recluses and brahmins outside of this Dispensation. The dart of uncertainty and doubt that has resided in my heart for a long time has been pulled out by the Exalted One."
185: 185 Thus he spoke. Then the Exalted One and Sakka, the Lord of Devas, conversed as follows: (The Buddha) "Lord of Devas, do you remember asking these questions to other recluses and brahmins?" (Sakka) "I remember, Venerable Sir." (The Buddha) "Lord of Devas, how did they answer? If it is not a burden to you, please tell me." (Sakka) "Venerable Sir, it is no burden for me to speak in the presence of the Exalted One or one like the Exalted One." (The Buddha) "Then speak, Lord of Devas." (Sakka) "Venerable Sir, I approached those recluses and brahmins whom I considered to be living in secluded forest dwellings and asked them these questions. Those recluses and brahmins, being unable to answer, asked me in return, 'Who is the venerable one?' Being thus questioned, I replied, 'Sirs, I am Sakka, the Lord of Devas.' Then they asked me further, 'Lord of Devas, what deed did you perform to reach this position of Sakka?' I preached the Dhamma to those ascetics and brahmins. They were delighted with just that much, thinking, “We have seen Sakka, the King of Gods, and Sakka, the King of Gods, has answered the questions we asked.” In truth, those ascetics and brahmins became my disciples; I did not become theirs. O Blessed One, I am a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer), a noble disciple of the Blessed One, who is no longer subject to rebirth in the four lower realms, is steadfast, and is destined for the three higher paths.

## Attaining Joy
Then the Blessed One asked Sakka, the King of Gods, “O Sakka, King of Gods, do you remember ever having experienced such joy and gladness before this?” Sakka, the King of Gods, replied, “O Blessed One, I do remember having experienced such joy and gladness before this.” When the Blessed One asked, “O Sakka, King of Gods, how do you remember having experienced such joy and gladness before this?”, Sakka, the King of Gods, said:

“Venerable Sir, in the past, a great war broke out between the Tāvatiṃsa gods and the Asuras. O Blessed One, in that war, the Tāvatiṃsa gods were victorious and the Asuras were defeated. O Blessed One,”
187: 187 "Because of winning that war, a sense of satisfaction and joy arose in me, thinking, 'Now there are two kinds of food—that of the Tāvatiṃsa devas and that of the Asuras—and the Tāvatiṃsa devas alone shall enjoy both.' Venerable Sir, that attainment of satisfaction and joy was of the kind that involves sticks, swords, and weapons. It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna. Venerable Sir, the satisfaction and joy I have gained now from hearing the Dhamma of the Exalted One is of the kind that does not involve sticks, swords, or weapons. It truly leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna." Thus he spoke. Again, the Exalted One asked, "Lord of Devas, seeing what special benefits do you proclaim the attainment of such satisfaction and joy?" Sakka, the Lord of Devas, replied as follows: "Venerable Sir, I see six special benefits and therefore proclaim the attainment of such satisfaction and joy. The six benefits are:"
188: 188 (1) "While staying right here, being a deva, I have gained a renewed life; know this, O Venerable One." O Venerable One, who has extinguished all suffering, I, known as Maghava, while staying in this Indasāla Cave and joyfully listening to the Dhamma that stills sorrow, being the Sakka, Lord of Devas, have obtained a renewed life—a lifespan in Tāvatiṃsa equivalent to thirty-six million human years—to be enjoyed due to another kamma. (By this, Sakka clearly indicates that after passing away from his current life, he has been reborn as Sakka again). O Venerable One, please take note of this. Venerable Sir, seeing this first special benefit, I proclaim the attainment of such satisfaction and joy. (2) "Having passed away from the divine body and left the non-human life, I shall enter a womb unconfused, where my mind finds delight." O Venerable One, when I pass away from this divine body and leave the Tāvatiṃsa lifespan of thirty-six million human years, I shall enter a womb unconfused and mindful, in whatever noble family of kings, brahmins, or householders my mind finds delight.
189: 189 "I shall reach rebirth without suffering. (The phrase 'I shall enter a womb unconfused' indicates that unlike ordinary worldlings who die in confusion and enter a womb without mindfulness, noble disciples die without confusion and enter a womb with mindfulness and clear comprehension. Because noble disciples have a fixed destiny, they are reborn only in good destinations such as the human or deva realms. Among these, if they are reborn in the human realm, they are reborn only in noble families of kings or brahmins; this is what Sakka desires). Venerable Sir, seeing this second special benefit, I proclaim the attainment of such satisfaction and joy. (3) "Delighting in the Dispensation of the One of Unconfused Wisdom, I shall live by the right method, clearly comprehending and mindful." O Venerable One, I, your disciple known as Maghava, delighting in the Dispensation of the Exalted One who possesses unconfused omniscient wisdom, shall live with a firm and balanced posture, being clearly comprehending and possessing ardent mindfulness, living in accordance with the state of an Ariya. Venerable Sir, seeing this third special benefit, I proclaim the attainment of such satisfaction and joy."
190: 190 (4) "As I practice by the right method, if Awakening should occur, I shall live as one who knows; that indeed will be my final birth." O Venerable One, as I practice the Dhamma in accordance with the state of an Ariya, if the higher path of Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi) should arise in me, I shall live with the intention to realize the paths of Non-returner and Arahatship. That human life in which I attain the path of Once-returner will surely be my final human birth. Venerable Sir, seeing this fourth special benefit, I proclaim the attainment of such satisfaction and joy.
191:
(5) Having passed away from the human body, and having abandoned human life,
I shall again become a god, a supreme one in the celestial world.

O Mārisa (the Buddha, the Destroyer of all suffering), I, who am known by the name Maghava, when I pass away from this human existence and abandon this human life, by the support of good merit, I shall become the king of gods, the supreme among all gods in the celestial realm of Tāvatiṃsa.

O Blessed One, seeing this fifth special benefit, I express my praise for attaining such a state of joy and delight.

(6) Those gods of the Akanittha realm are most sublime and glorious.
When my final existence comes to pass, that shall be my residence.

O Mārisa, those noble Brahma gods who dwell in the Akanittha realm (the highest plane of existence) are far superior to other gods and Brahmas in terms of lifespan, wisdom, and numerous other virtues. They possess great retinues. When my final existence arrives, that Akanittha Brahma realm will surely be my dwelling place, O Blessed One.
192:
O Blessed One, seeing this sixth special benefit, I express my praise for attaining such a state of joy and delight.

(In this context, the six special benefits are: (1) Having heard the Dhamma in this Indasāla Cave and becoming a Sotāpanna Ariya, then passing away from this state and becoming the King of Gods again; (2) After passing away from that state as Sakka, being reborn without confusion in a noble family of one's choice in the human world as a Sattakkhattuparama Sotāpanna; (3) While being reborn in such a state, living mindfully and practicing the Dhamma in accordance with being an Ariya; (4) By practicing the Dhamma in this way, attaining the knowledge of the Sakadāgāmi-magga and ending that human life; (5) After passing away from the human life as a Sakadāgāmi Ariya, becoming the King of Gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven once more; (6) After attaining the Anāgāmi-magga in that state as Sakka, and passing away from that life, becoming an Anāgāmi Ariya who goes upstream towards the Akanittha realm (Uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī), passing through the five Suddhāvāsa Brahma realms—Avihā, Atappā, Sudassā, Sudassī, and Akanittha—in succession, and finally becoming an Arahant in the Akanittha realm to end the cycle of rebirth. These are the six special benefits.

According to the sixth special benefit, when this Sakka passes away from his life as an Anāgāmi Ariya Sakka, he will spend one thousand great aeons (mahākappa) in the Avihā realm; after passing from there, two thousand great aeons in the Atappā realm; after passing from there, four thousand great aeons in the Sudassā realm; after passing from there, eight thousand great aeons in the Sudassī realm; and after passing from there, sixteen thousand great aeons in the Akanittha realm. Thus, for a total of thirty-one thousand great aeons, he will enjoy the lifespan and glory of a Brahma. (1) Sakka, the King of Gods, (2) Anāthapiṇḍika, the great merchant, and (3) Visākhā, the great lay devotee—these three noble ones have equal lifespans; there are no other beings delighted in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭābhirata) who share the same portion of happiness as these three.)
193:
O Blessed One, seeing these six special benefits, I express my praise for attaining such states of joy and delight."

After Sakka, the King of Gods, had spoken these words of praise for the joy he felt upon seeing the six special benefits, he further related through six verses how he had previously approached those who claimed to be recluses (samaṇa) and brahmins living in secluded forest dwellings with these questions, but they were unable to answer. Instead, he himself had to teach them the seven virtues that lead to becoming a Sakka (as mentioned previously). Then he said:

I pay homage to the Buddha, the destroyer of the dart of craving,
The peerless person, the Great Hero,
The Buddha who is a kinsman of the Sun.

To the Buddha, who is the destroyer of the dart called craving (taṇhā), having extracted it by the power of His Dhamma teachings; to the Buddha, who has personally and clearly realized the Four Noble Truths and taught them to gods and men; to the peerless and noble person; to the one possessed of great and noble energy (Mahāvīra); to the kinsman of the Sun (Ādiccabandhu), for both the Sun-god and the Buddha are of the Gotama lineage, thus being of the same ancestral line; (or) to the Ādiccabandhu, who is the supramundane father of the famous Sun-god; to that Buddha, the Lord of the World known as the Omniscient Buddha; I, who am known by the name Maghava,
194:
I pay homage with joined palms, O Blessed One.

Whatever homage we used to pay to Brahmā,
Together with the many gods, O Mārisa,
That we shall today offer to You;
Indeed, we personally perform this service of homage to You.

O Mārisa, the Blessed One who has extinguished all suffering, in the past, we, together with the multitude of gods, used to pay respect and homage to the Brahma King. From this day forward, we shall offer that respect and homage to You with faith. Now, we perform this effort of personal service and homage to You, the Blessed One, with overflowing faith.

You alone are the Fully Enlightened One; You are the unsurpassed Teacher.
In the world including the gods, there is no person equal to You.

O Mārisa, the Blessed One who has extinguished all suffering, You alone are the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) who has realized all things. You are the unsurpassed Teacher of gods and men. In the world of beings, including the gods and Brahmas, there is no person who can be compared to You in terms of physical or spiritual attributes.

## Sakka Granting a Boon to Pañcasikha

After Sakka, the King of Gods, had performed this act of homage and praise to the Buddha with these three verses, he addressed the Gandhabba deity Pañcasikha:

"Dear Pañcasikha, because you first obtained permission from the Buddha for me, we were able to approach and behold that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. Therefore, you have been of great service to me. I shall appoint you to the position held by your father (the position of the King of Gandhabbas); you shall become the King of Gandhabbas. I shall also give to you the goddess Suriyavacchasā, whom you so greatly desire and who is endowed with all auspicious signs."

Thus, he spoke words of gratitude and granted the boon.

Then, Sakka, the King of Gods, with a heart full of joy and delight (like one friend clapping the hand of another with his own), struck the ground with his hand and uttered this solemn exclamation three times: "Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa."

(In this regard, Sakka struck the ground with his hand because he was overjoyed, thinking, "While remaining on this very earth, I have attained this wonderful Supramundane Dhamma," and also because he was struck with intense wonder and praise, thinking, "How marvelous that such a Buddha-treasure has appeared on this great earth!")

While this discourse consisting of questions and answers was being delivered by the Buddha,
196:
The stainless and pure Eye of Dhamma (the knowledge of the Sotāpatti-magga) arose in Sakka, the King of Gods: "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." The Eye of Dhamma (the knowledge of the Sotāpatti-magga) also arose in eighty thousand other deities.

## Why it is called Sakkapañha

Because the Buddha answered these questions requested by Sakka, the lord of gods, the name of this discourse is known as the Sakkapañha.

The account of the preaching of the Sakkapañha Sutta ends here.

## Chapter 40
## Teaching the Aparihāniya Dhamma (Conditions of Welfare)
The Blessed One (as previously mentioned) spent the first twenty years of His Enlightenment (Paṭhama-bodhi) residing in various towns and villages, offering the nectar of the Dhamma to all beings. During the subsequent twenty-four years, known as the Pacchima-bodhi, He resided primarily in Sāvatthī during the rainy seasons. After each rainy season, He wandered through the three circuits as appropriate, offering the nectar of the Dhamma to those beings ready for liberation. The teachings He gave are so vast and numerous that they cannot be fully described in this (Maha Buddhavamsa) chronicle. Like a man who takes one or two drops of clear water from the vast ocean to demonstrate its salty taste, we have written and presented only a few discourses to give the readers a taste of the Dhamma from that great collection of teachings. Devout people who wish to study the vast teachings should examine and note the Burmese translations of the Piṭaka (in consultation with the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries). We shall now describe only the events and teachings starting from about the forty-fourth year of the Blessed One’s ministry, near the time of His Parinibbāna.
Once, when the Blessed One, endowed with the six glories and attributes, was staying (around the 44th year)...

At that time, King Ajātasattu was desirous of marching against the Licchavis, the Vajjian princes, to subdue them. He was speaking boastful words of royal pride: "I shall uproot these Vajjis, though they be so powerful and mighty; I shall destroy them; I shall bring them to utter ruin." The reason for this speech was as follows:

Between the cities of Rājagaha and Vesālī, the great river Gaṅgā flows (from east to west), separating them. Rājagaha is situated to the south of the Gaṅgā. Near that river, there is a large ferry village (called Paṭṭanagāma). (The great city that Indians today call "Patna" is likely that very village from that time.) Dependent on this Paṭṭanagāma, half a league (yojana) was within the sphere of King Ajātasattu’s authority, and half a league was within the sphere of the Licchavi princes’ authority.

In that village of Paṭṭanagāma, valuable treasures would descend from the foot of the mountains. Upon hearing of this, while King Ajātasattu was still planning, saying, "I shall go today, I shall go tomorrow," the Licchavi princes, being united and joyful, would arrive first and take all the valuable treasures. When King Ajātasattu arrived later and heard the news, he would return in anger.

Then again, King Ajātasattu reflected: "To engage in battle with an entire army of warriors is a heavy burden. There is no such thing as a strike or a thrust that does not result in destruction or is without consequence; (indeed, every strike and thrust results in destruction). However, if one acts after consulting a wise person, there is no fault. And there is no wise person in the world equal to the Buddha. At this time, the Buddha is staying at the Gijjhakūṭa Hill monastery at the head of my city. Well then, I shall send a wise minister to inquire. ## The Seven Conditions for Welfare of Kings

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him. (In this regard, the Venerable Ānanda fanned the Buddha primarily as an act of service. In truth, for the Buddha, there is no unbearable cold or heat. At the time when a Buddha appears, the climate remains temperate and balanced due to the power of the Buddha’s merit.) When the Buddha heard the words spoken by the Brahmin, he did not engage in any consultation or discussion with the Brahmin, but desiring to speak back and forth with the Venerable Ānanda, he said:

## (1) The First Condition for Welfare

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis meet frequently and have many meetings?"

(Venerable Ānanda)
"Venerable Sir, I have heard that the Vajjis meet frequently and have many meetings."

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, as long as the Vajjis meet frequently and have many meetings, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline."
202:
202
(In this context: If they meet three times a day, or meet at regular intervals, it is called "meeting frequently." If they do not fall into discouragement, thinking, "We met yesterday, and the day before; why should we meet again today?" then it is called "having many meetings."

The benefits and faults of meeting frequently or not are as follows: (a) If they do not meet frequently, they do not hear news coming from various directions and corners. Because they do not hear such news, they cannot know, "Such and such villages or border regions are in turmoil and being destroyed; in such and such a place, wicked people are rising up and causing trouble." Wicked people, knowing that "the kings are negligent," will then plunder, attack, and oppress the villages and towns, destroying the entire district. When this happens, decline occurs for those who rule the country.

(b) If they meet frequently, they hear various reports. Because they hear them, they can send the army and subdue the enemies in time. Wicked people will also consult among themselves, saying, "The kings are not negligent; we are no longer able to roam and forage in groups," and they will disperse and flee. When this happens, growth and progress occur for those who rule the country.)

## (2) The Second Condition for Welfare

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis meet in harmony, rise in harmony, and carry out the affairs of the Vajjian state in harmony?"

(Venerable Ānanda)
"Venerable Sir, I have heard that the Vajjis meet in harmony, rise in harmony..."
203:
203
...and carry out the affairs of the Vajjian state in harmony."

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, as long as the Vajjis meet in harmony, rise in harmony, and carry out the affairs of the Vajjian state in harmony, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline."

(In this context: If, when the drum or bell is sounded for a meeting, they make excuses such as, "I have another matter today; I have a wedding ceremony," and thus act with distraction and fail to attend, it is not called "meeting in harmony." If, upon hearing the sound of the drum or bell, even those who are eating, those who are adorning themselves, or those who are dressing, go to the meeting even if they have only half-finished eating, half-finished adorning, or half-finished dressing, then it is called "meeting in harmony."

If they all meet in harmony, deliberate on what should be deliberated, do what should be done in unity, and then do not rise from the meeting place together (at the same time), it is not called "rising in harmony." If they rise in disharmony, with some leaving and some remaining behind, those kings who have left may develop wrong thoughts and suspicions that lead to discord, thinking, "We only heard unimportant external talk; now that we have left, the important final decisions will be made."

Only if they all rise from the meeting place (the assembly hall) together in unity after the consultation and meeting are finished is it called "rising in harmony." (Alternatively) Upon hearing news that "In such and such places, the villages and borders are in turmoil and being destroyed; wicked thieves are rising up and causing trouble," and asking, "Who will go to these enemies..."
204:
204

When they deliberate, saying, “How shall we suppress [the enemy]?” and if they say, “I shall go first, I shall go first,” and rush to go before others, they are said to rise in unity from their assembly.

If the affairs of any one king are declining and the other kings send their sons or brothers to assist and support that king’s affairs; or if guest kings arrive and they do not speak words of evasion such as, “Go and stay at the house of such-and-such a king,” but all kings unitedly and harmoniously provide hospitality and care; or if any king has an auspicious occasion, or an illness, or any other matter of happiness or sorrow, and all the kings assist as companions in that matter—this is what is meant by conducting Vajjian state affairs in unity.

## (3) The Third Principle of Prosperity

(The Buddha)
“Ananda, have you heard that the Vajjis do not enact what has not been enacted, do not abolish what has been enacted, and follow and practice the ancient Vajjian traditions as they have been enacted?”

(Venerable Ananda)
“Bhante, I have heard that the Vajjis do not enact what has not been enacted, do not abolish what has been enacted, and follow and practice the ancient Vajjian traditions as they have been enacted.”

(The Buddha)
“Ananda, as long as the Vajjis do not enact what has not been enacted, do not abolish what has been enacted, and follow and practice the ancient Vajjian traditions as they have been enacted, the Vajjis may be expected to prosper and not decline.”
205:
205

(In this context: If they collect taxes, fines, and so forth that were not collected during the reigns of previous kings, they are said to enact what was not enacted. If they do not collect the taxes, fines, and so forth that have been handed down through generations since the reigns of previous kings, they are said to abolish what has been enacted. If, when someone is arrested and handed over as a “criminal or thief,” they decide to execute or mutilate them without investigation, they are said to not follow or practice the ancient Vajjian traditions. In the kingdoms of kings who newly enact what was not enacted by previous kings, the citizens who are oppressed by new taxes and such will lament in despair, saying, “We are being greatly oppressed; who would live in the kingdom of such unjust kings?” They may then flee to the border regions and become criminals themselves, or join existing gangs of criminals and plunder, destroy, and strike at the districts. 

In the kingdoms of kings who abolish what has been enacted by not collecting the taxes, fines, and so forth handed down from previous kings, the royal treasury and granaries will diminish day by day. Then, the elephants, horses, soldiers, and the harem attendants, not receiving their usual provisions and rewards, will lose their strength and become unable to fight in war or serve the king.

In the kingdoms of kings who do not follow or practice ancient Vajjian traditions, the people will become angry, saying, “These kings have executed and mutilated our sons, fathers, and brothers, making them out to be thieves when they were not.” They will then flee to the border regions and become criminals themselves, or join existing gangs of criminals and plunder, destroy, and strike at the districts. When this happens, it leads to the decline of those who rule the country.)
206:
206

In the kingdoms of kings who enact only what was enacted by previous kings, the citizens, thinking, “The kings only do what has been handed down through the royal lineage and have not enacted anything anew,” become joyful and fulfill their duties such as farming and trading.

In the kingdoms of kings who do not abolish what has been enacted and collect the taxes and so forth handed down from previous kings, the royal treasury and granaries increase day by day. Then, the elephants, horses, soldiers, and harem attendants, receiving their usual provisions and rewards, become endowed with both physical and intellectual strength, and are able to fight in war and serve the king.

In ancient times, when the Vajjian kings were presented with someone said to be a thief, they would not say lightly or easily, “Arrest that thief,” but would hand them over to the Ministers of Justice (Vinicchayamahāmatta). Those ministers would investigate and question the person thoroughly, and if he was not a thief, they would release him. If they considered him a thief, out of fear of wrongdoing themselves, they would not pass any judgment but would hand him over to the Judges (Vohārika). Those judges would also investigate and question him, and if he was not a thief, they would release him. If they considered him a thief, they would hand him over to the Legal Experts (Suttadhara). Those experts would also investigate and question him, and if he was not a thief, they would release him. If they considered him a thief, they would hand him over to the Council of Eight (Aṭṭhakulika) [who were born of the eight noble clans and avoided the four biases]. Those elders would act as before and hand him over to the General (Senāpati). From the General, he was handed to the Crown Prince (Uparāja), and from the Crown Prince to the King. The King would investigate and question him, and if he was not a thief, he would release him. If he was truly a thief, the King would have the Book of Law (Dhammasattha), handed down through generations, read out.
207:
207

In that book, it is clearly written: “If a person commits such-and-such an act, such-and-such a punishment must be given.” The King, after comparing the person’s case with that Book of Law, would then pass a sentence appropriate to the offense.

In this way, the people do not blame the kings who follow these ancient Vajjian traditions, but thinking, “The kings have decided the case according to ancient traditions; there is no fault in these kings, it is not their fault but only our own fault,” they remain satisfied and diligently and honestly perform their work. When this is done, it leads to the progress and prosperity of those who rule the country.)

## (4) The Fourth Principle of Prosperity

(The Buddha)
“Ananda, have you heard that the Vajjis respect, honor, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian elders, and think that they should listen to their words?”

(Venerable Ananda)
“Bhante, I have heard that the Vajjis respect, honor, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian elders, and think that they should listen to their words.”

(The Buddha)
“Ananda, as long as the Vajjis respect, honor, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian elders, and think that they should listen to their words, the Vajjis may be expected to prosper and not decline.”
208:
208

(To respect means to acknowledge a special benefit or favor. To honor means to repeatedly generate a mind of esteem, thinking, “These are the ones we should hold in high regard like a stone umbrella.” To esteem means to act with heartfelt affection. To venerate means to act with humility, setting aside pride. To think that their words should be listened to means to visit them two or three times a day and listen to what they have to say.

Young kings who do not perform such acts as respecting the elder kings and do not visit them to receive guidance will be neglected and abandoned by those elder kings. Consequently, not receiving advice and instructions, they will indulge in revelry and heedlessness, and thus decline and lose their royal sovereignty.

To the kings who show respect and so forth to the elder kings, the elder kings will speak of ancient traditions, saying, “This should be done; this should not be done.” When war arises, they will show the methods and strategies, saying, “One should enter in this way; one should withdraw in this way.” Those kings, being instructed and guided by the elder kings, act according to the advice and are thus able to maintain the royal lineage and history for a long time.)

## (5) The Fifth Principle of Prosperity

(The Buddha)
“Ananda, have you heard that the Vajjis do not abduct women and girls of the clans and forcibly detain them?”

(Venerable Ananda)
“Bhante, I have heard that the Vajjis do not abduct women and girls of the clans and forcibly detain them.”
209:
209

(The Buddha)
“Ananda, as long as the Vajjis do not abduct women and girls of the clans and forcibly detain them, the Vajjis may be expected to prosper and not decline.”

(In this context: In the kingdoms of kings who, thinking “I am the king,” abduct and forcibly detain housewives and young daughters, the people will become angry, saying, “These kings have forcibly taken the mothers of our children and our young daughters whom we have cherished and raised with great care, and have kept them in their palaces.” They will then flee to the border regions and become criminals themselves, or join existing gangs of criminals and plunder, destroy, and strike at the districts. When this happens, it leads to the decline of those who rule the country.

In the kingdoms of kings who do not forcibly detain housewives and young daughters, the people, being free from anxiety and worry, perform their respective duties and increase the king’s wealth and granaries. When this happens, it leads to the progress and prosperity of those who rule the country.)

## (6) The Sixth Principle of Prosperity

(The Buddha)
“Ananda, have you heard that the Vajjis respect, honor, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian shrines (cetiyas) both inside and outside the city, and do not allow the righteous offerings (bali) previously given and performed to those shrines to decline?”
210:
(Venerable Ānanda)
"Venerable Sir, I have heard that the Vajjīs honor, respect, revere, and worship the Vajjian shrines (cetiyas) both within and outside their city. They do not allow the righteous offerings (bali) formerly given and performed to these shrines to fall into neglect."

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, as long as the Vajjīs honor, respect, revere, and worship the Vajjian shrines both within and outside their city, and do not allow the righteous offerings formerly given and performed to these shrines to fall into neglect, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjīs, not decline."

(Regarding kings who do not honor, respect, and worship the ancient shrines within and outside the city, and who allow the righteous offerings formerly given and performed to fall into neglect—that is, they do not give them—the deities (devas) do not provide proper protection and guardianship. Although they may not be able to cause new suffering and distress, they can increase existing ailments such as coughs and headaches. When war or battle arises, they do not become allies; when this happens, it leads to the decline of the kings.

As for the kings who do not allow the righteous offerings to fall into neglect—that is, they give and perform them as before—the deities provide proper protection and guardianship. Although they may not be able to create new happiness and bliss, they cause existing ailments such as coughs and headaches to be quickly cured. When war or battle arises, they become allies by making their own side's forces appear double or triple in strength at the front of the battle, and by showing terrifying forms to the enemy. When this happens, it leads to the growth and prosperity of the kings.)
