## (7) The Seventh Principle of Non-decline

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, have you heard whether the Vajjīs provide righteous protection, defense, and security for Arahants, so that Arahants who have not yet come might come to the Vajjian territory, and those who have already come might live there in comfort? What have you heard, dear son?"

(Venerable Ānanda)
"Venerable Sir, I have heard that the Vajjīs provide righteous protection, defense, and security for Arahants, so that Arahants who have not yet come might come to the Vajjian territory, and those who have already come might live there in comfort."

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, as long as the Vajjīs provide righteous protection, defense, and security for Arahants, so that Arahants who have not yet come might come to the Vajjian territory, and those who have already come might live there in comfort, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjīs, not decline."

(In this context: Providing protection so that undesired dangers do not arrive is called 'protection and defense' (rakkhā-varaṇa). Maintaining desired objects so they are not destroyed is called 'security' (gutti). In providing such protection, defense, and security, surrounding them with a large army of soldiers is not called 'righteous protection, defense, and security' for monks. Rather, it means preventing trees from being cut down in the forest near the monastery, preventing hunters from catching, shooting, or killing animals, and preventing people from catching fish in the ponds near the monastery.)
212:
Doing such things is called 'righteous protection, defense, and security.'

In the Pali language, terms like 'kattuṃ', 'karaṇatthaṃ', and 'kātukāmo' are used, and in Burmese, phrases like 'in order to do' or 'desiring to do' are written to express the 'manasā-vatthāpita', which is the mental inclination or intention of the person concerned.

Therefore, the phrase 'so that Arahants who have not yet come might come, and those who have already come might live in comfort' describes the mental state and intention of the Vajjī kings, such as: 'By what means will Arahants who have not yet come to our country arrive? By what means will those who have already come live in comfort?'

In this regard, kings who do not desire the arrival of Arahants who have not yet come are those without faith (saddhā) and those who do not have confidence in the Triple Gem. Furthermore, when monks arrive in their country, these kings do not go out to welcome them, do not visit them, do not engage in polite conversation, do not ask questions about problems, do not listen to the Dhamma, do not give offerings (dāna), do not listen to the words of appreciation (anumodanā), and do not arrange any seating or lodging for those monks. At that time, a bad reputation spreads for those kings: 'Such and such a king has no faith, no confidence in the Triple Gem; when monks arrive in his country, he does not welcome them... (etc.)... and does not arrange any lodging at all.' Hearing this, monks no longer travel by the road through that king's city gate. Even if they must travel near the city gate, they no longer enter the city. When this happens, it results in the non-arrival of Arahants who have not yet come.
213:
If the monks who have already arrived do not find comfort in living there, even those who came without knowing will say, 'We came thinking we would stay in this city, but if these kings continue to behave in this way, who would stay?' and they will depart after speaking words of blame. Thus, if monks who have not yet come do not arrive, and those who have arrived live in misery, that place is no longer a residence for monks. At that time, there is no protection from the deities. When there is no protection from the deities, the ogres (yakkhas) find an opportunity. When those ogres become numerous, they cause new diseases (diseases that have never occurred before) to arise. Meritorious deeds rooted in visiting virtuous persons and asking questions about problems also do not flourish. When this happens, it leads to the decline of the kings. (Conversely, growth and prosperity should be understood by following the previous method.)

Then the Blessed One said to the Brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha:

"Brahmin, once I was staying at the Sārandada shrine in the city of Vesālī, and I taught these seven principles of non-decline (aparihāniya dhamma) to the Vajjīs.

Brahmin, as long as these seven principles of non-decline endure among the Vajjīs, and as long as the Vajjīs continue to practice these seven principles of non-decline well, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjīs, not decline."

At that time, the Brahmin Vassakāra said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Gotama, if they are endowed with even one of these principles of non-decline, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjīs,
214:
not decline; how much more so if they are endowed with all seven principles of non-decline?

Venerable Gotama, King Ajātasattu cannot conquer the Vajjian territory through mere warfare without using (1) persuasion/bribery or (2) sowing mutual discord.

Venerable Gotama, well then, we shall depart now; we are busy and have much to do."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One gave him permission, saying, "Brahmin, you may go at your own convenience (literally: you know the time for going)." Then the Brahmin Vassakāra, greatly pleased and appreciative of the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat and departed.

(Before the Buddha appeared, that place was a shrine and residence for the yakkha Sārandada. Later, when the Buddha appeared, a monastery was built and offered to the Blessed One at that site, and thus the monastery became known as the Sārandada Shrine Monastery.

In the words spoken by the Brahmin upon his return: (1) 'Persuasion' (upalāpana) refers to saying words of peace such as, 'There is no benefit in us quarreling; let us be united now,' and sending gifts such as elephants, horses, chariots, gold, and silver to win over the enemy's mind to one's own will. The intention is that after performing such acts of hospitality and persuasion and becoming intimate and familiar, one can easily capture and seize them. (2) The second term indicates that they could also be captured and seized by causing the Vajjī kings to become divided among themselves.)
215:
This expresses the meaning that they could be captured and seized. The Brahmin Vassakāra spoke these two strategic methods by drawing from the Buddha's teaching. Here, there are questions and answers:

(Question)
Did the Blessed One not know that if He taught in this way, the Brahmin Vassakāra would gain the strategy (to conquer the Vajjī kings)?

(Answer)
It is not that He did not know; He did know.

(Question)
Knowing this, why did He teach it?

(Answer)
He taught it out of compassion and protection for the Vajjī kings. To elaborate: In the Blessed One's golden knowledge, He considered: 'If I do not teach this, King Ajātasattu will go within two or three days and capture, seize, and kill all the Vajjī kings. But if I teach it, he will use the strategy of discord (bheda-upāya) to cause the united Licchavīs (Vajjī kings) to become divided, and only after three years will he go and capture, seize, and kill all the Vajjī kings. To live for these three years is itself praiseworthy and noble. Indeed, if they live for these three years, the Licchavī/Vajjī kings will be able to perform meritorious deeds that will be their support.' Thus, He taught it out of compassion and protection for the Vajjī kings.

## The Destruction of Vesālī

After the Brahmin Vassakāra departed from the Blessed One and reached King Ajātasattu, the King asked him, "Teacher, what did the Blessed One say?" Vassakāra replied, "O Great King, according to the words of the ascetic Gotama, it is not possible to capture and seize the Vajjī kings by any other means, but only through persuasion or..."
216:
“Only by these two means—either by persuasion or by sowing discord—is it possible to capture and conquer them.”

Then King Ajātasattu said to the Brahmin Vassakāra, “If we use the method of persuasion, our elephants, horses, and so on will be ruined. I shall capture those Vajjī kings only by the means of sowing discord (bheda-upāya). How should we proceed, teacher?”

The Brahmin Vassakāra replied, “Great King, if that is the case, please speak in the presence of the full assembly of ministers and troops about your intention to go to war with the Vajjī kings. At that time, I will say, ‘Great King, what benefit is there for you in warring with those Vajjī kings? Let those Vajjī kings live by their own wealth, engaging in farming, trade, and so forth.’ Having said this, I will rise from my seat and depart (with an air of disagreement). Then, Great King, you must speak as if in anger, saying, ‘Friends, why does this Brahmin Vassakāra forbid my words about going to war against the Vajjī kings?’ Furthermore, I will send gifts to the Vajjī kings in broad daylight. You should have those gifts seized and then blame me. Without imprisoning or beating me, simply have my head shaved and banish me from the city. Then I will say defiantly, ‘The walls and moats in your city were not supervised by others; they were supervised by me. I am the one who knows the fire-barriers of the walls in your city...’
217:
‘...I am the one who knows the weak spots, the shallow places in the moats, and the deep places. Now, before long, I will bring the enemy kings and work to destroy your city walls and moats until they are level with the ground.’ When you hear this, Great King, you must sternly pronounce the sentence of banishment, saying, ‘You must leave the country immediately!’” Thus he offered his counsel. King Ajātasattu then carried out everything as the Brahmin had advised.

The Licchavī kings heard the news that the Brahmin Vassakāra had departed from Rājagaha and strongly protested, saying, “The Brahmin Vassakāra is a crafty and deceitful man. Do not allow him to cross to this side of the Gaṅgā River.” Among those Licchavī kings, some said, “It is said that King Ajātasattu has thus banished the Brahmin Vassakāra because he spoke on our behalf.” When these words of appeasement were presented, all the Licchavī kings agreed, saying, “Friends, if that is the case, let the Brahmin come.”

When the Brahmin Vassakāra arrived and met the Licchavī kings, they asked, “Why have you come?” and he explained the situation to them. The Licchavī kings remarked, “It was not right to impose such a heavy punishment for such a trivial reason,” and they asked, “What was your rank in that city of Rājagaha?”
218:
The Brahmin Vassakāra replied, “I was the Chief Minister of Justice.” The Licchavī kings then said, “Let that same position of Chief Minister of Justice be for you here,” and they appointed the Brahmin to the post of Minister of Justice.

The Brahmin Vassakāra administered justice exceedingly well. The Licchavī princes also studied various arts and sciences under the Brahmin.

## Sowing Discord

When the Brahmin Vassakāra had attained such great virtue and merit that he was respected as a teacher, he one day called a Licchavī king aside to a suitable place and asked, “Do your young men plow the fields, O King?” When the Licchavī king replied, “Yes, teacher, they plow,” he asked again, “Do they plow by yoking two oxen?” The Licchavī king answered, “Yes, teacher, they plow by yoking two oxen.” Having said only this much, he returned to his place. (This act of taking a Licchavī king aside and appearing to speak of important matters was the use of the means of sowing discord, bheda-upāya, to divide the kings). Then, another Licchavī king asked the one who had spoken with the Brahmin, “What did the teacher say?” When the questioned king replied, the other could not believe him and thought, “This Licchavī king is not telling me the truth.” Thus, he became suspicious and alienated from the king who had been questioned.
219:
On another day, the Brahmin Vassakāra took another Licchavī king to a suitable place and asked only, “O King, with what curry did you eat your royal meal?” and then returned. When another Licchavī king questioned him, he could not believe the truthful answer of the questioned king, and discord arose again.

Furthermore, on another day, the Brahmin Vassakāra took a Licchavī prince to a suitable place and asked, “O Prince, is it true that you are very poor?” When the questioned Licchavī prince asked, “Who said such a thing?” the Brahmin slandered him by saying, “Such-and-such a Licchavī king said so.” Because of the Brahmin’s slander, those two Licchavī kings became so divided that they could not be reconciled.

The Brahmin took another Licchavī king to a suitable place and asked, “O Prince, is it true that you are a coward?” When the questioned Licchavī king asked in return, “Who said this?” the Brahmin slandered him by saying, “Such-and-such a Licchavī king said so.” Those two Licchavī kings also became so divided that they could not be reconciled.

## The Destruction of the Whole Country of Vesālī

In this manner, the Brahmin Vassakāra told one Licchavī king things that had not been said by another. Within three years, he had caused such discord among the Licchavī kings that no two kings would
220:
walk together on the same path. Then, (to demonstrate the extent of their division), he had the great assembly drum sounded.

The Licchavī kings said, “Let the wealthy and powerful kings assemble; we are but poor and powerless. Let the brave kings assemble; we are but cowards. What business have we to do by going to that assembly?” Speaking such words of resentment and dissatisfaction, they did not attend the meeting.

The Brahmin Vassakāra then sent a secret message to King Ajātasattu, saying, “Now is the time to capture the entire city of Vesālī. May the Great King quickly set forth with his army.” As soon as King Ajātasattu heard this news, he had the war drums sounded and departed from the city of Rājagaha.

When the kings of Vesālī heard of this, they said, “We shall not even allow King Ajātasattu to cross the Gaṅgā River,” and they had the great assembly drum sounded again. Even upon hearing this, the Licchavī kings spoke words of dissatisfaction, saying, “Let the brave kings go,” and so forth, and did not attend the meeting.

Again, when King Ajātasattu had crossed to this side of the Gaṅgā River, the kings of Vesālī said, “We shall not allow him to enter our city; let us close the city gates, stand firm, and mount a defense.” They had the great assembly drum sounded once more, but not a single Licchavī king attended the meeting.
221:
King Ajātasattu, along with his great army, easily entered the city of Vesālī through the gates that were already open. He brought all the Licchavī kings to their end and destruction, and then returned to Rājagaha victorious. This is the account of the destruction of Vesālī.

(These events of the “Destruction of Vesālī” took place within the three-year period between the year the Buddha was to attain final Parinibbāna and two years after His Parinibbāna. These events are presented in this text as they are explained in the Commentaries when the occasion arises. I wish for the virtuous readers of the Chronicle of Buddhas to keep in mind the time when the Brahmin Vassakāra departed from the monastery on Mount Gijjhakūṭa in Rājagaha, after the Buddha had preached the seven principles of non-decline for kings, Rāja-aparihāniya Dhamma, to him.)

## The Seven Principles of Non-decline for Monks

Even while the Buddha was preaching the seven principles of non-decline for kings to the Brahmin Vassakāra, He reflected and considered: “This discourse on the principles of non-decline for kings is a talk that does not lead to liberation from the round of rebirths (saṃsāra), but pertains only to saṃsāra. Indeed, in my Sāsana, this discourse on the principles of non-decline—Aparihāniya Dhamma—should be preached. The Aparihāniya Dhamma preached for the Sāsana leads to liberation from saṃsāra and pertains to Nibbāna, the state free from the round of rebirths. Because of this discourse, the Sāsana of the three trainings (sikkhā) will remain for a very long time after my Parinibbāna.”
222:
Therefore, not long after the Brahmin Vassakāra had departed, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, and assemble all the monks who are living in the vicinity of Rājagaha in the Dhamma Hall." The Venerable Ānanda replied, "Very well, Bhante," and acknowledging the Blessed One's command, he sent monks with psychic powers to those living in distant monasteries and went personally to those in nearby monasteries, saying, "Venerables, please assemble; the Blessed One desires your assembly." Having thus assembled them in the Dhamma Hall, he went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and standing in a suitable place, addressed the Blessed One: "Bhante, all the monks have assembled. Bhante, the Blessed One may now go at his convenience (i.e., it is according to the Blessed One's will)."

Then the Blessed One went to the Dhamma Hall, sat on the prepared seat, and addressed the monks: "Monks, I will teach you the seven conditions for welfare (aparihāniya dhamma). Listen and pay close attention; I will speak in detail." The monks replied, "Very well, Bhante." The Blessed One then taught these seven conditions for welfare:
223:
(1) Monks, as long as the monks meet often and meet in large numbers, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.

(2) Monks, as long as the monks meet in harmony, adjourn in harmony, and carry out the duties of the Saṅgha in harmony, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.

(3) Monks, as long as the monks do not authorize what has not been authorized, do not abolish what has been authorized, and proceed according to the training rules as they have been laid down, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.

(4) Monks, as long as the monks show respect, honor, esteem, and veneration towards the elder monks of long standing, the fathers of the Saṅgha and leaders of the Saṅgha, and deem that their words should be listened to, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.

(5) Monks, as long as the monks do not fall under the influence of arisen craving (taṇhā) which leads to renewed existence, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.

(6) Monks, as long as the monks maintain a desire for forest dwellings, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
224:
(7) Monks, as long as the monks maintain mindfulness individually so that well-behaved fellow practitioners who have not yet come may come, and those who have already come may live at ease, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.

Monks, as long as these seven conditions for welfare endure among the monks, and as long as the monks practice these seven conditions for welfare, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline. (The Blessed One's discourse has not yet ended).

(These seven principles mentioned above are called the "First Seven Conditions for the Welfare of Monks.")

(1) Among these seven, the first condition, "meeting often," is similar to what was said in the first condition for welfare taught for the Vajjī princes.

In this first condition for welfare, if they do not meet often, they will not hear news occurring in various places or matters concerning the Saṅgha coming from those places. Because of not hearing such news, they will not know matters such as: "The boundary (sīmā) of such-and-forth monastery is overlapping/confused. Because of such confusion, Uposatha and Pavāraṇā have been suspended. In such-and-forth place, monks are practicing medicine, acting as messengers, etc. They are making a living by excessive begging, giving flowers, and so on."

Corrupt monks, thinking "The Saṅgha is negligent," will form groups, grow in strength, and cause the Sasana to decline.
225:
If they meet frequently, because they hear such news, they can send monks to rectify the boundary (sīmā) and enable the performance of Uposatha and Pavāraṇā deeds. In places where corrupt monks who make a living through wrong livelihood are numerous, they can send noble disciple monks to preach the Dhamma of the Noble Lineages (ariyavaṃsa). They can send masters of the Vinaya to suppress the corrupt monks. The corrupt monks, saying "The Saṅgha is not negligent; we are unable to wander in groups," will split up and flee in disorder. When this happens, the three trainings (sikkhā) will flourish for the monks.

(2) In the second condition for welfare, "meeting in harmony" means: when the drum or bell is struck to signal an assembly for cleaning a shrine, roofing a Bodhi-tree house or Uposatha house, establishing a covenant, or giving instruction, if monks make excuses like "I have a robe to sew," "I have a bowl to fire," or "I have construction work (navakamma)," and thus act with distraction and fail to attend, it is not called meeting in harmony. Only when they set aside all personal matters like robe-sewing and assemble simultaneously with the thought "I will arrive first, I will arrive first," is it called meeting in harmony.

After consulting and performing what needs to be done, if they do not depart from the assembly place together (simultaneously), it is not called adjourning in harmony. If they adjourn without harmony, with some leaving and some remaining, those who left first might have wrong thoughts and misconceptions that lead to dissent, thinking: "We only heard unimportant external talk; now that we have left, the important decision-making talk will occur."
226:
Only when everyone leaves and rises from the assembly place (hall) in unison after the consultation is finished is it called adjourning in harmony. (Alternatively) If, upon hearing news that "The boundary of such-and-forth monastery is overlapping, and Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are suspended," or "Corrupt monks practicing medicine are numerous in such-and-forth place," and when the consultation arises, "Who will go to suppress those corrupt monks?", they go with the spirit of "I will go first, I will go first," then it is also called adjourning in harmony.

Furthermore, if they see a visiting monk (āgantuka) and do not speak words of avoiding responsibility such as "Go to this precinct" or "Go to that precinct; who is this monk?", but all monks perform the duties for the guest in harmony; or if they see a monk whose bowl and robes are worn out and scarce, and they seek bowl and robes for him by going on almsround; or if they seek medicine for a sick monk in harmony; or if they do not avoid responsibility for a helpless sick monk by saying "Go to this precinct," but instead take him into their own precinct or monastery and care for him; or if they encounter a situation where a scripture of the Buddha's teaching is about to be lost either in text (Pāli) or meaning, and they collectively support a wise monk with the four requisites so that he can learn the text and meaning without loss—all this is called "carrying out the duties of the Saṅgha in harmony."

(3) In the third condition for welfare, if they establish new covenants or new training rules that are not in accordance with the Dhamma, it is called "authorizing what has not been authorized."
227:
The fifth training rule in the second Kosiyavagga on page 336 of the Vinaya Pārājika Pāli is called the Nisīdanasanthata training rule or the Purāṇasanthata training rule. Regarding that rule, while the Blessed One was staying at Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, he once told the monks: "Monks, I wish to stay in retreat alone for three months. No monk should come to me except the one who brings my almsfood." Then the monks living in Sāvatthī made a covenant: "Friends, the Blessed One wishes to stay in retreat alone for three months. No monk should go to the Blessed One except the one who brings almsfood. Any monk who goes to the Blessed One must be made to confess a Pācittiya offense." (The full story can be seen in the Burmese translation of the Pitaka, Vinaya Vol 1, pages 355-359). This covenant of the Sāvatthī monks, "Let it be understood that any monk who goes to the Buddha incurs a Pācittiya offense and must confess it," is completely inconsistent with the Dhamma-Vinaya. Thus, establishing such new covenants not in accordance with the Dhamma is called "authorizing what has not been authorized."

One hundred years after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, if one acts like the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī by abolishing the training rules laid down by the Buddha and presenting the ten unlawful points (adhamma vatthu), it is called "abolishing what has been authorized." (The account of the Vajjiputtaka monks presenting the ten unlawful points can be seen in the Burmese translation of the Vinaya Cūḷavagga Pāli, Sattasatikakkhandhaka, pages 495-515).

If, like the monks Assaji and Punabbhasuka during the Buddha's time, one transgresses minor offenses (khuddānukhuddaka āpatti) with the intention to do so...
228:
228
It is not called "practicing well by undertaking the rules of training prescribed by the Buddha."

If one does not establish or form new types of commitments or new types of training rules that are not in accordance with the Dhamma—like the Arahant Elder Upasena (the younger brother of Ven. Sāriputta) in the Purāṇasanthata story—it is called "not enacting what was not enacted by the Buddha."

If one presents the Sāsana (the Buddha's teaching) in accordance with the Dhamma-Vinaya—like the Great Arahant Elder Yasa (the leader of the Second Council)—it is called "not abolishing what was enacted by the Buddha."

Just before the First Council was held, in the assembly of the Saṅgha (although the Buddha, near his Parinibbāna, had permitted that the Saṅgha could abolish the minor and lesser [khuddānukhuddaka] training rules if they so desired after his Parinibbāna), the Great Arahant Elder Mahākassapa (the leader of the First Council) firmly submitted a motion [ñattikammavācā] not to abolish those minor and lesser training rules. If one follows and practices without abolishing or transgressing even the minor training rules like him, it is called "practicing well by undertaking the rules of training prescribed by the Buddha."

(4) Regarding the fourth Aparihāniya Dhamma: If monks do not show respect and so forth to the elder monks who are leaders of the Saṅgha, and do not approach those elders two or three times a day to receive instruction, then the elder leaders of the Saṅgha do not give them advice and exhortation; they do not preach the Dhamma discourse handed down through the lineage of teachers; they do not teach the essential, core doctrines. Those monks who are thus abandoned by the elder leaders of the Saṅgha decline and lose spiritual qualities such as the five virtues [sīla, etc.] and the seven treasures of the noble ones [ariya-dhana].

If they show respect and so forth to the elder monks who are leaders of the Saṅgha, and approach those elders two or three times a day to receive instruction—
229:
229
—to those monks who approach, the elder monks give advice and exhortation. They preach the Dhamma discourse handed down through the lineage of teachers, saying: "In this way, friend, you should move forward; in this way, friend, you should move backward; in this way, friend, you should look ahead; in this way, friend, you should look aside; in this way, friend, you should bend your arm; in this way, friend, you should stretch your arm. In this way, friend, you should wear and carry the double robe, the bowl, and the upper robe," and so forth. They also teach the essential, core doctrines. They restrain them with the thirteen dhutaṅga practices and the ten kathāvatthu (subjects of discourse). Those monks, established in the advice and exhortation of those elders, prosper in spiritual qualities such as virtue and reach the fruit of the noble path [ariya-phala], which is the benefit of monkhood.

(5) Regarding the fifth Aparihāniya Dhamma: If, due to the desire for the four requisites, monks follow closely behind donors, wandering from village to village and town to town, they are said to be following the whims and desires of craving [taṇhā]. If they follow in such a way, spiritual qualities such as virtue decline for those monks. If they do not follow the whims of craving in that way, spiritual qualities such as virtue increase and flourish.

(6) Regarding the sixth Aparihāniya Dhamma: A dwelling that is five hundred bow-lengths [dhanu] away is called a "forest dwelling" [araññaka]. It means there should be a desire and longing to reside in such forest dwellings. Indeed, even if one dwells in a monastery near a town or village and enters into meditative absorption [jhāna], upon emerging from that jhāna, one hears the sounds of women, men, children, and so forth. Because of hearing such sounds, the mundane jhānas already attained by that monk can decline, perish, and be lost.

In a forest dwelling, however, upon waking from sleep, one hears the sounds of lions, leopards, tigers, peacocks, and so forth. Because of hearing such sounds, one attains the joy and rapture [pīti] born of the forest, and by contemplating that very rapture, one can reach the fruit of Arahantship [arahatta-phala].
230:
230
In this way, the Blessed One praised a monk who is sleeping in a forest dwelling more than a monk who is dwelling in meditative absorption in a monastery near a town or village. Therefore, looking forward to the benefit of easily obtaining the supportive causes for reaching the fruit of Arahantship easily for that forest-dwelling monk, the Blessed One taught: "As long as the monks have a desire to reside in forest dwellings, growth is to be expected for them, not decline."

(7) Regarding the seventh Aparihāniya Dhamma: Resident [āvāsika] monks who do not desire the arrival of virtuous [lajjī] fellow monks who love virtue at their own monastery are those who are deficient in faith and have no devotion to the Triple Gem. Consequently, those resident monks do not perform the duties that resident monks should perform for the visiting [āgantuka] monks who arrive at their monastery, such as welcoming them, receiving their bowl and robes, preparing a seat, or fanning them. Then, a bad reputation spreads for those resident monks: "These resident monks are deficient in faith and have no devotion to the Triple Gem; they do not perform the major and minor duties for the visiting monks who enter the monastery."

Hearing that bad reputation, even if monks are traveling past the gate of the monastery, they do not enter that monastery. When this happens, virtuous monks who have not yet arrived simply do not come. Furthermore, if there is no comfortable living for those good monks who have already arrived, the monks who came without knowing will say words of reproach: "We came thinking we would stay; but with this way of living where these resident monks do not fulfill their duties, who would stay?" and they depart. When this happens, that monastery becomes a place where other virtuous monks do not reside. Then, the resident monks do not get the opportunity to see the virtuous and noble—
231:
231
—venerable ones. Because they do not get to see them, they do not get to dispel their doubts, nor do they get a good teacher who will instruct them in moral conduct and training, nor do they get to hear the sweet Dhamma. For those resident monks, there is no learning of the Dhamma not yet learned, nor the recitation and rehearsal of the Dhamma already learned; thus, spiritual qualities such as virtue diminish and decline day by day.

Resident monks who desire and long for the arrival of virtuous fellow monks at their monastery are those with great faith and devotion to the Triple Gem. Consequently, they perform the welcoming and other duties for the virtuous fellow monks who arrive at their monastery and prepare beds and seats for them. They lead those visiting virtuous monks into the village for alms; they dispel their own doubts; they get the opportunity to hear the sweet Dhamma. Then, a good reputation and fame arise for those resident monks: "The monks residing in such-and-such a monastery are endowed with faith in this manner. They have devotion to the Triple Gem; they are endowed with the major and minor duties; they support the visiting virtuous fellow monks."

Hearing that news, virtuous monks from afar also arrive. The resident monks perform the major and minor duties for those visiting virtuous monks. They approach the visiting virtuous monks, and after bowing to the visiting virtuous monk who is senior in training [vassa], they sit respectfully. They take their own seats and sit near the visiting monk who is junior. Having sat thus, they ask: "Venerable sirs, will you reside in this monastery, or will you continue your journey?" If the visiting monk says, "I will continue my journey," they say: "This monastery's bedding and seating are suitable and comfortable for you; alms are also easy to obtain"—
232:
232
—and so forth, speaking words that make them want to stay, they do not give them leave to go. If the visiting monk is an expert in the Vinaya [vinayadhara], they learn and rehearse the Vinaya in his presence. If he is a bearer of the Suttas [suttantika] and so forth, they learn and rehearse the respective collections of Dhamma that he bears in his presence. Those resident monks, established in the advice and exhortation of the visiting virtuous monks, reach the fruit of Arahantship together with the four analytical insights [paṭisambhidā]. (This means they become Arahants attained to the analytical insights).

The visiting virtuous monks say words of joy: "We came thinking we would stay for only a day or two; however, because living together with these resident monks is so pleasant, we shall stay for a long time, ten or twelve years." When this happens, only the increase and growth of spiritual qualities such as virtue occurs for those monks.

## The Second Seven Conditions for Non-decline

The Blessed One, wishing to teach the second seven conditions for non-decline to the monks once more, said: "Monks, I shall teach you another seven conditions for non-decline [aparihāniya] besides those already mentioned. Listen to that, pay close attention, I shall speak in detail." When he said this, the monks replied, "Very well, Bhante."

The Blessed One taught these following seven conditions for non-decline:

(1) Monks, as long as the monks do not live delighting in, being fond of, and exerting effort in worldly activities [kammārāmatā], growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline.
233:
(2) Monks, as long as monks do not delight in, take pleasure in, and devote themselves to talk, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
(3) Monks, as long as monks do not delight in, take pleasure in, and devote themselves to sleep, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
(4) Monks, as long as monks do not delight in, take pleasure in, and devote themselves to company, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
(5) Monks, as long as monks are free from evil desires—which manifest as displaying virtues one does not possess—and do not fall under the influence of evil desires, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
(6) Monks, as long as monks do not have evil friends and companions and do not incline their minds towards those who are evil, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
(7) Monks, as long as monks do not stop halfway in their progress (before reaching the fruit of Arahantship) merely by attaining some minor distinction, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
Monks, as long as these seven conditions for non-decline (aparihāniya) remain among the monks, and as long as the monks practice these seven conditions for non-decline,
234:
only growth is to be expected for them, not decline. (The discourse is not yet finished).
(These aforementioned seven conditions are called the "Second Seven Conditions for the Growth of Monks.")
(1) Among those seven, the term "major and minor affairs" mentioned in the first condition for non-decline refers to: preparing robes, sewing robes, layering robes (making double-layered robes, etc.), making needle cases, sewing bowl bags, sewing shoulder straps, sewing waistbands, sewing water filters, making alms bowls, making foot-scrubbing pots, making brooms, and so on.
If a certain monk performs these major and minor affairs and spends the whole day doing only those tasks, it is with reference to such a monk that this prohibition is made. However, a monk who performs these major and minor affairs only at the appropriate time, and who studies during study time, recites during recitation time, performs duties at the pagoda courtyard at the proper time, and practices meditation at the time for meditation—such a monk is not called "one who delights in, takes pleasure in, and devotes himself to major and minor affairs."
(2) A monk who spends the day and night speaking only words that do not lead to the paths and fruits, such as praise of women or praise of men, and who does not set a limit to such talk, is called "one who delights in, takes pleasure in, and devotes himself to talk." A monk who preaches the Dhamma throughout the day and night or who answers questions is called "one who speaks little, and who speaks with consideration and limits." The reason is that the Blessed One taught (in M. i. 217): "Monks, when you have gathered together, there are two things to be done: 1. Dhamma talk, or 2. Noble silence while entering into meditative attainments."
235:
Because the Buddha has taught thus.
(3) Regarding the third condition for non-decline, a monk who sleeps while walking, sitting, or lying down (or even while moving), being overwhelmed and oppressed by sloth and torpor (thina-middha), is called "one who delights in, takes pleasure in, and devotes himself to sleep." However, a monk whose mind enters the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) because the physical body (karaja-kāya) is exhausted from striving in the monk's duties is not called "one who delights in sleep."
(4) Regarding the fourth condition for non-decline, a monk who always lives in entanglement with companions—being the second if there is one, the third if there are two, the fourth if there are three, and so on—and who finds no comfort when living alone, is called "one who delights in, takes pleasure in, and devotes himself to company." A monk who finds comfort only when living alone without relying on companions in the four postures of lying, sitting, standing, and walking is not called "one who delights in company."
(5) Regarding the fifth condition for non-decline, a monk who, being immoral himself, displays virtues he does not possess, is called a monk with evil desires. Conversely, one should understand the monk who is free from evil desires.
(6) Regarding the sixth condition for non-decline, one who is loved with affection is called a friend (mitta); one who is a companion in going, coming, eating, and drinking is called a companion (sahāya).
(7) Regarding the seventh condition for non-decline, it means: "As long as monks do not stop and rest merely with purity of virtue, or merely with insight, or merely with meditative absorption (jhāna), or merely with the state of a Stream-enterer, or merely with the state of a Once-returner, or merely with the state of a Non-returner,
236:
only growth is to be expected for them, not decline."
## The Third Seven Conditions for Non-Decline
Wishing to teach the third set of seven conditions for non-decline to the monks, the Buddha said: "Monks, I shall teach you another seven conditions for non-decline (aparihāniya) besides those already mentioned. Listen to them, pay close attention, and I shall speak in detail." The monks replied, "Very well, Bhante," and the Buddha taught these seven conditions for non-decline:
(1) Monks, as long as monks are endowed with faith (saddhā), only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
(2) Monks, as long as monks possess moral shame (hiri), (etc.),
(3) As long as they possess moral dread (ottappa), (etc.),
(4) As long as they possess great learning (bāhusacca), (etc.),
(5) As long as they possess aroused energy (viriya), (etc.),
(6) As long as they are endowed with established mindfulness (sati), (etc.),
237:
(7) Monks, as long as monks are endowed with insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
Monks, as long as these seven conditions for non-decline (aparihāniya) remain among the monks, and as long as the monks practice these seven conditions for non-decline, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline. (The discourse is not yet finished).
(These aforementioned seven conditions are called the "Third Seven Conditions for the Growth of Monks.")
(1) Among those seven, in the context of the first condition for non-decline, faith (saddhā) is of four types: (a) Āgamanīya-saddhā, (b) Adhigama-saddhā, (c) Pasāda-saddhā, and (d) Okappana-saddhā. Among these four: (a) Āgamanīya-saddhā is the faith that arises in the continuum of Bodhisattas due to the practice of the path (āgamanīya-paṭipadā) consisting of the noble perfections (pāramī), renunciation (cāga), and conduct (cariya) which lead to the attainment of Omniscience; it is a faith that enters into and becomes clear regarding the objects of devotion without being misled by others' instructions.
(b) Adhigama-saddhā is the faith that arises in the continuum of Noble Ones (ariyas) due to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths through the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa); it is a faith that cannot be destroyed by anyone (like the faith of the Ariya Surambhaṭṭha). (The story of the Ariya Surambhaṭṭha will be written when reaching the section on the Saṅgha Ratana).
(c) Pasāda-saddhā is the faith that arises, like that in the continuum of King Mahākappina and others, upon merely hearing the words "Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha." Even without a detailed explanation of the virtues of the Triple Gem, such as "The Blessed One has such and such virtues, the Dhamma has such and such virtues, the Saṅgha has such and such virtues,"
238:
but simply by hearing "Sammāsambuddho Bhagavā = The Blessed One is the fully enlightened one who knows all things clearly," faith and devotion arise toward the Triple Gem. (This is the kind of faith possessed by Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant, as described earlier starting from page 180 of Volume 3).
(d) Okappana-saddhā is the faith that, when others speak of "Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha," one investigates and contemplates the virtues of the Triple Gem with wisdom, and then believes with unshakeable conviction as if seeing it for oneself. In this first condition for non-decline, Pasāda-saddhā and Okappana-saddhā are to be taken.
(2-3) In the second and third conditions for non-decline, moral shame and disgust toward evil (hiri) and moral dread or fear of evil (ottappa)—the difference in their nature should be understood through the following simile: Suppose there are two iron balls, 1. an iron ball that is cold but smeared with excrement and filth, and 2. an iron ball that is glowing red-hot and burning. A wise person 1. would not dare to hold the first iron ball because of disgust and loathing for being smeared with excrement; 2. would not dare to hold the second iron ball because of fear of being burned. Similarly, a virtuous person 1. avoids and does not dare to commit evil because of hiri, which is the loathing of the base and filthy nature of misconduct, like the first iron ball; 2. avoids and does not dare to commit evil because of ottappa, which is the fear of the danger and punishment to be suffered in this life and the next due to that misconduct, like the second iron ball.
(4) In the fourth condition for non-decline, regarding "one who has great learning (bāhusacca)": (1) One who has scriptural learning (pariyatti-bāhusacca) = a person who has much learning in the Piṭaka scriptures.
239:
(2) One with penetrative knowledge (paṭivedha-bahussuta) = a person who possesses much supramundane knowledge of the Path and Fruit (magga-ñāṇa and phala-ñāṇa) that penetrates the Four Noble Truths. Thus, there are two types of learned persons (bahussuta). In this context, only the person of scriptural learning (pariyatti-bahussuta) is to be taken. This person of scriptural learning is further divided into four types: 1. Nissayamuccanaka-bahussuta = a person endowed with sufficient learning and qualifications to be independent of a teacher's guidance (nissaya); 2. Parisūpaṭṭhāka-bahussuta = a monk endowed with sufficient learning and qualifications to look after a following (sufficient to serve as an abbot); 3. Bhikkhunovādaka-bahussuta = a monk endowed with sufficient learning and qualifications to be formally designated as an exhorter of nuns; (The detailed meanings of these three types of persons should be studied and noted in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary on the Pācittiya, Ovāda-vagga, Vin.A. ii, 54). 4. Sabbatthaka-bahussuta = a monk who is not merely learned in a portion of the Tipitaka as defined for the previous three types, but like the Venerable Ānanda, is endowed with the learning and ability to speak and teach the entirety of the three Pitakas. In this context of the fourth condition for non-decline (aparihāniya-dhamma), the fourth type, the Sabbatthaka-bahussuta, is to be taken. The reason is that only such a person is well-established in the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-saddhamma), which is the root foundation of the Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti-saddhamma) and the Dhamma of penetration (paṭivedha-saddhamma).

(5) In the fifth condition for non-decline, regarding the phrase "those who have initiated effort (vīriya)," energy is of two kinds: 1. Kāyika-vīriya = bodily energy; 2. Cetasika-vīriya = mental energy. 1. Bodily energy refers to the energy that arises in the continuum of monks who live in solitude, having discarded the mingling with groups known as kāyasaṅgaṇikā, and who develop the eight grounds for the initiation of effort (vīriyārambhavatthu) in the four postures of lying, sitting, standing, and walking. 2. Mental energy refers to the energy of monks who, having discarded the mingling known as cittasaṅgaṇikā—where the six sense objects and defilements arise repeatedly—
240:
practice and enter the eight meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti) while living in solitude. They do not allow defilements that arise during walking to persist into the time of standing; they do not allow defilements that arise during standing to persist into the time of sitting; and they do not allow defilements that arise during sitting to persist into the time of lying down. Instead, they suppress the defilements right where they arise. This is called mental energy (cetasika-vīriya). The meaning is: "As long as the monks live endowed with these two kinds of energy—bodily and mental—they can be expected only to prosper and not to decline."

(6) In the sixth condition for non-decline, "those endowed with established mindfulness" refers to persons who can remember bodily and verbal actions performed or spoken a long time ago, such as the Elder Mahāgatimbaya Abhaya, the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, and the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. Among these three Elders cited as examples:

1. On the fifth day after his birth, during the festival of feeding the auspicious milk-rice, the Elder Mahāgatimbaya Abhaya saw a crow stretching its beak to eat the milk-rice from a bowl and made the sound "Hum, hum." Later, when that child became a monk and then a senior Elder, his disciples asked, "Venerable Sir, from what time do you remember your bodily and verbal actions?" He replied, "Friends, I remember from the time I made the sound 'Hum, hum' to scare away the crow on the fifth day after my birth."

2. On the ninth day after the birth of the child who would become the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, his mother, out of great love for her son, leaned over his face to kiss him. At that moment, her large hair-knot loosened and fell. A measure of jasmine flowers (mullai) then fell onto the child's chest, causing him pain and discomfort. When that child became the great Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, his disciples asked, "From what time
241:
do you remember, Venerable Sir?" He replied, "Friends, I remember from the ninth day after my birth."

3. As for the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, when his disciples asked, "Venerable Sir, how much can you remember and retain?" he replied, "Friends, if three of the four main gates of the city of Anurādhapura were closed, and people were made to exit through only one gate, and I were to ask each person, 'What is your name? What is your name?' and record all their names, and then in the evening when they were made to enter the city again, I could call out each person's name correctly without asking anew, saying, 'This person has this name, that person has that name.'"

(7) In the seventh condition for non-decline, "insight wisdom" (vipassanā-paññā) refers to the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-paññā) which discerns the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. Alternatively, the two terms mindfulness and wisdom mentioned in the sixth and seventh conditions refer to the right mindfulness (sammā-sati) and insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) that form the structure of insight for monks practicing vipassanā. (This means taking the mindfulness and wisdom that occur during the time of insight practice. This is a special point to be noted).

## The Fourth Set of Seven Conditions for Welfare
The Blessed One, in the same manner as before, further taught another seven conditions for non-decline:

(1) Monks, as long as the monks develop the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga), which is a cause for the Path, they can be expected only to prosper and not to decline.
242:
(2) Monks, as long as the monks develop the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga), which is a cause for the Path, (as above),
(3) the enlightenment factor of energy (vīriyasambojjhaṅga), which is a cause for the Path, (as above),
(4) the enlightenment factor of rapture (pītisambojjhaṅga), which is a cause for the Path, (as above),
(5) the enlightenment factor of tranquillity (passaddhisambojjhaṅga), which is a cause for the Path, (as above),
(6) the enlightenment factor of concentration (samādhisambojjhaṅga), which is a cause for the Path, (as above),
(7) Monks, as long as the monks develop the enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhāsambojjhaṅga), which is a cause for the Path, they can be expected only to prosper and not to decline.

Monks, as long as these seven conditions for welfare (aparihāniya-dhamma) endure among the monks, and as long as the monks practice these seven conditions for welfare, they can be expected only to prosper and not to decline. (The discourse has not yet ended).

(By these seven factors of enlightenment as conditions for welfare, the Buddha taught the factors of enlightenment associated with insight, the Path, and the Fruit, which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane states).

## The Fifth Set of Seven Conditions for Welfare
The Blessed One, in the same manner as before, further taught another seven conditions for non-decline:
243:
(1) Monks, as long as the monks develop the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā), they can be expected only to prosper and not to decline.
(2) Monks, as long as the monks develop the perception of non-self (anattasaññā), (as above),
(3) the perception of foulness (asubhasaññā), (as above),
(4) the perception of danger (ādīnavasaññā), (as above),
(5) the perception of abandoning (pahānasaññā), (as above),
(6) the perception of dispassion (virāgasaññā), which is the perception of Nibbāna as the state free from attachment, (as above),
(7) Monks, as long as the monks develop the perception of cessation (nirodhasaññā), (or) the perception of Nibbāna as the state of cessation, they can be expected only to prosper and not to decline.

Monks, as long as these seven conditions for welfare (aparihāniya-dhamma) endure among the monks, and as long as the monks practice these seven conditions for welfare, they can be expected only to prosper and not to decline. (The discourse has not yet ended).

(In this context: The perception (saññā) that occurs together with the wisdom of contemplation (anupassanā-paññā) which repeatedly observes things as impermanent is called the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā). The same applies to the perception of non-self, and so on. The wisdom (aniccavipassanā) which is the cause for contemplating the formations of the three planes (tebhūmaka-saṅkhāra) as impermanent is called the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā).
244:
When one develops the perception (saññā) that occurs together with that wisdom, it is also said that one develops wisdom (paññā). Therefore, in the Pali text, it is taught as "perception of impermanence" (aniccasaññā), etc. (Alternatively) It is a teaching that points specifically to insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) by making perception the primary factor. The same applies to the perception of non-self, and so on.

Among these seven perceptions as conditions for welfare, the first five are exclusively mundane (lokiya), while the last two are a mixture of mundane and supramundane (lokuttara). This is a special point to be noted).

## The Six Conditions for Welfare of Monks
The Blessed One, wishing to further teach the six conditions for welfare to the monks, said: "Monks, I shall teach you the six conditions for welfare. Listen to them, attend well to them, and I shall speak in detail." When he had said this, the monks replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir." The Blessed One then taught these six conditions for welfare (aparihāniya-dhamma):

(1) Monks, as long as the monks maintain acts of body (kāyakamma) based on loving-kindness (mettā) towards their fellow practitioners, both in public and in private, they can be expected only to prosper and not to decline.

(2) Monks, as long as the monks maintain acts of speech (vacīkamma) based on loving-kindness (mettā) towards their fellow practitioners, both in public and in private, they can be expected only to prosper and not to decline.
245:
(3) Monks, as long as monks maintain mental acts of loving-kindness (manokamma) toward their fellow practitioners, both openly and privately, they may be expected to prosper and not decline.
(4) Monks, as long as monks share their lawful gains (dhammiya lābha) acquired in accordance with the Dhamma—even if it be only the contents of their alms bowl—without reservation, and use them in common with their virtuous fellow practitioners, they may be expected to prosper and not decline.
(5) Monks, as long as monks live among their fellow practitioners, both openly and privately, endowed with those virtues (sīla) that are conducive to liberation from the slavery of craving, praised by the wise, not misapprehended, leading to concentration, and which are unbroken, untorn, unblotched, and unmottled, they may be expected to prosper and not decline.
(6) Monks, as long as monks live among their fellow practitioners, both openly and privately, endowed with that noble wisdom (ariya paññā) which leads to the cessation of suffering for those who follow it, they may be expected to prosper and not decline.
Monks, as long as these six conditions for non-decline (aparihāniya dhamma) remain established among the monks, and as long as the monks abide by these six conditions for non-decline,
246:
they may be expected to prosper and not decline. Thus, the Blessed One taught the monks the conditions for non-decline in six sets: five sets of seven conditions and one set of six conditions.
(1-2-3) All bodily actions performed with a mind of loving-kindness are called mettā-kāyakamma. All verbal actions spoken with a mind of loving-kindness are called mettā-vacīkamma. All mental actions thought with a mind of loving-kindness are called mettā-manokamma.
In the Pāḷi texts, these three—mettā-kāyakamma, mettā-vacīkamma, and mettā-manokamma—are taught in relation to monks because they are the foremost among the fourfold assembly. However, since the Buddha's teaching concerns the entire fourfold assembly, these three types of loving-kindness are also applicable to laypeople. The manner of application is as follows:
For monks, performing major and minor duties with a mind of loving-kindness is called mettā-kāyakamma. For laypeople, actions such as going to worship a stupa, venerating a Bodhi tree, or going to invite the Saṅgha; and upon seeing a monk entering the village for alms, welcoming him, taking his bowl, preparing a seat, and accompanying him when he departs—all such actions are called mettā-kāyakamma.
For monks, explaining and demonstrating the training rules (sikkhāpada) to be followed with a mind of loving-kindness,
247:
teaching meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), preaching other Dhamma, and in short, teaching and transmitting the three Piṭakas, is called mettā-vacīkamma. For laypeople, saying things such as, "Let us go to worship the stupa; let us go to venerate the Bodhi tree; let us go to listen to the Dhamma; let us perform the act of listening to the Dhamma; let us offer lamps, water, and flowers; let us well-establish and practice the three types of good conduct (sucarita); let us offer food by lottery (salāka-bhatta); let us offer rainy-season robes; let us today offer the four requisites to the Saṅgha; (after inviting the Saṅgha) prepare the food and snacks; arrange the seats; set out drinking water; welcome and escort the Saṅgha; have them sit in the prepared seats; and perform the service (veyyāvacca) with ardent desire and effort"—all such speech is called mettā-vacīkamma.
For monks, waking up early, performing duties such as cleaning the stupa courtyard, and then sitting in a secluded place and reflecting, "May the monks residing in this monastery be happy, be free from enmity, and be free from ill-will and distress"—this is called mettā-manokamma. For laypeople, reflecting and keeping in mind, "May the noble ones be happy, be free from enmity, and be free from ill-will and distress"—this is called mettā-manokamma.
248:
## Sammukhā-mettā and Parammukhā-mettā
## (Open Loving-kindness and Private Loving-kindness)
All actions, speech, and thoughts performed with a mind of loving-kindness in the presence of others are called sammukhā-mettā. All actions, speech, and thoughts performed with a mind of loving-kindness in the absence of others are called parammukhā-mettā.
Among these two, when elder monks assist junior monks in tasks such as sewing robes, it is the elders' sammukhā-mettā-kāyakamma (open bodily act of loving-kindness). When junior monks perform respectful acts for elders, such as washing their feet, bowing, or fanning them, it is the juniors' sammukhā-mettā-kāyakamma. When both juniors and elders see property, such as wooden utensils, left in disorder by their owners and, without any contempt for the owners, respectfully put them away as if they were their own, it is parammukhā-mettā-kāyakamma (private bodily act of loving-kindness).
When speaking in someone's presence, addressing them with praise such as "Venerable Deva Thera" or "Venerable Tissa Thera" is sammukhā-mettā-vacīkamma (open verbal act of loving-kindness). When wishing to ask about a monk who is not in the monastery, saying with affection and respect, "Where is our Venerable Deva Thera? Where is our Venerable Tissa Thera? When will he return?"
249:
inquiring in such a manner is parammukhā-mettā-vacīkamma (private verbal act of loving-kindness).
When one looks with eyes that are gentle and moist with the essence of loving-kindness and with a very clear and joyful face in someone's presence, the mental volition (cetanā) that causes such a look is sammukhā-mettā-manokamma (open mental act of loving-kindness). (Opening eyes that are gentle and moist with loving-kindness and looking with a clear, joyful face are themselves mettā-kāyakamma). Reflecting in someone's absence, "May the Venerable Deva Thera and Venerable Tissa Thera be free from illness," is parammukhā-mettā-manokamma (private mental act of loving-kindness).
(4) Regarding the fourth condition for non-decline, the phrase "without reservation" (lit. "without dividing separately") refers to two types of division: 1. Division of material gains (āmisa), and 2. Division of persons (puggala). Among these, 1. Thinking, "I will give only this much; I will not give that much," is the division of material gains. 2. Thinking, "I will give to this monk; I will not give to that monk," is the division of persons.
In this fourth condition, the characteristic of a monk who uses gains "in common with his virtuous fellow practitioners" is as follows:
250:
Whatever excellent alms-food he receives, he does not give it to laypeople with the primary aim of seeking further gains through that gift, nor does he eat it himself first. He eats only what remains after distributing it to the Saṅgha. From the moment of receiving, he accepts it with the thought, "Let this be shared with the Saṅgha," and regards it like communal property (sāṅghika) to be consumed after the sounding of the bell or gong. This practice is called the sāraṇīyavatta (duty of courtesy) in the Dispensation.
## Facts to Note Regarding Sāraṇīyavatta
Which monk can practice this sāraṇīyavatta, and which monk cannot? Firstly, an immoral monk (dussīla) cannot fulfill it. Indeed, virtuous monks will not accept the property of an immoral monk in any way. Therefore, an immoral monk cannot fulfill this sāraṇīyavatta.
Only a monk with perfectly pure virtue can fulfill it. Such a virtuous monk must fulfill this sāraṇīyavatta without break or interruption. The following is the method of practice in the context of these sāraṇīyadhamma:
If a monk gives to his mother, his father, or his teachers and preceptors (upajjhāya) by making a specific designation, he is merely a monk who gives what ought to be given. His giving is not the fulfillment of the sāraṇīyavatta; in the Dispensation, it is called "clearing away impediments" (palibodha).
251:
Indeed, the sāraṇīyavatta is suitable only for a monk who has already cleared his impediments.
A monk who truly wishes to fulfill the sāraṇīyavatta may give by designation to a sick monk, a monk attending the sick, a visiting monk (āgantuka), a traveling monk, or a new monk who is not yet proficient in handling his robes and bowl. After giving to them, if alms-food still remains in his bowl, he should offer as much as the elder monks wish to receive, starting from the seat of the most senior elder. If no alms-food remains in the bowl (and there is still time for alms-round), he should go for alms again and, starting from the senior elder's seat, offer whatever excellent food they desire. Only if alms-food still remains in the bowl should he eat it himself. (If no food remains and the time for alms-round has passed, he should not be discouraged, but should remain with joy and rapture, reflecting on the sāraṇīyavatta he has fulfilled). A special note: Since the Pāḷi text specifies "with virtuous fellow practitioners," it is also permissible not to give to an immoral monk. If one wishes to give, one may do so out of compassion, but it is not for the purpose of fulfilling the duty (vatta).
In a community of monks (Saṅgha) that is well-versed and proficient in the procedure for fulfilling the sāraṇīyavatta, it is easy to practice this duty. Regarding the procedure for the Saṅgha to fulfill that duty—
252:
252
If it is an unskilled and undisciplined assembly, it is not easy to fulfill [the practice]; it is very difficult.

If it is a well-informed, skilled, and disciplined assembly of the Saṅgha, the fulfillment is easy and pleasant. In such a skilled assembly, a monk who has already received alms-food from elsewhere does not accept more. A monk who has not received alms-food from elsewhere accepts only in moderation (so as not to cause hardship to the monk performing the duty) and does not take in excess. Thus, if it is a well-informed and skilled assembly of the Saṅgha, it is very easy and pleasant to fulfill the Sāraṇīya duties. However, in an assembly of the Saṅgha that is uninformed and unskilled in the procedure of fulfilling that practice, even a monk who has received alms-food from elsewhere might accept more out of greed. A monk who has not received alms-food might also accept more than the proper measure. In such a case, the monk performing the duty has to go for alms repeatedly throughout the time, and whatever is obtained is exhausted. Since the practitioner monk may face hunger day after day, it is not easy and is very difficult to fulfill the Sāraṇīya duties in an uninformed and unskilled assembly.

## Success Only After Twelve Years of Practice
For the monk who fulfills the duty by repeatedly going for alms as described and offering whatever alms-food is obtained to his virtuous fellow practitioners, this Sāraṇīya duty is only successfully completed after fulfilling it for a full twelve years.
253:
253
If twelve years are not completed, success cannot be achieved.

Suppose on the day the twelve years are completed, the monk fulfilling the Sāraṇīya duty leaves his bowl full of alms-food in a suitable place and goes to bathe. If a senior elder (Mahāthera) asks, "Whose bowl is this?" and the other monks reply, "It is the bowl of the monk who fulfills the Sāraṇīya duty," and the senior elder then says, "If that is so, bring that bowl," and distributes all the food according to seniority for them to eat, leaving the bowl empty; if the monk fulfilling the Sāraṇīya duty later sees the empty bowl and feels displeasure, thinking, "They have eaten it all without leaving anything for me," then his Sāraṇīya duty is broken. He must fulfill it again for another twelve years. Indeed, this Sāraṇīya duty is similar to the probation for sectarians (tittiya-parivāsa); if it is broken once, it must be practiced anew from the beginning.

However, if the monk fulfilling the Sāraṇīya duty sees the empty bowl after his fellow practitioners have eaten in his absence and (unlike the previous case) feels joy, thinking, "Oh, the venerable fellow practitioners have enjoyed the food in my bowl even without asking me; it is a great gain for me," then that monk's Sāraṇīya duty is said to be successfully completed.
254:
254
## Benefits of Practicing the Sāraṇīya Duties
In the continuity of a monk who has successfully fulfilled the Sāraṇīya duties for twelve years, the following benefits occur:

(1) Envy (issā) and stinginess (macchariya) do not arise because they have been removed by long-term cultivation of meditation.
(2) Because he is purified by the habit of generosity, he is loved and cherished by all people who see him.
(3) He easily obtains the four requisites because the meritorious intention of individuals with strong desire for giving has the nature of yielding the benefit of obtaining material things even in this very life.
(4) Because he has fulfilled the noble practice without interruption for twelve years with the alms-food in his bowl, the food in his bowl will not be exhausted no matter how much he gives to others.
(5) Because he has offered alms-food daily to noble recipients among his fellow practitioners, starting from the seniors, he receives the best and most excellent goods at the place where the Saṅgha's property and goods are distributed.
(6) Because he has a heart purified by long-term practice of the duty of giving without discriminating between the objects to be given or the recipients, and without any selfish desire for himself, deities will take care to help him escape from any dangers or famines (dubbhikkha) that may arise.
255:

## Illustrative Stories
(1) Tissa Thera, who resided at the mountain monastery called Sena, lived depending on the village of Mahāgiri as his resort village. At one time, fifty elders went to worship the Nagadīpa Cetiya. They wandered for alms in Mahāgiri village but did not receive anything at all and left the village. The aforementioned Tissa Thera, who was a resident monk (āvāsika), saw those fifty elders as he was entering for alms and asked, "Venerable sirs, did you receive alms-food?"

When the fifty elders replied suggestively, "We have wandered for alms, friend," Tissa Thera clearly understood that they had not received any food and said, "Venerable sirs, please remain right here until I return."

The fifty elders said, "Friend, all fifty of us did not get even enough to coat a bowl; (how can you alone get it?)" Tissa Thera replied, "Venerable sirs, those who are permanent residents (nevāsika) and local monks (āvāsika) are capable. Even those who do not have great merit or many gains know the alms-routes where food can be obtained." The fifty elders then waited there.

Tissa Thera entered the village of Mahāgiri for alms. At the very first house at the entrance of the village,
256:
256
the female lay devotee of the house had prepared milk-rice and was standing waiting for Tissa Thera. Then, as soon as he reached the door of her house, she offered a bowl full of milk-rice to the noble Tissa Thera.

Tissa Thera took the milk-rice offered by the devotee, went to the elders, and said to the senior elder, "Please accept this, venerable sirs." The senior elder thought, "We fifty, being so many, did not receive even a tiny bit to coat a bowl. This monk, however, has brought milk-rice so quickly. What is the meaning of this?" With a look of amazement, he looked at the faces of the other forty-nine monks. Tissa Thera understood the elder's thought just by his expression and said, "Venerable sir, this is alms-food obtained in accordance with the Dhamma. Please accept it without any doubt or remorse (kukkucca)." Starting from the senior elder, he offered the milk-rice to all fifty elders until they were satisfied, and finally, he himself ate the milk-rice until he was satisfied.

When the meal was finished, the fifty elders asked Tissa Thera, "Friend, at what time did you penetrate the Supramundane Dhamma?" Tissa Thera replied, "Venerable sirs, I do not yet possess the Supramundane Dhamma."
257:
257
The fifty elders asked again, "Friend, if that is so, are you one who has attained mundane jhāna?" Tissa Thera replied, "Venerable sirs, I do not possess that jhāna you mention either."

The fifty elders said, "Friend, while all fifty of us did not get even a coating of a bowl, is it not a miracle of your psychic power that you easily obtained such excellent milk-rice?"

Then, because the Sāraṇīya practice is not a superhuman state (uttari-manussa-dhamma), and because he wished to remove the doubts of the fifty elders, Tissa Thera confessed, "Venerable sirs, I have fully practiced the Sāraṇīya duties. For me, from the time I completed those Sāraṇīya duties, even if there were a hundred thousand fellow monks and I offered them alms-food, the food in my bowl would not be exhausted." The fifty elders expressed their joy, saying, "O virtuous one, well done, well done! This miracle is very fitting and suitable for a virtuous person like you."

This story is the evidence for the fourth benefit: "The food in his bowl will not be exhausted no matter how much he gives to others."

Regarding the second benefit, "Being loved and cherished by all people," and the third benefit, "Easily obtaining the four requisites,"
258:
258
this same story serves as evidence. However, because the inexhaustibility of the food in the bowl is particularly prominent in this story, the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) states that this story is the evidence for the fourth benefit.

(2) This same Venerable Tissa Thera arrived at the place of distribution during the Giribhaṇḍa Mahāpūjā festival held at the Cetiya Mountain monastery. He asked his fellow monks, "What is the best and most excellent gift in this place of distribution?" The monks replied, "Two pieces of smooth and fine cloth for robes are the best and most excellent gifts." Tissa Thera then said, "Those two pieces of cloth will come to me."

Hearing those words, a minister reported to the King, "A young monk spoke in this manner." The King said, "Even if such a thought arises in a young monk, those smooth and fine robe-cloths are only suitable and fitting for the senior elders." Thinking, "I will offer them to the senior elders," he kept them aside.

* The Giribhaṇḍa Mahāpūjā festival is a "grand island-wide festival of worship" held at Cetiya Mountain and throughout the entire island of Sri Lanka, where offerings of lamps, flowers, and perfumes are made, even on rafts and boats in the ocean for about a league (yojana) around.

259
Then, when the Saṅgha of monks stood according to their seniority, and the King himself was making the offerings, those two robes did not come into the King's hand even though they were placed at the very front; instead, only other offerings came to him. However, when he was about to offer to the young monk, Venerable Tissa, those two wondrous robes came into the King's hand.

The King offered those two robes into the hand of Venerable Tissa. Looking at the face of his minister, he had the young monk Venerable Tissa remain seated and continued to offer the gifts. After dismissing the Saṅgha, he sat near the young monk Venerable Tissa and asked, “Venerable Sir, when did you attain this special Dhamma?” The Elder Tissa, not wishing to speak of supramundane (lokuttara) Dhamma that he did not actually possess, even by way of metaphor, replied honestly, “Great King, I do not yet possess the supramundane Dhamma.” The King then said, “Venerable Sir, did you not say before the offering, ‘Those two robes will come to me’?” The Elder Tissa replied, “Great King, yes, I did say that. I am a monk who fulfills the duties of friendliness (sāraṇīya-vatta). From the time I fulfilled those duties of friendliness, at the place where the Saṅgha’s offerings and property are distributed, the foremost and most excellent

offerings and property come only to me.” The King said, “Venerable Sir, well said, well said! This miraculous power is indeed suitable and worthy of you.” Having spoken thus and paid homage, he returned to the golden palace. This is the testimonial story for the 5th benefit: “One receives the best and most excellent property at the place where the Saṅgha’s property is distributed.”

(3) Furthermore, when the great peril of Brāhmaṇa Tissa occurred on the island of Sri Lanka, all the people living in the village named Bhātara fled to another place due to the danger of the rebel Brāhmaṇa Tissa, without informing the Elder Nun (Therī) named Nāgā. At dawn, the Elder Nun Nāgā said to the young nuns, “The village of Bhātara is very silent. Go and investigate.” The young nuns went and found that all the villagers had fled. They returned and reported the matter to the Elder Nun Nāgā.

Upon hearing this, the Elder Nun Nāgā said, “Sisters, do not worry or have various anxious thoughts about the fact that all the villagers have fled. Just strive diligently in your respective duties of learning the Pāḷi, learning the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), and practicing meditation (kammaṭṭhāna).” Having said this, when the time for alms-round arrived, she robed herself and, being the twelfth in the group (leading eleven other nuns),
261:
261
(leading eleven other nuns behind her), she stood at the foot of a great banyan tree near the gate of Bhātara village. The deity guarding the banyan tree offered a complete meal to all twelve nuns and then invited them, saying, “Venerable ladies, please do not go elsewhere; please always come only to this banyan tree.”

In particular, there was an Elder named Nāga, who was the younger brother of the Elder Nun Nāgā. That Elder Nāga thought, “The peril is great; I cannot survive on this island of Sri Lanka. I shall go to the other side of the ocean.” Being the twelfth in his group (taking eleven other monks with him), as he left his monastery, he thought, “I will go after seeing my elder sister, the Elder Nun Nāgā,” and thus he came to Bhātara village. The Elder Nun Nāgā heard the news that the Elders had arrived, went to them, and asked, “Venerable sirs, what is the reason for your coming?” Elder Nāga explained the situation. The Elder Nun Nāgā pleaded, “Venerable sirs, please rest in the monastery for just this one day and proceed only tomorrow.” The twelve Elders then went and stayed in the monastery.

The next day, the Elder Nun Nāgā went for alms at the foot of the banyan tree, approached Elder Nāga, and said, “Venerable sirs, please accept and consume this alms-food.”
262:
262
Elder Nāga asked, “Elder Nun, is it truly allowable (kappa)?” and remained standing in silence. The Elder Nun Nāgā replied, “Younger brother, this alms-food is rightfully obtained. Please consume it without any hesitation (kukkucca) as to whether it is allowable or not.” Elder Nāga asked again, “Is it truly allowable, Elder Nun?” expressing his hesitation repeatedly.

## The Bold Spirit of Elder Nāga

Then, the Elder Nun Nāgā took the alms-bowl and threw it into the air. The bowl remained suspended in the sky. Elder Nāga said, “Elder Nun, even if it stays at the height of seven palm trees, it is still the food of a bhikkhunī. Peril does not last forever. When this famine subsides, I, who preach the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma, will not be able to stand firm if my own mind reproaches me, saying, ‘O you who observed the dhutaṅga of alms-food, you survived the peril of Brāhmaṇa Tissa by consuming the food of a bhikkhunī.’ Therefore, sisters, remain diligent (appamāda).” Having given this exhortation of diligence, he set out on his journey.

The deity guarding the banyan tree thought, “If Elder Nāga accepts and consumes the food from the hand of the Elder Nun Nāgā, I will not
263:
263
request him to stay. But if he does not consume it, I will plead with him to stay.” While standing there, the deity witnessed Elder Nāga continuing his journey without consuming the Elder Nun’s food. The deity descended from the banyan tree, said, “Venerable sirs, please give me the bowl,” took the bowl from the Elder’s hand, and invited Elder Nāga back to the foot of the banyan tree. After preparing a seat and offering alms-food, and once Elder Nāga had finished his meal, the deity pleaded with him to stay in that very place. Having received the Elder’s promise to stay, the deity supported the twelve nuns and twelve monks for seven years. This is the testimonial story for the 6th benefit: “Deities take care to help them escape from those perils.” In this story, the Elder Nun Nāgā was one who had fulfilled the practice of the duties of friendliness (sāraṇီya-vatta). As for Elder Nāga, the deity took care of him due to the power of his virtue (sīla).

(5) Regarding the fifth condition of non-decline (aparihāniya-dhamma), “virtues that are unbroken, untattered, unspotted, and unblemished”: For monks, this refers to the seven categories of offenses (āpatti) according to the Pātimokkha; for laypeople and novices, it refers to the precepts (sikkhāpada) they have undertaken. If a precept is broken at the beginning or at the end, that person’s virtue is called “broken virtue” (khanda-sīla), like a cloth torn at the edges or borders. If a precept is broken in the middle,
264:
264
that person’s virtue is called “untattered virtue” (chidda-sīla), like a cloth with a hole in the middle. If two or three precepts are broken in succession, that person’s virtue is called “spotted virtue” (sabala-sīla), like a cow with patches of a different color on its back or belly.
