If precepts are broken here and there, that monk’s virtue is called “blemished virtue” (kammāsa-sīla), like a brindled cow. Only virtue that is not broken in any of these four ways—not broken at the beginning or end, not broken in the middle, not broken in succession, and not broken here and there—is called “virtue that is unbroken, untattered, unspotted, and unblemished.” (See also Mahā Buddhavaṃsa, Vol. 1, Part 1, Anudīpanī, page Pa-Pa-Pha).

Virtues endowed with these four qualities can serve as a strong support (upanissaya-paccaya) for the Path and Fruit (Magga-Phala). Thus, one endowed with such virtue can live freely and happily as they wish; such virtues are called those that liberate one from being a slave to craving (taṇhā). Being extremely pure, they are called virtues praised by the wise, such as the Buddha. Because they are not grasped by craving, such as thinking, “By this virtue, may I become a certain prominent or obscure deity,” nor by wrong view (diṭṭhi), such as thinking that such a divine life is “permanent, stable, and eternal,” and because others cannot accuse or destroy them by pointing out any of the four failures (vipatti), saying, “This is a fault in your virtue,”
265:
265
...these are called virtues that are not misapprehended (aparāmaṭṭha-sīla). Because they can beautifully bring about both access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), they are called virtues conducive to concentration (samādhi-saṃvattanika-sīla). Since the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) of a worldling (puthujjana) cannot be perfectly consistent, whereas only the virtue of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) is perfectly consistent, the Blessed One taught this fifth condition of welfare (aparihāniya dhamma) with reference to the supramundane Path-virtue (lokuttara-magga-sīla). Similarly, in the sixth condition of welfare, the Blessed One taught the supramundane wisdom of the Right View of the Noble Path (lokuttara-ariyama-magga-sammādiṭṭhi-paññā). (These six conditions of welfare were also taught by the Blessed One as the six principles of cordiality (sāraṇīya dhamma) in Aṅguttara Nikāya 2-255 and Dīgha Nikāya 3, 202).
## Teaching Frequently on Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom
Thus, while the Blessed One was staying at the Gijjhakūṭa hill monastery in Rājagaha (knowing that He would pass into Parinibbāna in one year and three months), as the time for His Parinibbāna drew near, He frequently gave this specific Dhamma teaching to the monks:
“Such is virtue (sīla); such is concentration (samādhi); such is wisdom (paññā). Concentration, when firmly established on virtue, brings great fruit and profit. Wisdom, when firmly established on concentration, brings great fruit and profit. The mind, when firmly established on wisdom...”
266:
The mind that is thus developed is fully liberated from the taints (āsavas), namely, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava), without leaving even a trace.

## Departure for Ambalaṭṭhikā

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Rājagaha as long as he liked, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to Ambalaṭṭhikā." "Very well, Bhante," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.

(Note: The Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda because he was the Buddha's constant attendant, not because there were no other monks present. In fact, at that time, the number of monks staying with the Blessed One was very large.)

After replying to the Blessed One, the Venerable Ānanda urged the monks: "Friends, take your bowls and robes; the Blessed One wishes to depart for Ambalaṭṭhikā."

Then the Blessed One, accompanied by a large community of monks, went to Ambalaṭṭhikā and stayed at the royal rest house (Rājāgāraka). While staying at the royal rest house in Ambalaṭṭhikā, the Blessed One, as the time for his Parinibbāna was drawing near, gave this same discourse to the monks many times:
267:
"Such is virtue (sīla), such is concentration (samādhi), such is wisdom (paññā). Concentration, when supported by virtue, brings great fruit and profit. Wisdom, when supported by concentration, brings great fruit and profit. The mind, when supported by wisdom, is fully liberated from the taints, namely, the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance, without leaving even a trace."

(Note: In the phrase "Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom," virtue refers to the mundane fourfold purification of virtue (lokiya catupārisuddhi-sīla), concentration refers to mundane access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), and wisdom refers to mundane insight-wisdom (lokiya vipassanā-paññā), which serve as the foundation for the Path.

In "concentration supported by virtue," concentration refers to the supramundane concentration of the Path (magga-samādhi) and Fruition (phala-samādhi). Of these two, Path-concentration has the great fruit of the Noble Fruition (the primary result is called 'phala'). It has the great profit of the cooling of the suffering of the round of rebirth (the secondary result is called 'āniśaṃsa'). The same applies hereafter. Fruition-concentration has the primary result of abandoning the defilements through tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna) and the secondary result of producing the bliss of the cessation of defilements (nibbuti-sukha).

In "wisdom supported by concentration," wisdom refers to the supramundane wisdom of the Path and Fruition. The primary and secondary results of these two types of wisdom are similar to those of concentration.

In "the mind supported by wisdom," wisdom refers to mundane insight-wisdom and the wisdom associated with jhāna-concentration. The mind refers to the supramundane Path-consciousness and Fruition-consciousness. It means that the Path-consciousness liberates from the taints through the abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), and the Fruition-consciousness liberates through abandonment by tranquilization, leaving not even a trace or scent of the taints.)
268:
## Departure for Nāḷandā

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Ambalaṭṭhikā as long as he liked, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to Nāḷandā." "Very well, Bhante," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and then urged the monks as before.

## Venerable Sāriputta's Bold Declaration

Then the Blessed One, together with a large community of monks, arrived at Nāḷandā and stayed at Pāvārika's Mango Grove.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down. He then addressed the Blessed One with these bold words:

(Venerable Sāriputta): "Bhante, I have such faith in the Blessed One that I believe there has not been, will not be, nor is there now any other ascetic or brahmin who is greater or more enlightened than the Blessed One in terms of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)."

(The Buddha): "Sāriputta, you have spoken these grand and imposing words; you have spoken with certainty. You have roared a bold lion's roar, saying: 'Bhante, I have such faith in the Blessed One that I believe there has not been, will not be, nor is there now any other ascetic or brahmin who is greater or more enlightened than the Blessed One in terms of omniscience.'"
269:
"Sāriputta, what do you say? Have you encompassed with your own mind the minds of all the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas of the past, and known that those Blessed Ones had such virtue, such concentration, such wisdom, such dwelling, and such liberation?"

(Venerable Sāriputta): "No, Bhante."

(The Buddha): "Sāriputta, what do you say? Have you encompassed with your own mind the minds of all the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas of the future, and known that those Blessed Ones will have such virtue, such concentration, such wisdom, such dwelling, and such liberation?"

(Venerable Sāriputta): "No, Bhante."

(The Buddha): "Sāriputta, what do you say? Have you encompassed with your own mind my mind, I who am now the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, and known that the Blessed One has such virtue, such concentration, such wisdom, such dwelling, and such liberation?"

(Venerable Sāriputta): "No, Bhante."

(The Buddha): "Sāriputta, since you do not have the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa) to know the minds of the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas of the past, future, and present, why then, Sāriputta, have you spoken these grand, imposing, and certain words, roaring a bold lion's roar, saying: 'Bhante, I have such faith in the Blessed One that I believe there has not been, will not be, nor is there now any other ascetic or brahmin who is greater or more enlightened than the Blessed One in terms of omniscience'?"
270:
(Venerable Sāriputta): "Bhante, I do not have the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa) to know the minds of the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas of the past, future, and present. However, Bhante, I have the knowledge of inference from the Dhamma (dhammanvaya-ñāṇa).

Bhante, suppose there were a royal frontier city with strong foundations, strong walls and towers, and a single gate. There would be a wise, intelligent, and prudent gatekeeper who would stop those he did not know and allow only those he knew to enter. As he patrols the path around the city, he might not see a gap or an opening in the wall even large enough for a cat to pass through. He would then conclude:

'Whatever large creatures enter or leave this city, they all enter or leave through this single gate.'

In the same way, Bhante, I have the knowledge of inference from the Dhamma. Bhante, all the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas of the past, having abandoned the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) that defile the mind and weaken wisdom,
271:
with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and having correctly developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) which lead to the realization of Nibbāna, attained the supreme perfect enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa) and became Buddhas. (The knowledge of the Path of Arahantship and the knowledge of omniscience, which belong only to the Buddhas, are called Sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa).

Bhante, all the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas of the future, will also abandon the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, and with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, and having correctly developed the seven factors of enlightenment, will attain the supreme perfect enlightenment and become Buddhas.

Bhante, the Blessed One, who is now the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, has also abandoned the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, and with his mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, and having correctly developed the seven factors of enlightenment, has attained the supreme perfect enlightenment and become the Buddha. Thus, Bhante, I have the knowledge of inference from the Dhamma." (This is the account of the bold dialogue between the Venerable Sāriputta and the Blessed One.)
272:
While the Blessed One was staying in the mango grove of the wealthy merchant Pāvārika in the city of Nālandā, as the time for his Parinibbāna drew near, he frequently gave this Dhamma discourse to the monks:
"Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom. Concentration, when fortified by virtue, brings great fruit and great benefit. Wisdom, when fortified by concentration, brings great fruit and great benefit. The mind, when fortified by wisdom, is fully liberated from the taints—namely, the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance."
## The Five Dangers for One Who Fails in Virtue
Then, the Blessed One, having stayed in Nālandā as long as he desired, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to Pāṭaligāma." "Yes, Bhante," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. He then informed and urged the monks as before. Then the Blessed One, together with a large company of monks, proceeded to Pāṭaligāma.
When the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma heard the news that the Blessed One had arrived at Pāṭaligāma, they thought: "We should have gone to invite the Blessed One ourselves, but now the Blessed One has come to our village of Pāṭaligāma on his own without being invited."
273:
"Today, let us invite the Blessed One and have him deliver a discourse of blessing and appreciation in the rest-house we have just finished building." Having consulted and agreed, they went to the presence of the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down at a respectful distance, and requested: "Bhante, may the Blessed One accept the rest-house that we have recently constructed." The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent.
Then the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma, knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and went to the rest-house. There, they spread mats everywhere, prepared seats, set up a large water pot, and lit lamps. After arranging for the children in the village to be fed, nursed, and put to bed early, they returned to the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood to one side, saying:
"Bhante, the rest-house has been fully carpeted with mats, seats have been prepared, the large water pot has been set up, and the lamps have been lit. Bhante, the Blessed One may now go whenever he deems it the right time."
(Note: The officials of the Licchavī kings and the Magadhan kings frequently came to Pāṭaligāma, which was a border village, and forced the villagers out of their homes to stay there for a month or half a month. The villagers, constantly facing such hardships, agreed among themselves: "When these officials come, let there be a place for them to stay." Thus, they built a large rest-house in the middle of the village, with elegant and well-furnished rooms for living, sitting, and storing goods. Just as the construction of this large rest-house was completed, they heard the good news of the Blessed One's arrival in their village and, as mentioned, went to invite him.
274:
Initially, the villagers thought, "The Buddhas delight in forest dwellings and might not wish to stay within the village." Not knowing the Blessed One's preference, they did not clean or prepare the rest-house before coming to him. However, once they knew the Blessed One's intention, they went ahead to prepare the rest-house and then invited him.)
When they had invited him, the Blessed One dressed in the evening, took his bowl and robe, and went to the rest-house with the company of monks. After washing his feet, he entered the rest-house and sat down, leaning against the central pillar, facing East. The company of monks also washed their feet, entered the rest-house, and sat down against the West wall, facing East, with the Blessed One in front of them. The lay followers of Pāṭaligāma also washed their feet, entered the rest-house, and sat down against the East wall, facing West, with the Blessed One in front of them.
Then the Blessed One addressed the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma regarding the five dangers for one who fails in virtue and the five benefits for one who possesses virtue, as follows:
275:
"Householders, there are these five dangers for an immoral person through their failure in virtue. What five?
(1) Householders, here an immoral person, failing in virtue, suffers great loss of wealth through heedlessness. This is the first danger for an immoral person through their failure in virtue.
(2) Furthermore, householders, an immoral person, failing in virtue, gets a bad reputation. This is the second danger for an immoral person through their failure in virtue.
(3) Furthermore, householders, an immoral person, failing in virtue, whenever they enter an assembly—whether of kings, brahmins, householders, or ascetics—enters timidly and with a downcast face. This is the third danger for an immoral person through their failure in virtue.
(4) Furthermore, householders, an immoral person, failing in virtue, dies confused. This is the fourth danger for an immoral person through their failure in virtue.
(5) Furthermore, householders, an immoral person, failing in virtue, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell. This is the fifth danger for an immoral person through their failure in virtue.
276:
Householders, these are the five dangers for an immoral person through their failure in virtue.
## The Five Benefits for One Who Possesses Virtue
(1) Householders, here a virtuous person, accomplished in virtue, acquires a great mass of wealth through heedfulness. This is the first benefit for a virtuous person through their accomplishment in virtue.
(2) Furthermore, householders, a virtuous person, accomplished in virtue, gets a good reputation. This is the second benefit for a virtuous person through their accomplishment in virtue.
(3) Furthermore, householders, a virtuous person, accomplished in virtue, whenever they enter an assembly—whether of kings, brahmins, householders, or ascetics—enters confident and without a downcast face. This is the third benefit for a virtuous person through their accomplishment in virtue.
(4) Furthermore, householders, a virtuous person, accomplished in virtue, dies unconfused. This is the fourth benefit for a virtuous person through their accomplishment in virtue.
(5) Furthermore, householders, a virtuous person, accomplished in virtue, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
277:
This is the fifth benefit for a virtuous person through their accomplishment in virtue.
Householders, these are the five benefits for a virtuous person through their accomplishment in virtue." Thus he taught.
(In this context:
"Loss of wealth, bad reputation spreads, fear in assemblies, dying confused, and going to hell—these five dangers should be noted for the immoral.
Acquiring wealth, good reputation spreads, no fear in assemblies, dying unconfused, and going to heaven—these five benefits should be noted for the virtuous."
This mnemonic verse should be memorized. Although this teaching was given in relation to laypeople, it also applies to monks. The way it applies to both laypeople and monks is as follows:
A layperson, while earning a blameless living through farming, trade, etc., if they neglect their conduct and become heedless by killing living beings and so on, they can no longer perform their regular farming or trading at the proper time. In that case, let alone profit, even their capital is lost and destroyed. When kings announce by beat of drum that no one should kill animals, if one commits the act of taking life (pāṇātipāta) or stealing others' property, they will face royal punishment and suffer great loss of wealth. An immoral monk, failing in virtue, through heedlessness, suffers loss and ruin from virtue, from the Buddha's word, from meditative absorptions (jhāna), and from the seven types of noble wealth. (1)
For an immoral person who fails in virtue: "This person born in such-and-such a family is immoral, of bad conduct, and has been abandoned by both this world and the next. They do not even give a small portion of food (salāka-bhatta) and are very stingy." In this way...
278:
...and so on, an evil reputation spreads among the four assemblies. For an immoral monk, an evil reputation spreads among the four assemblies in this way: 'This monk is unable to guard his virtue, he cannot learn or listen to the Buddha's words, he is a practitioner of wrong livelihood who makes a living through medical treatments and such which are loathed by the Buddha, and he is also one who is full of the six types of disrespect.' (2)

An immoral layperson, whose virtue is broken, approaches the four assemblies with fear and hesitation, thinking, 'Surely, in the place where many people gather, some will know of my deeds; then they will rebuke me,' or 'They will take me before the King.' When he reaches the midst of the assembly, he sits with a downcast face, drooping shoulders, and head bowed (not daring to look at the assembly), scratching the ground; he cannot speak with confidence. Likewise, an immoral monk, whose virtue is broken, approaches the assembly of monks with fear and hesitation, thinking, 'Many monks are gathered here. Surely, one of these monks will know of my deeds. Then they will prohibit me from the Sangha acts such as Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, causing me to fall from monkhood and expel me from the Dispensation'; he cannot speak with confidence. In particular, some immoral monks, even though they are immoral, may wander about boastfully with their heads held high; however, no matter how much such an immoral monk acts boastfully on the outside, in his inner mind, he is truly unhappy and very dejected. (3)

Whether a monk or a layperson, for an immoral person, although they may live and move about boastfully while in normal health, when they lie upon their deathbed, the places where they committed their immoral deeds appear at the respective sense-doors. That person, looking at this world with eyes open and looking at the next world with eyes closed, becomes helpless and—
279:
—remains there; the four lower realms appear clearly to him. It is as if his head were pierced by a spear. That person dies crying out repeatedly, 'Stop it! Prevent it!' Therefore, the Blessed One taught: 'He dies confused.' (4). The fifth disadvantage is obvious. These are the points to be noted regarding the five disadvantages of one who lacks virtue. (The points regarding the five advantages of one who possesses virtue should be understood as the reverse of what has been said).

Then the Blessed One, until late at night, made the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma see the benefit, urged them to take up the Dhamma, and inspired and gladdened them with other Dhamma talks besides the five disadvantages of the immoral and the five advantages of the virtuous, as well as with a talk of appreciation (anumodanā) concerning the donation of the rest house. Then, saying, 'Lay followers, the first watch of the night has passed; you now know the time to depart (= your departure is according to your own will),' he dismissed them.

'Very well, Bhante,' the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma replied, accepting the Blessed One's words. Having paid respects to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, they departed. Not long after the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma had left, the Blessed One entered a secluded place.

(In this regard: There was no separate secluded place; rather, in that very rest house, at one side, a curtain was drawn around, and the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma had previously prepared a couch, thinking, 'The Blessed One will rest here.' The Blessed One, reflecting, 'If I make use of this rest house through the four postures—lying, sitting, standing, and walking—it will be of great benefit to these lay followers,'—
280:
—rested on that couch on his right side.

## The Founding of Pāṭaliputta
At that time, the chief ministers of Magadha, the Brahmin Sunīdha and the Brahmin Vassakāra, were building a city at Pāṭaligāma to repel the Vajjis. At that time, many devas in groups of thousands (= one thousand by one thousand) were occupying sites in Pāṭaligāma.

In the districts where powerful devas occupied sites, the minds of the wise city-builders were inclined toward building the residences of powerful kings and chief ministers. In the districts where middle-power devas occupied sites, the minds of the wise city-builders were inclined toward building the residences of middle-power kings and ministers. In the districts where low-power devas occupied sites, the minds of the wise city-builders were inclined toward building the residences of low-power kings and ministers.

(In this regard: The wise city-builders, who were skilled in the science of geomancy, could perceive through the power of their science up to thirty cubits deep into the earth: 'In this area, there is occupation by Nāgas. In this area, there is occupation by Yakkhas. In this area, there is occupation by spirits and ghosts. In this area, there is a stone slab or a tree stump.' Then, those wise men, after reciting their scientific verses and mantras, would build the city as if consulting with the devas.
281:
Alternatively, devas would possess the bodies of those wise men and incline their minds to build palaces and houses in those various places. After those devas had marked the palace sites by driving stakes at the four corners and taken possession of the sites, they would leave the bodies of those city-building wise men. For those with faith, faithful devas would possess them and perform such marking and occupying of sites. For those without faith, faithless devas would possess them and perform such marking and occupying of sites. The reason is: in the minds of faithful devas, they thought, 'In this place, people with faith will build houses, and after first inviting the Sangha of monks and providing them with seats, they will increase auspiciousness. Then, we shall have the opportunity to see virtuous monks; we shall have the opportunity to hear the Dhamma talks, questions and answers, and talks of appreciation taught by those venerable ones; people will give gifts and share the portion of merit with us.' Thinking thus, they would possess them and occupy the sites.)

The Blessed One, seeing with his divine eye those devas who were occupying sites in Pāṭaligāma in groups of thousands, arose from his bed at the end of the night, at dawn, and asked the Venerable Ānanda, 'Ānanda, who is building a city at Pāṭaligāma?' When Venerable Ānanda replied, 'Bhante, the chief ministers of Magadha, the Brahmin Sunīdha and the Brahmin Vassakāra, are building a city at Pāṭaligāma to repel the Vajjis,' the Blessed One said:
282:
'Ānanda, it is as if the chief ministers of Magadha, Sunīdha and Vassakāra, are building the city at Pāṭaligāma after consulting with the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

Ānanda, I have seen with the divine eye the devas occupying sites in Pāṭaligāma in groups of thousands.

Ānanda, in the districts where powerful devas occupy sites, the minds of the wise city-builders are inclined toward building the residences of powerful kings and chief ministers. In the districts where middle-power devas occupy sites, the minds of the wise city-builders are inclined toward building the residences of middle-power kings and ministers. In the districts where low-power devas occupy sites, the minds of the wise city-builders are inclined toward building the residences of low-power kings and ministers.

Ānanda, among the gathering places and trading centers of the Ariyans, this new city will be the greatest city, named "Pāṭaliputta," a place for the breaking of bundles (a center of commerce).

Ānanda, for Pāṭaliputta, there will be three dangers of destruction: from fire, from water, and from internal dissension.'—
283:
—Thus he spoke. (The meaning is that one part of Pāṭaliputta will be destroyed by fire. Another part will be washed away by the Ganges River. The other part will be destroyed by people's internal dissension due to believing the words of slanderers.) After the Blessed One had spoken thus, he went to the bank of the Ganges at dawn, washed his face, and sat waiting for the time to collect alms.

At that time, the Brahmin Sunīdha and the Brahmin Vassakāra thought, 'Our lord, King Ajātasattu, is a supporter of the four requisites for the recluse Gotama. That King Ajātasattu will ask us, "The Blessed One has gone to Pāṭaligāma, they say; did you go to that Blessed One or not?" If we say, "We went," he will further ask, "Did you invite him and offer alms or not?" If we say, "We did not invite him," he will blame and rebuke us. We are currently building a new city here in Pāṭaligāma. Furthermore, wherever the recluse Gotama goes, ill-omened (kāḷakaṇṇī) beings(*) [are absent]...'

* Ill-omened beings (kāḷakaṇṇī): This refers to beings who are called "kāḷakaṇṇī = devoid of glory and fortune" because they themselves are full of dark, unwholesome states, and because they are the cause for the arising of dark, unwholesome results and misfortune for others; they are beings of little power who cause harm to others. (Such as persons like Losaka Tissa).

Kāḷakaṇṇī sattāti attanā kaṇhadhammabahulatāya paresaṃca kaṇhavipākānatthanibbattinimittatāya “Kāḷakaṇṇī”ti laddhanāmā parūpaddavakara appesakkhasattā. [From Mahāvagga-ṭīkā, page 139].
284:
They were accustomed to clearing the way. They thought, "We shall invite the ascetic Gotama and have him deliver a discourse for the auspicious inauguration of this new city." Having approached the Blessed One, they stood in a suitable place, exchanged pleasant and memorable greetings with the Blessed One, and then addressed him: "May the Venerable Gotama, together with the Saṅgha of monks, accept our meal for today." The Blessed One accepted the invitation of the brahmins by remaining silent.

Then Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, went to their residence. There, they had choice food, both hard and soft, prepared and then sent word to the Blessed One: "Venerable Gotama, it is time; the meal is ready."

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, went together with the assembly of monks to the residence of Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, and sat down on the prepared seat. Sunidha and Vassakāra personally served and satisfied the assembly of monks headed by the Buddha with choice food, both hard and soft, until they refused further offerings. Then, when the Blessed One had finished his meal and removed his hand from the bowl, Sunidha and Vassakāra took a low seat and sat down in a suitable place.
285:
As Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers, were sitting in a suitable place, the Blessed One expressed his appreciation (anumodanā) with these verses:

In whatever place a wise person
Makes his dwelling,
Having fed the virtuous here,
The self-controlled practitioners of the holy life, (1)

Whatever deities are there,
He should dedicate the merit to them.
Being honored, they honor him;
Being respected, they respect him. (2)

Then they have compassion for him,
As a mother for her own son.
A person whom the deities compassionate
Always sees auspicious things. (3)

"O brahmins Sunidha and Vassakāra, in whatever place a wise person of good birth establishes his home and makes his dwelling, he should first, with faith, offer alms-food to those of good conduct and virtue, the self-controlled ones who practice the holy life. (1)

Whatever deities are present and guarding that dwelling place, he should share the portion of the merit of his gift with them. When the merit is thus shared, those deities who have been honored by the sharing of merit, will in turn protect that householder so that no danger befalls him. (2)

Being honored with offerings and respect, those deities will in turn cherish that householder by warding off and destroying any dangers that arise. (2)
286:
Therefore, just as a mother protects the son born of her own breast and causes him to prosper, so do the deities guarding the dwelling place protect that wise man of good birth with loving-kindness. A man who is thus compassionately protected by the house-guarding deities always hears, knows, encounters, and sees auspicious and pleasant things at all times, day and night. (3)

Then the Blessed One, having expressed his appreciation to Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, with these verses, rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, Sunidha and Vassakāra thought: "The gate by which the ascetic Gotama departs today shall be called the 'Gotama Gate'. The ferry by which the ascetic Gotama crosses the river Gaṅgā shall be called the 'Gotama Ferry'." And they followed closely behind the Blessed One.

The gate by which the Blessed One departed came to be known as the 'Gotama Gate'. Then the Blessed One
287:
approached the river Gaṅgā. At that time, the river Gaṅgā was full to the brim, so that a crow could drink from it.

Some people who wished to go from one bank to the other were looking for boats. Some were looking for log rafts. Some were binding bamboo rafts.

Then, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, even so the Blessed One vanished from this bank of the river Gaṅgā and appeared on the opposite bank together with the assembly of monks.

The Blessed One saw those people who, wishing to go from one bank to the other, were some looking for boats, some looking for log rafts, and some binding bamboo rafts. Then the Blessed One, understanding this matter, uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) at that time:

Those who cross the ocean and the lake,
Making a bridge and leaving the pools behind,
While the people are binding a raft,
The wise ones have already crossed over.

Those Noble Ones (Ariyas) who cross the great river of craving (taṇhā), which is vast and deep, they do so by building the bridge of the Noble Path (Ariyamagga), having abandoned the muddy pools of defilements which cause one to sink into the river of craving in the round of rebirths.
288:
While the common people, wishing to cross even a minor river like this Gaṅgā, must bind a raft, the wise ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples—have already crossed the river of craving by means of the eightfold bridge of the Path, without needing to bind a raft.

## Teaching the Four Noble Truths

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go; let us go to Koṭigāma." "Very well, Bhante," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and as before, he assembled the monks. Then the Blessed One, together with the assembly of monks, arrived at Koṭigāma and stayed there. (This village was called Koṭigāma because it was situated at the place where the pinnacle of King Mahāpanāda's palace fell).

There, the Blessed One addressed the monks concerning the Four Noble Truths as follows:

"Bhikkhus, it is through not understanding and not penetrating the Four Noble Truths that both you and I have wandered and roamed for so long in this saṃsāra, from one birth to another, without rest. We have circled and stayed repeatedly in various existences. What are these four?"
289:
"Bhikkhus, it is through not understanding and not penetrating the Noble Truth of Suffering (Dukkha Ariyasacca) that both you and I have wandered and roamed for so long in this saṃsāra. (1). Bhikkhus, it is through not understanding... the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (Samudaya Ariyasacca). (2). Bhikkhus, it is through not understanding... the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (Nirodha Ariyasacca). (3). Bhikkhus, it is through not understanding and not penetrating the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (Magga Ariyasacca) that both you and I have wandered and roamed for so long in this saṃsāra.

Bhikkhus, now I have understood and penetrated that Noble Truth of Suffering. I have understood and penetrated the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering... the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering... the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering. The craving for existence (bhavataṇhā), which leads to attachment to life, has been completely uprooted. The craving for existence, which like a cord pulls one toward a new life, has been exhausted in me. Now there is no more renewed existence for me."

(In this context, knowing through mundane insight (lokiya vipassanā) prior to the Path is called 'anubodha' in Pali, translated as 'understanding accordingly'. Knowing by breaking through and destroying defilements with the knowledge of the Path is called 'paṭivedha' in Pali, translated as 'penetrative understanding').

Having said this, the Blessed One further said:
290:
"Through not seeing the Four Noble Truths
As they really are,
There has been long wandering
In various births.

O Bhikkhus, because of not knowing and not seeing the four profound truths that truly make one a Noble One, through the analytical and penetrative power of insight and the Path, we have wandered for a long time in this saṃsāra, through various low and high births.

These have now been seen,
The cord of existence is uprooted.
The root of suffering is cut off;
There is now no more renewed existence.

O Bhikkhus, I, the Teacher of the three worlds, have fully seen and understood these four profound truths, reaching the fruit of Arahantship. The evil cord of craving that leads to further existence has been well removed and cut to pieces. The root cause of the suffering of the round of rebirths, which is craving and greed, has been uprooted and cut off without any latent tendency remaining. For me, the Teacher of the three worlds, there is no longer any rebirth or renewed existence."

He taught this verse of Dhamma as well.
291:
291
While the Blessed One stayed at Koṭigāma, as the time for His Parinibbāna drew near, He frequently gave this specific Dhamma teaching to the monks:
“Such is virtue (sīla); such is concentration (samādhi); such is wisdom (paññā). Concentration, when firmly established on virtue, brings great fruit and profit. Wisdom, when firmly established on concentration, brings great fruit and profit. The mind, when firmly established on wisdom, is thoroughly liberated from the taints (āsavas)—namely, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava)—without even a trace remaining.” He taught this Dhamma discourse many times.
## Proceeding to Nādika Village and Teaching on Those Destined for the Higher Path
Then, after staying at Koṭigāma as long as He liked, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Come, Ānanda, let us go; we shall proceed to Nādika village.” “Very well, Venerable Sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied, and as before, he assembled the monks. Then the Blessed One, together with the company of monks, arrived at Nādika and stayed at the Brick House (Giñjakāvasatha) in Nādika. (In this regard, there were two villages established by the two sons of two brothers near a large reservoir. These villages were called Ñātika, meaning 'village of relatives', but the letter 'Ñ' was...)
292:
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One and asked:

“Bhante, the bhikkhu named Sāḷha has passed away in Nādika. What is his destination? What is his future state?

Bhante, the bhikkhunī named Nandā has passed away in Nādika. What is her destination? What is her future state?

Bhante, the lay follower (upāsaka) named Sudatta has passed away in Nādika. What is his destination? What is his future state?

Bhante, the laywoman follower (upāsikā) named Sujātā has passed away in Nādika. What is her destination? What is her future state?

Bhante, the lay follower named Kukkuta... the lay follower named Kāḷimba... the lay follower named Nikaṭa... the lay follower named Kaṭissaha... the lay follower named Tuṭṭha... the lay follower named Santuṭṭha... the lay follower named Bhadda... the lay follower named Subhadda has passed away in Nādika. What is his
293:
destination? What is his future state?”

Thus he asked. Then the Blessed One answered in order:

“Ānanda, the bhikkhu Sāḷha, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom (arahattaphala-samādhi and arahattaphala-paññā), and having entered upon it, he dwells therein as an Arahant.

Ānanda, the bhikkhunī Nandā, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) that lead to rebirth in the lower sensual realm, has been spontaneously reborn in the Brahma realm and will attain Parinibbāna there, without ever returning from that world (to the lower sensual realm); she is a Non-returner (Anāgāmī).

Ānanda, the lay follower Sudatta, with the total destruction of the three fetters (personality view, doubt, and adherence to rules and rituals) and with the diminishing of greed, hatred, and delusion, is a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī) who will come back to this world only once more to make an end of suffering.

Ānanda, the laywoman follower Sujātā, with the total destruction of the three fetters,
294:
is a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and with the three higher paths as her ultimate destination.

Ānanda, the lay follower Kukkuta... the lay follower Kāḷimba... the lay follower Nikaṭa... the lay follower Kaṭissaha... the lay follower Tuṭṭha... the lay follower Santuṭṭha... the lay follower Bhadda... the lay follower Subhadda, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters that lead to rebirth in the lower sensual realm, have been spontaneously reborn in the Brahma realm and will attain Parinibbāna there, without ever returning from that world to the lower sensual realm; they are Non-returners (Anāgāmīs).

Ānanda, more than fifty lay followers who passed away in Nādika, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters that lead to rebirth in the lower sensual realm, have been spontaneously reborn in the Brahma realm and will attain Parinibbāna there, without ever returning to the lower sensual realm; they are Non-returners.

Ānanda, more than ninety lay followers who passed away in Nādika, with the total destruction of the three fetters and with the diminishing of greed, hatred, and delusion, will come back to this world
295:
295
...they are Sakadāgāmīs (Once-returners) who, after returning to this world only once, will make an end of suffering.

Ānanda, the more than five hundred lay followers who passed away in the village of Nātika, through the total destruction of the three fetters (namely: personality belief, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals), are Sotāpannas (Stream-enterers), no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and having the three higher paths as their final destination.

## Teaching the Mirror of Dhamma (Dhammādāsa)

Ānanda, it is not a strange or wonderful thing that a human being should die. But if you should come to the Tathāgata and ask about the fate and future state of every person who dies, it would be wearisome to the Tathāgata. 

Therefore, Ānanda, an Ariyan disciple who possesses the Mirror of Dhamma may, if he so desires, declare of himself: 'I am one for whom hell is destroyed, for whom the animal realm is destroyed, for whom the realm of hungry ghosts is destroyed. I am one for whom the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the abyss are destroyed. I am a Sotāpanna, no longer subject to downfall, fixed in destiny, and having the three higher paths as my final destination.' Thus he may declare of himself—
296:
about himself. And what, Ānanda, is that Dhamma discourse called the Mirror of Dhamma?

Ānanda, here a noble disciple (a male or female disciple of mine) is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus:

(1) ‘The Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’ Thus, through wisdom, he enters into and understands the qualities of the Jewel of the Buddha and is possessed of unwavering confidence. 

(2) ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.’ Thus, through wisdom, he enters into and understands the qualities of the Jewel of the Dhamma and is possessed of unwavering confidence.
298:
298
...I am one for whom the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the abyss are destroyed. I am a Sotāpanna, no longer subject to downfall, fixed in destiny, and having the three higher paths as my final destination.' Thus he may declare of himself. This, indeed, is that discourse known as the Mirror of Dhamma."

While the Blessed One stayed at the Brick House (Giñjakāvasatha) in the village of Nātika, as the time for his Parinibbāna drew near, he frequently gave this Dhamma discourse to the monks:

"Such is virtue (sīla), such is concentration (samādhi), such is wisdom (paññā). Concentration, when fortified by virtue, brings great fruit and profit. Wisdom, when fortified by concentration, brings great fruit and profit. The mind, when fortified by wisdom, is thoroughly liberated from the taints (āsavas)—namely, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava)."

## Proceeding to Ambapālī’s Mango Grove in the City of Vesālī

Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Nātika as long as he liked, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to Vesālī." "Very well, Bhante," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, together with a large community of monks, arrived at Vesālī.
299:
Then the Blessed One, together with a large community of monks, arrived at the city of Vesālī and stayed in the mango grove of the courtesan Ambapālī. 

At that time, among the many monks following the Blessed One, about five hundred were young and newly ordained. They were also lax in their efforts. Knowing that the courtesan Ambapālī would soon come to visit him, the Blessed One gave a prior warning to the monks so that those five hundred young monks would remain mindful when seeing her:

“Monks, a monk should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending; this is our instruction to you.

And how, monks, is a monk mindful? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and grief for the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and grief for the world. (etc.) He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind (etc.). He dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and grief for the world. In this way, monks, a monk is mindful.
300:
And how, monks, does a monk clearly comprehend? Here, monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; when looking ahead and looking aside; when bending and stretching his limbs; when wearing his robes and carrying his outer robe and bowl; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when defecating and urinating; when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and keeping silent. In this way, monks, a monk dwells clearly comprehending.

Monks, a monk should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending; this is our instruction to you,” he said.

## Ambapālī's Visit to the Buddha

When the courtesan Ambapālī heard that the Blessed One had arrived in Vesālī and was staying in her mango grove, she had her finest carriages harnessed. Mounting a fine carriage, she drove out from Vesālī with her train of magnificent vehicles toward her own grove. She went by carriage as far as the ground allowed, then dismounted and approached the Blessed One on foot. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side.
301:
301
Sitting there to one side, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened Ambapālī the courtesan with a talk on the Dhamma. Then Ambapālī the courtesan, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One's Dhamma talk, said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, may the Blessed One together with the community of monks accept my invitation for tomorrow's meal." The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent.

Then Ambapālī the courtesan, knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, rose from her seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on her right, departed.

## The Licchavī Princes Come to Visit the Blessed One

The Licchavīs of Vesālī heard that the Blessed One had arrived in Vesālī and was staying in Ambapālī’s mango grove. They ordered many magnificent carriages to be prepared, mounted them, and set out from Vesālī with their splendid retinues.

Among those Licchavīs, some were blue in color, with blue clothes and blue ornaments. Some were yellow in color, with yellow clothes and yellow ornaments. Some were red in color, with red clothes and red ornaments.
302:
Some Licchavīs were white, with white clothes and white ornaments, and of white complexion.

(Note: The natural complexion of the Licchavīs was not actually blue. Because they were anointed with blue-tinted sandalwood paste, their complexion appeared blue like sapphire. Their outfits were also blue, and they were adorned with blue gems and blue flowers. Their chariots were inlaid with sapphires, covered with blue cloth, flew blue banners, and were harnessed to horses with blue trappings. Even the goads were blue. The same logic applies to the yellow, red, and white groups.)

Then the courtesan Ambapālī drove her carriage against the carriages of the young Licchavīs, axle to axle, wheel to wheel, and yoke to yoke. The Licchavīs said to her: “Hey, Ambapālī! Why do you drive your carriage against the carriages of the young Licchavīs, axle to axle, wheel to wheel, and yoke to yoke?” 

Then the courtesan Ambapālī replied to the Licchavīs: “My lords, I have invited the Blessed One and the community of monks for tomorrow's meal. That is why I did so.”

Then the Licchavīs said: “Hey, Ambapālī! Give us this meal for a hundred thousand kahāpaṇas.” But Ambapālī replied: “My lords, even if you were to give me...
303:
...all of Vesālī with its revenues, I would not give up this meal.” She spoke these bold words. Then the Licchavīs snapped their fingers, saying: “We have been beaten by the mango-girl, friends! We have been outdone by the mango-girl!”

Then those Licchavīs drove their carriages toward Ambapālī's mango grove. The Blessed One saw the Licchavīs coming from afar in their grand assembly and addressed the monks:

“Monks, let those monks who have not seen the Tāvatiṃsa gods look at the assembly of Licchavīs! Behold the assembly of Licchavīs! Compare the assembly of Licchavīs to the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa gods!”

(Note: This instruction to look at the Licchavī assembly was not to encourage the perception of beauty (subha-nimitta). Rather, it was a discourse on the heavenly realms (saggakathā) within the graduated teaching (anupubbikathā), showing that the splendor of the Licchavīs' sovereignty was like that of the gods. However, for some monks listening, it might have triggered a perception of beauty. Thus, a question arises: “Why did the Blessed One, who in hundreds of suttas forbade the grasping of signs of beauty in forms, etc., now encourage it with such great effort?”
304:
The answer is: He encouraged them “out of desire for the monks' welfare.” To elaborate: Among the many monks listening, some were lax in their practice. He wished to inspire them with the splendor of sovereignty, showing that “for those who practice the Dhamma diligently, such splendor is easily attainable” (similar to showing the heavenly realm to Venerable Nanda). Thus, he spoke this way to make them strive in their practice.

Furthermore, he spoke this way so that the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) would become clear to the monks regarding the Licchavīs' splendor. To elaborate: All these Licchavīs would soon meet their destruction at the hands of King Ajātasattu. When that happened, the monks who had seen their current glory would reflect: “Even such grand and magnificent sovereignty has come to ruin.” By contemplating impermanence, they would reach the fruit of Arhatship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa). Thus, he spoke this way to make impermanence evident. This is the answer.)

Then those Licchavīs went by carriage as far as the ground allowed, then dismounted and approached the Blessed One on foot. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened the Licchavīs with a Dhamma talk. Then, the Blessed One, having instructed...
305: The Licchavīs, having been encouraged, urged, and gladdened by the Dhamma talk, said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One together with the community of monks accept tomorrow's meal from us." Then the Blessed One said to those Licchavīs: "Licchavīs, I have already accepted tomorrow's meal from the courtesan Ambapālī." Then those Licchavīs snapped their fingers, saying: "Friends, we have been beaten by the girl! Friends, we have been outdone by the girl!" Then the Licchavīs, greatly rejoicing in the words of the Blessed One and having expressed their appreciation, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and departed. (Here, one might ask: "Why did the Licchavīs invite the Buddha even though they knew, from Ambapālī's words, that she had already invited the Buddha and the community of monks?" The answer is: (1) Because of their lack of trust in Ambapālī, and (2) because they prioritized the duty to be performed by lay devotees. To elaborate: (1) Within the minds of those Licchavīs, they thought: "This courtesan Ambapālī is a frivolous and fallen woman; she might say she has invited him even if she has not." (2) Furthermore, it is a customary duty of lay devotees to extend an invitation after listening to a Dhamma talk. Thus, they invited him for these two reasons: lack of trust in Ambapālī and prioritizing the duty of devotees.)
306:
## The Donation of Ambapālī's Mango Grove
Then Ambapālī the courtesan, after that night had passed, had choice food prepared in her own park and had the time announced to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, it is time; the meal is ready." Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and outer robe, went together with the community of monks to the house (*) of Ambapālī the courtesan and sat down on the prepared seat. (Here * [indicated by the asterisk], regarding the "house" of Ambapālī, if one takes it not as her residence inside the city of Vesālī, but as the rest house constructed within the mango grove, it will be consistent with the words in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga and the preceding and following passages of this section in the Mahāvagga of the Dīgha Nikāya. Indeed, in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga, it is stated that Ambapālī the courtesan, after offering a meal to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head in the rest house within her own park, donated her mango grove to the community of monks with the Buddha at its head. Furthermore, at the beginning of this paragraph in this section of the Mahāvagga, it is mentioned that "she had choice food prepared within her own park," and later she offers it saying, "Imāhaṃ bhante ārāmaṃ buddhapamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dammi = Venerable Sir, I give this park to the community of monks with the Buddha at its head." Since the Pali word "ima" and the Burmese word "ဤ" (this) are used in her request and donation, the "house" of Ambapālī here should be understood as her rest house within the mango grove, rather than her residence inside the city of Vesālī.) Then Ambapālī the courtesan, with her own hands, served and satisfied the community of monks with the Buddha at its head with choice food...
307:
...having served them respectfully, she sat down in a suitable place and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I give this park to the community of monks with the Buddha at its head." The Blessed One accepted the park, and after teaching Ambapālī the courtesan with a Dhamma talk, he rose from his seat and departed. While the Blessed One was staying in Ambapālī's mango grove in Vesālī, he frequently gave the same Dhamma talk on the three trainings: virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā).
## Spending the Last Rains Retreat in Beluva Village
Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Ambapālī's mango grove as long as he liked, addressed the Venerable Ānanda as before to go to Beluva village, and together with a large community of monks, he arrived at the small village of Beluva, which was near Vesālī. While the Blessed One was staying in that small village of Beluva (around the full moon day of the month of Āsāḷha, the start of the final forty-fifth Rains Retreat), he addressed the monks: "Go, monks, enter the Rains Retreat in the vicinity of Vesālī, wherever you have friends and acquaintances. I shall spend the Rains Retreat right here in this small village of Beluva." Then the monks replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and entered the Rains Retreat in various monasteries around Vesālī where they had friends and acquaintances. The Blessed One, however, spent the Rains Retreat right there in the small village of Beluva.
308:
308
(Note: In the small village of Veluvagāmaka, there were no monasteries large enough for many monks, nor would alms-food be sufficient. However, around Vesālī, there were many monasteries and alms-food was easy to obtain. Therefore, so that the monks could spend the rains retreat comfortably, the Buddha said: "Go and spend the rains retreat in the monasteries around Vesālī where you have friends and acquaintances."

One might ask: "Why did the Buddha not simply release the monks to go wherever they pleased?"

The answer is: He did not release them because of his compassion for them. To elaborate—the Blessed One thought: "I will remain for only ten more months before entering Parinibbāna. If these monks go to very distant places, they will not be able to see me when I enter Parinibbāna. If that happens, they might feel distressed, thinking: 'The Blessed One was about to enter Parinibbāna but did not warn us. If we had known, we would not have stayed in such distant places.' If they spend the rains retreat around Vesālī, they can come eight times a month to hear the Dhamma and receive the Buddha's instructions." Thus, out of compassion for those monks, he did not release them to go wherever they wished.)

## The Onset of a Severe Illness for the Blessed One

Soon after the Blessed One had entered the rains retreat at Veluvagāmaka, a severe illness struck him, and he suffered sharp pains as if he were about to die.
309: ...arose. Then the Blessed One endured those pains, mindful and clearly comprehending, without regarding them as a burden. (Here, he endured those pains by discerning and reflecting on the nature of impermanence, suffering, and non-self of the painful feelings through insight knowledge.) Then the Blessed One thought: "It is not fitting for me to attain Parinibbāna without addressing my attendants and taking leave of the community of monks. It would be well if I were to suppress this illness with the preliminary insight-effort (vipassanā-vīriya) and the fruition-attainment-effort (phalasamāpatti-vīriya) which are the basis for the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, and dwell having entered the attainment that can sustain life." Then the Blessed One, as he had planned, suppressed that illness with the two efforts—preliminary insight-effort and fruition-attainment-effort—and dwelt having entered the attainment that can sustain life. Then the illness that had afflicted the Blessed One subsided. (Here, the continuity of the physical and mental life-faculties is called jīvitasaṅkhāra (life-formations conditioned by kamma). The fruition attainment that can prolong that physical and mental life for a period of time is also called jīvitasaṅkhāra. That same jīvitasaṅkhāra is also called āyusaṅkhāra. Here, the Blessed One's attainment of the fruit of Arahantship should be understood in three ways: (1) Maggānantara Phalasamāpatti, (2) Valañjana Phalasamāpatti, (3) Āyusaṅkhāra Phalasamāpatti (or) Āyupālaka Phalasamāpatti. Among these three, (1) the three moments of fruition that occur immediately after the Path of Arahantship in the Blessed One's Arahantamagga-vīthi (due to the attribute of being 'timeless' (akālika)...
310: ...which gives results without delay) should be understood as Maggānantara Phalasamāpatti. (2) The Blessed One's attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, which is entered at any time he desires, should be understood as Valañjana Phalasamāpatti (meaning the fruition attainment used for the enjoyment of the bliss of Nibbāna). Because he is the Lord of Mastery over Mind (Cittissariya), the Blessed One enters this Valañjana Phalasamāpatti even during the brief intervals when the audience is saying 'Sādhu' after a Dhamma talk, thereby enjoying the bliss of Nibbāna. Needless to say, he does so at other times when he is free. (3) Now, after entering the Rains Retreat in the small village of Beluva, when a severe and violent illness arose that could have cut short his life, the Blessed One—just as he did before becoming a Buddha at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree—developed preliminary insight by applying the three characteristics through the methods of the sevenfold contemplation of materiality (rūpasattaka) and the sevenfold contemplation of mentality (nāmasattaka). Then, as he was about to enter the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, he resolved: "From now until the full moon of Kason (Vesākha), for these ten months, may these illnesses not arise." Then he entered the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. (The methods of rūpasattaka and nāmasattaka should be studied from the Visuddhimagga, Vol. 2, pp. 253-264). Due to the power of that fruition attainment, those life-threatening illnesses did not occur and remained subsided in the Blessed One's continuity for ten months. Therefore, the fruition attainment entered in this way, based on insight developed through the rūpasattaka and nāmasattaka methods (because it has the power to sustain life), is called Jīvitasaṅkhāra Phalasamāpatti, or Āyupālaka Phalasamāpatti, or Āyusaṅkhāra Phalasamāpatti. Among these three types of fruition attainment, (1) Maggānantara Phalasamāpatti and (2) Valañjana Phalasamāpatti are referred to in the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries as Khaṇika Phalasamāpatti (momentary fruition attainment). (3) [Indicated by the mark]...
311: The Attainment of Fruition (Phalasamāpatti) is also referred to as the Attainment of the Life-Force (Jīvitasaṅkhāra) or the Attainment of the Vitality-Force (Āyusaṅkhāra). After the final rainy season retreat in the small village of Beluva, the Buddha suppressed and dispelled the life-threatening illness that had arisen by means of the aforementioned Jīvitasaṅkhāra Phalasamāpatti (also known as Āyusaṅkhāra Phalasamāpatti or Āyupālaka Arahattaphala Samāpatti). This means that the illness ceased and did not reappear until the full moon of Kason (Vesākha). Here, one might ask: "Did the Buddha not enter the Attainment of Fruition in the period before this?" The answer is: It is not that he did not enter it; he did. However, the Attainment of Fruition entered previously was only the momentary attainment (Khaṇika-samāpatti). (This means it was an attainment based on ordinary insight at the moment he wished to enter it). To elaborate, the momentary attainment of fruition can only dispel or repel the illness while one is within the attainment. Just as when a stone or brick is thrown into a pond covered with moss, the moss is cleared only for the moment the stone hits the water, and as soon as the stone sinks, the moss covers the surface again; similarly, when entering the momentary attainment of fruition, the illness is cleared only during the time of the attainment, and upon emerging, the illness overwhelms the body as before. The Attainment of Fruition entered by the Buddha when the life-threatening illness struck at the village of Beluva was based on the Great Insight (Mahā-vipassanā) using the methods of the sevenfold groups of materiality (Rūpasattaka) and the sevenfold groups of mentality (Nāmasattaka). By this attainment, the illness could be dispelled and held back for a long period. For example, just as when a strong man descends into a pond and vigorously clears away the moss with his hands and feet, it takes a long time for the moss to cover the water's surface again; in the same way, the aforementioned...
312: ...the illness of the Blessed One, who had emerged from the Attainment of Fruition based on the Great Insight (Āyupālaka Phalasamāpatti), remained subsided for a period of ten months. Thus, on the day that fatal illness struck, the Buddha practiced the Great Insight using the methods of Rūpasattaka and Nāmasattaka, just as he had practiced the Great Insight on the seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhi-pallaṅka) before becoming a Buddha. Having cleared the illness with that Great Insight, he made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), "May these illnesses not arise for ten months," and then entered the Arahattaphala Samāpatti. The illnesses dispelled by that Āyupālaka Phalasamāpatti, also called Jīvitasaṅkhāra, remained subsided and did not recur for ten months. Thereafter, the Blessed One, having recovered from the illness, soon came out of the monastery and sat on a prepared seat in the shade of the building. Then, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, sat in a suitable place, and addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I have seen the Blessed One in comfort. Venerable Sir, I have seen the Blessed One in health. Venerable Sir, although I see this now, because of the Blessed One's illness, my own body felt heavy and rigid. The directions were not clear to me, and the teachings such as the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna) were not clear in my mind. Venerable Sir, even so, I found some measure of relief because I thought that the Blessed One would not attain Parinibbāna until he had made some..."
313: "...pronouncement regarding the community of monks (Saṅgha)." Thus he spoke. Then the Blessed One replied and taught the Venerable Ānanda as follows: "Ananda, what more does the community of monks expect from me? Ananda, I have taught the Dhamma without making any distinction between inner and outer. Ananda, in the teachings of the Tathāgata, there is no 'teacher's fist' (ācariya-muṭṭhi) or secret. Ananda, if there were someone who thought, 'I shall lead the community of monks,' or 'The community of monks should depend on me,' then such a person would make a pronouncement regarding the community of monks. Ananda, the Tathāgata has no such thought as 'I shall lead the community of monks' or 'The community of monks should depend on me.' Ananda, since the Tathāgata has no such thought, why should he make a pronouncement regarding the community of monks? Ananda, I am now old, aged, and advanced in years. I have reached the end of my life. I am now eighty years old."
314: "Ananda, just as an old cart is kept going by being held together with thongs, even so the body of the Tathāgata is kept going by the Āyupālaka Phalasamāpatti, which is like being held together with thongs. Ananda, whenever the Tathāgata, by not attending to any signs and by the cessation of certain (worldly) feelings, enters and dwells in the signless concentration of the fruition of Arahantship (Arahattaphala-samādhi), then the body of the Tathāgata is more comfortable. Therefore, Ananda, you should live as islands unto yourselves, being your own refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as your island, with the Dhamma as your refuge, with no other refuge. And how, Ananda, does a monk live as an island unto himself, being his own refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, with no other refuge? Here, Ananda, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and grief for the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (p)... contemplating mind in mind... (p)... contemplating phenomena in..."
315:
315
...dwelling with a constant observation [of the body, etc.], having removed covetousness and grief regarding the world. Ānanda, in this way, a monk dwells with himself as an island, with himself as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.

Ānanda, whether now or after I have passed away, whoever shall dwell with themselves as an island, with themselves as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge—those monks, among all who are desirous of training in the three instructions, shall reach the very summit (i.e., become Arahants)."

Thus the Blessed One gave this Dhamma teaching, culminating in the fruit of Arahantship.

## The Parinibbāna of the Two Chief Disciples

After the Blessed One had spent his final rains retreat at Veluvagāmaka and the retreat was over, he departed from that village. Traveling back along the same route he had come, saying "I shall go to Sāvatthī," he eventually reached Sāvatthī and entered the Jetavana monastery. (That day was around the 8th day of the waxing moon of Tazaungmon).

On that very day, the Venerable Sāriputta, realizing that only seven days of his life-force (āyusaṅkhāra) remained, took leave of the Blessed One and traveled for seven days to his birthplace.
316: ...the village of Nālaka in the region of Rājagaha. There, in the very room where he was born, he attained Parinibbāna on the full moon day of Tazaungmon. (The details will be provided in the section on the Sangha Ratana). After the funeral rites of Venerable Sāriputta were completed, his younger brother, Venerable Cunda, brought the robes, bowl, and other requisites, as well as the bodily relics (sārīrika-dhātu) of Venerable Sāriputta to the Buddha. The Buddha had a stupa built in Sāvatthī and then traveled from Sāvatthī to Rājagaha. Upon reaching Rājagaha, the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna attained Parinibbāna on the new moon day of Tazaungmon. (The details will be provided in the section on the Sangha Ratana). After the Buddha had a stupa built for the bodily relics of Venerable Mahā Moggallāna in Rājagaha, he continued his journey and eventually reached Ukkacela. At the bank of the Ganges in Ukkacela, he taught the discourse concerning the Parinibbāna of the two Chief Disciples (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Vol 3, p. 141, Ukkacela Sutta). Departing from Ukkacela, he eventually arrived at the city of Vesālī. At that time, the Blessed One, having wandered for alms in Vesālī in the morning and finished his meal, said to Venerable Ānanda, "Ananda, take the sitting mat; let us go to the Cāpāla Shrine (Cāpāla Cetiya) to spend the day." "Very well, Venerable Sir," replied Venerable Ānanda, consenting to the Blessed One's words...
317:
317
...taking the sitting cloth, he followed closely behind the Blessed One.

## Giving a Hint and a Sign

Then the Blessed One went to the Cāpāla Cetiya and sat down on the prepared seat. The Venerable Ānanda paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, giving a clear hint and sign:

"Ānanda, Vesālī is delightful; the Udena Cetiya is delightful; the Gotamaka Cetiya is delightful; the Sattamba Cetiya is delightful; the Bahuputta Cetiya is delightful; the Sārandada Cetiya is delightful; and the Cāpāla Cetiya is delightful.

Ānanda, whoever has developed, practiced, employed as a vehicle, established as a foundation, consolidated, and properly undertaken the four bases of power (iddhipāda), could, if he so desired, remain for an entire aeon (kappa) or for the remainder of an aeon.

Ānanda, the Tathāgata has developed, practiced, employed as a vehicle, established as a foundation, consolidated, and properly undertaken the four bases of power..."
318:
...well-developed. Ānanda, if the Tathāgata so wished, he could remain for a kappa or for the remainder of a kappa.”

Even though the Blessed One gave such a clear hint and such a clear sign, the venerable Ānanda was unable to understand it. Therefore, he did not entreat the Blessed One, saying: “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One remain for a kappa, may the Fortunate One remain for a kappa, for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans.” It was as if the venerable Ānanda’s mind was possessed by Māra the Evil One.

(In this context: The monastery built at the site of the shrine of the yakkha Udena is called the “Udena Cetiya.” The same applies to the Gotamaka Cetiya and others.

Regarding the phrase “kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā = could remain for a kappa or for the remainder of a kappa,” the commentators of the Atthakathā and Ṭīkā unanimously take “kappa” to mean the lifespan of the people of that era, which was one hundred years.

However, the Elder Mahāsīva stated: “The Buddhas do not make boasts in matters that are not possible. To clarify—just as the life-threatening illness that arose at the village of Veḷuva was suppressed and dispelled for ten months through the attainment of the fruit of life-protection (āyupālaka-phalasamāpatti), in the same way, by repeatedly entering that attainment, he could suppress and dispel that illness every ten months and remain for the duration of this Bhadda-kappa. (If that is so, why...
319:
...does he not remain?) The physical body, the living human body (upādinnaka-rūpa), is overwhelmed and oppressed by the nature of decay (jarā), such as the whitening of hair and the falling out of teeth. It is the natural custom of the Buddhas that before they reach the stage of white hair and falling teeth, they divide the current human lifespan (āyu-kappa) into five parts, and when they reach the fifth part after completing the fourth, they enter Parinibbāna at a time when they are still loved, revered, and respected by the multitude. Furthermore, after the great disciples (Mahāsāvakas) who followed the Buddha have entered Parinibbāna, the Buddha would have to remain alone or surrounded only by young monks and novices, which would be unseemly. If that were the case, people might disparage them, saying, ‘Oh, look at what has become of the Buddha’s assembly!’ Therefore, he does not remain.” This was his firm assertion. However, this view of the Elder is not accepted. In the Commentary, it is firmly stated according to the ancient Pakinnaka teachings that “kappa” refers only to the lifespan (āyu-kappa). (From Dī. A. 2. 144-145).

Regarding this view of the Elder Mahāsīva, the author of the Sutta Mahāvāga Ṭīkā stated: “In the Elder’s argument, by saying ‘the living human body is overwhelmed and oppressed by decay, such as the whitening of hair and falling teeth,’ it implies that just as decay cannot be prevented by psychic power (iddhipāda), death likewise cannot be prevented by psychic power. Since this argument is like ‘aiming at one target but hitting another,’ the statement of the Commentary is more solid than the Elder’s view.” (From Dī. Ṭī. 2. 149).

In this matter, the Elder Mahāsīva considered only that the kamma which produced the final rebirth (pacchima-bhava) of a Bodhisatta has the potential to cause a lifespan of an incalculable number of years (asaṅkheyya). Because the Pāḷi text directly states that the Buddhas can ward off the danger to life through the attainment of the fruit of life-protection, he said, “He could remain for the duration of this Bhadda-kappa.” Even though he said so, the kamma that produces the rebirth of various beings can only cause a lifespan of an incalculable number of years...
320:
...if the human lifespan is of the type that lasts for an incalculable number of years. If the human lifespan is of the hundred-year type, it can only cause a life to last for one hundred years according to the limit of the lifespan (āyu-kappa). Indeed, kamma yields its fruit according to the success (sampatti) or failure (vipatti) of time (kāla), physical form (upadhi), effort (payoga), and destination (gati). Therefore, in the ancient Pakinnaka Commentary, the term kappa is interpreted as the lifespan (āyu-kappa). For this reason, the authors of the new Commentaries and Sub-commentaries, such as the Venerable Mahābuddhaghosa and the Venerable Mahādhammapāla, also accepted and adopted the interpretation of āyu-kappa.

Regarding the section on Māra’s interference, it should be noted that there are twelve types of perversions (vipallāsa)—distorted ways of perceiving. These twelve are:

Regarding the impermanent (anicca), perceiving it as permanent (nicca): 1. Perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa), 2. Perversion of thought (citta-vipallāsa), 3. Perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa)—making three.
Regarding suffering (dukkha), perceiving it as happiness (sukha): 1. Perversion of perception, 2. Perversion of thought, 3. Perversion of view—making three.
Regarding non-self (anatta), perceiving it as self (atta): 1. Perversion of perception, 2. Perversion of thought, 3. Perversion of view—making three.
Regarding the foul (asubha), perceiving it as beautiful (subha): 1. Perversion of perception, 2. Perversion of thought, 3. Perversion of view—making three. Thus, there are twelve perversions.

Māra cannot interfere with the mind of a person who has cleared and abandoned all twelve of these perversions. (One should reflect on the story of Venerable Moggallāna). However, Māra can interfere with the minds of worldlings (puthujjanas) who have not yet cleared or abandoned all twelve perversions, as well as Noble Ones (ariyas) who have abandoned some but still have others remaining.

Among the twelve perversions mentioned, the venerable Ānanda had not yet abandoned the four perversions consisting of the perversion of perception and the perversion of thought regarding suffering as happiness, and the perversion of perception and the perversion of thought regarding the foul as beautiful...
321:
...(he had already abandoned the other eight perversions). Therefore, Māra was able to interfere with the mind of the venerable Ānanda.

When Māra wishes to interfere with the minds of beings, how does he do it? The answer is: he may manifest a terrifying form (rūpārammaṇa) or he may cause a terrifying sound (saddārammaṇa) to be heard. At that time, beings who are not free from perversions, upon seeing that form or hearing that sound manifested by Māra, lose their mindfulness and remain with their mouths agape. Māra then inserts his hand into their mouths and holds their hearts as if crushing them. Then those beings lose their mindfulness and perception, becoming dazed and bewildered. In this way, he interferes with the minds of beings.

In the case of the venerable Ānanda, Māra was not able to torment him by inserting his hand into his mouth and crushing his heart; rather, he manifested a terrifying object. Having seen that terrifying object shown by Māra, the venerable Ānanda did not notice the clear hint and sign given by the Blessed One.

A second time... (p)... and a third time, the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda:

“Ānanda, Vesālī is delightful; the Udena Cetiya is delightful; the Gotamaka Cetiya is delightful; the Sattamba Cetiya is delightful; the Bahuputta Cetiya is delightful; the Sārandada Cetiya is delightful; the Cāpāla Cetiya is delightful.
322:
Ānanda, whoever has developed, practiced, used as a vehicle, used as a foundation, established, consolidated, and well-exerted the four bases of power (iddhipāda), if he so wished, could remain for a kappa or for the remainder of a kappa.
