Ānanda, the Tathāgata has developed, practiced, used as a vehicle, used as a foundation, established, consolidated, and well-exerted the four bases of power. Ānanda, if the Tathāgata so wished, he could remain for a kappa or for the remainder of a kappa.”

Thus did the Blessed One give a clear hint and a clear sign. Even though the Blessed One gave such a clear hint and sign, the venerable Ānanda was unable to understand it. Therefore, he did not entreat the Blessed One, saying: “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One remain for a kappa, may the Fortunate One remain for a kappa, for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans.” It was as if the venerable Ānanda’s mind was possessed by Māra the Evil One.
323:
(In this context, one might ask: “Why did the Blessed One speak in this way three times, even though he knew that Māra was interfering?”

The answer is: Later, when he is free from Māra’s interference and regains his mindfulness, Ānanda will entreat him, saying, “May the Blessed One remain for a kappa.” When he so entreats, the Blessed One wished to say, “Ānanda, it is your own fault that you did not entreat me then. it is your own failure,” thereby rebuking him to help thin out Ānanda’s grief and sorrow. This is the answer.)

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: “Go now, Ānanda, you know the time for whatever you think fit.” “Very well, Venerable Sir,” the venerable Ānanda replied, and having risen from his seat and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far from the Blessed One.

## The Entreaty of Māra

“Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One now enter Parinibbāna; may the Fortunate One now enter Parinibbāna. Venerable Sir, now is the time...
324:

Standing there, he thought, 'Now I will use a trick to make the Blessed One attain Parinibbāna. By doing this, the Blessed One's mind might change, and my desire will be fulfilled.' At that time, the Blessed One rejected Māra's request, saying he would not attain Parinibbāna until his disciples—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—were competent... (etc.)... and could well-refute the doctrines of others with the truth and
328:

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke to the Evil Māra:
'O Evil Māra, do not be concerned. The Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata will take place soon. Three months from today, the Tathāgata will attain Parinibbāna.'
## Relinquishing the Life-Principle
Then, while staying at the Cāpāla Cetiya, the Blessed One, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquished the life-principle (the Āyupālaka-phala-samāpatti that can prolong life). Then, a great earthquake occurred, hair-raising and terrifying. The thunders (celestial drums) also rumbled.
Then, the Blessed One, knowing this matter, uttered this Udāna at that moment:
Tulaṃ atulañca sambhavaṃ,
Bhava-saṅkhāram-avassaji muni.
Ajjhatta-rato samāhito,
Abhindi kavacam-ivatta-sambhavaṃ.
329:
Muni = The Buddha, who is the Buddha-Muni. Sambhavaṃ = The cause of the arising of the result of existence. Bhava-saṅkhāraṃ = That which prepares and conditions for the existence in the sense-sphere, etc. Tulañca = The Kāmāvacara-kamma which can be measured. Atulañca = The Mahaggata-kamma which cannot be measured. Avassaji = He has relinquished and cast away by means of the Ariyan Path. Ajjhatta-rato = Being delighted in contemplating the five aggregates within (ajjhatta) by applying the three characteristics with insight-wisdom (vipassanā). Samāhito = Being firm with the two types of concentration, access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā). Kavacam-iva = Like a coat of mail (armor). Atta-sambhavaṃ = The defilements that repeatedly arise within one's own continuity. Abhindi = He has cut away and destroyed with the sword of the four Path-knowledges.
(Alternatively) Muni = The Buddha, who is the Buddha-Muni. Atulañca = The incomparable Dhamma of Nibbāna. Sambhavañca = The three realms of existence that repeatedly arise. Tulaṃ = Tulento = Having compared and investigated with noble wisdom, deciding: 'The five aggregates, the conditioned things, are indeed impermanent; but this Dhamma called Nibbāna, which is the true cessation of the five aggregates, is not subject to destruction and is truly permanent.' Bhava-saṅkhāraṃ = The kamma leading to existence (bhava-gāmika-kamma) that prepares for new existence. Avassaji = He has relinquished and cast away by means of the Ariyan Path. (Kathaṃ avassaji = How did he relinquish it?) Ajjhatta-rato = Being delighted in contemplating the five aggregates within by applying the three characteristics with insight-wisdom. Samāhito = Being firm with the two types of concentration, access and absorption. Kavacam-iva = Like a coat of mail. Atta-sambhavaṃ = The defilements that repeatedly arise within one's own continuity. Abhindi = He has cut away and destroyed with the sword of the four Path-knowledges.
330:
The meaning is: By developing the two types of meditation, Samatha and Vipassanā, the Blessed One attained the four Ariyan Paths. Just as a brave warrior on the battlefield cuts off and throws away the armor tightly worn on his body with a very sharp sword, the Blessed One also completely cut off and destroyed the defilements with the sword of the four Ariyan Path-knowledges. As soon as the defilements were completely destroyed (just as the inherent fruit-bearing potential within a large tree ceases and can no longer bear fruit once the taproot is cut), the worldly kammas leading to the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-gāmika-lokiya-kamma) that had followed from the past saṃsāra also had their potential to produce rebirth and results in the course of existence ceased and were relinquished.
(In this context, regarding the phrase: 'The Blessed One, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquished the life-principle'—
With the attribute 'mindful', the Blessed One reflected: 'I have long and laboriously carried the great burden of suffering, which is the selfhood of the fourfold aggregates—body, feeling, mind, and mental objects—throughout the long saṃsāra. Now, I shall no longer carry it. To be able to relinquish and not carry this great burden of suffering, I have accumulated the various perfections, the requisites of the Ariyan Path, for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. I have now well-penetrated and attained that Ariyan Path which I had hoped for and desired. Because of that attainment, I have clearly seen these four things—body, feeling, mind, and mental objects—as they truly are: as foul, suffering, impermanent, and non-self.' Thus, he established the four types of mindfulness on their respective objects of body, feeling, mind, and mental objects...)
331:
After having done so, it is shown that He relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) without losing mindfulness. 

With the attribute “reflecting,” it is shown that the Blessed One relinquished the life-force only after deciding everything with His Buddha-knowledge, thinking: “In carrying this great burden of the aggregates, there are two kinds of benefits: 1. Attahita (one’s own benefit) and 2. Parahita (the benefit of others). For Me, 1. Attahita (one’s own benefit) was already completed at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree. As for the fulfillment of 2. Parahita (the benefit of others), which is the guidance and liberation of those to be taught by a Buddha, it will be completed in the coming third month (on the full moon day of Kason).”

In the phrase “The Blessed One relinquished the life-force,” the term āyu-saṅkhāra, as previously mentioned, refers to the continuum of physical and mental life (as it is a phenomenon conditioned by kamma). The previously mentioned āyupālaka-phalasamāpatti (the life-sustaining fruition attainment) is also called āyu-saṅkhāra because it can sustain and protect life to be long.

Between these two types of āyu-saṅkhāra, in this context of the phrase “relinquished the life-force,” āyupālaka-phalasamāpatti should be taken as the meaning of āyu-saṅkhāra. Therefore, “relinquishing the life-force” does not mean the Blessed One discarded it like one discarding a stone with a hand; rather, it means He made a mental resolution, a decision, thinking: “From now on, I will enter the āyupālaka-phalasamāpatti only for three months (until the full moon day of Kason). After that, I will no longer enter it.” By making the decision “I will not enter the āyupālaka-phalasamāpatti after three months,” He had already relinquished and decided not to produce the resultant āyu-saṅkhāra, which is the life-continuum sustained by that āyupālaka-phalasamāpatti.
332:
When He thus relinquished the life-force, this great earth (mahāpathavī) shook throughout the ten thousand world systems in six ways: 1. swaying from east to west, 2. swaying from west to east, 3. swaying from south to north, 4. swaying from north to south, 5. rising from below to above, and 6. sinking from above to below. For those not free from defilements, it was a terrifying tremor that made their hair stand on end.

After relinquishing the life-force, in the continuum of the Blessed One’s mind, joy and gladness (pīti-somanassa) arose repeatedly as He reflected: “The great burden of the aggregates, which I have carried with great hardship for a very long time throughout saṃsāra, I shall now discard in the coming third month.” Thus (just as when oil is poured into an oil jar, the excess oil overflows), the pīti and somanassa arising in the Blessed One’s body enveloped His entire being, and as if unable to be contained within His heart, they overflowed, and He uttered the verse of solemn utterance (udāna) beginning with “Tulam atulañca sambhavaṃ...”

By His uttering this solemn utterance, the meaning that “The Blessed One did not relinquish the life-force out of fear of Māra” is also established. Indeed, for one who is afraid, there is no such thing as uttering a joyful solemn utterance. Now, the Blessed One relinquished the life-force without fearing anyone, seeing with Buddha-knowledge that “I shall discard the burden of the aggregates and bring an end to suffering,” and thus He relinquished the life-force with joy and gladness, uttering a solemn utterance.

At that time, in the mind of the Venerable Ānanda, the thought arose: “Oh, how wonderful! How marvelous! This earthquake, which is terrifying and makes one’s hair stand on end, is truly great, exceedingly great!
333:
The sounds of thunder (celestial drums) also rumbled. What is the primary (janaka) cause of this great earthquake? What is the supporting (upatthambhaka) cause?”

Then, the Venerable Ānanda went to the presence of the Blessed One, and after paying respectful homage to the Blessed One, he sat in a suitable place and asked: “How wonderful, Bhante! How marvelous, Bhante! This earthquake, which is terrifying and makes one’s hair stand on end, is truly great, exceedingly great. The sounds of thunder (celestial drums) also rumbled. Bhante, what is the primary cause of this violent earthquake? What is the supporting cause?”

## Eight Causes of Earthquakes

Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, there are eight causes and conditions for the occurrence of a violent earthquake. What are the eight?

(1) Ānanda, this great earth is established on water; the water is established on air; the air is established on space. Ānanda, when great winds blow, those great winds shake the water; the shaking water shakes the earth. This is the first cause and condition for the occurrence of a violent earthquake.
334:
(2) Ānanda, furthermore, when an ascetic (samaṇa) or a brahmin (brāhmaṇa) who possesses psychic power and has mastered the mind of higher knowledge (abhiññā), or a deity of great power and majesty, has developed a weak perception of the earth-kasiṇa and a strong perception of the water-kasiṇa, he can make this earth shake, tremble, quake, and reel. This is the second cause and condition for the occurrence of a violent earthquake.

(3) Ānanda, furthermore, when the Bodhisatta, passing away from the Tusita heaven, descends into his mother’s womb, mindful and clearly comprehending, this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and reels. This is the third cause and condition for the occurrence of a violent earthquake.

(4) Ānanda, furthermore, when the Bodhisatta, mindful and clearly comprehending, is born from his mother’s womb, this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and reels. This is the fourth cause and condition for the occurrence of a violent earthquake.

(5) Ānanda, furthermore, when the Tathāgata attains the supreme self-enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) (meaning when He becomes a Buddha), this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and reels. This is the fifth cause and condition for the occurrence of a violent earthquake.
335:
(6) Ānanda, furthermore, when the Tathāgata sets in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka), this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and reels. This is the sixth cause and condition for the occurrence of a violent earthquake.

(7) Ānanda, furthermore, when the Tathāgata, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquishes the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and reels. This is the seventh cause and condition for the occurrence of a violent earthquake.

(8) Ānanda, furthermore, when the Tathāgata attains final liberation (Parinibbāna) through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), where the aggregates of mind and matter cease without residue, this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and reels. This is the eighth cause and condition for the occurrence of a violent earthquake.

Ānanda, these are the eight causes and conditions for the occurrence of a violent earthquake,” He said. (The Blessed One’s discourse did not end here).

(In this matter:
1. Disturbance of elements, 2. Psychic power of the powerful through meditative play, 3. Conception of the Supreme Buddha, 4. Birth, 5. Enlightenment, 6. Setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, 7. Relinquishing the life-force, 8. Attaining Nibbāna without remainder—

These are the eight causes of the earth shaking.
336:
After memorizing this mnemonic verse, one should specifically note the following explanation.

## 1. Disturbance of Elements

The earth also shakes due to the disturbance of elements. To elaborate: beneath this world-system, there is a layer of air with a thickness of 960,000 yojanas. Above that air layer lies a layer of water with a thickness of 480,000 yojanas. Above that water layer lies the earth with a thickness of 240,000 yojanas. Within that earth, the lower 120,000 yojanas consist of rocky earth (silā-pathavī), and the upper 120,000 yojanas consist of soil earth (paṃsu-pathavī).

When the elements are disturbed and violent winds blow excessively within the underlying natural air layer, violent winds called ukkhepaka-vāyo (winds caused by elemental disturbance that can displace the water from its original position by cutting through the air supporting the natural water layer) blow and strike the natural air layer that supports the water. At that time, the world’s water layer slides down into the open space (ajalakāsa) below. When the world’s water layer slides down, the world’s earth layer also slides down. Then (when the ukkhepaka-vāyo ceases blowing), the world’s air layer that supports the water, by its own power, pulls and holds the world’s water layer (just as air within a water-strainer holds the water from falling). At that time, the water layer rises back up. When the world’s water layer rises, the world’s earth layer also rises. In this way, when the ukkhepaka-vāyo blows, the world’s earth shakes (earthquake) because the world’s water layer trembles.

This shaking of the earth due to the disturbance of elements occurs from time to time even up to the present day.
337:
Even so, because the thickness of this great earth (mahāpathavī) is so immense, its sinking downwards or rising upwards is not clearly apparent.
## 2. Through the Psychic Power and Meditative Attainments of the Potent Ones
The earth also quakes due to the power of the supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) and meditative absorption (jhāna) of those possessed of psychic power (iddhi). When those of psychic power cause the earth to quake, they must do so by specifically entering the water-kasina jhāna (āpo-kasiṇa-jhāna). To elaborate: in causing the earth to quake, those of psychic power may do so (1) to cause a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in others, like the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera who shook the Vejayanta Palace of Sakka, the King of Devas; or (2) to test their own power, like the novice Saṅgharakkhita Sāmaṇera (the nephew of Mahānāga Thera) who also shook the Vejayanta Palace. I shall further elaborate on the second point:
## The Story of Saṅgharakkhita Sāmaṇera
The novice Saṅgharakkhita Sāmaṇera (the nephew of Mahānāga Thera) attained the fruit of Arahantship at the very tip of the razor.* Thinking, "On the very day I was ordained as a novice, I attained the fruit of Arahantship and [shook] the Vejayanta Palace of Sakka, the King of Devas..."
* The expression "at the tip of the razor" (khuragge) means attaining Arahantship at the conclusion of the act of shaving. This refers to taking the meditation on the fivefold skin (taca-pañcaka kammaṭṭhāna) while the hair is being cut for ordination, and attaining Arahantship at the same moment the last lock of hair is shaved off. This is in accordance with the explanation in the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā (Vol. 1, p. 128): "Khuraggeyevāti khurakamma-pariyosāneyeva..." (At the tip of the razor means at the very end of the work of the razor...). 
According to the Saṃyutta-ṭīkā (Saṃ. Ṭī. 2, 239), it means that as soon as the edge of the razor is placed on the head to shave the hair, one practices meditation beginning with the fivefold skin and attains Arahantship. Thus, it is called "attaining Arahantship at the tip of the razor." According to the Sārattha-ṭīkā, it should be translated as "at the very end of the razor's work," while according to the Saṃyutta-ṭīkā, it should be translated as "at the very beginning of the razor's work."
338: 338 At that time, the celestial dancing girls of Sakka said to the novice, "Dear Saṅgharakkhita, you are one whose head still bears the scent of rot (meaning he was very young in age), yet you wish to shake the Vejayantā Palace? Dear boy, this great palace is extremely firm, solid, and stable. How could you possibly shake it?" The novice Saṅgharakkhita thought, "These goddesses are mocking me. I have not yet received the proper method from a teacher who can instruct and guide me. Where is my teacher, Mahānāga Thera, residing now?" Upon reflection, he realized, "He has created a water-cave within the great ocean and is spending the day there." He went to that place, paid respects to the Elder, and stood there. Then Mahānāga Thera said to the novice, "Dear Saṅgharakkhita, did you enter the battle without being fully proficient?" He asked directly, "Dear boy, were you unable to shake the Vejayantā Palace?" When Saṅgharakkhita replied, "Venerable Sir, I have not yet received the proper method from a teacher who can instruct and guide me," Mahānāga Thera encouraged him, saying, "Dear boy, if a possessor of psychic power like you cannot shake it, who else could?" He continued, "Dear boy, have you not seen a piece of dried cow-dung floating on the surface of the water? Dear boy, those who fry cakes in a pan..."
339: 339 "...they turn and cut it away from the edges. Understand through this analogy, dear boy." The novice Saṅgharakkhita replied, "Venerable Sir, this much will be sufficient," and after resolving, "Let the place where the Vejayantā Palace stands become a single sheet of water," he proceeded towards the palace. Seeing the novice, the goddesses belittled him, saying, "The novice Saṅgharakkhita, who went away in shame the first time, has come again! He has come again!" Sakka, the king of gods, said, "Do not mock my son. Now my son has obtained a good teacher and a good method. In a moment, he will shake the great palace." The novice Saṅgharakkhita then touched the pinnacle of the Vejayantā Palace with his big toe. The great palace swayed in all four directions—front, back, left, and right. The goddesses cried out, "Dear boy, please let the palace stand still! Dear boy, please let the palace stand still!" After restoring the Vejayantā Palace to its original position, Saṅgharakkhita stood upon the palace and uttered these three verses of solemn utterance (udāna): (1) "Only today was I ordained; today I reached the destruction of taints. Today I shake the palace; oh, the magnificence of the Buddha!" (2) "Only today was I ordained; today I reached the destruction of taints. Today I shake the palace; oh, the magnificence of the Dhamma!" (3) "Only today was I ordained; today I reached the destruction of taints. Today I shake the palace; oh, the magnificence of the Saṅgha!" (In these three verses, only the fourth line differs. Therefore, I shall provide the combined word-for-word translation, highlighting the differences.)
340:
"I, the novice named Saṅgharakkhita, have truly reached the state of a monk this very day. Today, at the tip of the razor, I have reached the fruit of Arahantship, which is the total destruction of the four taints (āsavas). Today, having received the proper method from my teacher, I have momentarily shaken the Vejayanta Palace, the celestial mansion of Sakka."
1. "Oh! How magnificent (uḷāratā) is the excellence of the Buddha, the Teacher of the three worlds, known as the Omniscient Buddha! It is truly worthy of wonder and praise, a legend to be told with the snapping of fingers throughout the world."
2. "Oh! How magnificent (uḷāratā) is the excellence of the Dhamma, the tenfold Jewel of Truth that leads out of suffering (niyyānika)! It is truly worthy of wonder and praise, a legend to be told with the snapping of fingers throughout the world."
3. "Oh! How magnificent (uḷāratā) is the excellence of the Saṅgha, the Jewel of the Noble Ones (ariya) in the ultimate sense! It is truly worthy of wonder and praise, a legend to be told with the snapping of fingers throughout the world."
## 3. When the Supreme Bodhisattas Take Conception... (etc.) to 8. Depending on the Nibbāna without Remainder
3. When the Bodhisattas take conception in their final mother's womb, 4. when they are born, 5. when they attain Enlightenment, 6. when they preach the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka), 7. when they relinquish the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), and 8. when they enter the Parinibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-parinibbāna)—on these occasions, the earth also quakes. These eight causes of earthquakes should be noted.
Among these eight, the first type of earthquake occurs due to the disturbance of elements. This means it occurs due to the disturbance of the upward-tossing wind element (ukkhepaka-vāyodhātu). The second type of earthquake occurs due to the psychic power of a potent one, which is the power born of the result of kamma (kammavipākaja-iddhi). The third and fourth types of earthquakes occur due to the power of the Bodhisatta's merit.
341: 341 The 5th earthquake occurs through the majesty of the Knowledge of Penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa). The 6th earthquake occurs through the majesty of the Knowledge of Teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). When the Wheel of Dhamma was taught, the earthquake caused by the majesty of the Knowledge of Teaching was like the Great Earth giving its blessing; therefore, the Commentary explains this 6th type of earthquake as occurring "by way of the earth giving its blessing." In this commentarial explanation, the blessing given by the earth-deity is described as the earth's blessing through the figure of speech known as metonymy (ṭhānyūpacāra). The 7th earthquake occurs through the majesty of a special knowledge characterized by revulsion towards conditioned things (saṅkhata). When the life-principle was relinquished, the earthquake caused by the majesty of this special knowledge of revulsion was like this Great Earth standing in a state of compassion; thus, the Commentary explains this 7th type of earthquake as "the earth shaking out of compassion." This explanation should also be understood as the compassion of the earth-deity being described as the earth's compassion through metonymy. The 8th earthquake is caused by the power of the extremely sharp insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) occurring just before Parinibbāna, and the power of the fruition attainments (phala-samāpatti) based on that insight. When the Buddha reflected, "Today, the great element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna), which I have aspired to and gathered the merit of the perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, will be fulfilled," a special knowledge not shared with disciples arose, characterized by the diffusion of rapture (pīti) and other sublime qualities within the Buddha's continuum. The earthquake caused by the power of that knowledge is described in the Commentary, using the same figure of metonymy, as "the earth shaking by way of weeping," because at that time the earth seemed to be in a state of lamentation. (This is written by coordinating and harmonizing the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries.)
342: ## The Eight Assemblies. As soon as the Buddha preached these eight causes of earthquakes, the Venerable Ānanda, being a man of great wisdom, realized: "Surely, the Buddha has relinquished the life-principle today." Although the Buddha knew that the Venerable Ānanda had clearly realized this, He did not give him the opportunity to make a request. Instead, He continued to preach about the eight assemblies, the eight bases of overcoming (abhibhāyatana), and the eight liberations (vimokkha) as follows. (According to some teachers: "If He had immediately announced the relinquishing of the life-principle, great grief would have arisen in the Venerable Ānanda. To dispel that grief, the Buddha wished to prolong the discourse and thus continued to preach about the eight assemblies, the eight bases of overcoming, and the eight liberations without interruption.") "Ānanda, there are eight kinds of assemblies. What are the eight? The assembly of Nobles (Khattiya), the assembly of Brahmins, the assembly of Householders, the assembly of Ascetics, the assembly of the Devas of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa Devas, the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmas. Ānanda, I recall having attended countless assemblies of Nobles. In those assemblies, I have sat with them, spoken with them, and discussed with them. In those assemblies..."
343:
“In that assembly, my appearance was like their appearance, and my voice was like their voice. I instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened them with a talk on Dhamma. Yet, while I was speaking, they did not know me, wondering, ‘Who is this speaking? Is it a deva or a human?’ Having instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened them with a talk on Dhamma, I vanished. When I had vanished, they did not know me, wondering, ‘Who was that who just vanished? Is it a deva or a human?’

Ānanda, I well remember having attended many hundreds of assemblies of Brahmins... (p)... 

assemblies of householders... (p)... 

assemblies of ascetics (monks)... (p)... 

assemblies of the devas of the Four Great Kings... (p)... 

assemblies of the Tāvatiṃsa devas... (p)... 

assemblies of Māras... (p)...

Ānanda, I well remember having attended many hundreds of assemblies of Brahmas. In those Brahma assemblies, I have sat with them, spoken with them, and engaged in discussion with them. In those Brahma assemblies, my appearance was like their appearance, and my voice was like their voice. I instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened those Brahmas with a talk on Dhamma.
344:
I gladdened them. Yet, while I was speaking, those Brahmas did not know me, wondering, ‘Who is this speaking? Is it a deva or a human?’ Having instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened them with a talk on Dhamma, I vanished. When I had vanished, those Brahmas did not know me, wondering, ‘Who was that who just vanished? Is it a deva or a human?’

Ānanda, these are the eight assemblies,” the Blessed One said. (The Buddha’s discourse is not yet finished).

(In this context, “many hundreds of assemblies of kings” refers to meetings such as the first meeting with King Bimbisāra [described from page 579 of the second volume of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas], the meeting with the royal relatives upon the first visit to the city of Kapilavatthu [described from page 78 of the third volume of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas], and meetings with the Licchavī princes in the Sunakkhatta Sutta and Saccaka Sutta [described from page 434 of the third volume of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas]. Such assemblies of kings are found not only in this universe but also in other universes.

Regarding the phrase “my appearance was like their appearance, and my voice was like their voice,” among those kings, some have fair complexions, some have dark complexions, and some have complexions like the color of a bedbug’s back. The Blessed One, however, possesses a golden, radiant complexion. In the phrase “my appearance was like their appearance,” the word “appearance” (vaṇṇa) is taught with reference to the physical form and shape. To elaborate further: in that assembly, the Blessed One did not appear like a rustic
345:
villager, nor was he adorned with flexible ruby earrings and ornaments. He sat in his natural form as the Blessed One. However, those kings saw only a physical form and shape similar to their own. (With this point in mind, ancient scholars venerated the Buddha’s form in the scene of the conversion of Jambupati).

Regarding the phrase “my voice was like their voice,” some of those kings have broken voices, some have aged voices, and some have voices like the cawing of a crow. The Blessed One, however, possesses a voice endowed with the eight factors, like the voice of Great Brahma. This phrase “similarity of voice” is spoken with reference to the language and sound. If the Blessed One, while sitting on the royal throne of the kings, were to preach the Dhamma, the listeners would perceive him in their minds as having the form and appearance of a king, thinking, “Today our Great King speaks with a sweet voice.” When the Blessed One had finished preaching and departed, and they saw their actual king returning, only then, upon seeing their real king, would they reflect: “Who was this person who just now sat on the royal throne of the kings, preaching the Dhamma in the Magadhan language (or the Sinhalese language) in such a sweet manner and then vanished? Was it a deva or a human?” Even though they reflected thus, they did not know it was the Blessed One.

Here, one might ask: “For what purpose does the Blessed One preach the Dhamma to those who do not know him?” The answer is: He preaches so that they may develop a habitual tendency (vāsanā) for the Dhamma. To elaborate: even though the Dhamma is heard without knowing who the preacher is and without deeply understanding the nature of the Dhamma, because of the excellent qualities of the Dhamma, such as its being well-proclaimed (svākkhātatā), it can become a noble
346:
supportive condition (upanissaya) for attaining the Path and Fruit (magga-phala) in the future. Therefore, he preaches so that they may acquire the habitual tendency for the Dhamma in the future.

Regarding “many hundreds of assemblies of Brahmins,” etc., this should be understood through instances such as the assembly of the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, the assembly of the Brahmin Kūṭadanta, and assemblies occurring in other universes.

Here, one might ask: “For what purpose does the Blessed One bring forth and teach these eight assemblies?” The answer is: He brings them forth to demonstrate his own fearlessness (vesārajja). To elaborate: after bringing forth the explanation of these eight assemblies, the Blessed One revealed to the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, for the Blessed One who approaches all these eight assemblies and preaches the Dhamma, there is no fear or cowardice at all. This being so, who would be worthy of forming the perception that ‘the Blessed One might be afraid’ upon seeing a single Māra approaching now? It is not at all worthy. Ānanda, the Blessed One, without fear or trembling, mindful and clearly comprehending, has relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra).” (This passage is indeed the miscellaneous Dhamma teaching [pakiṇṇaka dhammadesanā] not included in the formal recension, as presented in various commentaries).

## The Eight Bases of Transcendence (Abhibhāyatana)

Then, the Blessed One, without breaking the flow of the discourse, continued to preach the eight bases of transcendence (abhibhāyatana jhāna) as follows:

“Ānanda, there are eight bases of transcendence which enable one to overcome opposing states and objects. What are the eight?
347:
A certain person, having the perception of form internally in his own continuity through preliminary meditation (meaning, after developing the preliminary perception of internal form), sees small external forms, whether beautiful or ugly, through meditative absorption (appanā). Overcoming those small forms, he enters into absorption. When he emerges from that jhāna, he also has the perception: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the first base of transcendence. (1). (Virtuous reader... as this is a discourse concerning those who have attained jhāna, it may not be immediately clear; do not be discouraged, you will understand well when the meaning is explained).

Another person, having the perception of form internally in his own continuity through preliminary meditation, sees large external forms, whether beautiful or ugly, through meditative absorption. Overcoming those large forms, he enters into absorption. When he emerges from that jhāna, he also has the perception: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the second base of transcendence. (2).

Another person, without the perception of form internally in his own continuity (meaning, no longer developing the preliminary perception), sees small external forms, whether beautiful or ugly, through the successive perceptions of preliminary meditation and absorption. Overcoming those small forms, he enters into absorption. When he emerges from that jhāna,
348:
he also has the perception: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the third base of transcendence. (3).

Another person, without the perception of form internally in his own continuity, sees large external forms, whether beautiful or ugly, through the successive perceptions of preliminary meditation and absorption. Overcoming those large forms, he enters into absorption. When he emerges from that jhāna, he also has the perception: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the fourth base of transcendence. (4).

Another person, without the perception of form internally in his own continuity, sees external forms that are blue, of blue color, and blue appearance, through the two perceptions of preliminary meditation and absorption. For example, just like the blue flax flower (ummā-puppha) which is blue, of blue color, and blue appearance, or like a cloth from Benares (Bārāṇasī) that is smooth on both sides and is blue, of blue color, and blue appearance; in the same way, this other person, without the perception of form internally, sees external forms that are blue, of blue color, and blue appearance, through the two perceptions of preliminary meditation and absorption. Overcoming those forms, he enters into absorption. When he emerges from that jhāna, he also has the perception: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the fifth base of transcendence. (5).

Another person, without the perception of form internally in his own continuity, sees external
349:
He perceives, in due order, the yellow kasiṇa-forms in the external continuity, which have yellow color, yellow appearance, and yellow luster, through both preparatory (parikamma) and absorption (appanā) meditative perceptions. Just as a kaṇikāra flower has yellow color, yellow appearance, and yellow luster, or as a fine Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, has yellow color, yellow appearance, and yellow luster; even so, this other person, without the perception of preparatory meditation on the internal forms of his own continuity, perceives, in due order, the yellow kasiṇa-forms in the external continuity, which have yellow color, yellow appearance, and yellow luster, through both preparatory and absorption meditative perceptions. Having mastered those kasiṇa-forms, he enters into absorption jhāna. When he emerges from that jhāna, he has the perception: 'I know, I see.' This jhāna is the sixth Abhibhāyatana jhāna. (6)

Another person, without the perception of preparatory meditation on the internal forms of his own continuity, perceives, in due order, the red kasiṇa-forms in the external continuity, which have red color, red appearance, and red luster, through both preparatory and absorption meditative perceptions. Just as a bandhujīvaka flower has red color, red appearance, and red luster, or as a fine Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, has red color, red appearance, and red luster; even so, this other person, without the perception of preparatory meditation on the internal forms of his own continuity, perceives, in due order, the red kasiṇa-forms in the external continuity, which have red color, red appearance, and red luster, through both preparatory and absorption meditative perceptions. Having mastered those kasiṇa-forms, he enters into absorption jhāna. When he emerges from that jhāna, he has the perception: 'I know, I see.' This jhāna is the seventh Abhibhāyatana jhāna. (7)
350:
"Another person, without the perception of preparatory meditation on the internal forms of his own continuity, perceives, in due order, the white kasiṇa-forms in the external continuity, which have white color, white appearance, and white luster, through both preparatory and absorption meditative perceptions. Just as the morning star (Osadhi-tārakā) has white color, white appearance, and white luster, or as a fine Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, has white color, white appearance, and white luster; even so, this other person, without the perception of preparatory meditation on the internal forms of his own continuity, perceives, in due order, the white kasiṇa-forms in the external continuity, which have white color, white appearance, and white luster, through both preparatory and absorption meditative perceptions. Having mastered those kasiṇa-forms, he enters into absorption jhāna. When he emerges from that jhāna, he has the perception: 'I know, I see.' This jhāna is the eighth Abhibhāyatana jhāna." (8) (The Buddha's discourse has not yet concluded).

(In this context, Abhibhāyatana jhāna means: (Abhibhu =) the jhāna that can master and overcome the opposing hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and the objects + (Āyatana =) the cause of special bliss for the yogi. Because the yogi is one of great wisdom, he can easily abandon and master the opposing hindrances, and can also masterfully perceive and develop the objects of jhāna, whether small or large. The jhāna thus obtained is called Abhibhāyatana jhāna.

In striving to attain this Abhibhāyatana jhāna, there is the practice of preparatory meditation (parikamma-bhāvanā) that begins by taking the internal forms (ajjhatta-rūpa) within one's own body as the object (1). There is also the practice of preparatory meditation that begins by taking the external forms (bahiddha-rūpa) as the object (2).)
351:
Between those two types, a yogi who wishes to develop the preparatory work for the blue/dark kasiṇa (nīla-kasiṇa) on internal forms must repeatedly practice the preparatory meditation as 'blue, blue, blue' (nīlaṃ nīlaṃ nīlaṃ) on the hair, or the bile, or the iris of the eye. A yogi who wishes to develop the preparatory work for the yellow kasiṇa (pīta-kasiṇa) on internal forms must repeatedly practice the preparatory meditation as 'yellow, yellow, yellow' (pītaṃ pītaṃ pītaṃ) on the fat, or the skin, or the back of the hands and feet, or the yellow parts within the eyes. A yogi who wishes to develop the preparatory work for the red kasiṇa (lohita-kasiṇa) on internal forms must repeatedly practice the preparatory meditation as 'red, red, red' (lohitaṃ lohitaṃ lohitaṃ) on the flesh, or the blood, or the tongue, or the reddish parts within the eyes. A yogi who wishes to develop the preparatory work for the white kasiṇa (odāta-kasiṇa) on internal forms must repeatedly practice the preparatory meditation as 'white, white, white' (odātaṃ odātaṃ odātaṃ) on the bones, or the teeth, or the fingernails and toenails, or the white of the eyes.

On those internal forms, only preparatory meditation (parikamma-bhāvanā) can be fulfilled; absorption meditation (appanā-bhāvanā) cannot be fulfilled. The kasiṇa-sign (kasiṇa-nimitta) obtained by practicing preparatory meditation on those internal forms cannot become pure enough to be a counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). Therefore, when the yogi practicing preparatory meditation on those internal forms gains strength in preparatory concentration (parikamma-samādhi), he must switch to external forms (bahiddha-rūpa) and practice meditation again to obtain the counterpart sign. When practicing thus, he obtains the counterpart sign, reaches access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), and attains jhāna.

(2) As for the yogi who practices preparatory meditation on external forms, the three types of signs (nimitta) appear on those external forms themselves, and by fulfilling the three types of meditation (parikamma-bhāvanā, upacāra-bhāvanā, appanā-bhāvanā), he attains jhāna.

The signs of those meditations may be small or large. Whether small or large, a yogi of very sharp wisdom—
352:
If the sign is small, (just as a person with good digestion, upon receiving a small portion of rice, thinks, 'How much food can there be in this rice?' and gathering all the available rice into a single mouthful, eats it quickly), even so, being one of pure vision, he thinks, 'Where is the difficulty in reflecting upon and entering into this small object? The work to attain absorption jhāna in this object is not a heavy burden for me.' Reflecting thus, he can master those color-forms—the small signs—and enter into absorption jhāna. He obtains the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) with ease, and immediately after attaining access jhāna (upacāra-jhāna), he can cause absorption jhāna to arise. The jhāna thus obtained is called Abhibhāyatana jhāna (because it arises by easily mastering the opposing hindrances and the objects).

If that yogi of very sharp wisdom encounters a large sign, (just as a man with very good digestion and a great appetite, upon receiving a large prepared meal, thinks, 'Even if there were another meal, what would it matter to me? I can eat it all without concern,' and without regarding the meal as being vast or numerous, eats it all up with ease), even so, being one of pure vision, he thinks, 'Where is the difficulty in reflecting upon and entering into this large object? This object is not so vast that I cannot reflect upon it or enter into it. There is not the slightest burden for me in working to attain concentration on this object.' Reflecting thus, he can master those large signs and enter into absorption jhāna. He obtains the counterpart sign with ease, and immediately after attaining access jhāna, he can cause absorption jhāna to arise. The jhāna thus obtained is called Abhibhāyatana jhāna (because it arises by easily mastering the opposing hindrances and the objects).
353:
Among the eight Abhibhāyatana jhānas mentioned above:

The 1st Abhibhāyatana jhāna is the jhāna attained by first establishing preparatory meditation on internal forms, and later obtaining the counterpart sign in small external kasiṇa-forms of good or bad color, thereby easily and quickly reaching access concentration and absorption concentration.

The 2nd Abhibhāyatana jhāna is similarly the jhāna reached through access and absorption concentration in large kasiṇa-forms.

The 3rd Abhibhāyatana jhāna is the jhāna attained without establishing preparatory meditation on internal forms, but by obtaining the three signs—preparatory sign, acquired sign (uggaha-nimitta), and counterpart sign—in order, in small external kasiṇa-forms of good or bad color, and by easily developing and reaching the three meditations—preparatory, access, and absorption—in order.

The 4th Abhibhāyatana jhāna is similarly the jhāna reached and attained in large kasiṇa-forms.

The four Abhibhāyatana jhānas numbered 5, 6, 7, and 8 are the four jhānas easily attained in the four external kasiṇa-forms of very pure color: blue, yellow, red, and white. They should be understood in order.

Among these eight types of Abhibhāyatana jhāna, in the first four jhānas, the jhāna on small kasiṇa-forms is for a person of discursive temperament (vitakka-carita). The jhāna on large kasiṇa-forms is for a person of deluded temperament (moha-carita). The jhāna on kasiṇa-forms of good color is for a person of angry temperament (dosa-carita). The jhāna on kasiṇa-forms of bad color is for a person of lustful temperament (rāga-carita). Indeed, those four types of kasiṇa-forms are suitable (sappāya) for those four types of persons respectively.

These eight types of Abhibhāyatana jhāna were not taught by the Blessed One without having attained and entered into them himself.
354:
Indeed, He preached what He Himself had attained and entered into repeatedly. For some individuals outside the Dispensation (bāhiraka), seeing a very vast and large kasiṇa-nimitta (meditation sign) might cause fear and terror, thinking, "What is this great object? It is covering and overwhelming the entire world (okāsaloka)." For the Blessed One, however, there is no such fear or terror at all. Therefore, to demonstrate His fearlessness, He preached and revealed these eight Abhibhāyatanas (Stages of Mastery) to the Venerable Ānanda.

After preaching these eight Abhibhāyatanas, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Dear Ānanda, for the Blessed One who enters into and emerges from such Abhibhāyatana-samāpattis, there is no fear or dread at all. This being so, who would be fit to perceive that 'the Blessed One might be afraid' upon seeing only Māra approaching now? It is indeed unfit. Dear Ānanda, the Blessed One, without fear or trembling, mindful and clearly comprehending, has relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra)." (This passage is a miscellaneous Dhamma teaching (pakiṇṇaka dhammadesanā) not included in the Council recitations; it is revealed in the Commentaries.)

## The 8 Vimokkhas

Then, the Blessed One, without breaking the flow of His elegant speech, continued to preach the eight Vimokkhas (Deliverances) to the Venerable Ānanda as follows:

"Dear Ānanda, there are eight deliverances. What are the eight?"
355: 355 Possessing internal form, one sees external forms. This is the first deliverance. (1) Not perceiving internal form, one sees external forms. This is the second deliverance. (2) One is focused only on 'the beautiful'. This is the third deliverance. (3) By completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite', one reaches and dwells in the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). This is the fourth deliverance. (4) By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking 'consciousness is infinite', one reaches and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana). This is the fifth deliverance. (5) By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking 'there is nothing', one reaches and dwells in the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). This is the sixth deliverance. (6) By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, one reaches and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). This is the seventh deliverance. (7) By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one reaches and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha). This is the eighth deliverance. (8) 'Dear Ānanda, these are the eight deliverances,' he said. (The Buddha's discourse was not yet finished.)
356: 356 (In this context, it is called 'deliverance' (vimokkha) because it is well-freed from opposing hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and the like, and because it occurs freely and without obstruction in its respective object, such as a kasina form, just as a young child sleeps comfortably and relaxed in his father's arms. Among the eight deliverances mentioned, the first three are the fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara jhāna). Among them, the 1st deliverance refers to the fine-material jhānas obtained by developing internal and external kasina forms. The 2nd deliverance refers to the fine-material jhānas obtained by developing external kasina forms. The 3rd deliverance refers to the fine-material jhānas obtained by developing the very pure and bright color kasinas (vaṇṇa-kasiṇa) of blue, yellow, red, and white. In this 3rd deliverance, although the person in attainment does not have the thought 'it is beautiful' while within the absorption (appanā), because they are dwelling in the attainment of color kasinas that are pure and extremely beautiful, it is said in the Pali text: 'One is focused only on the beautiful.' The 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th deliverances are the four immaterial jhānas (arūpa jhāna) in order. These jhānas are also called deliverances because they are freed from perceptions of form and the like, and because they occur freely and without obstruction in their respective objects. The 8th deliverance is the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). That attainment of cessation is called deliverance because it is freed from all mental states led by perception and feeling, and from a portion of matter known as mind-produced matter (cittaja-rūpa)—that is, from these conditioned mental and physical phenomena. Indeed, while dwelling in the attainment of cessation, the four mental aggregates and mind-produced matter cease to occur. Therefore, it is said to be freed from those four mental aggregates and mind-produced matter. For some individuals who delight in the cycle of birth (vaṭṭābhirata) and enjoy the round of existence in the three planes, because they are such people...)
357:
Let alone entering into the eight Vimokkhas, even hearing the word 'Vimokkha' causes great fear in some. For the Blessed One, however, there is only great joy when abiding in these Vimokkhas, and no fear at all. Therefore, to demonstrate His fearlessness, He preached and revealed these eight Vimokkhas to the Venerable Ānanda.

After preaching these eight Vimokkhas, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Dear Ānanda, for the Blessed One who enters into and emerges from these eight Vimokkhas, there is no fear or dread at all. This being so, who would be fit to perceive that 'the Blessed One might be afraid' upon seeing only Māra approaching now? It is indeed unfit. Dear Ānanda, the Blessed One, without fear or trembling, mindful and clearly comprehending, has relinquished the life-force." (He also spoke these words of miscellaneous Dhamma teaching.)

## On the Relinquishment of the Life-force
## Detailed Explanation

After preaching the eight Vimokkhas in this way, the Blessed One, without yet giving the Venerable Ānanda the opportunity to make a request and continuing His elegant speech, spoke the following matters again:

"Dear Ānanda, once, when I was newly enlightened (during the eighth week), while I was staying at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree near the banks of the Nerañjarā River in the Uruvelā forest, Māra the Evil One came to me, stood there, and addressed me thus:"
358: 358 "Blessed One, may the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna; may the Sugata (the Speaker of Good Words) now attain Parinibbāna. Blessed One, now is the time for the Blessed One's Parinibbāna." When this was said, Dear Ānanda, I spoke to Māra the Evil One as follows: "Evil One, I will not attain Parinibbāna until my monk disciples are accomplished, well-trained, confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma, practicing properly, living in accordance with the Dhamma; until they are able to explain, teach, proclaim, establish, disclose, analyze, and make clear their own teacher's doctrine after learning it; and until they are able to well-refute any opposing doctrine that has arisen by means of the truth and demonstrate the wonderful Dhamma. Evil One, I will not attain Parinibbāna until my nun disciples... (as above)... Evil One, I will not attain Parinibbāna until my laymen disciples... (as above)... Evil One, I will not attain Parinibbāna until my laywomen disciples are accomplished, well-trained...
359: 359 ...confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma, practicing properly, living in accordance with the Dhamma; until they are able to explain, teach, proclaim, establish, disclose, analyze, and make clear their own teacher's doctrine after learning it; and until they are able to well-refute any opposing doctrine that has arisen by means of the truth and demonstrate the wonderful Dhamma. Evil One, I will not attain Parinibbāna until this holy life (brahmacariya), this Dispensation (Sāsana), is successful, prosperous, widespread, known to many, and well-proclaimed by wise gods and humans. Dear Ānanda, today, just now, at the Cāpāla Shrine, Māra the Evil One approached me, stood in a suitable place, and addressed me again with these words: "Blessed One, may the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna; may the Sugata now attain Parinibbāna. Blessed One, now is the time for the Blessed One's Parinibbāna.
360: 360 Blessed One, the Blessed One once spoke these words: 'Evil One, I will not attain Parinibbāna until my monk disciples are accomplished, well-trained, confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma, practicing properly, living in accordance with the Dhamma; until they are able to explain, teach, proclaim, establish, disclose, analyze, and make clear their own teacher's doctrine after learning it; and until they are able to well-refute any opposing doctrine that has arisen by means of the truth and demonstrate the wonderful Dhamma.' Blessed One, now this holy life, this Dispensation of the Blessed One, is successful, prosperous, widespread, known to many, and well-proclaimed by wise gods and humans. ## Looking Back Like a Great Elephant

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms. After the meal, on his way back from the alms round, he turned his whole body around to look at Vesālī with an 'elephant's look' (nāgapalokita) and said: 'Ananda, this is the last time the Tathāgata will look upon Vesālī. Come, Ananda, let us go to Bhaṇḍagāma.' Ven. Ananda replied, 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' in agreement with the Blessed One's words.

(Note: It should be specifically noted here that the bones of ordinary people are joined end-to-end. The bones of Paccekabuddhas are joined like hooks. The bones of the Buddhas are not like that; the bones of the Buddhas are interlocked with one another like iron chains...)"
375:
They are joined together (meaning as a chain). Except for the twelve major bone joints, such as the shoulder and arm joints, and the minor joints of the fingers and toes, the bone joints (of the Buddhas) are like interlocking links of a chain. For this reason, the physical strength of these Buddhas is equivalent to the strength of a thousand Kāḷāvaka elephants or ten thousand Majjhimapurisa (average men).

Because the bone joints of the Buddhas are mostly interlocking like a chain, when they wish to look back, they cannot turn only the neck. Indeed, just as a great elephant turns its whole body when it wishes to look back, the Buddhas also turn their entire body to look back.

In this instance, when the intention to look at the city of Vesālī arose in the Buddha while standing at the city gate, this Great Earth (Mahāpathavī) revolved like a potter's wheel to make the Buddha face Vesālī, as if saying, "Venerable Sir, those like Your Lordship, who have fulfilled the Perfections (Pāramīs) for many billions of world-cycles, have not performed the action of turning only the neck (like ordinary people)." If this is so, a question arises: "How can this looking at Vesālī be called the 'Nāgāpalokita' (the elephant look), which means turning the whole body?" The answer is: At that time, the Buddha intended to turn his whole body like a great elephant; however, due to the power of his merit, the Great Earth on which he stood revolved of its own accord. Thus, based on the Buddha's intention to turn his whole body like a great elephant, this looking at Vesālī is called 'Nāgāpalokita'—looking by turning the body like a great elephant.
376:
Here, a question arises: "Was it not only when leaving Vesālī that he looked at the city for the last time? Indeed, when he departed for the last time from Sāvatthī, Rājagaha, Nālandā, Pāṭaligāma, Koṭigāma, and the village of Nātika, were those not also his final looks at those cities and villages? If so, why did he not perform the elephant look by turning his whole body in those cities and villages?"

The answer is: If he were to turn his whole body in every city and village, such a look would no longer be a marvel. Therefore, he did not perform the elephant look in those cities and villages.

Another answer (the essential one) is: At that time, the time for the destruction of the Licchavī princes of Vesālī was drawing near; three years from then, they would be destroyed by King Ajātasattu. Therefore, the Buddha reflected on a special benefit: "If I turn my whole body like a great elephant to look, these Licchavī princes will establish a shrine (Cetiya) named 'Nāgāpalokita' (The Elephant's Backward Look) at the place where I looked back like a great elephant at the gate of Vesālī, and they will honor it with perfumes, flowers, and so on. Such offerings will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time." Out of compassion and a desire to favor the Licchavī princes, he looked back at Vesālī alone with the elephant look. This is the answer.

## Preaching at Bhaṇḍugāma

Then the Blessed One, surrounded by a large company of monks, proceeded to Bhaṇḍugāma and stayed there.
377:
While staying in that village, the Blessed One addressed the monks and preached this Dhamma:

"Monks, it is through not understanding and not penetrating four things with the knowledge of understanding (anubodha) and the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha) that both I and you have wandered and hurried through this long course of Saṃsāra. What are the four?

1. Monks, it is through not understanding and not penetrating Noble Virtue (Ariya Sīla) with the knowledge of understanding and penetration that both I and you have wandered and hurried through this long course of Saṃsāra.

2. Monks, it is through not understanding... Noble Concentration (Ariya Samādhi). 3. Monks, it is through not understanding... Noble Wisdom (Ariya Paññā). 4. Monks, it is through not understanding and not penetrating Noble Liberation (Ariya Vimutti) with the knowledge of understanding and penetration that both I and you have wandered and hurried through this long course of Saṃsāra.

Monks, I have understood and penetrated that Noble Virtue. I have understood and penetrated that Noble Concentration (...), that Noble Wisdom (...), and that Noble Liberation. The craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) has been cut off at the root. Like a cord that leads to new existence,
378:
craving for existence has been exhausted in the Buddha. Now there is no more rebirth into a new existence."

Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Teacher further said:

Virtue, concentration, wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation;
These things have been understood by the renowned Gotama.

"O monks! The unsurpassed Noble Virtue, Noble Concentration, Noble Wisdom, and Noble Liberation—these groups of Dhamma have been understood according to the truth by the Buddha of the Gotama lineage, who has a great following."

Having thus known them through direct knowledge, the Buddha taught the Dhamma to the monks;
The Teacher, the ender of suffering, the one with vision, has attained Nibbāna.

"Thus, the Buddha, the Lord of the World known as the Omniscient One, having seen the truth with higher knowledge, has out of compassion preached the Dhamma that leads to Nibbāna to the monks. The Teacher, who is endowed with the five eyes—the Buddha-eye, Dhamma-eye, Samanta-eye, fleshly-eye, and divine-eye—and who has extinguished all defilements, has brought all the sufferings of the round of rebirth to a complete end within himself and for others."

This is what he further spoke.
379:
While the Blessed One stayed at Bhaṇḍugāma, as mentioned before, because the time for his Parinibbāna was drawing near, he gave this specific Dhamma discourse many times when instructing the monks:

"Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom. Concentration, when supported by virtue, brings great fruit and profit. Wisdom, when supported by concentration, brings great fruit and profit. The mind, when supported by wisdom, is thoroughly liberated from the taints (āsavas), namely, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava), without leaving even a trace."

## Preaching the Four Great Authorities at Bhoganagara

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Bhaṇḍugāma as long as he liked, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to Hatthigāma (...), Ambagāma (...), Jambugāma (...), and Bhoganagara." "Very well, Bhante," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, surrounded by a large company of monks, arrived at Bhoganagara and stayed at the Ānanda Cetiya. While staying at the Ānanda Cetiya, the Blessed One preached the Four Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa)—the four guidelines for judging whether a teaching attributed to great personages is true or false:

(1) "Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk might say:
380:
'Friends, I have heard and received this from the Blessed One's own lips: This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction.'

Monks, the words of that monk should neither be readily accepted nor rejected. Without accepting or rejecting them, those words and syllables should be carefully noted and compared with the Suttas and examined in the light of the Vinaya.

If, when compared with the Suttas and examined in the light of the Vinaya, those words and syllables do not fit into the Suttas and do not tally with the Vinaya, then you should conclude: 'Certainly, this is not the word of the Blessed One. It is a wrong grasp of that monk.' Thus, monks, you should reject it.

But if, when compared with the Suttas and examined in the light of the Vinaya, those words and syllables fit into the Suttas and tally with the Vinaya, then you should conclude: 'Certainly, this is the word of the Blessed One. It is a correct grasp of that monk.' Monks, bear in mind this first Great Authority.

(2) Monks, furthermore, in this Dispensation, a monk might say:"

If, when compared with the Suttas and scrutinized in the light of the Vinaya, those words and syllables do not fit into the Suttas nor conform to the Vinaya, then you should reach the conclusion: ‘Certainly, this is not the word of the Blessed One. If, however, when compared with the Suttas and scrutinized in the light of the Vinaya, those words and syllables fit into the Suttas and conform to the Vinaya, then you should reach the conclusion: ‘Certainly, this is the word of the Blessed One. It is a correct grasp by that Saṅgha.’ Monks, bear in mind this second Great Authority.

## Miscellaneous Meanings to be Noted
(In this section, the miscellaneous meanings to be noted will be presented as indicated in the Commentaries for clarity—
In this regard, one should understand the miscellaneous meanings to be noted: (1) the four Great Authorities mentioned in this Sutta Piṭaka, (2) the four Great Authorities mentioned in the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi, (3) the four types of answering questions according to the mnemonic “Ekaṃ, Vibhajja, Paṭi, Ṭha = the four Vyākaraṇas,” (4) the four types of Vinaya, and (5) the three Councils.)

## 1. The Four Great Authorities in the Sutta Piṭaka
The four Great Authorities in the Sutta Piṭaka should be understood as previously described.

## 2. The Four Great Authorities in the Vinaya Piṭaka
The four Great Authorities in the Vinaya Piṭaka (as mentioned in the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi, 6-Bhesajjakkhandhaka, pages 348-9) are as follows: “(a) Monks, whatever I have not rejected as ‘This is not allowable,’ if it conforms with what is not allowable and contradicts what is allowable, that is not allowable for you. (b) Monks, whatever I have not rejected as ‘This is not allowable,’ if it conforms with what is allowable and contradicts what is not allowable, that is allowable for you. (c) Monks, whatever I have not permitted as ‘This is allowable,’ if that unpermitted

(d) Monks, whatever I have not permitted as ‘This is allowable,’ if that unpermitted thing conforms with what is allowable and contradicts what is not allowable, that is allowable for you.” These are the four great principles taught.

## 3. The Four Types of Answers
According to the mnemonic verse “Ekaṃ, Vibhajja, Paṭi, Ṭha = the four Vyākaraṇas” (the meaning desired by the questioner is called Pañha = question; the answering of that question is called Pañhavyākaraṇa; those questions and answers are)—

(a) Ekāṃsavyākaraṇīya question = a type of question that should be answered categorically in one way; Ekāṃsavyākaraṇa answer = a type of answer that is given categorically in one way (e.g., if asked “Is the eye impermanent?”, one must answer categorically, “Yes, the eye is impermanent.” This type of question and answer is called Ekāṃsavyākaraṇīya question and Ekāṃsavyākaraṇa answer).

(b) Vibhajjavyākaraṇīya question = a type of question that should be answered by analytical division; Vibhajjavyākaraṇa answer = a type of answer that is given by analytical division (e.g., if asked “Is only the eye impermanent?”, one must answer by analytical division, “It is not only the eye that is impermanent; the ear is also impermanent, the nose is also impermanent, the tongue is also impermanent,” and so on. This type of question and answer is called Vibhajjavyākaraṇīya question and Vibhajjavyākaraṇa answer).

(c) Paṭipucchāvyākaraṇīya question = a type of question that should be answered only after asking the questioner a counter-question; Paṭipucchāvyākaraṇa answer = a type of answer given after
386:
asking the questioner a counter-question. (e.g., if asked “Should the ear be understood in the same way as the eye? Should the eye be understood in the same way as the ear?”, one must counter-question the questioner, “In what sense do you ask?” If the questioner says, “I ask in the sense of seeing—does the ear see just like the eye?”, then one must answer, “Nahi = No.” If the questioner says, “I ask in the sense of impermanence—is the ear impermanent just like the eye?”, then one must answer, “Āma = Yes, the ear is impermanent just like the eye.” This type of question and answer is called Paṭipucchāvyākaraṇīya question and Paṭipucchāvyākaraṇa answer).

(d) Ṭhapanīya question = a type of question that should be set aside without giving an answer; Ṭhapanīya answer = a type of answer where leaving the question unanswered without speaking any specific words of reply is itself the answer. (e.g., in the realm of self-view, there are the terms Jīva = soul and Sarīra = body; both Jīva and Sarīra are things that cannot be found in the ultimate sense. Therefore, if asked “Is the soul the same as the body?” or “Are the soul and the body one and the same?”—just as in the world, there is no such thing as the son of a barren woman, and if asked “Does the son of a barren woman behave well and respectfully toward his mother?”, one must simply set aside the question without speaking; similarly, in this question, because the soul is something that cannot be found in the ultimate sense, knowing that “The Buddha did not teach that this soul exists,” one must leave the question unanswered. Leaving it unanswered is indeed the answer. This type of question and answer is called Ṭhapanīya question and Ṭhapanīya answer). Thus, there are four types of questions and four types of answers.
387:
## (4) The Four Vinayas
1. Sutta = Refers to the three baskets of the Piṭaka. 2. Suttānuloma = Refers to the four Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa) mentioned in the Vinaya and the four Great Authorities mentioned in the Suttas. 3. Ācariyavāda = During the Buddha's lifetime, the miscellaneous teachings (Pakiṇṇaka Desanā) preached in various places regarding meanings and natures were called the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) because they explained the Piṭaka. After the elders of the Council first recited the three Piṭakas, they placed these Commentaries into the tradition of study (Vācanāmagga) in accordance with the explanations of the Piṭaka. This very Commentary or Pakiṇṇaka Desanā is called Ācariyavāda because it consists of the teachers' explanations of the Piṭaka. This body of speech, known by three names—Ācariyavāda, Aṭṭhakathā, and Pakiṇṇaka Desanā—was brought to the island of Sri Lanka by the Venerable Mahā Mahinda Thera. Later, the elders of Sri Lanka recorded it in the Sinhala script to prevent it from being mixed with the views of other sects. The Venerable Mahā Buddhaghosa Thera then composed the New Commentary by translating the Sinhala Commentary (the original Pakiṇṇaka Desanā) into the Māgadhī language, condensing repetitive parts, matching the explanations (Saṃvaṇṇanā) to be explained (Saṃvaṇṇetabba) with their respective Piṭaka locations, and in some places, presenting appropriate Theravāda views (Attanomati). Therefore, among these four Vinayas, the third, Ācariyavāda, refers to the Commentaries we see today. 4. Attanomati = Refers to the meanings and views (Theravāda) that are to be understood by analyzing and reflecting with one's own wisdom, following the methods obtained from the first three—Sutta, Suttānuloma, and Ācariyavāda—and being consistent with them. Thus, the four Vinayas—Sutta, Suttānuloma, Ācariyavāda, and Attanomati—should be understood.
388:
## (5) The Three Councils
1. The Council of the Five Hundred (Pañcasatika Saṅgāyana), the first council held by five hundred Arahants led by Venerable Mahākassapa. 2. The Council of the Seven Hundred (Sattasatika Saṅgāyana), the second council held by seven hundred Arahants with Venerable Mahāyasa as the leader. 3. The Council of the Thousand (Sahassika Saṅgāyana), the third council held by one thousand Arahants led by Venerable Mahāmoggaliputta Thera. In this way, there are three major official Councils. Thus, one should first note: (1) the four Great Authorities from the Suttas, (2) the four Great Authorities from the Vinaya, (3) the four types of questions and answers, (4) the four Vinayas, and (5) the three major official Councils.

After that: (1) If an occasion arises to decide whether something is Dhamma or Vinaya because a certain monk says, referencing the Buddha, the Saṅgha, many elders, or a single elder, "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction," it must be resolved and decided by comparing it with the four Great Authorities mentioned in the Suttas. In these four Great Authorities, only the speech that is consistent should be accepted as true. If the speech is inconsistent, it should not be accepted as true, no matter how eloquently the monk who spoke it may complain.

(2) If an occasion arises to decide regarding what is allowable or not allowable, saying, "This matter is allowable, this matter is not allowable," it must be resolved and decided by comparing it with the four Great Authorities mentioned in the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pali. (The detailed meaning of those four Great Authorities from the Vinaya should be noted from the Vinaya Commentary). After comparing and reflecting with those four Great Authorities from the Vinaya, a matter should be decided as "This matter is allowable" only if it aligns with the side of what is allowable. If, after comparing and reflecting with those four Great Authorities from the Vinaya, it aligns with the side of what is not allowable, it should be decided as "This matter is not allowable."
389:
(3) As mentioned before, if a question or problem arises regarding the nature of the Dhamma, it should be answered with the four types of answers in accordance with the four types of questions.

(4) Among the four Vinayas such as Sutta, if the words cited by the other person are the Sutta words, namely the Tipitaka recited in the three major official Councils, those words must not be rejected. To reject those Sutta words is to reject the Buddha himself. If the words presented by the other person are Suttānuloma, they should be accepted as true only if they are consistent with the Pali Piṭaka called Sutta; if not consistent, they should not be accepted. Regarding Ācariyavāda, Pakiṇṇaka Desanā, or the Commentary, one should not accept it as definitely true just because the Commentary says so. In that Ācariyavāda, Pakiṇṇaka Desanā, or Commentary, there may occasionally be instances that do not harmonize with the Pali Piṭaka due to errors in recitation (pamādapāṭha) or errors in writing (pamādalekha). Therefore, that Ācariyavāda should also be accepted as true only if it is consistent when compared with the Pali called Sutta; if it is an error in recitation or writing and is inconsistent with the Sutta Pali, it should not be accepted as true. Attanomati (the views and opinions of various elders) is the weakest of all; that Attanomati should also be accepted as true only if it is consistent with the Sutta Pali. If not consistent, it should not be accepted as true.

(5) Even if the Pali cited and presented by a person is said to be "Pali recited at a Council," it should be regarded as authoritative (pamāṇagaru) only if it is the Pali recited at the three major official Councils mentioned before. If it is a type of Sutta not recited at these three major Councils, it is only a despicable Sutta and should not be accepted as true. (This is the miscellaneous meaning to be noted in detail).

While the Blessed One was staying at the Ānanda Cetiya in the city of Bhoga, because the time for his Parinibbāna was drawing near as mentioned before, he gave the following Dhamma discourse many times when instructing the monks:
390:
"This is virtue (sīla), this is concentration (samādhi), this is wisdom (paññā). Concentration, when developed based on virtue, brings great fruit and benefit. Wisdom, when developed based on concentration, brings great fruit and benefit. The mind, when developed based on wisdom, is fully liberated from the taints (āsavas), namely the taint of sensuality (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava), without leaving even a trace."

## The Story of Cunda the Smith
Then the Blessed One, having stayed in the city of Bhoga as long as he liked, addressed the Venerable Ānanda, "Come, Ānanda, let us go; let us go to the city of Pāvā." The Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, "Very well, Bhante." Then the Blessed One, surrounded by a large company of monks, arrived at the city of Pāvā and stayed in the Mango Grove monastery built and donated by the son of a smith named Cunda in that city of Pāvā.

(In this context: The son of Cunda the smith was a very wealthy householder. This son of Cunda the smith had become a Sotāpanna Noble One after hearing the Dhamma when he first met the Blessed One, and he had built and donated a large monastery within his own mango grove. Now, the Blessed One was staying in that Mango Grove monastery for the last time).
391:
When Cunda the smith, the donor of the monastery, heard the news that the Blessed One had arrived and was staying in his Mango Grove monastery, he went to the presence of the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Blessed One then made Cunda the smith see the benefit through a Dhamma discourse, encouraged him to establish himself in the Dhamma, and made him enthusiastic and joyful in practicing the Dhamma. After hearing the Dhamma, Cunda the smith said to the Blessed One, "Bhante, may the Blessed One together with the community of monks accept my meal tomorrow for the sake of merit." The Blessed One accepted the invitation of Cunda the smith by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, Cunda the smith rose from his seat, paid respects to the Blessed One, and after performing an act of reverence, departed. After that night had passed, he had excellent hard and soft food prepared in his home, as well as "Sūkaramaddava," which is the tender meat of a wild boar that is neither too old nor too young, but middle-aged. Having had it well-cooked and prepared, he sent word to the Blessed One that it was time for the meal, saying, "Bhante, it is time for the meal; the meal is ready."

(In this context: *Some teachers (Eke) say that soft rice well-prepared with the five flavors of cow's milk is called Sūkaramaddava. Others (Keci) say that a type of food well-prepared according to a medicinal recipe (Rasāyana) is called Sūkaramaddava; Cunda the smith prepared this special food thinking, "May the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One not occur.")
392:
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robes, went to the home of Cunda the smith with the community of monks and sat on the prepared seat.

After sitting down, the Blessed One said to Cunda the smith, "Cunda, serve me with the tender wild boar meat you have prepared; serve the community of monks with the other hard and soft foods you have prepared."

Cunda the smith replied to the Blessed One, "Very well, Bhante," and according to the Blessed One's instruction, he served the Blessed One with the tender wild boar meat he had prepared, and served the community of monks with the other hard and soft foods he had prepared.

Then, immediately after finishing the meal, the Blessed One said to Cunda the smith, "Cunda, bury your remaining tender wild boar meat in a hole. Cunda, in this world of devas, including Māras and Brahmās, and in this world of humans, including recluses, brahmins, kings, and men, I do not see anyone who, if they ate that tender wild boar meat, could properly digest it, except for the Tathāgata."

Cunda the smith replied to the Blessed One, "Very well, Bhante," and...
393:
Following the Exalted One's instructions, after burying the remaining tender boar's meat (sūkaramaddava) in a pit, Cunda the smith's son approached the Exalted One, paid respectful homage, and sat down at a respectful distance. Then, the Exalted One, having encouraged, instructed, and gladdened Cunda the smith's son with a Dhamma discourse, rose from his seat and departed.

After partaking of the meal provided by Cunda the smith's son, a severe illness fell upon the Exalted One, and he suffered from dysentery with a violent discharge of blood, which was near to death. The Exalted One, mindful and clearly comprehending, endured these pains without being distressed.
