Then the Exalted One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, "Come, Ānanda, let us go; let us proceed to the city of Kusinārā." The Venerable Ānanda replied, "Very well, Bhante," in agreement with the Exalted One's command.

(Note: It was not because he partook of the meal from Cunda the smith's son that the Exalted One developed dysentery; rather, it simply means the dysentery occurred after he had eaten the meal. Had this dysentery occurred before he partook of that meal, his condition would have been so severe that he would have been unable to move at all. However, because he partook of Cunda's smooth and tender boar's meat, the illness was alleviated as much as possible; for this reason, he was able to travel to the city of Kusinārā on foot.)
394:
## Requesting Drinking Water

Then the Exalted One stepped off the road and approached the foot of a certain tree, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

"Come, Ānanda, please fold my double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) in four and spread it out. Ānanda, I am weary and wish to sit down."

"Very well, Bhante," the Venerable Ānanda replied, and he folded the double-layered robe in four and spread it out. After the Exalted One had sat down on the prepared seat, the Exalted One and the Venerable Ānanda spoke to each other as follows:

(The Buddha): "Ānanda, please bring me some drinking water. Ānanda, I am thirsty and wish to drink." (1)

(Venerable Ānanda): "Bhante, five hundred carts have just crossed the stream. Because those carts have crossed, the shallow water of the stream is flowing disturbed and turbid. Bhante, the Kakudhā River is not far away. That river has clear water, sweet water, cool water, and pure water; its banks are pleasant and delightful. There, the Exalted One may drink water and also cool his limbs."

(The Buddha): "Ānanda, please bring me some drinking water. Ānanda, I am thirsty and wish to drink." (2)
395:
(Venerable Ānanda): "Bhante, five hundred carts have just crossed the stream. Because those carts have crossed, the shallow water of the stream is flowing disturbed and turbid. Bhante, the Kakudhā River is not far away. That river has clear water, sweet water, cool water, and pure water; its banks are pleasant and delightful. There, the Exalted One may drink water and also cool his limbs."

(The Buddha): "Ānanda, please bring me some drinking water. Ānanda, I am very thirsty and wish to drink." (3)

When the Exalted One had requested drinking water for the third time, the Venerable Ānanda replied, "Very well, Bhante," and taking the alms-bowl, he went to the stream. Then, that shallow stream water, which was flowing disturbed and turbid because the carts had crossed, became clear, pure, and free from turbidity as soon as the Venerable Ānanda approached it. Then the Venerable Ānanda thought:

"Oh, how wonderful and marvelous is the great psychic power and majesty of the Exalted One! This shallow stream water, which was flowing disturbed and turbid because the carts had crossed, became clear, pure, and free from turbidity as soon as I approached it!"
396:
Having reflected with amazement, he drew drinking water with the alms-bowl, approached the Exalted One, and addressed him thus:

"Bhante, how wonderful and marvelous is the great psychic power and majesty of the Exalted One! Bhante, that shallow stream water, which was just now flowing disturbed and turbid because the carts had crossed, became clear, pure, and free from turbidity as soon as I approached it. May the Fortunate One drink the water! May the Well-Spoken One drink the water!"

Saying this, he offered the drinking water to the Exalted One. Then the Exalted One drank the water.

## The Twelve Karmic Retributions

(At this point, I shall briefly insert and describe the "Twelve Karmic Retributions" of the Exalted One:)

(1) The First Retribution: In a past life, while the Bodhisatta was a drunkard named Munāḷi, he falsely accused a Paccekabuddha named Surabhi, saying, "This man indulges in sensual pleasures in secluded places and is an immoral person without Dhamma."

Due to that evil unwholesome kamma, he suffered in hell for many years, and in this current final birth (pacchima bhava),
397:
when he became the Buddha, he had to endure the false accusation of the female wanderer Sundarī, which caused many people to have wrong views. This is the first retribution.

(2) The Second Retribution: In a past life, while the Bodhisatta was a disciple named Nanda of a Paccekabuddha named Sabbābhibhū, he falsely accused that Paccekabuddha Sabbābhibhū, saying, "He is merely an immoral and base person."

Due to that unwholesome kamma, he suffered in hell for ten thousand years, and in many subsequent human births, he was falsely accused by others. In this current final birth, when he became the Buddha, he had to endure the false accusation of the wicked woman Ciñcamāṇavika in the midst of a large assembly. This is the second retribution.

(3) The Third Retribution: In a past life, the Bodhisatta was a learned Brahmin teacher, a master of the three Vedas who was respected by many. While he was teaching the Vedas to five hundred young students in the Mahāvana forest, he saw a powerful hermit named Bhīma approaching. (Instead of showing devotion, he had wrong thoughts and) told his students, "This hermit is a rogue who enjoys sensual pleasures." Those five hundred students, accepting their teacher's words with delight, told the people in every house while the hermit Bhīma was on his alms round in the town, "This hermit is a rogue who enjoys sensual pleasures."

As a result of that unwholesome kamma, those five hundred students became five hundred monk disciples during the time of the Buddha in their final birth, and they had to endure the false accusations and insults of the people due to the death of the female wanderer Sundarī (who was killed by heretics). The accusation against the disciples is also considered an accusation against the Exalted One himself. This is the third retribution.
398:
(4) The Fourth Retribution: In a past life, the Bodhisatta, out of greed for wealth, killed his younger half-brother, threw him into a mountain cleft, and further crushed him with a stone.

As a result of that unwholesome kamma, in his final birth as the Buddha, he was subjected to Devadatta hurling a stone using a mechanical device; a splinter from the rock struck him, causing his toe to bleed. This is the fourth retribution.

(5) The Fifth Retribution: In a past life, the Bodhisatta was a mischievous and reckless boy (a street urchin). While playing on the road, he saw a Paccekabuddha and (instead of showing devotion, with a perverted mind) picked up stones from the road and threw them at the Paccekabuddha.

As a result of that unwholesome kamma, in his final birth as the Buddha, he was subjected to Devadatta sending archers to assassinate him. This is the fifth retribution.

(6) The Sixth Retribution: In a past life, the Bodhisatta was an elephant trainer. He repeatedly threatened a Paccekabuddha who was on his alms round, making it seem as if he would have the elephant trample him to death.

As a result of that unwholesome kamma, in the city of Rājagaha, he had to face the elephant Nālāgiri, who, being intoxicated and in a wild state, approached to trample the Exalted One. This is the sixth retribution.

(7) The Seventh Retribution: In a past life, the Bodhisatta was a ruling king, and becoming intoxicated with royal pride—
399:
(Without considering the evil of the deed), he himself stabbed and killed a man with a spear. 

Due to the consequence of that unwholesome kamma, he suffered in hell for many years. In this final birth (when Devadatta set up a rock-engine and a splinter of rock struck his toe, causing a bruise with clotted blood), he had to undergo surgery by the physician Jīvaka, who cut his toe with a knife to treat it. This is the seventh result of past kamma.

(8) The Eighth Result: When the Buddha was a Bodhisatta in a certain birth, he was a young son of a fisherman in a fishing village. When he saw his fisherman relatives cruelly killing fish, he felt joy (though he did not kill them himself).

Due to the consequence of that unwholesome kamma, in this final birth when he became the Buddha, he frequently suffered from headaches. (The fisherman relatives who cruelly killed fish in the past became the Sākyan princes in this life and were massacred by Viṭaṭūbha). This is the eighth result of past kamma.

(9) The Ninth Result: When the Buddha was a Bodhisatta during the dispensation of Phussa Buddha, he spoke wrongly to the disciple monks, saying, "You should chew and eat barley; do not eat fine rice alms-food."

Due to the consequence of that unwholesome kamma, in this final birth when he became the Buddha, while staying for the three months of the rainy season retreat in the city of Verañjā at the invitation of the Brahmin of Verañjā, he had to subsist only on barley powder. This is the ninth result of past kamma.

(10) The Tenth Result: When the Buddha was a Bodhisatta in a certain birth, he was a wrestler and struck another wrestler, breaking his back.
400:
Due to the consequence of that unwholesome kamma, in this final birth when he became the Buddha, he suffered the pain and affliction of backache. This is the tenth result of past kamma.

(11) The Eleventh Result: When the Buddha was a Bodhisatta in a certain birth, he was a physician and gave a purgative to the son of a wealthy merchant who did not want to pay the medical fees.

Due to the consequence of that unwholesome kamma, in this final birth when he became the Buddha, as he was nearing his Parinibbāna, he was afflicted with the disease of dysentery (passing blood). This is the eleventh result of past kamma.

(12) The Twelfth Result: When the Buddha was a Bodhisatta during the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was a young Brahmin named Jotipāla. He spoke disparagingly to Kassapa Buddha, saying, "Where could the Golden Omniscience come from for this shaveling monk? Omniscience is a state very difficult to attain."

Due to the consequence of that unwholesome kamma, in this final birth, when he went forth to attain Buddhahood and practiced austerities (dukkharacariyā), while other Bodhisattas practiced for only a few days or months as appropriate, our Buddha Bodhisatta had to practice austerities for six years because of the aforementioned result of verbal kamma. This is the twelfth result of past kamma. (The Buddha himself preached these twelve results of past kamma in the Khuddaka Nikāya, Thera-apadāna Pāḷi, 39. Avaṭaphalavagga, 10. Pubbakammāpilotika Buddha-apadāna, pages 343-346).
401:
## The Story of Pukkusa the Mallian

While the Buddha was sitting at the foot of a tree after drinking the water, Pukkusa the Mallian, a disciple of the great teacher Āḷāra Kālāma and of the Kālāma lineage, was traveling on the road from Kusinārā to Pāvā. Seeing the Buddha sitting at the foot of a tree, Pukkusa the Mallian approached the Buddha, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. He then said to the Buddha:

"It is wonderful, Lord! It is marvelous, Lord! How peaceful is the meditative attainment in which the monks abide!

Lord, once in the past, the great teacher Āḷāra Kālāma of the Kālāma lineage, while traveling, turned off the main road and sat at the foot of a nearby tree for his midday rest. Lord, at that time, about five hundred carts passed very close to the great teacher Āḷāra Kālāma.

Lord, then a man who was following behind those five hundred carts approached the great teacher Āḷāra Kālāma and asked:

(The Man)
'Venerable Sir, did you see the five hundred carts that just passed by?'

(Āḷāra)
'Layman, I did not see them.'

(The Man)
'Venerable Sir, how is that? Did you hear the sound of those carts?'
402:
(Āḷāra)
'Layman, I did not hear the sound either.'

(The Man)
'Venerable Sir, how is that? Were you asleep at that time?'

(Āḷāra)
'Layman, I was not asleep.'

(The Man)
'Venerable Sir, how is that? Were you conscious at that time?'

(Āḷāra)
'Layman, I was conscious at that time.'

(The Man)
'Venerable Sir, you say that while being conscious and awake, you neither saw nor heard the sound of the five hundred carts passing very close to you. Yet, is it not true that your double-layered robe is covered in layers of dust?'

(Āḷāra)
'Yes, layman, it is so.'

Lord, after the great teacher Āḷāra Kālāma and the man had finished their conversation of questions and answers, that man thought:

'Oh, it is wonderful! Oh, it is marvelous! How peaceful is the meditative attainment in which the monks abide! This great teacher Āḷāra, while being conscious and awake, neither saw nor heard the sound of the five hundred carts passing very close to him.'
403:
Reflecting thus, he expressed his supreme devotion to the great teacher Āḷāra Kālāma and then departed."

Then the Buddha asked Pukkusa the Mallian, "Pukkusa, what do you think of this? (1) One person, while being conscious and awake, neither sees nor hears the sound of five hundred carts passing very close to him. (2) Another person, while being conscious and awake, neither sees nor hears the sound when it is raining, thundering, lightning is flashing, and a thunderbolt strikes. Among these two, which is more difficult to perform and more difficult to occur?"

Pukkusa the Mallian replied to the Buddha, "Lord, what are five hundred carts, or six hundred, or seven hundred... or eight hundred, or nine hundred, or a thousand, or even a hundred thousand carts? It cannot be said that it is difficult for one not to see or hear those carts passing nearby. Indeed, it is far more difficult to perform and far more difficult to occur for one to remain conscious and awake, neither seeing nor hearing anything, while it is raining, thundering, lightning is flashing, and a thunderbolt strikes."

Then the Buddha said to Pukkusa the Mallian:

"Pukkusa, once I was staying at the town of Ātumā in a threshing-floor hut. At that time,
404:
while it was raining and thundering, with lightning flashing and thunderbolts striking, four oxen and two brothers who were farmers were killed near the threshing-floor hut.

Pukkusa, then a great crowd of people came out from the town of Ātumā and approached the place where the four oxen and the two farmer brothers had died. Pukkusa, at that time, I came out of the threshing-floor hut and was walking to and fro in the open air near the hut. Pukkusa, then a man from that great crowd approached me, paid homage respectfully, and stood in a suitable place. Pukkusa, the conversation that took place between me and that man was as follows:

(The Buddha)
'Layman, why has this great crowd of people gathered?'

(The Man)
'Lord, while it was raining and thundering, with lightning flashing and thunderbolts striking, four oxen and two brothers who were farmers were killed. It is for this reason that the crowd has gathered.'

(The Man)
'But Lord, where were you?'

(The Buddha)
'Layman, I was right here.'
405:
(The Man)
'Lord, how is that? Did you see it?'

(The Buddha)
'Layman, I did not see it.'

(The Man)
'Lord, how is that? Did you hear the sound?'

(The Buddha)
'Layman, I did not hear the sound either.'

(The Man)
'Lord, how is that? Were you asleep at that time?'

(The Buddha)
'Layman, I was not asleep.'

(The Man)
'Lord, how is that? Were you conscious at that time?'

(The Buddha)
'Layman, I was conscious at that time.'

(The Man)
'Lord, while it was raining and thundering, with lightning flashing and thunderbolts striking, were you conscious and awake, yet neither saw nor heard it?'

(The Buddha)
'Yes, layman, it is so.'

Pukkusa, after I and that layman had finished our conversation of questions and answers, that layman—
406:
“How wonderful, how marvelous! That those who have gone forth should dwell in such a peaceful state of attainment. While it was raining, with the clouds thundering and lightning flashing, and the thunderbolt striking, the Blessed One, being conscious and awake, neither saw it nor heard the sound.”

Reflecting thus, he expressed his exceeding devotion to me, paid homage, and after performing a respectful circumambulation, he departed.”

## The Extraordinary Faith and Devotion of Pukkusa the Mallaputta

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Pukkusa the Mallaputta said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable Sir, the faith I had in Āḷāra Kālāma, I blow it away as if in a strong wind, or I let it float away as if in a swift-flowing river.

Magnificent, Venerable Sir! Magnificent, Venerable Sir! It is as if, Venerable Sir, one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what had been hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. In the same way, the Blessed One has explained the Dhamma in many ways.
407:
“Venerable Sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forth as long as life shall last.”

Then Pukkusa the Mallaputta called a certain man and said, “Friend, go and bring me a pair of golden-hued robes, fine and ready to be worn.” When that man had brought the robes, Pukkusa the Mallaputta said, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One out of compassion accept this pair of golden-hued robes, fine and ready to be worn, from me.”

Then the Blessed One said, “In that case, Pukkusa, clothe me in one, and clothe Ānanda in the other.” Accordingly, Pukkusa the Mallaputta clothed the Blessed One in one and the Venerable Ānanda in the other.

(In this matter, if it is asked, “Did the Venerable Ānanda accept that robe offered by Pukkusa the Mallaputta?” the answer is, “He did.” If it is asked, “Why did he accept it? Did he not, when accepting the position of attendant, choose as one of the eight boons that he would not accept robes and such offered to the Blessed One?” the answer is:
408:
(1) He accepted it because his duties as an attendant (upaṭṭhāka) had reached their ultimate conclusion. To elaborate: although the Venerable Ānanda had accepted the position of attendant on the condition that he would not receive gifts such as robes offered to the Blessed One, his service as an attendant was now nearing its end. Therefore, he accepted it.

(2) Furthermore, there might be people who would say, ‘The Venerable Ānanda, it seems, could not serve the Blessed One to his satisfaction; though he served him like a shadow for twenty-five years, he received nothing from the Blessed One.’ To prevent such people from having the opportunity to speak wrongly, he accepted it.

(3) Alternatively, the Blessed One considered: ‘After Ānanda accepts this robe, he will not wear it himself but will offer it to me. Indeed, if Pukkusa the Mallaputta makes an offering to Ānanda, it is as if he makes an offering to the Saṅgha; in this way, a great mass of merit will accrue to Pukkusa.’ Knowing this, the Blessed One had him offer one to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda accepted it for that very reason. This is a special point to be noted.)

Then the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened Pukkusa the Mallaputta with a talk on the Dhamma. Having been thus instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s Dhamma talk, Pukkusa the Mallaputta
409:
rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and after performing a respectful circumambulation, he departed.

Not long after Pukkusa the Mallaputta had left, the Venerable Ānanda placed that pair of golden-hued robes upon the body of the Blessed One. When placed upon the radiant body of the Blessed One, the robes appeared as if they had lost their luster. The Venerable Ānanda, in amazement, reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda:

“It is so, Ānanda! It is so, Ānanda! There are two occasions, Ānanda, when the skin of the Tathāgata becomes exceedingly clear and radiant. What are the two?

Ānanda, they are: (1) the night on which the Tathāgata attains the supreme and perfect Enlightenment (Sammā-sambodhi), and (2) the night on which the Tathāgata attains final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without remainder (Anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

On these two occasions, Ānanda, the skin of the Tathāgata becomes exceedingly clear and radiant. Today, Ānanda, in the last watch of the night, in the Upavattana Sāla grove of the Mallas near Kusinārā, between the twin Sāla trees,
410:
the Tathāgata’s final passing (Parinibbāna) will take place.”

Having said this, he said, “Come, Ānanda, let us go to the Kakutthā River.” The Venerable Ānanda replied, “Yes, Venerable Sir.”

Then the Blessed One, together with a large community of monks, went to the Kakutthā River. Having gone down into the river, bathed, and drunk, he came back out and went to the mango grove nearby. (At that time, the Venerable Ānanda remained behind to wring out the Blessed One’s bathing robe, so the Blessed One spoke to the Venerable Cundaka who was nearby): “Come, Cundaka, fold my double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) in four and spread it out. I am weary, Cundaka, and would like to lie down.” The Venerable Cundaka replied, “Yes, Venerable Sir,” and folded the robe in four and spread it out. Then the Blessed One lay down on his right side in the lion posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the thought of rising (uṭṭhāna-saññā). The Venerable Cundaka sat right there in front of the Blessed One.

## The Equal Merit of the Two Meals

By this time, the Venerable Ānanda had arrived near the Blessed One. Then
411:
the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda with these words:

“Ānanda, it may be that someone might cause remorse in Cunda the smith, saying: ‘It is a loss for you, friend Cunda, it is an ill-fortune for you, that the Tathāgata passed away after having eaten his last meal from you.’

Ānanda, any such remorse in Cunda should be dispelled in this way:

‘Friend Cunda, it is a gain for you, it is a great fortune for you, that the Tathāgata passed away after having eaten his last meal from you. Friend Cunda, I have heard and received this from the very mouth of the Blessed One: 

“These two offerings of food are of equal fruit and equal result, and are far more fruitful and profitable than any other. Which two? (1) That offering of food after eating which the Tathāgata attains supreme and perfect Enlightenment, and (2) that offering of food after eating which the Tathāgata attains final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without remainder. These two offerings of food are of equal fruit and equal result, and are far more fruitful and profitable than any other.”’
412:
‘Thus, the lay follower Cunda the smith has accumulated a deed that leads to long life, he has accumulated a deed that leads to beauty, he has accumulated a deed that leads to happiness, he has accumulated a deed that leads to fame, he has accumulated a deed that leads to heaven, and he has accumulated a deed that leads to sovereignty.’

In this way, Ānanda, the remorse of Cunda the smith should be dispelled.”

Then the Blessed One, understanding the significance of this, uttered this inspired verse (Udāna) at that time:

“To him who gives, merit increases;
In him who restrains himself, enmity is not accumulated.
The skillful one discards evil;
By the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished (attained Nibbāna).”

(Word-for-word gloss): To the one who gives with a clear and faithful heart, pure merit alone increases day by day. To the one who restrains and controls body, speech, and mind, the five types of enmity such as killing do not increase, being suppressed by the power of virtue. The one who is accomplished in wisdom, from the level of insight-wisdom up to the Path of Arahatship, discards the base and defiled types of kileasā.
413:
Jahāti = abandons, relinquishes, or discards without remainder. Sa-so = that person who is well-endowed and complete with these four: dāna (generosity), sīla (virtue), samatha (tranquility), and paññā (wisdom). Rāgadosamohakkhayā = due to the total exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion. Nibbuto = has attained peace, having completely extinguished the fires of defilements.

(In this context: Regarding the two types of alms-food—the milk-rice offered by Sujātā and the meal of young pork offered by Cunda—the Buddha preached that they are equal in their fruit and result. Here, a question may arise:

“The Blessed One partook of the alms-food offered by Sujātā and attained Buddhahood on that very day. At the time he partook of that food, greed, hatred, and delusion were not yet extinguished in the Blessed One. Now, he partook of the alms-food offered by Cunda at a time when greed, hatred, and delusion had already been extinguished. Why, then, are these two types of alms-food equal in their fruit and result?”

The answer is: They are equal in their fruit and result because (a) they are equal as causes for the attainment of Parinibbāna, (b) they are equal as causes for the ability to enter meditative attainments (samāpatti), and (c) they are equal in the manner of subsequent reflection. [In this context, by mentioning the two types of alms-food, it should be specifically understood as referring to the two acts of offering alms-food].

(a) To elaborate further: Having partaken of the alms-food offered by Sujātā, the Blessed One entered Kilesa-parinibbāna (the extinguishment of defilements) through the Sa-upādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu (Nibbāna with the constituent groups of existence remaining); that is, he attained Buddhahood. Having partaken of the alms-food offered by Cunda, he entered Khandha-parinibbāna (the extinguishment of the aggregates) through the Anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu (Nibbāna without the constituent groups of existence remaining). By depending on and consuming the excellent alms-food offered by Sujātā, the Blessed One received nutritional support from that food, and excellent material qualities (rūpa) were produced in his physical continuity. Because he obtained a basis in those excellent material qualities, the Dhammakāya—consisting of the mental states of Insight (Vipassanā), the Path (Magga), and the Fruition (Phala) produced in his continuity—
414:
was able to abandon the defilements with ease; thus, he entered Kilesa-parinibbāna. Similarly, by depending on and consuming the excellent alms-food offered by Cunda, due to the fulfillment of nutritional suitability (bhojana-sappāya), he was able to abandon the aggregates (khandha) with ease; thus, he entered Khandha-parinibbāna. Therefore, as the two types of alms-food were equal in being the cause for the easy accomplishment of these two types of Parinibbāna—the abandonment of defilements (Kilesa-parinibbāna) and the abandonment of the aggregates (Khandha-parinibbāna)—they are equal in their fruit and result.

(b) On the day he was to become Buddha, the Blessed One partook of the alms-food offered by Sujātā and entered into and enjoyed the daily-used attainments (devasi-kavalañjana-samāpatti) numbering two million four hundred thousand kotis (2.4 trillion). Similarly, on the day he was to enter Parinibbāna, he partook of the alms-food offered by Cunda and entered into and enjoyed the daily-used attainments numbering two million four hundred thousand kotis. Because he partook of those alms-foods, he was able to enter those attainments with ease and comfort. Thus, because they are equal as causes for the ability to enter those daily-used attainments numbering two million four hundred thousand kotis, those two types of alms-food are equal in their fruit and result.

## The Two Million Four Hundred Thousand Kotis of Attainments

Here, I shall further describe the daily-used attainments (devasi-kavalañjana-samāpatti) numbering two million four hundred thousand kotis, as mentioned in the Saṃyutta-ṭīkā, Volume I, Sagāthāvagga-saṃyutta-ṭīkā, 6-Brahma-saṃyutta, 2-Dutiyavagga, 5-Parinibbāna-sutta-vaṇṇanā, pages 251–252:

According to the view of some teachers (Kecivāda): Every day, the Blessed One entered the Great Compassion Attainment (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) one million two hundred thousand koti times. He also entered the Arahatship Fruition Attainment (Arahatta-phala-samāpatti) one million two hundred thousand koti times. Thus, the two combined
415:
make two million four hundred thousand koti daily-used attainments. (Alternatively) In the case of the Buddhas, the habit of the occurrence of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) mind is extremely rapid, and their mastery in meditative attainments has reached the pinnacle. Therefore, entering and emerging from an attainment is completed in just a few—two or three—thought-moments. Thus, the Blessed One entered twelve types of attainments: 5 fine-material sphere attainments (rūpāvacara-samāpatti), 4 immaterial sphere attainments (arūpāvacara-samāpatti), 1 boundless state attainment (appamaññā-samāpatti), 1 attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), and 1 Arahatship fruition attainment (arahatta-phala-samāpatti). Every day, he entered each of these twelve types one hundred thousand koti times in the morning (thus, in the morning, there are one million two hundred thousand koti attainments). In the afternoon, he entered them in the same way; thus, the two combined make two million four hundred thousand koti daily-used attainments. This is the view of some teachers (Kecivāda).

According to another view (Aparevāda): Every day, the Blessed One entered the Arahatship Fruition Attainment (Arahatta-phala-samāpatti). It is the natural law that if one wishes to enter the Fruition Attainment, one must first practice insight contemplation (Vipassanā). (This means the process of insight, vipassanā-vīthi, occurs first, followed by the process of fruition attainment, phala-samāpatti-vīthi). In such insight contemplation, the Blessed One had the habit of contemplating with the twelve links of Dependent Origination (Paṭicca-samuppāda) as the basis. (One should recall the Mahāvajira-vipassanā in the section on becoming Buddha, Mahā-buddhavaṃsa, Volume II, pages 334–6). Thus, when the Blessed One wished to enter the Fruition Attainment (Arahatta-phala-samāpatti), among the twelve links of Dependent Origination, he would contemplate ignorance (avijjā) with insight in forward order (anuloma) and then enter Arahatship Fruition one hundred thousand koti times. Similarly, after contemplating mental formations (saṅkhāra) with insight, he entered Arahatship Fruition one hundred thousand koti times. In this manner, by contemplating consciousness (viññāṇa), mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), contact (phassa), feeling (vedanā), craving (taṇhā), clinging (upādāna), becoming (bhava), birth (jāti), and aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa) with insight, he entered Arahatship Fruition one hundred thousand koti times for each.
416:
In total, based on the twelve links of Dependent Origination in forward order (anuloma), there are one million two hundred thousand koti Arahatship Fruition Attainments.

Similarly, by way of reverse order (paṭiloma) Dependent Origination attainments, he contemplated aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa) with insight and entered Arahatship Fruition one hundred thousand koti times. In this manner, contemplating birth (jāti) ... becoming (bhava), clinging (upādāna), craving (taṇhā), feeling (vedanā), contact (phassa), the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa), consciousness (viññāṇa), and mental formations (saṅkhāra) with insight, he entered Arahatship Fruition one hundred thousand koti times for each. Then, contemplating ignorance (avijjā) with insight, he entered Arahatship Fruition one hundred thousand koti times. In total, based on the twelve links of Dependent Origination in reverse order (paṭiloma), there are one million two hundred thousand koti Arahatship Fruition Attainments. Combining the two, the total number of Arahatship Fruition Attainments entered daily by the Blessed One is two million four hundred thousand kotis. This is the view of another teacher (Aparevāda).

Here, if it is asked: “Since the Blessed One entered these two million four hundred thousand koti daily-used attainments every single day, why is it necessary to specifically mention those entered on the day of becoming Buddha and the day of entering Parinibbāna?” The answer should be: “On other days, he entered those attainments in an ordinary manner. However, on the day of becoming Buddha and the day of entering Parinibbāna, he entered those attainments uniquely, having thoroughly analyzed and mixed them with the fourteen modes—namely, the seven modes of material phenomena (rūpa-sattaka) and the seven modes of mental phenomena (nāma-sattaka)—and preceded by Great Insight (Mahā-vipassanā). Therefore, those attainments entered on those two days are specifically mentioned.” This passage is from the Sutta Mahāvagga-ṭīkā.

(c) To continue: After the Buddha had attained Enlightenment, the merchant’s wife Sujātā heard the news: “The person to whom I offered the milk-rice was not the guardian deity of the banyan tree; that noble person was the Bodhisatta. That Bodhisatta
417:
attained Buddhahood after partaking of that milk-rice I offered. It is said that while the Blessed One was staying at the seven locations, he subsisted for the entire forty-nine days on that very milk-rice I offered.” Upon hearing this good news, great rapture (pīti) and joy (somanassa) repeatedly arose in the continuity of the merchant’s wife Sujātā as she reflected again and again, “It is a great gain for me!” In the continuity of Cunda, the son of the goldsmith, after the Blessed One had entered Parinibbāna, he heard the news: “I have offered the final alms-food to the Blessed One. In connection with my alms-food, the Blessed One has attained Nibbāna, which is like the crown of all dhammas. Having partaken of my alms-food, the Blessed One entered Parinibbāna through the Anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu.” Upon hearing this news, great rapture (pīti) and joy (somanassa) repeatedly arose as he reflected again and again, “It is a great gain for me!” Because the manner of reflection of the two donors was thus equal, the two types of alms-food are equal in their fruit and result. This is a point especially worthy of note.

## Arrival at the City of Kusinārā

Thereafter, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: “Come, Ānanda, let us go to the Mallas’ Sāla Grove at the entrance of the city of Kusinārā, on the other side of the Hiraññavatī River.” “Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied, consenting to the Blessed One’s command. Then the Blessed One, together with a large community of monks, proceeded to the Mallas’ Sāla Grove at the entrance of the city of Kusinārā, on the other side of the Hiraññavatī River. Having arrived, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, prepare a bed for me between the twin Sāla trees, with the head to the north.”
418:
“Prepare the couch, Ānanda. I am weary and would lie down,” the Buddha said.

“Very well, Venerable Sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied, and in accordance with the Buddha's command, he prepared the couch between the twin Sāla trees with the head facing north. The Buddha then lay down on his right side, placing the left foot slightly over the right, remaining mindful and self-possessed in the noble lion's posture.

(At this point, a special note should be mentioned:
On this journey from the city of Pāvā to the city of Kusinārā, the accompanying Saṅgha of monks was so numerous they were beyond counting. To elaborate—from the time the Buddha dispelled his painful feelings at the village of Veḷuva, the news spread that “The Buddha will soon attain Parinibbāna.” Monks who came from various places did not depart elsewhere; thus, the Saṅgha was indeed countless.

Inside the Sāla grove of Kusinārā, at the place where the couch was to be prepared, there was a row of Sāla trees to the north (the head side) and another row to the south (the foot side). In these two rows, there was a young Sāla tree at the head side and another young Sāla tree at the foot side; these were called the “Twin Sāla Trees.” Alternatively, the “Twin Sāla Trees” refers to a pair of Sāla trees whose roots, trunks, branches, and leaves were intertwined. In that grove, there was a royal couch belonging to the Malla princes; the Buddha commanded it to be prepared, and the Venerable Ānanda prepared it for him.

Regarding the words “Ānanda, I am weary and would lie down,” the natural physical strength of the Buddha was equal to the strength of a thousand ordinary elephants, or the strength of ten Chaddanta elephants.)
419:
(The Buddha's strength was equal to) the strength of ten thousand average men. Yet all that strength and power, from the time he suffered from dysentery after partaking of Cunda's meal, became exhausted like water poured into a filter. The distance from the city of Pāvā to the city of Kusinārā is only three gāvutas. Although he traveled this distance with great effort, resting twenty-five times along the way, he reached the Sāla grove of Kusinārā only at sunset. Thus, the illness overcame and suppressed all his health. To show this condition, he spoke the words that would alarm the whole world: “Ānanda, I am weary and would lie down.”

A question may arise: “Why did the Buddha travel to Kusinārā with such great effort? Could he not have attained Parinibbāna in other places?” The answer is: There is no place where he could not have attained Parinibbāna. However, the Buddha traveled to Kusinārā with great effort for three reasons.

(1) To elaborate—the Buddha foresaw these three reasons. His foresight was: “If I were to attain Parinibbāna in a place other than Kusinārā, there would be no occasion to preach the great Mahāsudassana Sutta. Only by attaining Parinibbāna in Kusinārā will I be able to preach the Mahāsudassana Sutta, which describes the great glory I enjoyed as a Bodhisatta even in the human world—a glory fit only for the celestial realms—in a discourse spanning two bhāṇavāras (the length of two recitations during the Council). Upon hearing this great Mahāsudassana Sutta from me, many people will realize they should perform meritorious deeds.” This is one reason.

(2) Furthermore: “If I attain Parinibbāna in a place other than Kusinārā, the wanderer Subhadda will not have the opportunity to see me. This wanderer Subhadda is one who can only be converted by a Buddha (Buddha-veneyya).
420:
He is not one who can be converted by a disciple (Sāvaka-veneyya); therefore, the disciples would not be able to discipline or liberate him. If I attain Parinibbāna in Kusinārā, this wanderer Subhadda will approach me and ask questions. At the end of the explanation of his questions, he will take refuge, receive ordination as a monk in my presence, learn meditation, and while I am still alive, attain the fruit of Arahatship, becoming my last disciple (pacchima-sāvaka).” This is the second reason.

(3) Furthermore: “If I attain Parinibbāna in a place other than Kusinārā, there will be a great conflict during the distribution of my relics, and it will be as if a river of blood might flow. If I attain Parinibbāna in Kusinārā, the Brahmin Dona will settle that conflict and distribute the relics.” This is the third reason.

Because of these three reasons mentioned above, the Buddha traveled to Kusinārā with such effort. (This is the answer).

## The Sāla Trees and the Worship by Devas
When the Buddha thus lay down on the couch of Parinibbāna, the twin Sāla trees were entirely covered in blossoms, though it was not the season for flowering. In worship of the Buddha, those Sāla trees incessantly showered and scattered their blossoms over the body of the Buddha.

Celestial Mandārava flowers also fell from the sky. In worship of the Buddha, the devas incessantly showered and scattered those celestial flowers over the body of the Buddha.
421:
Celestial sandalwood powder also fell from the sky. In worship of the Buddha, the devas incessantly showered and scattered that sandalwood powder over the body of the Buddha.

Celestial musical instruments were also being played in the sky in worship of the Buddha. Celestial songs were also being heard from the sky in worship of the Buddha.

## The Highest Worship
Then the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

“Ānanda, the twin Sāla trees are entirely covered in blossoms, though it is not the season for flowering. In worship of the Buddha, those Sāla trees incessantly shower and scatter their blossoms over the body of the Buddha.

Celestial Mandārava flowers also fall from the sky. In worship of the Buddha, the devas incessantly shower and scatter those celestial flowers over the body of the Buddha.

Celestial sandalwood powder also falls from the sky. In worship of the Buddha, the devas incessantly shower and scatter that sandalwood powder over the body of the Buddha.

Celestial musical instruments are also being played in the sky in worship of the Buddha.
422:
Celestial songs are also being heard from the sky in worship of the Buddha.

Ānanda, it is not by this much that the Buddha is truly honored, respected, revered, worshipped, or paid homage to. Ānanda, whatever monk or nun, or layman or laywoman, dwells practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (Dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti), dwells practicing properly, and lives according to the Dhamma—it is such a person who honors, respects, reveres, worships, and pays homage to the Buddha with the highest worship.

Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall dwell practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma; we shall dwell practicing properly; we shall live according to the Dhamma.’ This is how you must strive.”

(In this context: Regarding the worship by the Sāla trees, it should be understood that the earth-dwelling devas (bhummasita devas) shook the branches of those Sāla trees to perform the worship.

The celestial Mandārava flowers are those that grow in Lake Nandā. Those celestial flowers have leaves the size of a large leaf-umbrella and carry pollen the size of a large grain-measure. Not only Mandārava flowers, but other celestial flowers such as the Pāricchattaka were also being cast down in worship by devas dwelling at the edge of the universe, devas of the Tāvatiṃsa realm, and Brahmas of the Brahma realm.
423:
They were falling incessantly from the sky in great abundance. 

The mention of celestial sandalwood powder falling is merely an illustration; in truth, it was not only celestial sandalwood powder. Sandalwood powder from the Naga realm, the Garuda realm, and the human realm, as well as all other kinds of celestial perfumes such as red sandalwood, orpiment, cinnabar, antimony, gold dust, and silver dust—all these celestial fragrances were being cast down from full gold and silver caskets by the aforementioned devas and Brahmas, falling incessantly in great abundance over the body of the Buddha.

In the section on worship with celestial musical instruments, it should be understood that all types of musical instruments belonging to devas, Nagas, Garudas, and humans from the ten thousand world systems were brought together in this universe and played in the sky.

## The Immense Celestial Flower Garland
Regarding the statement that celestial songs were being heard from the sky: To explain in detail—there were long-lived devas named Varuṇa and Vāraṇa. These devas had heard the news that “The Bodhisatta will be born in the human world and become a Buddha.” Thinking, “We will take a flower garland to worship the Bodhisatta on the day of his conception,” they began weaving the garland at that time. While they were still weaving, they heard, “The Bodhisatta has entered his mother's womb.” When other devas asked, “For whom are you weaving this?” they replied, “The celestial garland is not yet finished; we shall take it to worship him on the day he is born from his mother's womb.”

Again, when they heard the news, “The Bodhisatta is born,” they said, “We shall go and worship him on the day he renounces the world.” Twenty-nine years... (the text continues)
424:
424
While dwelling in the human realm, when they heard the news, "Today the Bodhisatta has renounced the world," they said, "We shall go and pay homage on the day he attains Buddhahood." After he had practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for six years, when they heard the news, "Today he has attained Buddhahood," they said again, "We shall go and pay homage on the day he preaches the first sermon of the Dhammacakka." When they heard the news, "After staying at the seven locations near the Mahābodhi seat for seven weeks each, he has now gone to Isipatana Migadāya and preached the first sermon of the Dhammacakka," they said again, "We shall go and pay homage on the day he performs the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) of water and fire." When they heard the news, "Today he has performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire," they said again, "We shall go and pay homage on the day he descends from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven after preaching the Abhidhamma." When they heard the news, "Today he has descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven," they said again, "We shall go and pay homage on the day he relinquishes the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra)." When other devas informed them and they heard the news, "Today he has relinquished the life-force," they said, "The great garland is not yet finished; we shall only go and pay homage on the day he enters Parinibbāna."

Now, as the final news, other devas said, "Today the Blessed One, between the pair of young Sal trees, mindful and clearly comprehending, has attained the noble reclining posture on his right side. At the time of dawn, he will enter Parinibbāna. For whom are you weaving this great garland?" When those long-lived devas named Varuṇa and Vāraṇa heard the news that the Blessed One was about to enter Parinibbāna:

"What kind of matter is this? It was only today that the Bodhisatta took conception in his mother's womb; only today was he born from his mother's womb;
425:
425
Only today did he renounce the world; only today did he attain Buddhahood; only today did he preach the first sermon of the Dhammacakka; only today did he perform the Twin Miracle of water and fire; only today did he descend from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; only today did he relinquish the life-force; and only today is he about to enter Parinibbāna! (It is as if he conceived just now, was born just now, renounced just now, became Buddha just now, preached the first sermon just now, performed the miracle just now, descended from heaven just now, relinquished the life-force just now, and is about to enter Parinibbāna just now). Truly, he should remain for at least the duration of drinking a cup of gruel the next day. That he should enter Parinibbāna in such a short time is indeed unsuitable for a Great Man who has attained Buddhahood by fulfilling the ten perfections to their zenith."

Lamenting thus, they brought even the unfinished garlands and came before the Buddha. Finding no space within this world system (cakkavāḷa), they hung that great garland in the sky at the very edge of the world system. Running along the edge of the world system, they passed it from hand to hand, joined together, and embraced one another neck to neck. Focusing on the virtues of the Triple Gem, they composed and sang soft, sweet songs and verses based on the 32 marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa), the 6-colored rays, the 10 perfections, the 550 Jātakas, and the 14 Buddha-knowledges. At the end of each song and verse, they uttered praises: "Mahāyaso! The Blessed One is of great fame and retinue! Mahāyaso! The Blessed One is of great fame and retinue!" Referring to this, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Divine songs also arose in the sky as an offering to the Blessed One."

While reclining on the couch of Parinibbāna, the Blessed One saw the great effort of the assembly of devas and brahmas gathered from the surface of the earth to the edge of the world system, and from the edge of the world system to the Brahma realm.
426:
426
Seeing their great effort, the Blessed One informed Venerable Ānanda about it. After showing this great material homage (āmisa-pūjā) of the devas and brahmas, he continued to teach that he is not truly honored with the highest and best homage by such material offerings; only when one honors him with the homage of practice (dhamma-pūjā) is he honored with the highest homage. The meaning of those words is:

"Dear Ānanda, I, who fulfilled the eight factors, prostrated at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha to form a bridge and made the aspiration for Buddhahood, and who fulfilled the perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, did not make that aspiration nor fulfill those perfections with the intention of receiving offerings of flowers, scents, music, and divine songs. Therefore, honoring me with these divine flowers, scents, music, and songs is not called honoring with the highest homage. Only honoring with the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti) is called honoring with the highest homage."

Here, a question arises: "The Blessed One has praised elsewhere that even offering a single sesame flower while reflecting on the Buddha's virtues brings great benefits beyond the scope of a Buddha's knowledge. Why then, in this instance, does he reject such a grand offering?"

The answer is: He rejected it because he wished to encourage the assembly and desired the long-term endurance of the Sāsana. To elaborate: If the Blessed One did not reject it in this way, in the future, people would not fulfill virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi) where they are required; they would not practice insight (vipassanā) where it is required. Instead, they would only teach and encourage lay devotees to make offerings of flowers, scents, and so on, and would spend their time performing only material homage (āmisa-pūjā). Material homage is not capable of sustaining the Sāsana of the three trainings even for the duration of drinking a cup of gruel for one day. Indeed—
427:
427
A thousand monasteries like the Mahāvihāra, or a thousand stupas like the Mahācetiya, cannot sustain the Sāsana for a long time. In truth, they are merely supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the donor to attain the three types of happiness: human, divine, and Nibbāna.

Only right practice (sammā-paṭipatti) is the suitable homage for the Blessed One. Indeed, the Blessed One desired only that homage of practice (dhamma-pūjā), which is right practice. Only this homage of practice is capable of sustaining the Sāsana for a long duration. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus (it was not because material homage has no benefit). This is the answer.

## Practice in Accordance with the Supramundane Dhamma

In this context, practicing the 'practice in accordance with the Dhamma' (dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti), which means the practice suitable for the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma), is the highest homage to the Blessed One. This practice in accordance with the Dhamma refers to the preliminary practices (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) occurring before the Path (magga), starting from taking refuge and virtue up to the stage of Gotrabhū.

Therefore, if a monk, established in the six types of irreverence, transgresses the training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed by the Blessed One, or seeks the four requisites through improper means of livelihood, that monk is said to be one who does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma. However, if a monk does not transgress even to the slightest degree the Buddha's discipline and rules—all the training rules prescribed for him—this monk is said to be one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma. The same applies to a nun.

If a lay follower (upāsaka) practices the five types of enmity (vera), such as killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), which bring only harmful results like an enemy,
428:
428
or the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha), this lay follower is said to be one who does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma. But if a lay follower keeps the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts securely, observes the Uposatha eight days a month (the four quarter-moon days), is habitually generous, and honors the Triple Gem with scents and flowers; and if he serves his parents and the virtuous ones known as Samana-Brāhmaṇa who abide in the Dhamma, then that lay follower is said to be one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma. The same applies to a female lay follower (upāsikā).

Honoring the Blessed One with this practice in accordance with the Dhamma is also called non-material homage (nirāmisa-pūjā). Only this highest homage, known as non-material, can sustain the Sāsana to endure for a long time. As long as these four groups of followers—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—continue to honor the Blessed One with this non-material homage, the Buddha's Sāsana will surely shine and be as beautiful as the full moon in the middle of the sky.

## Venerable Upavāṇa

At that time, Venerable Upavāṇa was standing in front of the Blessed One, fanning him. Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Upavāṇa, saying, "Monk, move aside; do not stand in front of me," and dismissed him. With just that single word, Venerable Upavāṇa put down his palm-leaf fan and stood in a place where he would not be an obstruction.

Then, a thought arose in the mind of Venerable Ānanda: "This Venerable Upavāṇa has been a long-time attendant who stayed near the Blessed One and was always in his presence (during the first twenty years after Enlightenment). Yet now, at this final moment when the Blessed One is about to enter Parinibbāna, he says, 'Monk, move aside; do not stand in front of me,' and dismisses him. What could be the reason for this dismissal?"
429:
429
Thinking thus, Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, this Venerable Upavāṇa has been a long-time attendant who stayed near the Blessed One and was always in his presence. Yet now, at this final moment when the Blessed One is about to enter Parinibbāna, you say, 'Monk, move aside; do not stand in front of me,' and have dismissed him. What, Venerable Sir, is the reason for this dismissal?"

Then the Blessed One thought, "Ānanda thinks I dismissed the monk Upavāṇa because of some fault. I shall now explain the faultless nature of the monk Upavāṇa," and he addressed Venerable Ānanda:

"Dear Ānanda, the devas and brahmas from the ten thousand world systems have mostly assembled to see the Buddha (excluding the non-percipient and formless brahmas). Dear Ānanda, within twelve leagues (yojana) around the Sal grove of Kusinārā, there is not a single spot even the size of the tip of a hair that is not crowded with powerful devas. (a)

Dear Ānanda, the devas are complaining about the monk Upavāṇa: 'We have come from afar to see the Blessed One...'
430:
430
'...have come; the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas, appear in the world only once in a long while. The Parinibbāna of the Blessed One will take place in the last watch of this very night. Yet, this powerful monk Upavāṇa is standing in front of the Blessed One, blocking the view. We will no longer have the opportunity to behold the Blessed One in these final moments,' thus they are complaining. (Therefore, I have asked the monk Upavāṇa to step aside) (b)."
Thus, He explained.

(Here, some special notes should be mentioned— (a) In this context, within a space as small as the tip of a single hair's breadth closest to the Blessed One, Devas and Brahmās, having created subtle bodies for themselves, are standing in groups of ten. Outside of them, they stand in groups of twenty; further out, in groups of thirty; further out, in groups of forty; further out, in groups of fifty; and further out, in groups of sixty. These Devas and Brahmās do not touch one another with their hands, feet, or garments. There is no such thing as having to say, "Move aside, do not touch me."

(b) In this context, the Elder Upavāṇa was naturally large in stature, like a young elephant, and since he was wearing a rag-robe (paṃsukūla), he appeared even more massive, effectively blocking the front of the Blessed One. Consequently, the Devas and Brahmās, unable to behold the golden countenance of the Blessed One, complained in that manner.

Here, one might ask: "Could the Devas and Brahmās not see the Blessed One's face by looking through the body of the Elder Upavāṇa?" The answer is: No, they could not. Indeed—
431:
431
Devas and Brahmās can see through ordinary persons (puthujjana), but they cannot see through Arahants. In particular, because the Elder Upavāṇa possessed such great power and majesty, they were unable even to approach near him.

Here, another question might arise: "Why was only the Elder Upavāṇa so great in power and majesty, while other Arahants were not as powerful as him?" The answer is: Because he had previously been a guardian deity of the Cetiya of Kassapa Buddha, he possessed such great power and majesty.

## The Guardian Deity of the Cetiya
To elaborate—ninety-one aeons ago, when Vipassī Buddha attained Parinibbāna, a Cetiya was built for the bodily relics (sārīrika-dhātu), which remained as a single solid mass like a block of gold. (Specifically, when Buddhas with long lifespans attain Parinibbāna, it is the natural law that the bodily relics remain as a single mass, and people build only one Cetiya to worship). For the Cetiya where the single mass of relics of Vipassī Buddha was enshrined, people used golden bricks measuring one cubit in length, a span in width, and two inches in thickness. Instead of mortar, they used realgar and orpiment powders, and instead of water, they used sesame oil to build it to a height of one league (yojana).

Then, the earth-bound deities (bhummasoc) added to it until it was one league higher. Then, the sky-bound deities (ākāsasoc) added another league. Then, the Unhavalāhaka deities added one league, the Abbhavalāhaka deities added one league, the Cātumahārājika deities added one league, and finally, the Tāvatiṃsa deities added one league. Thus, the Cetiya enshrining the single mass of relics of Vipassī Buddha reached a height of seven leagues.
432:
432
When many people came to worship the Cetiya bringing flowers, perfumes, robes, and so on, the guardian deity of the Cetiya would take those offerings and offer them to the Cetiya while the people were watching.

At that time, the future Elder Upavāṇa was a wealthy Brahmin who brought a golden-colored robe to offer to the Cetiya. The guardian deity took the robe from his hand and offered it to the Cetiya. Seeing the deity, the wealthy Brahmin was filled with devotion and made a wish: "May I also become a guardian deity of such a Buddha's Cetiya in the future." After passing away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm.

While he was wandering through the celestial and human realms, Kassapa Buddha appeared in the world and attained Parinibbāna. The bodily relics of Kassapa Buddha also remained as a single mass (as He was a Buddha with a long lifespan). Taking that single mass of relics, the king and the people built a Cetiya with a circumference and height of one league. The future Elder Upavāṇa became the guardian deity of that Cetiya of Kassapa Buddha. When the Dispensation (Sāsana) disappeared, he was reborn again in the celestial realm. When our Blessed One appeared, he passed away from the celestial realm, took conception in a noble family, went forth into homelessness, and attained the Fruit of Arahantship.

Thus, because he had been the guardian deity of Kassapa Buddha's Cetiya, the Elder Upavāṇa possessed great power and majesty. This is the answer.

When the Blessed One explained that "the Elder Upavāṇa was not asked to move because of any fault, but because the Devas were complaining,"
433:
433
Elder Ānanda further addressed the Blessed One:
"Exalted Blessed One, how does the Blessed One perceive the state of the Devas and Brahmās?"
(The underlying meaning of the question was whether the Devas and Brahmās were able to endure the fact that the Blessed One was about to attain Parinibbāna). Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show that the Devas and Brahmās could not endure it, said to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Dear Ānanda, those Devas who are in the sky with the perception of earth, disheveling their hair, they weep; raising their arms, they weep; they fall down as if falling from a precipice; they roll to and fro, they roll this way and that, lamenting: 'Too soon will the Blessed One attain Parinibbāna! Too soon will the Well-Spoken One attain Parinibbāna! Too soon will the Eye of Wisdom vanish from the world!'

Dear Ānanda, those Devas who are on the earth with the perception of earth, disheveling their hair, they weep; raising their arms, they weep; they fall down as if falling from a precipice; they roll to and fro, they roll this way and that, lamenting: 'Too soon will the Blessed One attain Parinibbāna! Too soon will the Well-Spoken One attain Parinibbāna! Too soon will the Eye of Wisdom...'
434:
434
...vanish from the world!' Thus they dishevel their hair and weep; they raise their arms and weep. They fall down as if falling from a precipice. They roll to and fro, they roll this way and that.

But those Devas who are free from passion (vītarāga) endure it mindfully and clearly comprehending, reflecting: 'Conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are impermanent. How could it be otherwise in this case?'"
Thus He said.

(In this passage, "Devas who are in the sky with the perception of earth" refers to Devas who, having created a surface of earth in the natural sky, stand there perceiving that created surface as earth. "Devas who are on the earth with the perception of earth" refers to Devas who, by their psychic power, created a 'new earth' upon this great earth (Mahāpathavī) capable of supporting their own bodies, and stand there perceiving that created surface as earth.

Because the natural earth is coarse and the natural bodies of Devas are extremely subtle and delicate, the natural earth cannot support the bodies of Devas. If a Deva's natural body were to stand on the natural earth, it would sink into the ground like a lump of butter. Therefore, once when a Brahmā named Hatthaka came to stand before the Blessed One, he could not remain standing and kept sinking into the earth. The Blessed One then gave him instructions, saying, "Hatthaka, create a coarse physical form for your body." Therefore, in this context as well, since the Devas were unable to stand on the natural earth, they created a surface capable of supporting their bodies...
435:
435
...having created the natural earth into a very soft form, they rolled and wept upon it).

## The Four Places that Arouse Spiritual Urgency
Then, the Venerable Elder Ānanda continued to address the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, in the past, monks who had spent the rains retreat (vassa) in various directions would come to behold the Blessed One. We used to have the opportunity to see and attend upon those monks who were worthy of devotion and esteem. Venerable Sir, after the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, we will no longer have the opportunity to see and attend upon such monks worthy of devotion and esteem as we did before."

During the Buddha's time, monks would gather at the Buddha's location on two occasions: 1. When the time for the rains retreat was near, to learn meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), and 2. When the rains retreat was over, to report the special attainments of the Path and Fruition (magga-phala) they had achieved through practicing the meditation subjects they had learned. Just as in the Buddha's time, in the island of Sri Lanka (Sīhaḷa), when the rains retreat was near, monks living on this side of the shore would gather at the Lohapāsāda palace, and monks living on the other side (the Mahāgāma side) would gather at the Tissa Mahā Vihāra built by King Kākavaṇṇatissa. Among those monks, those living on this side would bring baskets for disposing of rubbish and brooms, and gather at the Mahā Vihāra to perform necessary repairs (such as patching plaster or applying lime-wash) at the Mahā Cetiya, and then...
436:
“When the rains retreat is over, let us come and assemble at the Lohapāsāda,” they consulted and agreed. Having performed their duties such as sweeping and disposing of rubbish in their respective places, they spent the rains retreat in places where they found comfort. When the rains retreat was over, they came again and assembled in the Pavilion of the Five Nikāyas (Pañcanikāya Maṇḍalamāla) within the Lohapāsāda. The monks who studied the Pali recited the Pali, and the monks who studied the Commentaries (Atthakathā) recited the Commentaries. If a monk recited the Pali or the Commentary incorrectly, they would inquire, “Friend, from which teacher did you learn this?” and after investigating, they would correct it and have him recite and learn it properly. The monks living on the other side (the Mahāgāma side) did the same at the Tissa Mahāvihāra.

In this way, during the Buddha's time, among the monks who assembled on two occasions—those who went after learning meditation at the beginning of the rains and returned after the rains to report their special attainments of Path and Fruition (Magga-Phala) to the Buddha—Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha as previously mentioned.

Because Venerable Ānanda was one who fulfilled his duties, whenever he saw a senior monk arriving, he never remained seated with pride or harshness. He would go out to welcome them, take the umbrella, bowl, and robes from the hands of the visiting senior monk, and then dust the wooden seat to offer it to them. After the senior monk was seated and Ānanda had paid his respects, for that visiting senior monk...
437:
...he would clean and provide a suitable dwelling. Even upon seeing a junior visiting monk, he would not remain silent but would stand near him and perform all necessary duties. Therefore, Venerable Ānanda, desiring that these great and small duties he was accustomed to performing should not diminish, spoke thus to the Buddha.

Then the Buddha, reflecting, “Ānanda is worried and thinking, ‘I shall no longer have the opportunity to see the monks who are worthy of devotion and affection.’ Now, I shall tell Ānanda of the places where he can easily find the opportunity to see such monks. By staying in those places, he will easily have the opportunity to see monks worthy of devotion and affection without having to wander here and there,” addressed Venerable Ānanda:

“Ānanda, there are four places that a person of noble birth endowed with faith should visit, and which will cause a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in the one who visits them. What are the four?

(1) Ānanda, the place of the Lumbinī Sal grove is a place that a person of noble birth endowed with faith should visit, thinking, ‘Here the Buddha was born,’ and it is a place that will cause spiritual urgency in the one who visits it.

(2) Ānanda, the place of the Mahābodhi seat is a place that a person of noble birth endowed with faith should visit, thinking, ‘Here the Buddha attained the supreme Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi),’ and it is a place that will cause spiritual urgency in the one who visits it.”
438:
(3) Ānanda, the place of the Migadāya (Deer Park) is a place that a person of noble birth endowed with faith should visit, thinking, ‘Here the Buddha set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka),’ and it is a place that will cause spiritual urgency in the one who visits it.

(4) Ānanda, the place of the city of Kusinārā is a place that a person of noble birth endowed with faith should visit, thinking, ‘Here the Buddha attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu),’ and it is a place that will cause spiritual urgency in the one who visits it.

Ānanda, these are the four places that a person of noble birth endowed with faith should visit, and which will cause spiritual urgency in the one who visits them.

Ānanda, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen endowed with faith will come, thinking: (1) ‘In this Lumbinī place, the Buddha was born’; (2) ‘In this Mahābodhi place, the Buddha attained the supreme Perfect Enlightenment’; (3) ‘In this Migadāya place, the Buddha set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma’; (4) ‘In this Kusinārā place, the Buddha attained Parinibbāna through the...’
439:
...Nibbāna element without residue.’ Ānanda, those who travel to visit these shrines (cetiyas) with a devout heart, if they die while doing so, all of them, after the breaking up of the body after death, will reach a good destination, the heavenly world.”

Thus He spoke.

## Detailed Questions and Answers of Venerable Ānanda

Thereafter, Venerable Ānanda asked in detail, and the Buddha answered in detail as follows:

(Venerable Ānanda)
“Bhante, how should we conduct ourselves regarding women (mātugāma)?”

(The Buddha)
“Ānanda, you should conduct yourselves by not seeing them (meaning: do not look).”

(The meaning is that not looking at women is the best practice. Indeed, a monk who stays in his dwelling with the door closed does not experience greed or agitation of mind as long as he does not see a woman standing at the door. Only upon seeing can attachment and agitation of mind occur. Therefore, the Buddha gave the best practice by answering, “Do not look, Ānanda.”)

(Venerable Ānanda)
“Bhante, if we do see them, how should we conduct ourselves?”

(The Buddha)
“Ānanda, you should remain without speaking (meaning: the intention is to answer, ‘Do not speak, Ānanda’).”
440:
(When a woman stands bringing alms-food, etc., it is impossible not to see her; she will be seen. Venerable Ānanda asked how to behave when such a sight occurs. Then the Buddha taught: It is better to speak with a man who stands holding a sword saying, “If you speak to me, I will cut off your head right here so it falls like a basket,” or with an ogress who stands saying, “If you speak to me, I will chew and eat your flesh right here.” Indeed, such speech can only lead to ruin in one lifetime; it cannot cause one to suffer the boundless misery of the four woeful states. If there is initial talk (ālāpa) and repeated intimate conversation (sallāpa) with a woman, intimacy (vissāsa) arises. When intimacy arises, there is a descent into passion (rāga). When that happens, one's virtue is destroyed, and one falls into the woeful states to suffer great misery. Therefore, the Buddha answered, “Do not speak, Ānanda.”)

(Venerable Ānanda)
“Bhante, if we must speak (unavoidably), how should we conduct ourselves?”

(The Buddha)
“Ānanda, you should speak while maintaining mindfulness as if they were your own mother and so forth.”

(If a woman asks about the day, such as “What day is today?”, or requests the precepts, or asks for a Dhamma talk, or asks a question—answering in such instances is indeed a duty of monks. If one does not answer or speak in such cases, one might be criticized: “This monk is a mute; this monk is deaf. After eating, he just stays silent with his door closed.” Therefore, in such cases, one must certainly speak. Thus, Venerable Ānanda asked, “If we must speak, how should we conduct ourselves?” Then the Buddha, referring to the advice found in the...
441:
...Saṃyutta Nikāya (S.ii.329 = Saḷāyatana-vagga Saṃyutta, Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta, 13, 3-Gahapati-vagga, 4-Bhāradvāja Sutta): ‘Come, monks, establish the thought of a mother towards women who are of an age to be your mother; establish the thought of a sister towards women who are of an age to be your sister; establish the thought of a daughter towards women who are of an age to be your daughter,’ answered, ‘Ānanda, you should speak while maintaining mindfulness as if they were your own mother and so forth.’

(Venerable Ānanda)
“Bhante, when the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, how should we act regarding the Blessed One's physical remains (utujarūpakalāpa)?”

(The Buddha)
“Ānanda, do not trouble yourselves about the worship of the Buddha's physical remains. Ānanda, I urge you deeply: strive only for the supreme practice (brahmacariya). Be diligent and ardent in the supreme practice, and live with your minds directed towards Nibbāna. Ānanda, there are wise kings, wise brahmins, and wise householders who have great faith in the Buddha; they will perform the worship of the Buddha's physical remains.”

(Venerable Ānanda)
“Bhante, how should those wise kings, wise brahmins, and wise householders act regarding the Blessed One's physical remains? (When the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, those kings, brahmins...)”
442:
442

"Wise and wealthy people will surely ask me, 'Venerable Ānanda, how should we act regarding the physical remains (utujarūpakalāpa) of the Blessed One?' What answer should I give to them?" (This was the intent of the question).

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, as one acts towards the physical remains of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), so should one act towards the physical remains of the Tathāgata."

(Venerable Ānanda)
"Lord, how do they act towards the physical remains of a Universal Monarch?"

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, they wrap the physical remains of a Universal Monarch in new cloth from the Kāsī country. (Since that new Kāsī cloth is very fine and cannot absorb oil, but only a bale of cotton can absorb oil), after wrapping it in new Kāsī cloth, they wrap it again in carded cotton. After wrapping it in carded cotton, they wrap it again in new Kāsī cloth. After wrapping it in new Kāsī cloth, they wrap it again in cotton. In this manner, having wrapped the physical remains of the Universal Monarch in five hundred pairs of garments, they place it in a golden oil-vat (a golden coffin filled with oil) and cover it with another golden lid. Then, having built a pyre of all kinds of perfumes, they cremate the physical remains of the Universal Monarch. They build a stupa (cetiya) for the Universal Monarch at the crossroads. Ānanda, this is how they act towards the physical remains of a Universal Monarch as mentioned above."
443:
443

## A Stupa Should Be Built

"Ānanda, just as they act towards the physical remains of a Universal Monarch, so should they act towards the physical remains of the Tathāgata. A stupa for the Tathāgata should be built at the crossroads. Whoever places flowers, perfumes, or scented powder there, or pays homage, or develops a clear mind of devotion, it will be for their long-term welfare and happiness."

## Four Kinds of Persons Worthy of a Stupa

"Ānanda, these four kinds of persons are worthy of a stupa. The four are:
1. The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, is worthy of a stupa.
2. The Paccekabuddha is worthy of a stupa.
3. The Disciple (Ariya Sāvaka) of the Tathāgata is worthy of a stupa.
4. The Universal Monarch is worthy of a stupa.
These are the four.

Ānanda, for what special benefit is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, worthy of a stupa? Ānanda, many people develop a clear mind of faith and devotion, thinking, 'This is the stupa of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.' Having developed such faith and devotion at that stupa, after the breaking up of the body, after death,

they reach a good destination, a heavenly world. Ānanda, it is for this special benefit that the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, is worthy of a stupa.

Ānanda, for what special benefit is a Paccekabuddha worthy of a stupa? Ānanda, many people develop a clear mind of faith and devotion, thinking, 'This is the stupa of that Blessed One, the Paccekabuddha, who realized the Four Noble Truths by himself.' Having developed such faith and devotion at that stupa, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they reach a good destination, a heavenly world. Ānanda, many people develop a clear mind of faith and devotion, thinking, 'This is the stupa of that disciple, the Noble One, of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.' Having developed such faith and devotion at that stupa, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they reach a good destination, a heavenly world. Ānanda, it is for this special benefit that a disciple of the Tathāgata is worthy of a stupa.

Ānanda, for what special benefit is a Universal Monarch worthy of a stupa? Ānanda, many people develop a clear mind of faith and devotion, thinking, 'This is the stupa of that righteous king (Dhammarāja), the Universal Monarch.' Having developed such faith and devotion at that stupa, after the breaking up of the body,

after death, they reach a good destination, a heavenly world. Ānanda, it is for this special benefit that a Universal Monarch is worthy of a stupa.

Ānanda, these are the four kinds of persons worthy of a stupa."

This is the detailed explanation given by the Blessed One in response to the detailed inquiry of the Venerable Ānanda.

(A question may arise here: "Why did the Blessed One allow a stupa for a Universal Monarch who lived and died in the household life, but did not allow a stupa for a virtuous worldling (puthujjana) monk?"

The answer is: It should be answered briefly that "He did not allow it because it would not be a wonder." In detail: If stupas were allowed for virtuous worldling monks, there would be so many stupas that there would be no room for them even on the island of Sri Lanka, let alone other places. Thus, if stupas were allowed for virtuous worldling monks, they would be so numerous that they would not be a wonder; therefore, He did not allow it. A Universal Monarch, however, is unique, and his stupa can be a wonder; thus, He allowed a stupa for a Universal Monarch. Although a stupa is not allowed for a virtuous worldling monk, it is very appropriate and fitting to perform great offerings and honors for such a monk, just as for a monk who has attained Parinibbāna. This is the answer).
