## Preaching of the Mahāsudassana Sutta
After the Blessed One had spoken thus (regarding the virtues of Venerable Ānanda), Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

“Lord, may the Blessed One not attain Parinibbāna in this small, insignificant town, a mere wattle-and-daub town (Kusinārā). Lord, there are other great cities such as Campā, Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, and Bārāṇasī. May the Blessed One attain Parinibbāna in those great cities. In those great cities, there are many wealthy nobles, wealthy brahmins, and wealthy householders who have great faith in the Blessed One; those wealthy people will honor the physical remains (body) of the Blessed One in a grand and magnificent manner.”
456: Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Do not say so, Ānanda. Do not say, 'a small wattle-and-daub town, a town in the midst of the jungle, a mere outpost.' Do not say so, Ānanda.##In the past, Ānanda, there was a king named Mahāsudassana, a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti), a righteous king who ruled according to the Dhamma, a conqueror of the four quarters, who had established the security of his realm and was possessed of the seven treasures. This Kusinārā, Ānanda, was then the royal capital of King Mahāsudassana, named Kusāvatī. It was twelve yojanas in length from east to west and seven yojanas in breadth from north to south.##Kusāvatī, Ānanda, was prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-provided with food. Just as the royal city of the devas named Āḷakamandā, the city of King Vessavaṇa, is prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with spirits (yakkhas), and well-provided with food; even so, Ānanda, was the royal capital Kusāvatī prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-provided with food.##Kusāvatī, Ānanda, was never free from ten sounds by day or by night: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of drums, the sound of tabors, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, the sound of conchs, the sound of cymbals and gongs, and the tenth sound was 'Eat, drink, and be merry!'—the sound of invitation and feasting."
457: (In this context, in other towns, only inauspicious sounds prevail, such as 'Discard the rubbish!', 'Take the hoes!', 'Take the baskets!', 'Let us go elsewhere!', 'Take the rice-packets!', 'Take the food-packets!', 'Prepare the shields and weapons for war!' In the royal capital of Kusāvatī, however, it was not so. It means that the city was never silent, day or night, from auspicious sounds of invitation such as 'Eat, drink, and be merry!')##"Kusāvatī, Ānanda, was surrounded by seven walls"—in this manner, the Blessed One preached the great Mahāsudassana Sutta, which is two bhāṇavāras in length (for details, see the Burmese translation of the Sutta Mahāvagga Pāḷi). Having concluded the discourse, he said to the Venerable Ānanda:##"Go now, Ānanda, enter Kusinārā and say to the Mallas of Kusinārā: 'Tonight, Vāseṭṭhas, in the last watch of the night, the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata will take place. Come forth, Vāseṭṭhas, come forth! Do not let yourselves be regretful later, thinking: "The Tathāgata passed away within our own territory, yet we did not take the opportunity to see the Tathāgata in his last hours."'"##The Venerable Ānanda, having replied, "Very well, Bhante," to the Blessed One, entered Kusinārā together with another monk.##(In this regard, one might ask: "Did those Mallas not know that the Blessed One had arrived?" The answer is: It was not that they did not know; they did. Wherever the Buddhas arrive, it is natural for a great clamor and commotion to arise from the devas and faithful lay devotees who go before them. However, the Mallas were unable to come because they were assembled for some business. Furthermore, because there was no monastery built for the Buddha in that Sāla grove, and because the number of monks was very large, the Buddha considered, "Those Mallas will come and arrange seating and make offerings for the Saṅgha." Thus, he sent Ānanda even at an unusual time, during the night. In sending him, he intended that the Mallas should not feel regret, thinking, "Why did the Blessed One not let us hear the news of his condition in his final moments?" and thus he sent Ānanda to deliver the message as described.)
458: ## The Homage of the Mallas##When the Venerable Ānanda entered Kusinārā, the Mallas of Kusinārā were assembled in their assembly hall (Santhāgāra) for some public business. Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the Mallas' assembly hall and, as instructed by the Blessed One, said:##"Vāseṭṭhas, tonight in the last watch of the night, the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata will take place. Come forth, Vāseṭṭhas, come forth! Do not let yourselves be regretful later, thinking: 'The Tathāgata passed away within our own territory, yet we did not take the opportunity to see the Tathāgata in his last hours.'"

They lamented: "Too soon will the Blessed One pass away! Too soon will the Sugata pass away! Too soon will the Eye of the World vanish from the world!" Some tore their hair and wept; some raised their arms and wept; some fell down as if their legs were cut from under them; some rolled to and fro, and some tossed about this way and that.##Then the Mallas, their sons, their daughters-in-law, and their wives, being deeply grieved and sorrowful, went to the Sāla grove and approached the Venerable Ānanda. Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:##"If I allow the Mallas of Kusinārā to pay homage to the Blessed One one by one, the night will be over before they have all finished. It would be better if I arrange the Mallas of Kusinārā by families and present them to the Blessed One, saying: 'Bhante, the Malla named so-and-so, with his children, his wife, his ministers, and his retinue, pays homage at the feet of the Blessed One.'"

...thinking, "It would be good if I could let them pay homage to the Blessed One by announcing them one by one."

After having this thought, the Venerable Ānanda, according to his plan, arranged the Mallas of Kusinārā into groups by family and announced them repeatedly: "Venerable Sir, the Malla named so-and-so, together with his children, wife, ministers, and retinue, pays homage at the feet of the Blessed One." ## The Story of Subhadda the Wanderer

At that time, a wanderer named Subhadda was staying in Kusinārā. Subhadda heard the news: "Tonight, in the last watch of the night, the Parinibbāna of the Ascetic Gotama will take place." Then, a thought arose in Subhadda's mind:

"I have heard from elderly teachers and teachers of teachers among the wanderers that 'Arahants, Fully Enlightened Buddhas, arise in the world only rarely.' Tonight, in the last watch of the night, the Parinibbāna of the Ascetic Gotama will take place. A doubt has arisen in my mind. I have confidence that 'The Ascetic Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma so that I may abandon this doubt.'"
461: ## Subhadda's Past Story##This Subhadda the Wanderer was not the Subhadda who was the son of Upaka and Cāpā. Nor was he the old monk Subhadda who, after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, when the Venerable Mahākassapa was traveling from Pāvā to Kusinārā with a large company of monks, spoke rude and harsh words among the monks, saying, "Now that the Blessed One has passed away, we shall be free to do as we like." In fact, this Subhadda the Wanderer was a wanderer who wore clothes, born of a very famous and wealthy Brahmin family, and he was the last disciple to be converted by the Blessed One.##Why did such a thought occur to Subhadda the Wanderer only now, so close to the time of Parinibbāna? It was because he had accumulated past merits (upaniṣaya) that would allow him to attain liberation at the very last moment. Thus, this thought arose in him only today, just before the Parinibbāna.##To elaborate: In the past, while performing meritorious deeds, there were two brothers. These two brothers cultivated grain together. Among them, the elder brother had the thought: "From each harvest of grain, I should make nine offerings of the first-fruits (agga-dāna)."
462: The elder brother, acting on his thought, gave the first-fruits of the seeds when sowing the grain. Later, when the grain began to form milk, he consulted his brother, saying, "Brother, now that the grain is milky, let us extract the milk and make an offering of the first-fruits of the milky grain." The younger brother objected, saying, "Brother, you wish to destroy the young grain!"##The elder brother, realizing that the younger brother would not agree to his wish, divided the field into two halves. From his own portion, he took the milky grain, extracted the milk, mixed it with ghee and honey, and made an offering of the first-fruits of the milky grain. When the grain was suitable for making parched rice, he made an offering of the first-fruits of parched rice. When the grain was ripe and harvested, he took the first-reaped sheaves and made an offering of the first-fruits of the harvest. When the sheaves were bound, he took the first-bound sheaves and made an offering of the first-fruits of the sheaves. When the sheaves were gathered together, he took the first of the heap and made an offering of the first-fruits of the heap. When the grain was threshed, he made an offering of the first-fruits of the threshing. When the threshed grain was winnowed and piled on the threshing floor, he took the first of the pile and made an offering of the first-fruits of the grain-pile. When the grain was moved from the threshing floor to the granary, he took the first to enter and made an offering of the first-fruits of the granary. In this way, the elder brother...
463: At each harvest, he offered the first-fruits (u-ū dāna) nine times. The younger brother, however, only gave his donation from the granary after all his grain had been harvested and stored. Of these two brothers, the elder became the Venerable Aññāsi Koṇḍañña in this Buddha's Dispensation. When the Buddha reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He considered, "Aññāsi Koṇḍañña is one who offered the first-fruits nine times at each harvest. I shall preach this first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, to this donor of first-fruits, Aññāsi Koṇḍañña." Thus, He preached the supreme Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta first to him before all others. That Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, together with eighteen crores of Brahmas, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The younger brother, because he gave his donation later, became the wanderer Subhadda during the time of the Buddha's appearance. As the Buddha was about to attain Parinibbāna, he reflected as previously mentioned and desired to see the Buddha. (This is the past story of the wanderer Subhadda) (From Dīgha Nikāya Commentary Vol. 2, pp. 179-180). Driven by the impulse of his past meritorious perfections (pāramī), Subhadda did not delay and immediately went to the Sal-tree grove, approached the Venerable Ānanda, and said to him:
464: "O Venerable Ānanda, I have heard from elderly wanderers, teachers, and teachers of teachers, that Arahants, Sammāsambuddhas, appear only rarely in the world. This very night, in the last watch, the Parinibbāna of the recluse Gotama will take place. A doubt has arisen in my mind. I have complete confidence in the recluse Gotama, believing, 'The recluse Gotama is able to preach the Dhamma to me so that I may abandon this doubt.' O Venerable Ānanda, I entreat you, I wish to have the opportunity to see the recluse Gotama." Thus he made his request. When he had spoken, the Venerable Ānanda reflected: "These sectarians (titthiyas) outside this Dispensation hold firmly to their own views. If the Buddha were to preach many discourses to dispel this wanderer Subhadda's wrong view, it would only result in the physical and vocal exhaustion of the Blessed One. This wanderer Subhadda will not abandon his wrong view, and the Blessed One is already naturally exhausted." Having considered this, he replied to the wanderer Subhadda: "Enough, friend Subhadda, do not trouble the Blessed One. The Blessed One is weary."
465: The wanderer Subhadda thought, "The Venerable Ānanda does not grant me permission, yet one who has a need should act according to their wish." He made his request a second time in the same manner. The Venerable Ānanda replied in the same manner. A third time, the wanderer Subhadda made his request, and the Venerable Ānanda replied in the same manner. The Blessed One, hearing with His natural ear the conversation between the wanderer Subhadda and the Venerable Ānanda, and having come to the city of Kusinārā with great effort specifically for Subhadda's sake, said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Enough, Ānanda, do not hinder him. Let Subhadda have the opportunity to see the Buddha. Ānanda, whatever Subhadda asks me, he will ask from a desire for knowledge, not to harass me. And whatever I answer, he will quickly understand." Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the wanderer Subhadda, "Go, friend Subhadda, the Blessed One gives you permission." Then the wanderer Subhadda approached the Blessed One, exchanged pleasant and memorable greetings with Him, and sat down in a suitable place. Having sat there, he addressed the Blessed One with this question:
466: "O Venerable Gotama, those recluses and brahmins who have a following, a group, who are heads of a sect, famous, renowned, founders of schools, and regarded by many as holy men—namely, (1) Pūraṇa Kassapa, (2) Makkhali Gosāla, (3) Ajita Kesakambala, (4) Pakudha Kaccāyana, (5) Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, and (6) Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta—do they all have direct knowledge of everything as they claim, or do they not, or do some have knowledge while others do not?" Thus he asked. (Here, Subhadda's main point was: "Venerable Buddha, the six sectarian teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa each claim, 'We are omniscient (Sabbaññū), knowing all things.' Their many disciples also recognize them as truly holy men. Do all six of these sectarian teachers truly become omniscient Buddhas as they claim, or are all six not omniscient Buddhas, or are some omniscient and others not? If they were omniscient Buddhas, the doctrines they teach must be 'niyyānika' (leading out of the round of rebirth). Are all the doctrines taught by them niyyānika, or..."
467: "...are they all not niyyānika, or are some niyyānika and others not?" This was his intended question. When he asked this, the Buddha's arrival at Kusinārā was with the intention: "In the first watch, I shall preach to the Malla princes; in the middle watch, I shall preach to Subhadda; and in the last watch, I shall give an exhortation to the Saṅgha and attain Parinibbāna at dawn." Since explaining that the doctrines of those sectarian teachers were not niyyānika would be of no benefit to Subhadda, and since there was no longer time or opportunity for such an explanation, the Blessed One, desiring to preach the Middle Way (Majjhima Paṭipadā), the Noble Eightfold Path that truly leads out of the round of rebirth, said to the wanderer Subhadda: "Enough, Subhadda, let it be. Put aside this question: 'Do they all have direct knowledge of everything as they claim, or do they not, or do some have knowledge while others do not?' Subhadda, I will preach the Dhamma to you that leads to Nibbāna. Listen to that Dhamma, pay close attention, and I will speak in detail."
468: When Subhadda replied, "Very well, Bhante," the Blessed One spoke these words: "Subhadda, in whatever Dhamma-Vinaya (Doctrine and Discipline) the Noble Eightfold Path is not found, there the first recluse (Sotāpanna) is not found, the second recluse (Sakadāgāmī) is not found, the third recluse (Anāgāmī) is not found, and the fourth recluse (Arahant) is not found. Subhadda, in whatever Dhamma-Vinaya the Noble Eightfold Path is found, there the first recluse is found, the second recluse is found, the third recluse is found, and the fourth recluse is found. Subhadda, in this Dhamma-Vinaya of mine, the Noble Eightfold Path is clearly found. Only in this Dhamma-Vinaya of mine is the first recluse found. Only in this Dhamma-Vinaya of mine is the second recluse found. Only in this Dhamma-Vinaya of mine is the third recluse found. Only in this Dhamma-Vinaya of mine..."
469: "...is the fourth recluse found. Other systems of belief are empty of the twelve noble recluses (the four who have attained the paths, the four who have attained the fruits, and the four practicing insight to attain the paths) who realize the Dhamma. Subhadda, if these twelve noble recluses live rightly and teach correctly in succession, the world will not be empty of Arahants. Subhadda, I was twenty-nine years old when I went forth seeking the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Subhadda, more than fifty years have passed since I went forth. Outside this Dispensation of mine, there is no one who develops insight (vipassanā), which is the preliminary stage of the Noble Path; there is no first recluse, no second recluse, no third recluse, and no fourth recluse. Other systems of belief are empty of the twelve noble recluses mentioned before. Subhadda, if these twelve noble recluses live rightly and teach correctly in succession..."
470:
the world will not be empty of Arahants.”

Thus did the Blessed One deliver this discourse.

## Subhadda the Wanderer’s Ordination and Attainment of Arahantship

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Subhadda the Wanderer said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, O Blessed One! Excellent, O Blessed One! It is, O Blessed One, as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what had been hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Even so has the Dhamma been set forth in many ways by the Blessed One. I, Subhadda, go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha. May I, O Blessed One, receive the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the higher ordination (upasampadā) in the presence of the Blessed One.”

When he had thus requested, the Blessed One said:

“Subhadda, one who was formerly a member of another sect (titthiya) and wishes for the going-forth and the higher ordination in this Dhamma-Vinaya must undergo a four-month probation (parivāsa).
471:
After the lapse of four months, if the monks are satisfied, they may give him the going-forth and raise him to the status of a monk (higher ordination). However, in this matter, I recognize a distinction between individuals (i.e., whether one is fit for the sectarian probation or not).”

When this was said, Subhadda the Wanderer replied:

“Venerable Sir, if those who were formerly members of another sect and wish for the going-forth and higher ordination in this Dhamma-Vinaya must undergo a four-month probation, and after four months the monks, being satisfied, give them the going-forth and raise them to the status of a monk, then I will undergo the sectarian probation for four years. After the lapse of four years, if the monks are satisfied, let them give me the going-forth and raise me to the status of a monk.”

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “In that case, Ānanda, give the going-forth to Subhadda.” The Venerable Ānanda replied, “Very well, Venerable Sir.”

Then Subhadda the Wanderer said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, it is a gain for you, friend Ānanda, it is a great blessing for you,
472:
that you have received the consecration of discipleship in the presence of the Teacher in this Dhamma.”

(In the traditions of other sects, when a teacher says to a disciple, “Ordain this person, instruct this person, or perform the legal act for this person,” speaking on his behalf, the disciple to whom the responsibility is delegated is considered to have been placed in the teacher's own position. Therefore, for a disciple, such words of delegation from the teacher are considered a great gain. Subhadda the Wanderer spoke to the Venerable Ānanda in this manner according to the customs of those sects.)

Then the Venerable Ānanda took Subhadda the Wanderer to a suitable place, moistened his head with water from a vessel, taught him the meditation on the five skin-constituents (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna), and performed the three stages of novice ordination: shaving the hair and beard, donning the saffron robes, and administering the three refuges. He then led the novice Subhadda to the presence of the Blessed One.

The Blessed One had Subhadda ordained as a monk at that very moment and taught him the subject of meditation. Taking the meditation subject taught by the Blessed One, the monk Subhadda went to a secluded spot within the Sāla grove and practiced diligently, without rest, solely in the posture of walking meditation. That very night, before the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, he became an Arahant attained to analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-patta). He then went to the presence of the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down.

The Venerable Subhadda was one among the Arahants whose taints were exhausted, and he was the last direct disciple (pacchima-sakkhisāvaka) of the Blessed One.
473:
(Regarding the term 'last direct disciple' (pacchima-sakkhisāvaka): (1) One who receives novice ordination while the Buddha is alive, and after the Buddha's Parinibbāna, receives higher ordination, practices meditation, and attains the fruit of Arahantship—such a person is called a last direct disciple. (2) One who receives both novice and higher ordination while the Buddha is alive, but only after the Buddha's Parinibbāna practices meditation and attains the fruit of Arahantship—such a person is also called a last direct disciple. (3) One who receives novice ordination, higher ordination, and practices meditation while the Buddha is alive, but only attains the fruit of Arahantship after the Buddha's Parinibbāna—such a person is also called a last direct disciple. However, the Venerable Subhadda received novice ordination, higher ordination, practiced meditation, and attained the fruit of Arahantship all while the Buddha was still alive. Thus, he should be specifically noted as the foremost (ukkaṭṭha) last direct disciple.)

## The Story of Subhadda the Wanderer from the Dhammapada

The preceding account of Subhadda the Wanderer follows the sequence found in the Mahāvagga of the Sutta Piṭaka and its Commentary. I shall now briefly present the account of Subhadda the Wanderer as it appears in the Dhammapada:

While the Blessed One was reclining on the couch of the Parinibbāna in the Sāla grove of the Mallas, Subhadda the Wanderer thought: “I have had these three questions and doubts, but I only asked the elder wanderer teachers. I did not ask the Noble Gotama, thinking, ‘He is young in years.’
474:
I have underestimated him and failed to ask. Now the time for the Noble Gotama’s Parinibbāna is drawing near. If I do not ask now, later I will be troubled by the thought that I did not ask the Noble Gotama.” Having reflected thus, he went to the Mallas' Sāla grove where the Blessed One was staying and requested the Venerable Ānanda for an audience with the Buddha. Although the Venerable Ānanda refused him as previously described, the Blessed One gave permission, saying: “Ānanda, do not hinder Subhadda. Let him ask the Buddha his questions.” Subhadda then entered within the curtain, sat down beside the couch, and asked:

“O Noble Recluse, how is it? 
1. Can there be any footprint in the sky?
2. Can there be recluses (samanas) who have calmed their defilements in the doctrines of sects outside this Buddha’s Dispensation?
3. Can there be conditioned things (saṅkhāra) that are permanent, unchanging, and indestructible?”

He thus addressed these three questions to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to explain to Subhadda the Wanderer that all three are impossible and non-existent, taught the Dhamma with these following verses:

“In the sky there is no footprint,
Outside there is no recluse.
Beings delight in conceptual proliferation (papañca),
The Tathāgatas are free from proliferation. (1)”
475:
Subhadda = Dear Subhadda. Ākāse = In the open sky. Padaṃ = A footprint of anyone. Natthi = Truly does not exist. Natthi iva = Just as it truly does not exist. Bāhire = In the doctrines of sects outside this Dispensation. Samaṇo = The twelve types of noble recluses who have calmed all defilements. Natthi = Truly do not exist. Pajā = The multitude of beings including humans, devas, and brahmas. Papañcābhiratā = Delight and take pleasure only in conceptual proliferation (papañca), which is threefold: craving, conceit, and views. Tathāgatā = The Buddhas. Nippapañcā = Have absolutely cut them off at the foot of the Bodhi tree and possess no proliferation whatsoever.

“In the sky there is no footprint,
Outside there is no recluse.
There are no permanent conditioned things,
There is no agitation in the Buddhas. (2)”

Subhadda = Dear Subhadda. Ākāse = In the open sky. Padaṃ = A footprint of anyone. Natthi = Truly does not exist. Natthi iva = Just as it truly does not exist. Bāhire = In the doctrines of sects outside the Dispensation. Samaṇo = The twelve types of noble recluses who have calmed all defilements. Natthi = Truly do not exist. Sassatā = Having a permanent nature, unchanging and indestructible. Saṅkhārā = The conditioned things of the five aggregates. Natthi = Truly do not exist in the slightest. Buddhānaṃ = In the continuum of the All-Enlightened Buddhas. Iñjitaṃ = Agitation such as the agitation of craving or the agitation of conceit—
476:
any such agitation. Natthi = Truly does not exist.

At the conclusion of these verses of Dhamma teaching, Subhadda the Wanderer was established in the fruit of a Non-returner (anāgāmiphala). It was also a beneficial Dhamma teaching for the assembly gathered near the Blessed One.

This is the story of Subhadda the Wanderer as found in the Dhammapada. In this matter, if one considers that Subhadda the Wanderer asked the questions found in the Mahāvagga of the Sutta Piṭaka and heard the answers, then continued by asking the three questions found in the Dhammapada and heard those answers, becoming a Non-returner (anāgāmī), and then, as recorded in the Mahāvagga, took refuge, requested ordination, practiced the Dhamma of a monk, and attained Arahantship with the exhaustion of taints before the Buddha’s Parinibbāna, becoming the last direct disciple—then the two texts are not contradictory and the accounts are harmonized.

## The Final Exhortation of the Blessed One

After Subhadda the Wanderer, the last direct disciple, had become an Arahant, the Blessed One, wishing to give his final exhortation to the Saṅgha of monks, addressed the Venerable Ānanda (as the representative listener) in this manner:

“Ānanda, it may be that in the minds of you all there is the thought: ‘The word of the Dhamma is now without a Teacher who taught it; our Teacher is gone.’"
477:
477
'The Teacher's word has ended; we have no teacher anymore'—such a thought or feeling of discouragement might arise. Ananda, it should not be thought of in this way. Ananda, the Dhamma and the Vinaya that I have taught and proclaimed during these forty-five years shall be your teacher after I am gone. (a)

Ananda, whereas now the bhikkhus address one another as 'Āvuso' (friend) regardless of seniority, after my passing they should not do so. Ananda, a senior bhikkhu should address a junior bhikkhu by name, by clan, or as 'Āvuso'. A junior bhikkhu should address a senior bhikkhu as 'Bhante' (Venerable Sir) or 'Āyasmā' (Venerable). (b)

Ananda, if the Saṅgha wishes, after my passing, let them abolish the minor and lesser rules. (c)

Ananda, after my passing, the Brahma-punishment (Brahmadanda) should be imposed on the bhikkhu Channa."

Venerable Ananda then asked, "Bhante, what is the Brahma-punishment?" The Buddha replied, "Ananda, the bhikkhu Channa may say whatever he wishes, but the bhikkhus should not speak to him, advise him, or admonish him. This is the Brahma-punishment." (d)
478:
478
(Among these instructions, regarding note (a):

Ananda, while I am still alive, I have taught the Vinaya—the Ubhatovibhaṅga (Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga) together with the Mahāvagga, Cūḷavagga, Khandhaka, and Parivāra—along with the miscellaneous teachings and commentaries. I have explained which offenses are light and which are heavy, which are remediable and which are irremediable, which are 'Lokavajja' (wrong by worldly standards/inherently unwholesome) and which are 'Paṇṇattivajja' (wrong by regulation/prohibited by the Buddha). I have taught how a particular offense can be cleared before an individual, before a group (gaṇa), or only before the Saṅgha, in relation to the seven classes of offenses. This entire Vinaya Piṭaka will perform the duty of the Teacher for you after my Parinibbāna.

Ananda, while I am still alive, I have taught the Sutta Piṭaka, repeatedly analyzing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) in various ways: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path. This entire Sutta Piṭaka will also perform the duty of the Teacher for you after my Parinibbāna.

Furthermore, while I am still alive, I have taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, repeatedly analyzing the Dhamma such as the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four noble truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine roots, the four nutriments, the seven contacts, the seven feelings, the seven perceptions, the seven volitions, and the seven consciousnesses. Among those teachings,
479:
479
'these are Kāmāvacara (sensuous sphere) dhammas, these are Rūpāvacara (fine-material sphere) dhammas, these are Arūpāvacara (immaterial sphere) dhammas; these are included in the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and these are not; these are mundane (lokiya) and these are supramundane (lokuttara).' I have taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, analyzing these dhammas such as the aggregates, and crowning the teaching with the Great Book of Paṭṭhāna (Anantanaya Paṭṭhāna) which consists of twenty-four books of Samanta-Paṭṭhāna. This entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka will also perform the duty of the Teacher for you after my Parinibbāna. Thus, the collection of the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya that I have taught for forty-five years, from the time of my Enlightenment until my Parinibbāna, is vast in its divisions: three Piṭakas, five Nikāyas, nine Angas, and eighty-four thousand Dhammakkhandhas (Dhamma-groups). These eighty-four thousand Dhammakkhandhas, which can be regarded as eighty-four thousand Buddhas, remain clearly present. Only I, the single Buddha, pass away. While I am alive, I alone admonish and restrain you. After my Parinibbāna, these eighty-four thousand Dhammakkhandhas will take my place and continue to admonish and restrain you."

In this way, the Buddha admonished and encouraged the assembly of bhikkhus with many reasons.

Regarding note (b), the Buddha indicated the conduct to be followed by the Saṅgha after his Parinibbāna.

Regarding note (c), there is a question: Why did the Buddha not give a single, definitive command to "abolish the minor rules," but instead gave a double-edged instruction, "if they wish, let them abolish"?
480:
480
The answer is: He gave this double-edged instruction because he saw the strength of faith and the strength of wisdom of the Venerable Mahākassapa. To elaborate—even if the Buddha had given a definitive command to "abolish them," he knew clearly that when the Council was held, Venerable Mahākassapa would not abolish them in any way. Therefore, he said, "if they wish, let them abolish." (This is a special point to be noted).

After addressing Venerable Ananda in this way, the Buddha said to the bhikkhus:

"Bhikkhus, if any bhikkhu has any doubt or perplexity in his mind—'Is this the Buddha or not? Is this the true Dhamma or not? Is this the true Saṅgha or not? Is this the true Path (Magga) leading to Nibbāna or not? Is this the good practice leading to Nibbāna or not?'—if there is any doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the Path, or the practice, ask now, bhikkhus. Do not later regret, thinking: 'The Buddha was present before us, yet we were unable to ask him face to face.'"

When he had spoken thus, the bhikkhus remained silent. When he spoke a second time, they remained silent. When he spoke a third time, they remained silent.
481:
481
Because they remained silent, the Buddha addressed the bhikkhus again:

"Bhikkhus, perhaps you do not ask out of respect for the Buddha, thinking: 'We are those who have gone forth under the Buddha; our four requisites are the property of the Buddha; it is not proper for us, who have not had doubts for so long, to have doubts now when he is about to enter Parinibbāna.' Bhikkhus, if that is the case, let one friend tell another of his doubt."

Even when he spoke thus, the bhikkhus remained silent.

Then Venerable Ananda said to the Buddha:

"Bhante, it is wonderful! Bhante, it is marvelous! I have faith that in this assembly of bhikkhus, there is not even a single bhikkhu who has any doubt or perplexity concerning the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the Path, or the practice."

The Buddha then said to Venerable Ananda:

"Ananda, you speak thus out of faith. Ananda, the Tathāgata already knows that in this assembly of bhikkhus, there is not even a single bhikkhu who has any doubt or perplexity concerning the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the Path, or the practice. (It is not merely a matter of faith).
482:
482
Ananda, among these five hundred bhikkhus, even the most junior bhikkhu is a Stream-winner (Sotāpanna), no longer subject to rebirth in lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and having the three higher paths as his final destination (referring to Ananda)."

Then, giving his final exhortation to the bhikkhus, the Buddha said:

"Handa dāni bhikkhave āmantayāmi vo = Bhikkhus, I now wish to give you my final exhortation: Vayadhammā saṅkhārā = All conditioned things are subject to decay; Appamādena sampာdetha = Therefore, strive to complete your task with heedfulness."

These were the last words of the Buddha. Thus, while lying on his deathbed, the Buddha summarized all the exhortations he had given over forty-five years into this single word, 'Appamāda' (Heedfulness), and gave his final instruction.

## Entering Parinibbāna
O virtuous one of the lineage of the wise, reader of the Buddha's life... one thing I want you to note in your mind is that after the Buddha spoke the words "Appamādena sampādetha,"
483:
483
He did not utter even a single word anymore. The entire Sāla grove became silent. The Blessed One performed only the preparatory mental work (parikamma) for entering Parinibbāna. He practiced and developed only the preparatory meditation (parikamma-bhāvanā) for entering Parinibbāna, which is purely a mental act (manokamma) without the involvement of bodily or vocal acts:

First, he entered the first rūpāvacara-kiriya-jhāna. Emerging from that jhāna, he entered the second jhāna. Emerging from that jhāna, he entered the third jhāna. Emerging from that jhāna, he entered the fourth rūpāvacara-kiriya-jhāna. Emerging from that jhāna, he entered the arūpāvacara-kiriya attainment of the Base of Infinite Space (ākāsānañcāyatana-samāpatti). Emerging from that attainment, he entered the Base of Infinite Consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-samāpatti). Emerging from that attainment, he entered the Base of Nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana-samāpatti). Emerging from that attainment, he entered the Base of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-samāpatti). Emerging from that attainment, he entered the Cessation of Perception and Feeling (nirodha-samāpatti).

When he entered the Cessation of Perception and Feeling, the out-breath and in-breath of the Blessed One ceased. Seeing that the out-breath and in-breath of the Buddha had ceased, the Venerable Ānanda, with great anxiety, asked the Venerable Anuruddha, "Venerable Anuruddha, has the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna?" Then the Venerable Anuruddha replied, "Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One has not yet attained Parinibbāna; he is currently in the attainment of the Cessation of Perception and Feeling (nirodha-samāpatti)."
484:
484
(In this matter, a question may arise: "How did the Venerable Anuruddha know that the Blessed One was in the attainment of Cessation?" The answer is: The Venerable Anuruddha followed and entered those four rūpāvacara-jhāna attainments and four arūpāvacara-jhāna attainments along with the Blessed One. [That is to say, when the Blessed One entered the first rūpāvacara-jhāna, the Venerable Anuruddha also entered that jhāna; when the Blessed One emerged from the first rūpāvacara-jhāna, the Venerable Anuruddha also emerged from it. In this manner,] the Venerable Anuruddha followed and entered the attainments along with the Buddha until emerging from the nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-jhāna, and only when the Buddha entered nirodha-samāpatti did he remain behind.

Therefore, he knew, "At this moment, the Blessed One is still in the attainment of Cessation; and within the attainment of Cessation, there is absolutely no such thing as the falling away of the life-continuum (cuti) or passing away, which is called attaining Parinibbāna." In this way, the Venerable Anuruddha knew that the Blessed One was in the attainment of Cessation.)

Then, the Blessed One emerged from the attainment of the Cessation of Perception and Feeling and entered the attainment of the Base of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception. Emerging from that attainment, he entered the Base of Nothingness. Emerging from that attainment, he entered the Base of Infinite Consciousness. Emerging from that attainment, he entered the Base of Infinite Space. Emerging from that attainment, he entered the fourth rūpāvacara-kiriya-jhāna. Emerging from that fourth jhāna, he entered the third jhāna. Emerging from that third jhāna, he entered the second jhāna. Emerging from that second jhāna, he entered the first jhāna.
485:
485
(In this regard: The Blessed One entered the first rūpāvacara-kiriya-jhāna based on these twenty-four objects: the ten foulness (asubha) concepts, the first eight kasina concepts, the concept of the body-group which is the object of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati), the concept of out-breath and in-breath which is the object of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), the three types of concepts of immeasurable beings which are the objects of the three divine abidings (brahmavihāra) called loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), and appreciative joy (muditā), and the concept of limited space (paricchedākāsa).

From those twenty-four, excluding eleven (the ten foulness concepts and the concept of the body-group), he entered the second and third rūpāvacara-kiriya-jhānas based on the remaining thirteen objects. He entered the fourth jhāna based on fifteen objects: the eight kasina concepts, the concept of out-breath and in-breath, the concept of immeasurable beings which is the object of the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhā-brahmavihāra), the concept of limited space, and the four immaterial (arūpa) objects.

This statement is merely a brief explanation. In truth, the Blessed One, about to enter the Golden City of Nibbāna, entered all the two million four hundred thousand valañjana-samāpatti (attainments for dwelling in ease) mentioned previously [in the section on the two types of meals having equal fruit, pages 283-284]. Just as a person about to go to another place embraces and kisses all his relatives to his heart's content before leaving, it should be specially noted that the Blessed One fully enjoyed and made use of all the bliss of the attainments before entering the Golden City of Nibbāna.)

Then, the Blessed One emerged from the first jhāna and entered the second jhāna again. Emerging from the second jhāna, he entered the third jhāna again. Emerging from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna again. After emerging from that fourth jhāna, he reviewed the two jhāna factors, namely equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness (ekaggatā), both individually and together. At the end of those reviewing great functional impulsions (paccavekkhaṇa-mahākiriyā-javana),
486:
486
He entered Parinibbāna, ceased, and brought the drama of suffering to an end through the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta) which is the indeterminate truth of suffering (abyākata-dukkha-sacca) [specifically, the first great resultant consciousness, unprompted, associated with knowledge, and accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata ñāṇa-sampayutta asaṅkhārika paṭhama mahāvipāka)].

(In this regard: (1) When a person enters a jhāna, emerges from it, and then passes into the life-continuum, the attainment of Parinibbāna at that moment of the life-continuum is called jhāna-samanantara-parinibbāna = Parinibbāna immediately following jhāna. (2) When a person enters a jhāna, emerges from it, reviews the jhāna factors contained in that jhāna individually or collectively, and then passes into the life-continuum at the end of that reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa), the attainment of Parinibbāna at that moment of the life-continuum is called paccavekkhaṇa-samanantara-parinibbāna = Parinibbāna immediately following reviewing. Between these two types, it should be specially noted that the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna through the second type of Parinibbāna.)

## Here ends Chapter 40.
487:
487
## Chapter 41
## Verses of Urgency (Saṃvega-kathā)

When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, at the very moment of his Parinibbāna, there occurred a great, terrifying earthquake that made the hair stand on end. The thundering sounds of celestial drums also resounded.

When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, at the very moment of his Parinibbāna, the Great Brahmā Sahampati recited this verse of urgency:

Sabbēva nikkhipissanti,
Bhūtā lōkē samussayaṃ.
Yattha ētādisō satthā,
Lōkē appaṭipuggalō.
Tathāgatō balappattō,
Sambuddhō parinibbutō.

In this world where whatever arises must perish, even such a Teacher, the Peerless One in the world, the Tathāgata, possessed of the ten powers, the Fully Enlightened One, has attained Parinibbāna. In that world where whatever arises must perish, all living beings without exception will have to lay down this body, this heap of mind and matter, at the time of death.
488:
488
At the time of death, they will surely have to abandon this physical form.

When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, at the very moment of his Parinibbāna, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, recited this verse of urgency:

Aniccā vata saṅkhārā, uppādavaya-dhamminō.
Uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, tesaṃ vūpasamō sukhō.

Conditioned things are indeed impermanent; they are of the nature to arise and perish. Having arisen, they cease. The cessation of those conditioned things [the great unconditioned element, Nibbāna] is true bliss.

Alternatively: Conditioned things of the three planes (tebhūmaka-saṅkhāra) [because] they arise and become manifest, and then reach the moment of dissolution and cease. [Therefore] they have only the inherent nature of arising and perishing (meaning they have no nature of permanence at all). [Because] they have only the inherent nature of arising and perishing, they are indeed impermanent. The cessation and calming of those conditioned things of the three planes, which is the great unconditioned element, the ultimate Nibbāna, is indeed true bliss.
489:
489
When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, at the very moment of his Parinibbāna, the Venerable Anuruddha recited these verses of urgency:

Nāhu assāsapassāsō,
Ṭhitacittassa tādinō.
Anējō santimārabbha,
Yaṃ kālamakari muni.

"O friends, monks! The Buddha-muni, the peerless Teacher of the three worlds, who has extinguished all cravings (ejā) for existence, has attained Parinibbāna, intending to enter the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). Of that Buddha-muni, the peerless Teacher of the three worlds, who possessed a firm mind that remained unmoved even when the storms of worldly conditions blew, and who was endowed with the quality of steadfastness (tādi), the out-breath and in-breath have ceased and no longer appear, as he dwells in the peace of cessation."

Asallīnēna cittēna,
Vēdanaṃ ajjhavāsayi.
Pajjōtassēva nibbānaṃ,
Vimokkhō cētasō ahu.

"O friends, monks! Our Teacher, the Great Buddha, with a mind that was not at all shrinking or dejected, endured the painful feelings that arrived at his person. Like the extinguishing of a lamp, the liberation of his mind occurred."
490:
He endured the painful feeling. With the heart of patient endurance (khantī), he remained unperturbed and smiling, enduring without change. Like the extinguishing of a flame when its fuel is exhausted, such was the liberation of the mind of that Teacher of ours, an absolute cessation and release where no phenomenon could hinder it. It has indeed come to pass.

When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, at the very moment of his passing, the Venerable Ānanda recited this verse of spiritual urgency (saṃvega-gāthā):

"Then there was terror, then there was hair-raising awe,
When the Fully Enlightened One, endowed with all excellent qualities, attained Parinibbāna."

Friends, when our Teacher, who was endowed with all excellent and praiseworthy qualities and attributes, attained Parinibbāna and reached the end of the cycle of existence, at that moment, a terrifying and violent earthquake occurred. At that moment of Parinibbāna, a hair-raising and violent earthquake of six kinds occurred.

When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, those monks present at the place of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna who were not yet free from passion and anger—the worldlings (puthujjana), Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), and Once-returners (sakadāgāmī)—cried out: "The Blessed One...
491:
has attained Parinibbāna too soon! The Sugata (Well-Spoken One) has attained Parinibbāna too soon! The One with the Eye of Wisdom (the Eye of the World) has vanished from the world too soon!" Thus they lamented, raising their arms and weeping. They fell down as if falling from a precipice; they rolled back and forth, tossing this way and that.

However, those monks who were Non-returners (anāgāmī) and Arahants, being free from passion and anger, endured it with mindfulness and clear comprehension, reflecting: "Conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are impermanent by nature. How could it be possible to find permanence within these conditioned things? It is simply not possible."

Then the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the monks:

"Enough, friends! Do not grieve, do not lament. Has the Blessed One not already declared that there must be separation (nānābhāva) from all that is beloved and pleasing, parting (vinābhāva), and becoming otherwise (aññathābhāva)? Friends, how can it be that what is born, come into being, conditioned, and subject to disintegration should not disintegrate? Such a thing is impossible.

Friends, the deities are complaining, saying: 'If even the noble ones themselves cannot endure this, how can the rest of the people be comforted?'"
492:
Thus he spoke words of admonition and spiritual urgency.

Then the Venerable Ānanda asked the Venerable Anuruddha: "Venerable Anuruddha, what kind of state are the deities and Brahmās in? How do you perceive them?"

When asked, the Venerable Anuruddha said to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Friend Ānanda, there are deities in the sky who perceive the earth on the sky; they are weeping with disheveled hair, raising their arms and lamenting: 'The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna too soon! The Sugata has attained Parinibbāna too soon! The One with the Eye of Wisdom (the Eye of the World) has vanished from the world too soon!' They fall down as if falling from a precipice; they roll back and forth, tossing this way and that.

Friend Ānanda, there are deities on the earth who perceive the earth on the earth; they are weeping with disheveled hair, raising their arms and lamenting: 'The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna too soon! The Sugata has attained Parinibbāna too soon! The One with the Eye of Wisdom (the Eye of the World)...
493:
has vanished from the world too soon!' They fall down as if falling from a precipice; they roll back and forth, tossing this way and that.

But those deities who are free from sensual passion endure it with mindfulness and clear comprehension, reflecting: 'Conditioned things are impermanent. How could it be possible to find permanence within these conditioned things? It is simply not possible.'"

Then the Venerable Anuruddha and the Venerable Ānanda spent the remainder of that night in Dhamma discussion, saying: "Friend, even towards our Teacher, the Blessed One, who is peerless in the world including the deities, this Death has no shame. Why then should it have shame towards ordinary worldly people? It certainly will not."

Not long after the two Elders had been discussing the Dhamma, dawn broke.

Then the Venerable Anuruddha said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Go, friend Ānanda, enter Kusinārā and inform the Mallas of Kusinārā: 'O Vāseṭṭhas, the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna. Now is the time for you to do as you think fit.'" The Venerable Ānanda, having consented, took a companion monk and entered Kusinārā.
494:
At that time, the Mallas were assembled in their council hall (santhāgāra) to discuss matters concerning the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, such as: "What kind of flowers and perfumes should be offered at the place of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna? What kind of seating should be arranged for the Saṅgha of monks? What kind of food and offerings should be prepared?"

Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the council hall where the Mallas of Kusinārā were assembled and said:

"O Vāseṭṭhas, the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna. Now is the time for you to do as you think fit."

When they heard these words of the Venerable Ānanda, the Mallas, their sons, daughters, daughters-in-law, and queens were deeply grieved and distressed. They cried out: "The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna too soon! The Sugata has attained Parinibbāna too soon! The One with the Eye of Wisdom (the Eye of the World) has vanished from the world too soon!" Some wept with disheveled hair, some raised their arms and lamented, some fell down as if falling from a precipice, and some rolled back and forth, tossing this way and that.
495:
## Honoring the Physical Remains

Then the Mallas of Kusinārā gave orders to their men: "Friends, since the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, gather all the flowers and perfumes in Kusinārā, and all the musical instruments." They took various kinds of flowers and perfumes, all kinds of musical instruments, and five hundred pairs of garments (rolls of fine cloth), and went to the Sāla-grove where the physical remains (utuja-rūpakalāpa) of the Blessed One lay. There they honored, respected, revered, and paid homage to the Blessed One's remains with dance, song, music, flowers, and perfumes. They erected canopies and prepared circular pavilions, and in this way, they spent the rest of that day.

Then the Mallas of Kusinārā thought: "It is now too late to cremate the Blessed One's remains today. We shall cremate the remains tomorrow."

Then the Mallas, continuing to honor, respect, revere, and pay homage to the Blessed One's remains with dance, song, music, flowers, and perfumes, and by erecting canopies and preparing circular pavilions, spent the second day. In the same manner, they spent the third day, the fourth day, the fifth day, and the sixth day.

Then, on the seventh day, the Mallas of Kusinārā decided:
496:
"We shall carry the Blessed One's remains by a path to the south of the city, honoring, respecting, revering, and paying homage with dance, song, music, flowers, and perfumes, and we shall cremate the Blessed One's remains to the south of the city."

Then eight Malla chieftains, having washed their heads and dressed in new clothes, thinking, "We shall lift the Blessed One's remains," tried to lift them simultaneously, but they were unable to move the remains at all. Then the Mallas of Kusinārā, although other senior Elders were present, had great faith in the Venerable Anuruddha, who was the foremost (etadagga) in the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), thinking: "This Venerable Anuruddha will be able to explain this to us clearly."

They asked the Venerable Anuruddha: "Venerable Anuruddha, these eight Malla chieftains, having washed their heads and dressed in new clothes, intended to lift the Blessed One's remains, but even though they tried to lift them together, they are unable to move the remains. Venerable Anuruddha, what is the cause? What is the reason?"

The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "O Vāseṭṭhas, your intention is one thing,
497: "The intention of the deities is one way, while yours is another," he said. The Mallas asked, "Venerable Anuruddha, what is the intention of the deities?" Then Venerable Anuruddha said to the Mallas: "Vāseṭṭhas, your intention is: 'We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the physical remains of the Blessed One with dance, song, music, flowers, and scents, and carrying them by a route south of the city, we shall cremate the physical remains of the Blessed One to the south of the city.' Vāseṭṭhas, the intention of the deities is: 'We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the physical remains of the Blessed One with celestial dance, song, music, flowers, and scents, and carrying them by a route north of the city, we shall enter through the north gate, process through the center of the city, exit through the east gate, and cremate the physical remains of the Blessed One at the Mallas' shrine named Makuṭabandhana to the east of the city.'" The Mallas replied, "Venerable sir, let it be according to the intention of the deities." *The pavilion where the Mallas were adorned with crowns and such during their consecration is called the Makuṭabandhana Shrine because it was a place of great reverence.
498:
At that time, in the Mallas' city of Kusinārā, the grounds including house compounds, fences, and even places where waste and sweepings were discarded, were strewn with celestial Mandārava flowers to the depth of one's knees.
Then the deities and the Mallas of Kusinārā, showing respect, reverence, esteem, and worship with celestial and human dances, songs, and music, and with flowers and scents, carried the physical remains (utujaruūpakalāpa) of the Buddha to the north of the city via the northern route. Entering through the northern gate, they solemnly escorted the remains along the central road of the city.
## Mallikā, the Wife of General Bandhula, 
## Worships the Physical Remains 
## with the Mahālatā Ornament
While the physical remains of the Blessed One were being escorted along the central road of the city, Mallikā, the wife of General Bandhula, heard the news: "The physical remains of the Blessed One are being escorted!" She then had the Mahālatā ornament (similar to Visākhā's ornament) brought out from storage—an ornament she had not worn or used since the death of her husband, General Bandhula. Intending to worship the Blessed One with this ornament, she had the dust wiped off, washed it with scented water, and stood waiting at the door of her house.
It is said that this Mahālatā ornament existed in only three places: (1) with Visākhā, (2) with Mallikā, and (3) in the house of the thief named Devadāniya. In the present age, this Mahālatā ornament is also called the Mallikā ornament.
499: When the physical remains of the Blessed One reached the door of her house, Mallikā, the general's wife, requested, "Sirs, please set down the physical remains of the Blessed One for a moment," and she draped the Mahālatā ornament over the physical remains of the Blessed One. The Mahālatā ornament, placed starting from the head, reached down to the soles of the feet. The golden-hued physical remains of the Blessed One looked exceedingly beautiful, adorned with the Mahālatā ornament encrusted with the seven kinds of jewels. Seeing that beauty, Mallikā felt waves of faith and devotion, and she made an aspiration: "Blessed One, for as long as I wander in Saṃsāra, may I never have the need to adorn myself separately; may my body in every existence in Saṃsāra be as if naturally and permanently adorned." After she passed away, Mallikā became a goddess in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, her aspiration fulfilled. The details of this story should be noted from the commentary to the Mallikā-vimāna (Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā, page 150 onwards, 1-Itthivimāna, 3-Paricchatthakavagga, 8-Mallikāvimāna). Thereafter, the Mallas lifted the physical remains of the Blessed One along with the Mahālatā ornament, carried them out through the east gate, and placed the physical remains of the Blessed One at the Mallas' shrine named Makuṭabandhana on the eastern side of the city.
500: ## Procedures for the Physical Remains. Then the Mallas asked Venerable Ānanda, "Venerable Ānanda, how should we act regarding the physical remains of the Blessed One?" Venerable Ānanda replied, "Vāseṭṭhas, one should act regarding the physical remains of the Blessed One as one acts regarding the physical remains of a Wheel-turning Monarch." The Mallas further asked, "Venerable Ānanda, how do they act regarding the physical remains of a Wheel-turning Monarch?" Then Venerable Ānanda told the Mallas: "Vāseṭṭhas, the physical remains of a Wheel-turning Monarch are wrapped in new cloth. Having wrapped them in new cloth, they are wrapped in teased cotton. Having wrapped them in teased cotton, they are again wrapped in new cloth. In this manner, having wrapped the physical remains of the Wheel-turning Monarch in five hundred pairs of cloth, they are placed in a golden oil-vat, covered with another golden lid, and then, having prepared a pyre of all kinds of perfumes, the physical remains of the Wheel-turning Monarch are cremated. A stupa for the remains of the Wheel-turning Monarch is built at the crossroads of four highways. Vāseṭṭhas, this is how they act regarding the physical remains of a Wheel-turning Monarch."
501: "Vāseṭṭhas, just as they act regarding the physical remains of a Wheel-turning Monarch, so should they act regarding the physical remains of the Blessed One. A stupa for the remains of the Blessed One should be built at the crossroads of four highways. If any persons there offer flowers, scents, or perfumes, or pay homage, or feel serene faith in their hearts, that will be for their long-term welfare and happiness." He spoke this in accordance with what the Blessed One had previously instructed. Then the Mallas of Kusinārā gave orders to their men, "Friends, if that is so, collect the teased cotton of the Mallas." Then, as Venerable Ānanda had instructed, the Mallas wrapped the physical remains of the Blessed One in new cloth, then in teased cotton. Having wrapped them in teased cotton, they wrapped them again in new cloth. In this manner, having wrapped the physical remains of the Blessed One in five hundred pairs of cloth, they placed them in a golden oil-vat, covered them with a golden lid, and having prepared a pyre of all kinds of perfumes, they placed the physical remains of the Blessed One upon that pyre.
502: ## The Story of Venerable Mahākassapa. At that time, the Great Elder Mahākassapa, having wandered for alms in the city of Pāvā, considered, "I shall go to Kusinārā," and was traveling from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with five hundred monks. Then Venerable Mahākassapa stepped off the main road and sat down with the monks at the foot of a certain tree. It should be specifically noted that he sat there not for a midday rest, but to recover from fatigue. To elaborate: all the monks in the Elder's retinue were those who had grown up in luxury and comfort. These monks were extremely exhausted, having traveled on foot over the ground that was as hot as a burning stone slab in the midday sun. Venerable Mahākassapa, seeing that the monks were very tired, thought, "The monks are very exhausted, and the remaining distance is not very far. After resting a bit to cool down from the heat, I will go to Kusinārā in the evening to pay respects to the Blessed One." He stepped off the road, spread his outer robe at the foot of a tree, cooled his hands and feet with water from a flask, and rested for a while. The monks of his retinue also sat at the foot of the tree, some practicing meditation and others discussing the virtues of the Triple Gem.
503: At that time, an ascetic was coming from Kusinārā toward Pāvā, carrying a large celestial Mandārava flower on a stick like an umbrella. Venerable Mahākassapa saw the ascetic coming from afar and thought: "I see this large Mandārava flower clearly in the ascetic's hand. Such a Mandārava flower is not seen at all times in the human world. Indeed, it only appears when a powerful being performs a miracle, or when Bodhisattas descend into their mother's womb, and so on. Today, no powerful being has performed a miracle, nor has my Teacher, the Blessed One, descended into his mother's womb, nor was he born from his mother's womb. Today is not the day my Teacher attained the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience, nor the day he preached the first sermon of the Dhammacakka, nor the day he performed the Twin Miracle, nor the day he descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, nor the day he relinquished the life-force. Indeed, my Teacher is advanced in age; he must surely have attained Parinibbāna." After thinking this, he felt, "I must ask that ascetic," and then considered, "If I ask while sitting, it would be a sign of disrespect toward my Teacher." So he rose from his seat and, while standing...
504:
Moving slightly away, the Great Elder Mahākassapa, wearing the dark-cloud-colored rag-robe (paṃsukūla) exchanged and given by the Blessed One—as if the Chaddanta elephant king were draped in a jeweled branch—placed his hands together in a gesture of reverence above his head. Out of respect for the Buddha, he faced the direction of the naked ascetic and asked, "Friend, do you know our teacher, the Blessed One?"

(In this regard, a question may be asked: "Did the Elder Mahākassapa ask while knowing that the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, or did he ask because he did not know?" Regarding this question, the commentators do not accept the argument that he asked because he did not know. The explanation accepted by the commentators is as follows:

"In this matter, there is no reason at all for him not to know that the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna. The Parinibbāna of the Blessed One was very evident through great signs such as the trembling of the ten thousand world systems.

In fact, the true reason was that among the retinue of the Elder Mahākassapa, some monks had seen the Blessed One before, while others had not. Among those monks, those who had seen him before still wished to see him again, and those who had never seen him before also wished to see him.

If they did not know beforehand that the Buddha had attained Parinibbāna because he did not ask now, those monks who had never seen him before, out of their intense desire to see him, would ask upon reaching the city of Kusinārā, 'Where is the Blessed One?' If they were to hear the news that 'The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna' upon asking so, they would not be able to compose themselves. They would discard their robes and bowls, and being poorly clad or having only a single robe, they would beat their breasts and weep bitterly."
505:
"In such weeping, the people who see them will surely blame me, saying, 'These rag-robe-wearing dhutaṅga monks who arrived with the Elder Mahākassapa are weeping loudly like women. How can these monks provide us with solace? They cannot.' This place is a quiet, secluded forest. In this great forest, if they weep as they please, no blame will fall on me. If they hear the news beforehand, their grief (soka) might be lessened.' Reflecting thus, he asked the question even though he already knew, in order to arouse mindfulness in the monks following him.")

When the Elder Mahākassapa asked thus, the naked ascetic replied, "Friend, yes, I know. It has been seven days since the ascetic Gotama attained Parinibbāna. I brought this celestial Mandārava flower from the place of his Parinibbāna."

At that time, among the five hundred monks following the Elder Mahākassapa, those who were not yet free from passion wept, raising their arms and saying, "Too soon has the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna! Too soon has the Well-Spoken One attained Parinibbāna! Too soon has the Eye of the World vanished from the world!" They fell down as if falling over a precipice, rolling back and forth and to and fro.

Those monks who were free from sensual passion reflected, "Conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are impermanent. In these
506:
conditioned things, where can permanence be found? It is simply not possible." Reflecting thus, they remained composed.

## Subhadda, the Old Monk

At that time, an old monk named Subhadda, who had gone forth in his old age, was among that company of five hundred monks. When the monks were weeping uncontrollably, this old monk Subhadda said to the monks:

"Friends, enough! Do not grieve, do not lament, do not weep. Now we are well rid of that Great Ascetic. That Great Ascetic used to harass us, saying, 'This is allowable for you; this is not allowable for you.' Now we shall do whatever we want, and we shall not do what we do not want."

Thus he spoke these rude and harsh words.

## About Subhadda, the Old Monk

(In this regard, it may be asked: "Why did the old monk Subhadda speak such rude and harsh words?" The brief answer is: "He spoke such rude and harsh words because he held a grudge (āghāta) against the Blessed One."

To elaborate—this old monk Subhadda, who had been a barber when he was a layman, had pleasant speech and extraordinary skills. He was living in the city of Ātumā together with
507:
his two young novice sons, who were also skilled in their teacher's craft of barbering. When the Blessed One was traveling from the city of Kusinārā to Ātumā with a company of one thousand two hundred and fifty (1,250) monks, the old monk Subhadda heard the news of the Buddha's arrival. Thinking, "I will offer a great gruel (yāgu) donation when the Buddha reaches Ātumā," he sent his two young novice sons, saying, "Dear sons, the Blessed One is coming to Ātumā with one thousand two hundred and fifty monks. Go, dear sons, take your barber's kits and go from house to house with bowls and bags. Collect as much salt, oil, rice, and food as you can. When the Blessed One arrives, we shall offer a great gruel donation."

The novice sons did exactly as their father, the old monk, had told them. The townspeople, seeing these two novices with pleasant voices and extraordinary skills, both those who wanted their hair and beards trimmed and those who did not, all asked for their services. After the service, when the people asked, "Dear sons, what shall we give you?" the two novices replied, "We do not want anything else for ourselves. However, our father, the old monk, wishes to offer a gruel donation when the Blessed One arrives."
508:
Hearing this, the people did not count the cost but gave everything the novices could carry, and even sent their servants to deliver the rice, oil, salt, and food that the novices could not carry.

Later, when the Blessed One arrived at Ātumā and entered the threshing-floor monastery, the old monk Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening and said to the people, "Lay devotees, I do not desire anything else from you. The rice, oil, salt, and food brought by my sons are sufficient for the Saṅgha. You only need to provide me with manual labor." He then had them bring all the pots, bowls, ladles, and trivets. Inside his monastery, he had the trivets set up. Wearing one brown robe and draping another brown robe over himself, he personally supervised the work all night, saying, "Do this, do that." Having spent a sum worth a hundred thousand, he had a great quantity of thick gruel (bhojja-yāgu) and honey-balls prepared. (Bhojja-yāgu: This refers to a type of thick gruel that must be chewed before swallowing. In this gruel, various ingredients like ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, flower nectar, and fruit juice are added and cooked.
509:
For those who seek pleasure, it could even be used as a thick hair oil for the head and had a fragrant scent.)

Then, the Blessed One, having risen early and performed his personal duties, set out toward the city of Ātumā for alms, surrounded by a company of monks. The people said to the old monk Subhadda, "The Blessed One is entering for alms. For whom have you prepared this gruel, venerable sir?"

The old monk Subhadda, still wearing his large brown robes, holding a ladle in one hand, sat in the Brahma-pose (kneeling with the right knee on the ground), paid homage to the Blessed One, and invited him, saying, "Exalted Blessed One, may the Lord accept my offering of thick gruel (bhojja-yāgu)."

Then the Blessed One (as recorded in the Vinaya Mahāvagga, 6-Bhesajjakkhandhaka), having inquired and learned the facts, rebuked the old monk for many reasons. Regarding this matter, he laid down two training rules: (1) Akappiya-samādāna Sikkhāpada (the rule prescribing a dukkhaṭa offense for a monk who causes others to accept unallowable things) and (2) Khura-bhaṇḍa-pariharaṇa Sikkhāpada (the rule prescribing a dukkhaṭa offense for a monk who was formerly a barber and carries a barber's kit).
510:
The Blessed One laid down these two training rules and said:

"Monks, for many millions of eons, you have spent your time seeking food and sustenance. This gruel offered by the old monk Subhadda is unrighteous food that is entirely unallowable for you. For those who consume this food, it will lead to rebirth in the four woeful states for thousands of lifetimes. Monks, cast it away; do not accept it."

Having said this, he proceeded toward the village for alms. Not a single monk accepted even a small portion of the old monk Subhadda's gruel.

Consequently, the monk Subhadda became displeased and went around saying, "This Great Ascetic claims 'I know everything.' If he did not want to accept it, he should have sent someone to tell me. This cooked food could have lasted at most seven days. If this food had been kept raw, I could have eaten it for my whole life. Now, the Great Ascetic has destroyed it all. This Great Ascetic is one who desires my harm; he is an enemy." Thinking thus, he harbored a grudge against the Blessed One, saying, "This Great Ascetic is an upper-class person who went forth from the noble Sakyan clan."
511:
“If I say anything, he will only threaten me,” he thought. Thus, while the Buddha was still alive, he did not dare to say anything. Now, having heard the news that “The Buddha has attained Parinibbāna,” that old monk Subhadda felt as if he had found relief and spoke with great joy in this manner.

## The Thought of Ven. Mahākassapa

When the Elder Mahākassapa heard the harsh and rude words of the old monk Subhadda, he felt as if his heart had been struck, or as if a thunderbolt had fallen upon his head. Within the Elder’s mind, he reflected: “Alas! It has been only seven days since the Buddha attained Parinibbāna. Even today, the golden-hued physical remains (utujarūpa-kalāpa) of the Buddha are still clearly present. In this noble Sāsana, established with such hardship and fatigue by the Buddha himself, such rubbish, thorns, and obstacles in the form of wicked monks have appeared so quickly. If this wicked monk is not restrained and is allowed to grow, he will gain other wicked companions like himself and cause the decline of the Sāsana.” Reflecting thus, a great sense of spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in him.
512:
Subsequently, within the Elder’s mind, thoughts of holding a Dhamma Council (Saṅgāyanā) continued to arise as follows:

“If I were to make this old monk, who went forth in his old age, wear coarse cloth, sprinkle him with ash, and expel him right here, many people would blame us, saying, ‘While the physical remains of the Monk Gotama are still present, his disciples are already quarreling.’ I shall endure and be patient for now.

Indeed, the teachings preached by the Buddha are like a great pile of flowers that have not yet been strung together. Just as unstrung flowers in a pile can be scattered and blown away by the wind, so too, if time passes under the influence of wicked persons like this old monk Subhadda, the rules of training (sikkhāpada) in the Vinaya Piṭaka will disappear one by one or two by two. In the Suttanta Piṭaka, the questions and answers will disappear one by one or two by two. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the extraordinary teachings such as the Kāmāvacara, Rūpāvacara, Arūpāvacara, and Lokuttara dhammas will disappear one by one or two by two. In this way, if the Sutta, Vinaya, and Abhidhamma Piṭakas, which are the roots of the Sāsana, gradually disappear—to use a worldly metaphor—just as an ogre (peta) clinging to a tree can still stay by the trunk if the branches disappear, and can still stay by the roots if the trunk disappears, but has no place to cling to at all if the roots disappear, so too shall we become those without a refuge.
513:
(Alternatively—just as a father ogre gives his young son a certain invisibility root, and if that young ogre loses that root through forgetfulness or by it being snatched away, he can no longer find a footing or support; in the same way, if the Piṭakas disappear, we too shall be without support or footing). Therefore, we shall hold a Council of the Dhamma and Vinaya. If we hold such a Council, this Dhamma-Vinaya Sāsana will be firm, unshakable, and steady, like flowers well-strung with a floral thread.

It was for the very purpose of holding this Dhamma-Vinaya Council that the Buddha traveled as far as three gāvutas to welcome me. He granted me the status of a monk through the three-fold exhortation (ovāda). He removed the robe he was wearing and exchanged it with the robe I was wearing. While moving his hand in the sky, he preached the Candūpama practice, using me as a living witness. Three times he entrusted me with the entire heritage of the Sāsana (referring to the three Suttas of exhortation in the Kassapa Saṃyutta). While a son of the Buddha like myself is still present, let not this wicked person find growth in the Sāsana.
514:
“Before Adhamma (unrighteousness) flourishes and Dhamma (righteousness) is obstructed; before Avinaya (what is not the Buddha's discipline) flourishes and Vinaya (the Buddha's discipline) is obstructed; before those who speak Adhamma gain strength and those who speak Dhamma lose strength; before those who speak Avinaya gain strength and those who speak Vinaya lose strength—I shall hold a Council of the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya teachings. When such a Council is held, monks will learn according to their ability and wisdom, and they will discuss and debate what is allowable and what is not according to the Vinaya. Then, this wicked person will naturally be suppressed and will not dare to raise his head again, and the Buddha’s Sāsana will reach a state of completeness and prosperity.”

Thus, the thoughts of holding a Dhamma Council continued to arise.

The Elder did not mention to any other monk or person that “such a thought has arisen in my mind.” Instead, he preached a discourse to comfort the grieving and weeping monks as follows:

“Friends, enough! Do not grieve, do not lament, do not weep. Has the Buddha not already preached long ago that there is separation from all that is beloved and dear—
515:
being parted (nānābhāva), being separated (vinābhāva), and becoming otherwise (aññathābhāva)? Friends, how can it be obtained in this case that what is born, come into being, conditioned, and subject to disintegration should not disintegrate? There is no possibility of such a thing. Has the Buddha not preached this word in advance?”

Thus he preached to comfort them.

## The Cremation of the Physical Body

At that time, four Malla chiefs, having washed their heads and dressed in brand-new clothes, intended to light the Buddha’s sandalwood pyre. However, they were unable to make the fire catch by any means.

(In this regard: The sandalwood pyre was one hundred and twenty cubits high. When the four Malla chiefs could not light it, they increased the number to eight, sixteen, and thirty-two. They held large torches in pairs on the left and right, fanned with palm-leaf fans, and used leather bellows, trying various ways to make the fire burn, but they were unable to make the fire catch by any means.

To elaborate: Eighty thousand households who were the primary supporters of the eighty great disciples (asīti-mahāsāvaka) had been reborn in the celestial realms. Among those devas, those who had special devotion to the Elder Mahākassapa—
516:
looked and reflected, “Where is our alms-collecting Elder Mahākassapa?” Seeing the Elder traveling on the road from Pāvā to Kusinārā, they made a resolution: “Let this sandalwood pyre not catch fire until our alms-collecting Elder Mahākassapa has paid his respects.” Because of this, the fire would not catch.

Then the Mallas asked Ven. Anuruddha about the reason why the fire would not catch. Ven. Anuruddha replied, “Mallas of the Vāseṭṭha clan, the intention of the devas is different.” When the Mallas asked, “Venerable sir, what is the intention of the devas?” Ven. Anuruddha told them:

“Mallas of the Vāseṭṭha clan, the devas’ intention is this: ‘Ven. Mahākassapa is traveling from Pāvā to Kusinārā with five hundred monks. Let the Buddha’s sandalwood pyre not catch fire until Ven. Mahākassapa has bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet.’”

Upon hearing this, the Mallas said, “Venerable sir, let it be according to the devas’ intention.”

When the people heard this news, they thought, “O friends, a monk named Mahākassapa is coming with five hundred monks to pay respects to the Buddha’s feet. It is said the sandalwood pyre will not burn until that monk Mahākassapa arrives. Friends, is that monk Mahākassapa dark-skinned or fair-skinned? Is he tall or short? What is his appearance and form like? While such a monk exists, how could the Buddha’s Parinibbāna be like this?” Some took perfumes and flowers and went out to meet him. Others decorated the roads and stood waiting for his arrival.
517:
Then Ven. Mahākassapa arrived at the sandalwood pyre at the Makuṭabandhana shrine of the Mallas in Kusinārā. He arranged his robe over one shoulder, clasped his hands in reverence, and circumambulated the sandalwood pyre three times to the right. While reflecting, he clearly discerned, “Here is the Buddha’s head; here are the Buddha’s feet.” Standing at the foot of the physical body, he entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for higher knowledge (abhiññā). After emerging from that jhāna, he made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna): “May the pair of the Buddha’s feet, adorned with the thousand-spoked wheel marks, together with the layers of cotton and the five hundred pairs of cloth, the golden coffin, and the sandalwood pyre, part in two and appear upon my head.”

Simultaneously with his resolution, the five hundred pairs of cloth parted in two, and like the full moon emerging from behind a cloud, the pair of the Buddha’s feet came forth. The Elder, like a newly blossomed red lotus—
518:
Spreading his reddish-hued hands, the Elder Mahākassapa firmly grasped the Buddha's golden-colored, radiant feet up to the ankles and placed them upon his own head, paying homage with deep reverence.
