## (4) The Attribute of Sugato
Regarding this attribute of Sugato, the Commentary provides four explanations:
(1) Su = beautifully + Gata = He who has gone by means of going. In this context, the Noble Path (Ariya-magga) is called the Buddha's 'going'. That Noble Path is beautiful because it is faultless and pure. Thus, the Buddha is called 'Sugato' because He has gone without attachment to the safe place of Nibbāna by means of the 'going' of knowledge, which is the faultless, pure, and beautiful Noble Path. (In this sense, the Noble Path is the attribute, and the Buddha's personhood is the possessor of the attribute).

(2) Su = to the good place of Nibbāna + Gata = the Buddha who has gone by the 'going' of knowledge. Since the state of Nibbāna is free from any kind of suffering or conditioned things (saṅkhāra) and is purely blissful, that Nibbāna is the best place. Because the Buddha has gone to that best place of Nibbāna in a single sitting by means of the four path-knowledges, He is called 'Sugato'. (In this sense also, the four path-knowledges are the attribute, and the Buddha's personhood is the possessor of the attribute). In both of these methods, the direct realization of Nibbāna through the Noble Path is called 'going to Nibbāna'. This type is called Ñāṇa-gati (going by knowledge), whereas the arrival of the physical body at a village, town, forest, or various regions is called Kāya-gati (going by body).
576:
(3) Su-sammā = well + Gata = the Buddha who is able to go to Nibbāna by path-knowledge. In this method, 'going well' means going without being overwhelmed by the opposing defilements (kilesa). It means the Buddha who goes to Nibbāna without allowing the defilements already abandoned by the four respective paths to return to His mental continuum.

In all three of these methods, if one looks at the ultimate reality (paramattha), they all result in a single essential meaning: the realization of Nibbāna through the four paths. Therefore, in the meaning of the attribute, the first method (I) is translated as: "Because He has gone straight to the Golden Realm of Nibbāna, the Great Seat of Victory, by means of the fourfold path-knowledge without ever returning."

(4) Su-sammā = well + Gada = the Buddha who speaks appropriate words in appropriate places. (In this method, the word is intended as 'Sugada', but the letter 'da' is changed to 'ta' to say 'Sugato').

According to the saying, "Six types of speech appear among humans; reject four, keep two":

1. Speech that is not true, not beneficial, and not liked by others (e.g., saying a virtuous person is "immoral"). The Buddha does not speak such words.

2. Speech that is true but not beneficial and not liked by others (e.g., calling an immoral person
577:
"immoral" not out of a desire to admonish but out of malice). The Buddha does not speak such words either.

3. Speech that is true and beneficial, but not liked by the person spoken to (e.g., saying out of Great Compassion to Devadatta, who was headed for hell, "Devadatta, who will fall into hell"). The Buddha speaks such words if it is appropriate, after considering the right time and opportunity.

4. Speech that is not true and not beneficial, yet liked and enjoyed by others (e.g., saying that performing acts like killing according to Vedic rituals can lead to the celestial realms). The Buddha does not speak such words either.

5. Speech that is true but not beneficial, yet liked and enjoyed by others (e.g., slanderous speech that is true but causes loss of love and increases hatred between people). The Buddha does not speak such words either.

6. Speech that is true, beneficial, and liked and enjoyed by others (e.g., Dhamma talks concerning generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), etc., preached in appropriate places). The Buddha speaks such words after considering the right time and opportunity.

Among these six types of speech in the world, the Buddha speaks only two types: type 3, which is true and beneficial but disliked by the recipient, and type 6, which is true, beneficial, and liked by others.
578:
Regarding these two types of speech spoken by Him, even the 3rd type—which is true and beneficial but disliked only by the person spoken to—is considered well-spoken and faultless because it brings about the welfare and happiness of the world when heard by others.

Thus, according to this method, speaking these two types of faultless words—which are true and beneficial, whether they are liked or disliked (by the other party)—is called the attribute, and the Buddha's personhood is the possessor of the attribute. (Please reflect on this in connection with the meaning of the attribute).

## Summary of the Abhaya Rājakumāra Sutta
The account of the six types of speech mentioned above is found in the Majjhima Nikāya, Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, 1. Gahapati Vagga, 8. Abhaya Rājakumāra Sutta. The summary of the story is as follows:

At one time, while the Buddha was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha, Prince Abhaya, the son of King Bimbisāra, went to his teacher, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, paid respects, and sat in a suitable place. Then, the teacher Nātaputta said to Prince Abhaya:

"Prince, go. Raise a challenge of doctrine against the Samana Gotama. If you do so, it will be said of you, 'Prince Abhaya
579:
‘The doctrine of the ascetic Gotama, who is of such great power and majesty, can indeed be refuted.’ In this way, a very good reputation will spread far and wide.”

When this was said, Prince Abhaya asked, “Venerable sir, how can I refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama, who is of such great power and majesty?” (meaning, it would not be possible). Then the teacher Nātaputta said to Prince Abhaya:

“Prince, go. Go to where the ascetic Gotama is and ask him: ‘Venerable sir, would the Tathāgata speak words that are unloved and disagreeable to others?’ If, when you ask this, the ascetic Gotama answers you: ‘Prince, the Tathāgata would speak words that are unloved and disagreeable to others,’ then you should say to him: ‘Venerable sir, if that is so, then what is the difference between you and an ordinary person? For an ordinary person also speaks words that are unloved and disagreeable to others.’ This is the first way to refute his doctrine (1).

But if, when you ask this, the ascetic Gotama answers you: ‘Prince, the Tathāgata would not speak words that are unloved and disagreeable to others,’ then you should say to him: ‘Venerable sir, if that is so, then why did you say of the Venerable Devadatta: “Devadatta is destined for the states of deprivation,
580:
Devadatta is destined for hell, Devadatta will remain in hell for an aeon, Devadatta is incurable”? To continue, Venerable sir, because of those words of yours, the Venerable Devadatta became angry and dissatisfied.’ This is the second way to refute his doctrine (2).

Prince, if you ask the ascetic Gotama this two-pronged problem from which there is no escape, the ascetic Gotama will certainly be like a man with a fishhook stuck in his throat, unable to spit it out and unable to swallow it.”

Thus did he instruct him.

(In this regard: The teacher Nātaputta had contemplated this problem for four months before teaching it to Prince Abhaya. To clarify further—before the Buddha appeared, the six sectarian teachers boasted and claimed, “I am a Buddha, I am a Buddha,” and many people became their disciples, believing them to be true Buddhas. From the time the Buddha appeared and became well-known, many of those disciples, being people with great merit and perfections, became disciples of the Buddha in large groups.

At that time, the teacher Nātaputta thought, “The ascetic Gotama has taken away my disciples. Well then, if I ask the ascetic Gotama a certain problem, he will be unable to rise from his seat in dejection; I must devise such a problem.” He reflected thus while receiving and eating fine food at the house of his supporter, Prince Abhaya. He devised many problems in his mind, thinking, “In this problem, the ascetic Gotama will point out such-and-such a fault; in that problem,
581:
he will point out such-and-such a fault.” After considering and discarding all those problems, after four months had passed, the problem mentioned earlier—“Would the Tathāgata speak words that are unloved and disagreeable to others?”—appeared in his mind.

Then, the teacher Nātaputta thought, “In both the question and answer of this problem, the ascetic Gotama will not be able to point out a fault. This problem is a very profound ‘pocket-sized’ dilemma. Who can take this problem and refute the ascetic Gotama?” He then considered, “Prince Abhaya is a wise man. He will be able to take this problem and refute the ascetic Gotama. Therefore, I will teach this problem to Prince Abhaya.” Having made this decision, when Prince Abhaya came to him, he taught and spoke to him as described above.)

When the teacher Nātaputta taught him thus, Prince Abhaya, having a strong desire to find fault with others, agreed, saying, “Very well, venerable teacher.” He rose from his seat, paid respects to the teacher Nātaputta, and went to the Veluvana monastery where the Buddha was staying. After paying respectful homage to the Buddha, he sat in a suitable place and looked at the sun. At that time, as it was near sunset, Prince Abhaya thought, “The teacher devised this problem over four months. If I spend time asking and answering each side of such a profound problem, the short time remaining in the day will not be enough.” He then thought, “There is no more time to refute the Buddha today. Tomorrow, in my own palace, I shall
582:
refute the Buddha.” Having considered this, Prince Abhaya said to the Buddha, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One, for the sake of merit, together with three other monks (making four in total including the Buddha), accept my meal tomorrow.”

(In this regard: Prince Abhaya’s intention was: (1) If I invite the Buddha along with many monks, while many monks are seated, even if I ask the problem with a few words, because there are many people, they might speak of other suttas, other matters, or other stories as if everyone is talking at once. If that happens, there might be arguments or a great commotion. (2) If I invite only the Buddha, the thought might arise, “This Prince Abhaya is very stingy and mean; although he sees the Buddha going for alms daily with hundreds and thousands of monks, he invites only the Buddha alone.” Thus, the danger of blame (garahā-bhaya) would come upon me. If I invite the Buddha as the fourth with three other monks, the two aforementioned faults will not occur.” Thus he reflected. Therefore, he invited the Buddha as the fourth, with three monks following.)

The Buddha accepted Prince Abhaya’s invitation by remaining silent. Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, Prince Abhaya rose from his seat, paid respects to the Buddha, and returned to his palace.

The next morning, when the Buddha arrived at Prince Abhaya’s palace (according to the prince’s invitation) and had finished his meal, Prince Abhaya
583:
sat in a low seat and asked the Buddha, just as the teacher Nātaputta had taught him:

“Venerable sir, would the Tathāgata speak words that are unloved and disagreeable to others?”

Then the Buddha said to Prince Abhaya:

“Prince, there is no one-sided (categorical) answer to the problem you have just asked. (That is: The Tathāgata might speak such words, and he might not. If he sees that speaking such words will be beneficial, he would speak them. If he does not see that speaking such words will be beneficial—that is, if he sees they will be unbeneficial—he would not speak them.)”

Having said this, the Buddha crushed the problem that the teacher Nātaputta had devised over four months into pieces with a single sentence, just as a thunderbolt destroys a mountain peak with a single strike.

Then Prince Abhaya, unable to find even a speck of fault in the Buddha, said:

“Venerable sir, in this problem, all the Nigaṇṭhas have been defeated and ruined.”

The Buddha asked, “Prince, why do you say, ‘Venerable sir, in this problem, all the Nigaṇṭhas have been defeated and ruined’?” Then Prince Abhaya
584:
disclosed everything that had happened when he went to the teacher Nātaputta and how that teacher had instructed him (as previously described). (Refer back to page 578).

At that time, a very young infant, who could only lie on his back, was sitting on Prince Abhaya’s lap. (This was done intentionally. Indeed, when debaters engage in a debate with one another, they often sit holding a fruit, a flower, or a book in their hands. If they win, they speak over and dominate the other side. if signs of defeat appear, they act as if they are eating the fruit, smelling the flower, or reading the book, showing a distracted manner. Now, this Prince Abhaya thought, “Oh, the Buddha with whom I must now debate is one who has fought and won many battles of doctrine and can suppress the doctrines of others. If I win, it is well; but if signs of my defeat appear, I will pinch this child and make him cry. Then I will say, ‘O sirs, this child is crying; let us rise, let us consider this later,’ and thus I will scatter the conversation.” For this reason, he sat holding the child.)

The Buddha, being hundreds and thousands of times more skilled in debate than Prince Abhaya, thought, “I will refute his doctrine by using this very child on the prince’s lap as a simile.” Having reflected thus,
585:
and before Prince Abhaya could pinch the child, the Buddha said:

“Prince, what do you think of the words I am about to ask? (You may answer as you please.) Suppose this child on your lap, through your negligence or the nurse’s negligence, being an ignorant child, were to put a stick or a shard of pottery or glass into his mouth. What would you do to that child?”

Then Prince Abhaya said to the Buddha:

“Venerable sir, I would quickly take out that stick or shard of pottery or glass from the child’s mouth. Venerable sir, if I could not take it out easily at the very first, I would hold the child’s head firmly with my left hand so he could not move, and then, hooking my right forefinger, I would pull out that stick or shard of pottery or glass, even if it drew blood. I would do so because of my great love and compassion for that child.”

Then the Buddha said to Prince Abhaya:
586:
586
1. Prince Abhaya, such words that are not true, not beneficial, and are disagreeable and unpleasant to others, the Buddha does not speak.
2. Such words that are true but not beneficial, and are disagreeable and unpleasant to others, the Buddha also does not speak.
*3. Such words that are true and beneficial, but are disagreeable and unpleasant to those spoken to, the Buddha, having considered the proper time and occasion, speaks them if it is appropriate (i.e., if speaking will be beneficial).
4. Such words that are not true and not beneficial, yet are agreeable and pleasant to others, the Buddha does not speak.
5. Such words that are true but not beneficial, yet are agreeable and pleasant to others, the Buddha also does not speak.
*6. Such words that are true and beneficial, and are also agreeable and pleasant to others, the Buddha, having considered the proper time and occasion, speaks them if it is appropriate (i.e., if speaking will be beneficial).
Prince Abhaya, the reason for avoiding those four types of speech and speaking only these two types is because of the Buddha's great loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā) toward all beings.
Thus he spoke. (It should be noted in summary that whether it is agreeable or disagreeable to others, the Buddha speaks only that which is true and
587:
587
beneficial).
(In this context, regarding point 4, 'words that are not true and not beneficial, yet are agreeable and pleasant to others,' the Commentary states that this refers to 'aṭṭhānīyakathā'—illogical or impossible talk that is spoken randomly. To illustrate this, the following story of the Old Woodsman is presented. For the sake of general knowledge, I shall recount that story—
## The Story of the Old Woodsman
An old man from the forest came to the city and was drinking at a tavern. Many city drunkards, wishing to deceive him, gathered at the drinking place and drank together with the old man. They plotted, saying, 'We shall trick this forest-dweller and take all his clothes and the goods he has in his hands.' They made a pact: 'We shall each tell a personal experience. Whoever says "It is not true" or does not believe the story shall be made a slave and taken as property.' They then asked the old man, 'Grandfather, do you agree to this pact?' The old man replied, 'My grandsons, yes, very well. Let it be as you say.'
Then, one of the city drunkards began to tell his personal experience—
588:
588
'Friends, while my mother was pregnant, she had a craving to eat wood-apples. Since she could find no one else to pick them, she sent me to pick the wood-apples.
I, while still dwelling in my mother's womb, went to the wood-apple tree. Being unable to climb the tree, I grabbed myself by my own feet and threw myself up into the tree like a club. Then, moving from branch to branch in the tree, I picked the wood-apples. Unable to climb down, I went back home, fetched a ladder, set it against the tree, and climbed down. Then I went to my mother and gave her the wood-apples. Those wood-apples I brought were very large, about the size of a large storage pot.
My mother ate sixty of those wood-apples in one sitting to satisfy her craving. Of the wood-apples I brought in a single fold of my lower garment, those left over by my mother were enough for all the people, young and old, in our entire village. Our house's reception hall was sixteen cubits wide. After removing all the household furniture, large and small, from that hall, we stored the wood-apples there, and they filled the room up to the roof. The wood-apples that exceeded the capacity of the hall were taken outside and piled at the door, forming a heap about the size of a mountain eighty cubits high.'
589:
589
'Friends, what do you think? Can you believe this event I have just told?' he asked.
The old woodsman remained still and silent. After all the other city drunkards had finished their stories, they asked, 'Well, grandfather, do you believe this event?' He replied, 'My grandsons, if it is said to happen, it must happen. The country itself is so large; since the country is very large, I can believe it.'
Just as the first drunkard had spoken, all the other drunkards each told different kinds of groundless stories (stories that lack a reasonable cause to be possible). When they had finished, finally, the old woodsman said—
'My grandsons, please listen to my personal experience as well. It is not only the houses in your city that are grand; the houses in our forest are also very grand. What I particularly want to say is that in my home, the cotton field is much larger than other fields. It is very vast. In the middle of our cotton field, which is many hundreds of acres wide, there is a single giant cotton tree growing exceptionally tall, about eighty cubits high. It has five main branches. While the other branches bear no fruit at all, from the branch that grows toward the east,
590:
590
a single, extraordinary cotton fruit grows, with a circumference about the size of a large storage pot. Within the six segments of that large cotton fruit, six large clusters of cotton flowers bloomed.
After I had shaved my hair and beard, bathed, and applied perfumes, I went to the cotton field. Seeing those six large clusters of cotton flowers blooming so strangely, I stood there with great joy, reached out my hand, and plucked those six clusters. What was even more strange was that as soon as those six clusters reached my hand, they lost their appearance as flowers and became six strong male slaves. All six of them abandoned me and ran away to another place. For such a long time, I did not see those six slaves of mine, and only today do I see them again. Those six slaves are none other than you six! You are the slave named Nanda, you are the slave named Puṇṇa, you are the slave named Vaḍḍhamāna, you are the slave named Citta, you are the slave named Maṅgala, and you are the slave named Poṭṭhiya!' Saying this, he rose quickly from his seat and stood there, firmly grasping all six city drunkards by their topknots.
The six city drunkards could not say, 'We are not your slaves,'
591:
591
(for if they did, according to the original pact, they would indeed have to become slaves). Thereafter, the old man dragged all six of them to the court, had them branded as slaves and registered, and used them as slaves for the rest of their lives. The Buddha, even if others might find such talk entertaining and refreshing, never speaks it because it is neither true nor beneficial. (From Ma-ṭṭha, Vol. 3, pages 70, 79).
Then Prince Abhaya asked the Buddha, 'Exalted Buddha, when wise kings, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise recluses prepare questions and approach the Buddha to ask them, has the Buddha already reflected and considered in his mind beforehand, "If these wise men approach me and ask in this manner, I shall answer them in that manner"? Or does that answer appear in the Buddha's knowledge at that very moment?' The Buddha replied, 'Prince Abhaya, if that is so, I shall ask you a question in return. You may answer as you please. Prince, what do you think of this? Are you not one who is skilled and proficient in the various parts and components of a chariot?' Prince Abhaya replied, 'It is so, Exalted Buddha. I am
592:
592
one who is skilled and proficient in the various parts and components of a chariot.'
Then the Buddha asked Prince Abhaya, 'Prince, what do you think of this? If someone were to approach you unexpectedly and ask, "What is the name of this particular part of the chariot?", would you have already reflected and considered in your mind beforehand, "If someone approaches me and asks in this manner, I shall answer them in that manner"? Or would that answer appear in your knowledge at that very moment?' Prince Abhaya replied, 'Exalted Buddha, I am well-known as one who has reached the far shore of the art of chariotry. I am skilled and proficient in the various parts of a chariot. All the various parts of a chariot are already well-clarified to me. Therefore, the answer to any question asked regarding the parts of this chariot appears in my knowledge at that very moment.'
Then the Buddha said to Prince Abhaya, 'Prince, in the same way, when wise kings, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise recluses prepare questions and approach me to ask them, the answer to the question appears in my knowledge at that very moment. If you ask why it appears so—Prince, it is because the Buddha has well-penetrated the Dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) which is the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).'
593:
“...I have attained it; because I have well-penetrated and attained this Dhamma-element, which is the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), the answers to these questions appear in My knowledge in an instant.” When the Buddha spoke these sweet and gentle words, Prince Abhaya took refuge and became a lay follower (upāsaka) right there. This is the summary of the Abhayarājakumāra Sutta.

(It is mentioned in detail in the Apadāna Pāḷi, Part II, pages 158, 159, 160, that this Prince Abhaya later entered the Order, practiced the Dhamma, and became an Arahant endowed with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā) and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). He was one possessed of the five kinds of wisdom: sharp wisdom, witty wisdom, swift wisdom, great wisdom, and profound wisdom. Those who wish to know more should consult the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka.)

Here ends the attribute of Sugato.
