Meaning of the First Poem: In the first poem, the section from "With the jewel of Bodhi as a wheel-chariot" to "I pay homage with the three doors" expresses the salutation (paṇāma) to the Buddha. The meaning is: Just as a Universal Monarch (Sammuti-deva) possesses the great ruby jewel named Jotirasa and circles the four islands with his wheel-treasure, so too the Buddha, the peerless Visuddhi-deva, who is the King of Dhamma, possesses the great jewel of the four Path-knowledges (magga-ñāṇa) and circles the four islands of the Four Truths with the great wheel-chariot of the Dhamma-teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). I pay homage to Him with the three doors of body, speech, and mind.

Here, the fact that the Buddha tirelessly taught the Four Noble Truths in various ways through His knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) for forty-five years is described as "circling the four islands of the Four Truths with the wheel-treasure of desanā-ñāṇa." The devas and brahmas in the celestial and brahma realms are called Upapatti-deva. The humans who rule countries in the human world are called Sammuti-deva. This means they are those designated by human society as "Deva = mundane Sammuti-deva," similar to the higher devas. The Buddhas and Arahats whose taints (āsava) are exhausted are called Visuddhi-deva = noble persons who are pure from defilements and shine beautifully through the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). Among those Visuddhi-devas, the Buddha is the peerless King of Visuddhi-devas.
696:
The section from "The three realms of existence, roaring through" to "I shall now recite the introductory verses" expresses the pledge (paṭiññā), which is the commitment to compose the poem-treatise on Paṭiccasamuppāda. The meaning is: The great cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra), where the aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) arise continuously and without stopping in the three realms of existence—the sense realm (kāma-bhava), the fine-material realm (rūpa-bhava), and the immaterial realm (arūpa-bhava)—is described as "the great wheel-chariot of Saṃsāra roaring through the three realms of existence." The occurrence and account (atthuppatti) of this great chariot of Saṃsāra, when identified in terms of ultimate reality, is Paṭiccasamuppāda—the arising of effects depending on causes. Therefore, it means: "In order that the Paṭiccasamuppāda, which is the account of the nature of the great chariot of Saṃsāra, may be clearly and precisely understood, I shall recite the introductory verses."

"The four truths, deep in nature" refers to the Four Noble Truths, which are very profound in their natural essence. "Obscuring and hiding, a great darkness called Avijjā falls" means that in the continuity of ignorant worldlings, the great darkness of the four types of moha mentioned earlier obscures and hides those Four Noble Truths so that they cannot be seen or known as they truly are. In the world, when four conditions are met—the day of the new moon, midnight, being in the middle of a forest, and thick, dark clouds—it is called the falling of a great darkness with four factors. When such darkness falls, nothing can be seen or known. Similarly, in the continuity of an ignorant worldling, there is the falling of a great darkness complete with the four factors of moha mentioned earlier,
697:
meaning that because of this darkness, nothing is known or seen as it truly is.

"The nest of existence, intensely hot; this body, which is fuel for the fire, based on attachment to it" means: In the three realms of existence—kāma, rūpa, and arūpa—the eleven fires such as the fire of lust (rāga), the fire of hatred (dosa), and the fire of delusion (moha) are roaring and burning. Thus, it is true that they are always intensely hot and oppressive. Within this intensely hot and oppressive nest of the three realms, the aggregates (khandha) that manifest are merely the fuel for those eleven fires. Because ignorant worldlings are in the darkness of ignorance (avijjā) mentioned before, they do not realize the heat, the burning, or the intensity within the nest of existence; instead, they strongly cling to and crave the five aggregates of mind and matter, which are the fuel for the fire. This means "because of such attachment and craving."

"Unwholesome... the seed of the path to lower realms, apuñña..." means: Based on this craving (lobha) and attachment to the five aggregates which are the fuel for the fires of existence, and not realizing it is unwholesome, people focus only on the happiness of their present life. They commit the twelve types of unwholesome volition (akusala cetanā) known as apuññābhisaṅkhāra—foul and evil states—such as killing and stealing, which are the seeds for the existence in lower realms. (This is how apuññābhisaṅkhāra arises due to ignorance).

With the section "Desiring a good future... ten merits, āneñja," the arising of puññābhisaṅkhāra and āneñjābhisaṅkhāra due to ignorance is shown. The meaning is: Among the Four Noble Truths, Dukkha-sacca and
698:
Samudaya-sacca are mundane truths; they are truths that are hot and burning. Nirodha-sacca and Magga-sacca are supramundane truths; they are truly peaceful states. However, in the continuity of worldlings (especially those worldlings who delight in the cycle of rebirth, vaṭṭābhirata puthujjana), because the four types of ignorance obscure and hide the truth, they do not know at all that the two burning mundane truths are hot. Consequently, craving (taṇhā-lobha) arises, which pursues, clings to, and delights in those two burning mundane truths.

When such craving arises, among the worldlings who delight in the cycle (as explained in the commentary on the attribute Lokavidū on page 598 of this Volume V), those worldlings with the underlying tendency of annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) do not believe in the world beyond. Therefore, they do not think at all about prosperity and happiness in the next life; they think only of being happy for the duration of this present life and thus commit unwholesome volitions (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) such as killing (pāṇātipāta). Those worldlings who delight in the cycle and have the underlying tendency of eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) look forward to prosperity and happiness in future lives. They diligently perform puññābhisaṅkhāra, which are ordinary wholesome volitions of the sense and fine-material spheres, and āneñjābhisaṅkhāra, which are wholesome volitions of the immaterial sphere. These are vaṭṭapādaka (supporting the cycle of the three planes) and not vivaṭṭapādaka (the foundational wholesome deeds for the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna). (This is how puññābhisaṅkhāra and āneñjābhisaṅkhāra arise due to ignorance).

"The capital for existence, thus prolonged; the field and lineage of the cycle are long." The meaning here is: as already stated—
699:
The arising of the three types of volitional formations (saṅkhāra) due to ignorance (avijjā) means the increase of the 'capital' for the ceaseless rotation of the great chariot of the three rounds of existence (vaṭṭa). It means that when this capital of existence increases, the three rounds—the round of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa), the round of action (kamma-vaṭṭa), and the round of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa)—which are the grounds and lineages of the suffering of existence, become so long that they cannot be cut or faded away. (This is the concise meaning of the first verse. For a detailed explanation, one should consult the Paṭiccasamuppāda Dīpanī by the Most Venerable Ledi Sayadaw. The same applies to the subsequent verses).

## (2) Saṅkhārapaccayā Viññāṇaṃ

When the capital of existence increases, intending to lengthen the grounds and lineage of the rounds, through the ten types of meritorious and non-meritorious volitional formations; then in the four lower realms and various realms of Brahmas, humans, and devas—the three spheres of existence—the six types of consciousness, which are the predominant and presiding masters of the doors, appear as the 'Lord of Elements'. They govern and manage the various mental and physical phenomena that surround them in abundance at the six internal and external gates. Due to the sharp power and radiance of this consciousness, delusions such as 'I', 'you', 'human', or 'deva' arise, and the lineage of the rounds in various hells and lower realms stretches far and wide. This is the power of the six types of consciousness. (Thus, take the meaning).

## Concise Meaning

Regarding the statement 'Conditioned by volitional formations, the six types of consciousness appear': due to unwholesome volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), which are unwholesome volitions, rebirth-consciousness in the lower realms and unwholesome resultant consciousness (akusala-vipāka viññāṇa) in the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere during the course of existence arise as appropriate.
700:
Through meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), which are sense-sphere wholesome volitions, nine types of rebirth-consciousness arise in the seven happy sense-sphere realms (human and deva realms), and sixteen types of sense-sphere wholesome resultant consciousness arise during the course of existence in the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere as appropriate. Through meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), which are fine-material wholesome volitions, fine-material resultant rebirth-consciousness and life-continuum consciousness arise in the fifteen fine-material Brahma realms. Through imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), which are immaterial wholesome volitions, immaterial resultant rebirth-consciousness and life-continuum consciousness arise in the four immaterial Brahma realms.

In this context, the manner in which resultant consciousness arises due to wholesome and unwholesome volitions (saṅkhāra) should be briefly understood through the four types of endowments (samangitā, also called samangī). The method of understanding is as follows:

(1) When performing a good or bad deed, wholesome or unwholesome volitions that complete that action arise. The state where that volition is clearly present in the present moment is called Cetanā-samangitā (Endowment of Volition), meaning being complete with the act of instigation.

(2) When those wholesome or unwholesome volitions cease after their three sub-moments (unlike other resultant consciousness), they do not cease by being completely cut off from this continuum of aggregates. Instead, they cease after leaving behind a special potency (satti) that can cause a resultant consciousness to appear as a distinct mental phenomenon when conditions are met. This special potency remains latent in this continuum of aggregates as long as it has not yet become a 'lapsed kamma' (ahosi-kamma). Being endowed with this special potency is called Kamma-samangitā (Endowment of Action).
701:
(3) When it is time for those wholesome or unwholesome kammas to bear fruit, there appears at the respective door either the kamma itself, or the sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta)—the objects or instruments that were present when the kamma was performed—or the sign of destination (gati-nimitta)—the objects to be experienced or encountered in the next life. (For beings near death, except for Buddhas and Arahants, these signs appear to everyone. They pass away from this life only after firmly grasping such an appearing sign with enough strength to follow into the next life). Being endowed with the appearance of one of these three—kamma, kamma-nimitta, or gati-nimitta—is called Upaṭṭhāna-samangitā (Endowment of Appearance).

(4) Thereafter, passing away from this life, rebirth (resultant) consciousness arises in the appropriate existence. Following the moment of rebirth (during the course of existence), resultant consciousnesses, which are the fruits of that kamma, arise repeatedly to maintain the flow of existence whenever other cognitive processes (vīthi-citta) are not occurring (acting as life-continuum or bhavaṅga). This state of being endowed with the arising of rebirth-resultant consciousness and resultant consciousness during the course of existence is called Vipāka-samangitā (Endowment of Result).

In this context, 'resultant' (vipāka) refers to the ripening of the special potency of the previously mentioned Kamma-samangitā into the ultimate reality of a mental consciousness (resultant citta). By reflecting on and studying these four types of endowments, one should understand that resultant consciousness arises based on and conditioned by saṅkhāra, known as Cetanā-samangitā. Therefore, the Buddha taught in summary: 'Saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ'—Conditioned by volitional formations, the six types of consciousness arise.
702:
Meaning of the second verse: "The grounds and lineage of the rounds, intended to be long... (etc.)... the Lord of Elements appears" means: As previously stated, when the three types of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), the capital of existence, increase and grow, the resultant consciousness called Vipāka-samangitā arises in the four lower realms, the human realm, the deva realms, and the Brahma realms as appropriate. This resultant consciousness is the predominant and chief factor among mental phenomena (nāma). Indeed, just as the fire element (tejo-dhāt) is the predominant chief on the side of materiality (rūpa), consciousness (viññāṇa) is the predominant chief on the side of mentality (nāma). (For details, see Paṭiccasamuppāda Dīpanī).

If we classify resultant consciousness by function, there are six types: seeing-consciousness, hearing-consciousness, smelling-consciousness, tasting-consciousness, touching-consciousness, and cognizing-consciousness. In the body, where the six doors—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are present: in the eye (cakkhu-dvāra), seeing-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) is the presiding master; in the ear (sota-dvāra), hearing-consciousness (sota-viññāṇa) is the presiding master; in the nose (ghāna-dvāra), smelling-consciousness (ghāna-viññāṇa) is the presiding master; in the tongue (jivhā-dvāra), tasting-consciousness (jivhā-viññāṇa) is the presiding master; in the body (kāya-dvāra), touching-consciousness (kāya-viññāṇa) is the presiding master; and in the mind (mano-dvāra), cognizing-consciousness (mano-viññāṇa) is the presiding master.

"Internal and external gates... (etc.)... governing and managing in abundance" means: (I shall explain using eye-consciousness as an example). Just as when a prince of great merit and power appears, his attendants, the royal throne he occupies, and the surrounding palace and regalia also arise and appear.
703:
For the sake of a single eye-consciousness (seeing-consciousness), which is like a prince of merit and power, there appear: the seven universal mental factors (cetasika), which are like his attendants; the eye-base (cakkhu-vatthu/cakkhu-dvāra), which is the sensitive eye-matter like a royal throne; and the physical phenomena contained within the eye-decad kalāpa, which are like the surrounding palace and regalia. Just as a prince brilliantly governs the aforementioned attendants and regalia while enjoying royal pleasures, the 'prince' of eye-consciousness brilliantly governs the seven attendant mental factors and the physical phenomena such as the eye-decad kalāpa while grandly experiencing the taste of the visible object (rūpārammaṇa). (The same should be understood for hearing-consciousness and the others).

If one reflects on a person's daily activities through the eye of ultimate reality (paramattha), one can clearly see that they are merely the functioning of the six types of consciousness: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. Thus, it becomes evident that all the bustling activities, speech, and thoughts throughout the day are in fact the six types of consciousness.

"Due to his sharp power and radiance... (etc.)... is the power of the six types of consciousness" means: Because these six types of consciousness are constantly and busily arising throughout the days, months, and years, due to the power, radiance, and potency of these six types of consciousness, the delusions arise: 'It is I', 'It is he', 'It is a man', 'It is a deva', 'I see', 'I hear', 'I smell', 'I eat', 'I touch', 'I know',
704:
'He sees', 'He hears', and so on, in various ways. When such delusions arise, the roots of the cycle of existence, such as the hells and other lower realms, become longer and larger. It is meant that this occurs due to the power of the six types of consciousness.

## (3) Viññāṇapaccayā Nāmarūpaṃ

Due to the power of the six types of consciousness, just as radiance follows closely within a fire, there arise without separation: contact (phassa), feeling (vedanā), volition (cetanā), perception (saññā), and initial application (vitakka). Like various colors interwoven in a cat's eye gem, the various lineages of the mental body (nāma-kāya) arise beautifully. And based on the four great elements—earth, water, air, and fire—as the foundation, there are twenty-four derived physical phenomena. Combined together, these twenty-eight types of materiality are called the physical body (rūpa-kāya). These two distinct phenomena, mentality (nāma) and materiality (rūpa), appear together in full. Thus, infinite and various bodies, physical forms, shapes, and behaviors arise—different species of humans, various devas, water-dwellers, land-dwellers, good, bad, superior, and inferior—all distinctly and abundantly separated. This is the power of the two factors, mentality and materiality. (Thus, take the meaning).

## Concise Meaning

Just as when a prince of great merit and power appears, his attendants, retinue, and royal regalia appear ready-made due to the prince's own merit; similarly, when the six 'princes' of the six types of consciousness appear, due to the cause of those six types of consciousness, their attendants and retinue appear as follows:
705:
The associated mental factors (cetasikas) and the physical phenomena (rupas), which are like the royal regalia and accessories of that consciousness, manifest clearly.

Meaning of the third verse: Just as when fire arises, its radiance follows immediately, and just as in a cat's eye gem, various colored streaks follow in succession, so too, when the six types of consciousness arise, due to the power of those consciousnesses, the mental phenomena called cetasikas manifest. These include Phassa (contact), the nature of touching and grinding the object; Vedanā (feeling), the nature of fully experiencing the essence and flavor of the object; and Cetanā (volition), the nature of urging and inciting the associated factors to perform their respective duties without fail. Furthermore, physical phenomena consisting of the four great elements (mahabhūta) and the twenty-four derived matters (upādā-rupa) also manifest clearly.

When these two, mind and matter (nāma-rūpa), manifest completely, infinite beings appear in various forms, shapes, behaviors, lineages, and types—such as humans, devas, aquatic beings, and terrestrial beings. They are distinguished as superior or inferior, each distinct in its own species and lineage, manifesting in countless and immeasurable numbers.

In this regard, even if beings are as closely related as brothers and sisters, the reason why they differ in appearance, shape, temperament, and behavior, and why they are so diverse and extraordinary—
706:
—is due to the diversity and difference of the mind associated with craving (taṇhā). Craving, being associated with and clinging to the mind, delights in and desires a certain kind of appearance, shape, and temperament. Driven by the incitement of that craving, one performs good or bad kamma to obtain a body with the appearance, shape, and temperament that the craving delights in (because craving is diverse, kamma is diverse). Since the kamma performed is of various kinds, when the resultant aggregates of that kamma arise, they manifest as various states of existence (gati), lineages, appearances, shapes, and temperaments, differing and being diverse from one another. This means that because kamma is diverse, the states of existence and so on manifest diversely.

## (4) Nāmarūpapaccayā Saḷāyatanaṃ

When the collection of mind and matter, called the body, appears in full and established form, whether large or small, the six types of clarity known as doors (dvāra) also appear, shimmering and revolving. Pervading the entire body, arranged within the structure, are: the eye (cakkhu) for seeing, the ear (sota) for hearing, the nose (ghāna) for smelling, the tongue (jivhā) for tasting, the body (kāya) for touching, and the mind (mano) for knowing. They are unmixed and sparkling, like the brilliance of a diamond. All six objects—forms, signs, and appearances—manifest completely. Because of these, there arise the perceptions and mistaken views such as "this is a woman," "this is a man," "this is the sun or moon," and the recognition of various forms, sounds, scents, tastes, heat, cold, and touches. To fuel the pride of thinking "this is my body" or "I am a young prince," the six doors illuminate the entire body; such is the power of the six-fold mirror-like elements. (Memorize the meaning).
707:
From this paragraph onwards, I shall explain the meaning based on the verse. Among the physical body (rūpa-kāya) and the mental body (nāma-kāya) that arise because of consciousness, the five physical sensitive matters—eye-sensitivity, ear-sensitivity, nose-sensitivity, tongue-sensitivity, and body-sensitivity—arise due to the power of the physical body. Due to the power of the mental body, the mind-sensitivity known as mano arises.

There are four types of beings: (1) Aṇḍaja beings = beings born from an egg; (2) Jalābuja beings = beings born from a womb; (3) Saṃsedaja beings = beings born from moisture, such as in moss, lotuses, or foam; (4) Opapātika beings = beings who manifest instantaneously with a full body, appearing as if they are sixteen or twenty years old from the moment of conception.

Just as all fruits like coconuts, palm fruits, mangoes, and jackfruits develop their seed-vessels and kernels when the time is right, so too for aṇḍaja and jalābuja beings, after conception, during the course of existence (pavatti), when it is time for the four physical sensitivities—eye, ear, nose, and tongue—to appear, they manifest along with their respective bases (the eye-socket, ear-canal, etc.). They come into being as if the kernel of sensitive matter is being added. Body-sensitivity, however, arises simultaneously with the rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa).
709:
and there are times when Anger (dosa) is excessive, like fire falling on gunpowder. Thus, there are turns where each factor becomes dominant. In such cases, when Vitakka is dominant, the consciousness arises following the lead and guidance of Vitakka. When consciousness arises repeatedly with the mental factors such as Vitakka, Vicāra, Lobha, and Dosa as the inciters, it is said that the mind-base (manāyatana), which is consciousness, arises because of the mental factors (cetasikas). (Alternatively) Just as it is said "fire causes wind, and wind causes fire to spread," so too, because of consciousness (like fire), the mental factors (like wind) arise, and because of those mental factors, consciousness is further propagated in stages.

Alternatively, just as the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are inseparable and when one arises, the other three must also arise, so too, when consciousness arises, the appropriate mental factors must arise with it. When the group of mental factors arises, consciousness is always included. (This explains how the mind-base, manāyatana, arises due to the mental body).

In the continuity of living beings, these six sensitivities are useful only because they manifest and exist. If they did not exist, one would be as useless as a log of wood. These six sensitivities are also called the six doors (dvāra). When we say "door," we do not mean an open space like a physical doorway, but rather clear doors that shimmer and revolve, like doors made of crystal or glass.
710:
Eye-sensitivity arises in the eye-socket; ear-sensitivity in the inner ear; nose-sensitivity in the nose; tongue-sensitivity on the surface of the tongue; and body-sensitivity pervades the entire body, inside and out. The mind-sensitivity (mano) arises within the heart-base. This is what is meant in the verse by "six types of clarity, pervading the entire body."

Just as when a bird perches on a branch, the branch shakes and a shadow appears on the ground simultaneously, so too, various visible forms (rūpārammaṇa) strike the eye-sensitivity and the mind-sensitivity simultaneously. At that moment, with eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) leading, the eye-door cognitive process and the subsequent mind-door cognitive processes occur according to the law of the mind (citta-niyāma). Thus, one sees and knows: "this is the sun," "this is the moon," "this is a person," "this is an ox or buffalo," and so on.

Similarly, various sounds (saddārammaṇa) such as thunder, wind, drums, harps, human voices, and animal sounds strike the ear-sensitivity and mind-sensitivity simultaneously... (etc.) ...Various scents (gandhārammaṇa), such as fragrant or foul smells, strike the nose-sensitivity and mind-sensitivity simultaneously. Various tastes (rasārammaṇa), such as sweet or sour, strike the tongue-sensitivity and mind-sensitivity simultaneously. The collection of various touches (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa), such as heat, cold, roughness, or softness, strikes the body-sensitivity and mind-sensitivity simultaneously. All six types of objects, including the remaining mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) and the aforementioned five objects like forms and sounds, strike the mind-sensitivity. At that time, the mind-door
711:
cognitive processes occur, and various types of knowledge arise abundantly. Referring to this, the verse says: "arranged within the structure, the eye for seeing... (etc.) ...knowing and thinking are fulfilled."

Because seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, knowing, and thinking occur incessantly day and night, in the continuity of worldlings (puthujjana), the flames of unwholesome states such as greed, hatred, delusion, pride, envy, and stinginess burn fiercely within the great hell-pot of personality-belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), with thoughts like "I see," "I hear," "I smell," "I eat," "I touch," "I know," "I think," "I am foolish," or "I am wise." The unwholesome hell-fires illuminate the entire body right at the six great doors. This happens due to the power of the six sense bases. Therefore, the verse says: "knowing and thinking are fulfilled, this body of mine... (etc.) ...the power of the six-fold mirror-like elements."

## (5) Saḷāyatanapaccayā Phasso

When the six types of mirror-like sensitivities are established, all six objects manifest throughout the body in the form of shapes, shadows, and signs. When the six levels of consciousness bloom repeatedly, to give a comparison: it is like the power of Sakka's thunderbolt (vajira), flashing and brilliant, grinding and crushing. The six types of contact (phassa) arise sharply, and by grinding the six kinds of essence and flavor of the objects, they encounter them. Then, the causes are incited, and it becomes urgent to distinguish: "this is desirable (iṭṭha)," "this is undesirable (aniṭṭha)," "this is this much bad," or "this is this much good." The qualities and essences of the six objects emerge fully and vividly, painting the proportions of what is to be desired and what is to be hated. Such is the power of the six-fold contact. (Memorize the meaning).
712:
The meaning is as follows: When the six types of sensitive transparency, known as the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), arise and are established in their respective places within this body, the forms and signs of various visible objects (rūpārammaṇa) appear in the eye-door (cakkhudvāra)—the sensitive transparency of the eye—just as a reflection appears on the surface of a mirror. In the ear-door (sotadvāra)—the sensitive transparency of the ear—the forms and signs of various sounds (saddārammaṇa) appear. In the nose-door (ghānadvāra)—the sensitive transparency of the nose—the forms and signs of various odors (gandhārammaṇa) appear. In the tongue-door (jivhādvāra)—the sensitive transparency of the tongue—the forms and signs of various tastes (rasārammaṇa) appear. In the body-door (kāyadvāra)—the sensitive transparency of the body—the forms and signs of various tangible objects (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa) appear. In the mind-door (manodvāra)—the sensitive transparency of the mental consciousness—the forms and signs of the six types of objects appear as appropriate.

When the respective objects appear in those respective doors, the six types of consciousness—namely seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing—arise vividly at their respective doors (just as sparks fly when a flint and a striker are struck together).

Based on the meeting of these three—the door, the object, and the consciousness—eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa) arises vividly due to the meeting of the eye-transparency, the visible object, and eye-consciousness. Ear-contact (sotasamphassa) arises vividly due to the meeting of the ear-transparency, the sound, and ear-consciousness. Nose-contact (ghānasamphassa) arises vividly due to the meeting of the nose-transparency, the odor, and nose-consciousness. [In the case of] the tongue-door, the tongue-transparency...
713:
...various tastes (rasārammaṇa), and the act of tasting (jivhāviññāṇa)—due to the meeting of these three, tongue-contact (jivhāsamphassa) arises vividly. Due to the meeting of the body-transparency, various tangible objects (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa), and the act of touching (kāyaviññāṇa), body-contact (kāyasamphassa) arises vividly. Due to the meeting of the mind-transparency, any one of the six types of objects, and the act of cognizing (manoviññāṇa), mind-contact (manosamphassa) arises vividly.

These six types of contact, like the Vajira weapon of Sakka, press and grind the objects so that their pleasant essence (iṭṭharasa) and unpleasant essence (aniṭṭharasa) become manifest. Eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa) presses and grinds the various visible objects appearing at the eye-door to make their pleasant and unpleasant essences manifest. The other five types of contact also press and grind the objects appearing at their respective doors to make their pleasant and unpleasant essences manifest. Just as if eye-contact were pressing and chewing various visible objects, through this touching, the pleasant essences from pleasant visible objects and the unpleasant essences from unpleasant visible objects become manifest, as if they were flowing out steadily. Similarly, ear-contact (sotasamphassa) [grinds] various sounds... (etc.), nose-contact (ghānasamphassa) various odors, tongue-contact (jivhāsamphassa) various tastes, body-contact (kāyasamphassa) various tangible objects, and mind-contact (manosamphassa) any one of the six objects appearing at the mind-door; through this touching, as if pressing and chewing, the pleasant essences from pleasant objects and the unpleasant essences from unpleasant objects...
714:
...become manifest as if they were flowing out steadily. The stronger the contact, the more clearly the pleasant and unpleasant essences of the object manifest. When the pleasant essences manifest, they are perceived as desirable things, good things, or attractive things. When the unpleasant essences manifest, they are perceived as undesirable things, bad things, or repulsive things.

This act of touching, which is like pressing and chewing to make the pleasant and unpleasant essences of the object manifest so that they can be perceived as desirable, undesirable, good, bad, attractive, or repulsive, is the functional power of contact (phassa).

## (6) Phassa-paccayā Vedanā

There are six types of contact; by their power,
They grind and chew with the force of a machine,
Causing the six objects to tremble and break,
So that the six kinds of essence, both unpleasant
And pleasant, flow out steadily like liquid.
Then the six great elements of feeling (vedanā)
Arise in various forms and play,
Abundantly partaking of those six essences.
Only when they are experienced and enjoyed distinctly,
Do beauty and ugliness, pleasure and pain,
And various other qualities, good and bad,
Become clearly and prominently known.
If it is good, the mind overflows with radiance,
The heart is joyful and wears a bright smile.
If something hateful is encountered, it withers and fades,
The heart turns sour, and like rising steam or boiling water,
It becomes hot and anxious, joyless and dull,
And the mind becomes exhausted.
In a single moment of pleasure (sukha),
715:
The entire mass of the world's [desires] is gathered.
Whatever is seen moving or bustling about,
Is all for the sake of pleasure (sukha), with intense effort.
Setting aside the Noble Ones and the ultimate reality (paramattha),
For the rest of the world, as much as there is,
They perform many actions that increase suffering (dukkha).
Such is the power of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). (Take this as the meaning).

Among the six types of objects, it is clear that due to the pressing and grinding by the respective contacts, a pair of pleasant and unpleasant essences emerges from each type of object. When the respective objects strike and appear at the six doors (the six transparencies), the six types of consciousness that arise like sparks are only capable of the mere acts of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. Beyond that, the six types of consciousness are not capable of making the pleasant and unpleasant essences (iṭṭharasa, aniṭṭharasa) manifest. The act of pressing and grinding so that the pleasant and unpleasant essences of the object manifest as if flowing out steadily is solely the work of the six types of contact (phassa).

When the six types of contact thus press and grind their respective objects, and the object is of a pleasant kind so that pleasant essences emerge, the great elements of pleasant and joyful feeling (sukha-somanassa vedanā) arise vividly and enjoy those pleasant essences of the object with relish. When the object is of an unpleasant kind and unpleasant essences emerge, the great elements of painful and displeasurable feeling (dukkha-domanassa vedanā) arise vividly and experience those essences unpleasantly, painfully, and with distress. With this meaning in mind, it is taught in the Pali: "Phassa-paccayā vedanā = Due to the six types of contact, the six types of feeling arise."
716:
(In this context: Sukha-vedanā refers to bodily pleasure (kāyika-sukha). Somanassa-vedanā refers to mental pleasure (cetasika-sukha). Dukkha-vedanā refers to bodily pain (kāyika-dukkha). Domanassa-vedanā refers to mental pain (cetasika-dukkha). Sometimes sukha and somanassa are combined and called sukha-vedanā, and dukkha and domanassa are combined and called dukkha-vedanā.

Although feeling is of three types—pleasant (sukha), painful (dukkha), and neutral (upekkhā)—in this verse, unwholesome upekkhā and unwholesome-resultant upekkhā are included under dukkha, while wholesome and functional upekkhā and wholesome-resultant upekkhā are included under sukha. This should be specially noted.

The detailed explanation of this verse should be sought in the Paṭiccasamuppāda Dīpanī. In this book, the meaning of the verse is provided only enough to maintain the connection; the same applies to subsequent verses).

"The six great elements of feeling" refers to: (1) Cakkhusamphassajā vedanā = feeling born of eye-contact, (2) Sotasamphassajā vedanā = feeling born of ear-contact, (3) Ghānasamphassajā vedanā = feeling born of nose-contact, (4) Jivhāsamphassajā vedanā = feeling born of tongue-contact, (5) Kāyasamphassajā vedanā = feeling born of body-contact, (6) Manosamphassajā vedanā = feeling born of mind-contact. These are the six great elements of feeling.

Only these great elements of feeling can fully experience the taste of the object. Therefore, the verse says, "Only when they are experienced and enjoyed distinctly." When the elements of feeling thus fully experience the taste of the object, perceptions and signs such as being beautiful or not, being pleasant or not, being good or...
717:
...not good arise abundantly. If it is a good object, both body and mind are endlessly joyful, and one remains smiling. If it is a hateful or bad object, one experiences it with a withered, fading, and sour heart, as if steam were rising in distress.

The sole aim of all people in the world is to obtain the great element of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). All the bustling efforts seen in the world are merely intense strivings to obtain this great element of pleasant feeling. This element of pleasant feeling, excluding the Noble Ones (Ariyas), tends to cause the increase of suffering (dukkha) for the majority of the worldlings (puthujjanas). All the hardships people endure are solely because they desire that pleasant feeling. Even those who, at the lowest level, wish to end their lives by swallowing poison, hanging themselves, jumping into water, or killing themselves with a weapon, do so because they desire happiness, thinking, "Only in death will there be happiness; only in death will there be peace."

## (7) Vedanā-paccayā Taṇhā

When the power of pleasant feeling spreads,
And its delicious taste thoroughly permeates,
There arises a bubbling and surging love (piya)
For that very pleasure (sukha).
To easily and quickly provide those six
Delicious feelings whenever desired,
Like a wealthy treasurer or a precious gem,
Are spouses, clothing, gold and silver,
Farmlands, food and sustenance,
Various shows and festivals,
Flowers and perfumes of all kinds,
Visible objects (rūpārammaṇa) and the rest,
The five sense objects and the six contacts,
The eye and other six doors,
The sensitive transparencies, the delicate internal elements,
All these in their various and numerous forms,
Are mental objects (dhammārammaṇa), the mass of sensual things,
718:
Indulging in the six sense objects, with intense longing and increasing attachment daily, without seeing even in a dream the essence of the Dhamma or its profound nature, one remains within the prison of sensuality, devoid of the realization of the aggregates—such is the power of the six groups of craving. (Memorize the essence).

When a visible form is seen, through the power of eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa), a desirable essence (iṭṭharasa) emerges from that object. At that time, the pleasant feeling born of eye-contact (cakkhusamphassajā sukha vedanā), which experiences and enjoys that desirable essence as "Excellent! Excellent! Beautiful and radiant!", arises in the mental continuum, overflowing with delicious relish. Then, just as dry rice becomes moist when poured over with melted butter, the mental continuum becomes saturated. Just as a withered lotus becomes fresh and flourishing when sprinkled with cool water, the mental continuum becomes joyful and flourishing. The facial complexion becomes bright, moist, and radiant. This pleasant feeling that saturates the mental continuum through the eye is called the relishing of the eye, the delight of the eye, and the sweetness of the eye. (When a sound is heard, when an odor is smelled, etc., the relishing of the ear, the relishing of the nose, the delight and sweetness of the ear and nose, etc., should be understood in the same way for all six sense objects).

When these six types of pleasant feelings arise, and the relishing and sweetness of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind occur, the six great elements of craving and passion (taṇhā-rāga), which desire to experience that sweetness and obtain that relish, arise repeatedly. Regarding this, it is taught in the Pāḷi scriptures: "Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā = With feeling as condition, the sixfold craving arises."
719:
The six types of craving are: craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā), craving for sounds (sadda-taṇhā), craving for odors (gandha-taṇhā), craving for tastes (rasa-taṇhā), craving for tangibles (phoṭṭhabba-taṇhā), and craving for mental objects (dhamma-taṇhā).

Beings are naturally attached to their life and body. Because they are attached to life and body, they must be attached to the rice that sustains life, the husked rice that produces the rice, the paddy that produces the husked rice, and the cattle, buffaloes, fields, rain, and land that produce the paddy. Because of attachment to all these, they must be attached to the money that can acquire all these. In this way, when craving and greed (taṇhā-lobha) become attached to one object as a root, the attachment spreads through hundreds and thousands of successive stages related to that one attached object. Similarly, because of being attached to and lusting after the single relish of the eye, which is the feeling born of eye-contact (cakkhusamphassajā vedanā), the attachment and lust increase stage by stage for the good form (rūpārammaṇa) that can provide that eye-relish, for all animate and inanimate objects endowed with that form, and for everything related to those objects. (The same should be understood for the successive increase of attachment and lust for good sounds, odors, etc., that provide the relishes of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, starting from the feeling born of ear-contact).

When the vast and wide collection of objects of craving and greed—consisting of concepts, physical things, names, and types—is viewed through the eye of ultimate reality (paramattha), there are only the six sense objects. Therefore, summarizing them by these six objects, the Blessed One taught the six types of craving: craving for forms,
720:
craving for sounds, and so forth. (In the verse, these six sense objects are composed as a metaphor, comparing them to the Treasurer Jewel of a Universal Monarch, who can fulfill all desires).

Because craving and greed for these six sense objects and various sensual things increase daily, beings do not see the profound points of the Dhamma even in their dreams, and they pass away and die within the prison of sensuality, which is the collection of sensual objects.

## (8) Taṇhāpaccayā Upādānaṃ
With the six cravings as the root, when they increase and persist for a long time, the four types of clinging (upādāna) truly arise. In the internal body and in all sensual objects, there is a deep-rooted and intense attachment. 1. Clinging to the various and endless sensual objects such as sons, wives, and so forth, is kāmupādāna. 2. Furthermore, the sixty-two types of wrong views (diṭṭhi) that are distorted and perverted through false knowledge constitute diṭṭhupādāna. 3. Moreover, the firm belief that cow-vows (go-sīla) can lead to liberation from the round of suffering is sīlabbatupādāna. 4. Firmly grasping and regarding the five aggregates, the collection of phenomena, and the subtle elements as 'self' is attavādupādāna. With such intense and rigid clinging, one remains constantly stuck in the field and ocean of Saṃsāra without any chance of escape—such is the power of the four types of clinging. (Memorize the essence).

It is best if one can abandon the six types of craving mentioned above while they are still weak and new. If they are not abandoned,
721:
but are allowed to increase over many days and years, the four types of clinging (upādāna)—which are intense attachment through craving and intense attachment through wrong view—will clearly arise toward one's own internal (ajjhatta) body as well as all external (bahiddha) sensual objects and sensual things. The four types of clinging are: 1. Kāmupādāna, 2. Diṭṭhupādāna, 3. Sīlabbatupādāna, and 4. Attavādupādāna.

1. Among these four, just as it is said, "A large monitor lizard becomes a crocodile, a large snake becomes a dragon," the previously mentioned six cravings themselves, when they become strong and intense as attachments, are called kāmupādāna. (By this statement, one should understand the distinction: weak craving and greed are called taṇhā, while strong and intense craving and greed, which are difficult to solve or remove, are called upādāna).

2. The collection of intense wrong views, such as the three fixed wrong views (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) and the sixty-two wrong views mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta, is called diṭṭhupādāna. (Since the three fixed wrong views are included among the types of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) within the sixty-two wrong views, the verse states, "the sixty-two types of wrong views"). (The 62 wrong views should be studied in the Sīlakkhandhavagga of the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka).

3. During the time of the Buddha, the clinging to the practices of cattle and the practices of dogs, as held by ascetics like Puṇṇa and Seniya, with the false view that such practices lead to liberation from the suffering of Saṃsāra, is called sīlabbatupādāna. (The story of the ascetics Puṇṇa and Seniya should be noted from the Kukkuravatika Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka).
722:
Ascetics who wrongly believe that one can be liberated from Saṃsāra through the practice of cattle are called Govatika ascetics. Their view is: if one endures the hardships and miseries of a cow throughout this life, the entire collection of old bad kamma from previous lives will be exhausted in this very life because it is forced to give its bad results daily. No new bad kamma is created in this life. If this happens, all old and new bad kamma will be eradicated, and one will attain eternal happiness. One who practices this view walks on all fours like a cow, sleeps like a cow, and if given food, eats like a cow. They adopt the entire system of cattle. If this practice is taken lightly and practiced lightly, one may become a cow after death. If taken rigidly and practiced intensely, one will fall into hell after death.

Ascetics who wrongly believe that one can be liberated from Saṃsāra through the practice of dogs are called Kukkuravatika ascetics. Their view is: to walk, go, live, eat, and sleep exactly like dogs. It is the adoption and practice of the entire system of dogs. This practice also leads to becoming a dog if practiced lightly, and to falling into hell if practiced intensely.

4. The twenty types of personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), which occur through the false perception of 'atta' (soul) or 'I', are called attavādupādāna. Among the five aggregates, four types of personality view occur for each aggregate. Regarding the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha): 1. The wrong view that form is the self (atta/soul/I), where form and self are seen as indistinguishable; 2. Taking mental phenomena as the self and wrongly viewing that the self possesses form, just as a tree has a shadow; 3. Taking mental phenomena as the self and
723:
wrongly viewing that form is in the self, just as fragrance resides in a flower; 4. Taking mental phenomena as the self and wrongly viewing that the self (soul) resides in form, just as a ruby resides in a casket. Thus, there are four types of personality view related to the aggregate of form. Since there are also four types of personality view related to each of the four mental aggregates, there are twenty types of personality view in total. These twenty types of personality view are called attavādupādāna.

When these four types of clinging arise, it is no longer easy to be liberated from the field, the lineage, and the ocean of the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), and one remains firmly and continuously within the round of Saṃsāra.

## (9) Upādānapaccayā Bhavo
Through intense clinging (upādāna), the attachment to 'self' (atta) in the phenomena of the aggregates and the physical body becomes firmly established. For the sake of oneself, one boldly and ruthlessly commits acts such as killing and stealing, resulting in the ten types of unwholesome actions (akusala kamma) and overflowing with faults. On the other hand, with the hope that "I shall be well in the future," and looking far ahead, one follows the ways of the virtuous—hermits and monks—practicing giving, sharing, and observing the five, eight, or ten precepts. One also strives in the ten types of meritorious deeds (puñña-kiriya-vatthu), including the four sublime abidings (brahmavihāra jhānas), the ten kasinas, and various meditations (bhāvanā). Due to the various seeds of these two types of kamma—wholesome and unwholesome—in whatever existence (bhava) one is born, the results continue to multiply—such is the power of the two types of existence (bhava). (Memorize the essence).

The summary of the verse is: because of the intensity of clinging (upādāna) in the continuum of beings, the attachment to self (sakkāyadiṭṭhi = attavādupādāna) in one's own phenomena of the aggregates and physical body...
724:
It becomes firmer and firmer; because it has become so firm, for the sake of one's own temporary happiness in this life, faults of unwholesome kamma-process (akusala-kammabhava), such as the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha) like killing and stealing, arise. Aiming for future happiness just as one is happy in this present body and life, and looking far ahead, one exerts effort in the practices of the virtuous—generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), and meditation (bhāvanā)—which are wholesome deeds leading to mundane existence. Thus, the states of wholesome kamma-process (kusala-kammabhava), namely sense-sphere wholesome kamma, fine-material wholesome kamma, and immaterial wholesome kamma, arise. These two—the unwholesome kamma-process consisting of the ten unwholesome courses of action, and the wholesome kamma-process consisting of mundane wholesome deeds like generosity, virtue, and meditation—are called 'kammabhava' (kamma-process). Due to that kammabhava, resultant mental aggregates (vipāka-nāmakhandha) and kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) arise in the appropriate sensual planes, fine-material planes, or immaterial planes; these resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter are called 'upapattibhava' (rebirth-process). (Mundane wholesome and unwholesome courses of action are called 'bhava' because they cause rebirth-process to occur, and the resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter are called 'bhava' because they arise as the fruit of the kamma-process). This is the summary of the meaning of the verse.

In this regard, I shall further describe in brief the detailed arising of the two types of becoming—kammabhava and upapattibhava—due to the four types of clinging (upādāna), as stated in the Vibhaṅga Commentary named Sammohavinodanī.

If it is asked, "Which clinging can be the cause (paccaya) for which becoming?", the answer should be, "All four types of clinging can be the cause for both types of becoming." To elaborate: a worldling (puthujjana) is like a madman; thus, that worldling,
725:
without being able to judge or discriminate, "This is proper, this is improper," through the power of all four types of clinging, and desiring all three types of rebirth-process (upapattibhava)—sensual, fine-material, and immaterial—performs and exerts in all mundane wholesome and unwholesome kamma-processes (kammabhava) that lead to existence. Regarding the manner of performance:

In this world, some worldlings, either through hearsay or by following what they see, think and consider, "These sensual pleasures and riches are abundant among wealthy royal families in the human world and in the six celestial realms of the sense-sphere." To obtain those sensual pleasures and riches, having encountered bad luck and bad company, and having heard the unjust words of the wicked, they are deceived and misled. Thinking wrongly, "By such acts as killing, one can be fully endowed with sensual pleasures in the human and celestial realms," and prompted by the clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna), they commit misconducts (duccarita) such as killing. Due to the abundance of such misconducts, that worldling reaches and dwells in rebirth in the four woeful states (apāya). (Alternatively) A worldling, either desiring the sensual pleasures seen clearly before them or wishing to secure and prolong the sensual objects they have already obtained (without understanding what is righteous or unrighteous), commits bodily misconduct and so on, prompted by the clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna). Due to the abundance of misconducts, that worldling reaches and dwells in rebirth in the four woeful states. In such a case, the unwholesome kamma of misconduct, which is the cause of that worldling's rebirth in the woeful states, is called 'kammabhava', and the resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter of the woeful states produced by that kamma are called 'upapattibhava'. (This is
726:
the manner in which unwholesome kammabhava and its fruit, upapattibhava, arise due to kāmupādāna).

Another worldling, thinking and considering in the same way as before, but with the support of good kamma, associates with the virtuous and hears the True Dhamma. As their wisdom grows and matures stage by stage, they know correctly, "By these wholesome deeds (sucarita), one can be fully endowed with sensual pleasures in the human and celestial realms," and they perform bodily good conduct and so on. Due to the abundance of wholesome deeds, that worldling reaches and dwells in rebirth in either the celestial realm or the human realm. In such a case, the wholesome kamma of good conduct, which is the cause of that worldling's rebirth in the human or celestial realm, is called 'kammabhava', and the resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter of the human or celestial realm produced by that kamma are called 'upapattibhava'. (This is the manner in which sense-sphere wholesome kammabhava and its fruit, upapattibhava, arise due to kāmupādāna).

Another worldling, either having heard or having reasoned, "In the fine-material Brahma realms and immaterial Brahma realms, sensual pleasures are even more complete and abundant than in this sensual realm," and prompted by the clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna), brings about fine-material wholesome and immaterial wholesome meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti). By the power of those attainments, they reach and dwell in rebirth in the fine-material Brahma realm or the immaterial Brahma realm. In such a case, the fine-material wholesome and immaterial wholesome kamma, which are the causes of that worldling's rebirth in the fine-material or immaterial Brahma realms, are called 'kammabhava', and the resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter of those Brahma realms produced by those kamma are called 'upapattibhava'. (This is the manner in which sublime (mahaggata) wholesome kammabhava and its fruit,
727:
upapattibhava, arise due to kāmupādāna). This is how kammabhava and upapattibhava arise due to kāmupādāna.

Another worldling, based on the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna) in the form of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi), thinking, "This so-called 'atta-soul' can only be properly and completely terminated when it ceases in the sensual happy destination (sugati) realm, or the fine-material Brahma realm, or the immaterial Brahma realm," performs sense-sphere wholesome kamma or sublime wholesome kamma that leads to those realms. Those sense-sphere wholesome and sublime wholesome kamma of that worldling are called 'kammabhava', and the resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter produced by those kamma are called 'upapattibhava'. This is how kammabhava and upapattibhava arise due to diṭṭhupādāna.

Another worldling, prompted by the clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna), thinking, "This so-called 'atta-soul' will certainly find happiness and the cooling of distress in the sensual happy destination realm, or the fine-material Brahma realm, or the immaterial Brahma realm," performs sense-sphere wholesome kamma or sublime wholesome kamma that leads to those realms. Those sense-sphere wholesome and sublime wholesome kamma of that worldling are called 'kammabhava', and the resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter produced by those kamma are called 'upapattibhava'. This is how kammabhava and upapattibhava arise due to attavādupādāna.

Another worldling, prompted by the clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna), thinking, "This practice or observance (sīlabbata) can only be easily and fully accomplished in the continuum of one who fulfills it in the sensual happy destination realm, or the fine-material Brahma realm, or the immaterial Brahma realm," performs sense-sphere wholesome kamma or sublime wholesome kamma that leads to those realms. Those sense-sphere wholesome and sublime wholesome
728:
kamma are called 'kammabhava', and the resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter produced by those kamma are called 'upapattibhava'. This is how kammabhava and upapattibhava arise due to sīlabbatupādāna.

## (10) Bhava paccayā jāti

Due to the power of becoming (bhava) and the two types of kamma, for all beings (sabba-sattā), when the current life ends, in the place where kamma casts them, whether it be one, four, or five aggregates, birth (jāti) occurs repeatedly and in various ways according to the natural law (dhammatā). Entangled in rebirth throughout the three realms, beings arise in various forms, high or low in power and glory, bad or good in conduct, as diverse beings with various bodies. This is the power of the fourfold birth. (Memorize this verse).

In this point, "Bhava paccayā jāti" (Birth dependent on Becoming), for the term 'bhava', only the causal wholesome kammabhava and unwholesome kammabhava should be taken. For 'jāti', one should take the arising (uppāda) of the wholesome resultant mental aggregates, unwholesome resultant mental aggregates, and kamma-born matter produced by those wholesome and unwholesome kammabhava. To make it clearer: under the previous "Saṅkhāra paccayā viññāṇaṃ" (Consciousness dependent on Volitional Formations), it was said that resultant consciousness arises due to wholesome and unwholesome formations—this refers to the arising of resultant consciousness at the moment of rebirth and during the course of life in this present existence due to the wholesome and unwholesome formations of a past life. Under this present "Bhava paccayā jāti", it refers to the manifest arising of birth (jāti), which is the arising (uppāda) of resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter in a future period due to the wholesome and unwholesome kammabhava of this present life. (This will be clarified later).
729:
In the point below, "Saṅkhāra paccayā viññāṇaṃ", the manner in which resultant consciousness arises according to the four types of endowments (samangitā) due to wholesome and unwholesome formations was described on page 700. In that context, just as resultant consciousness arises at the moment of rebirth and during the course of life in this present existence due to the wholesome and unwholesome formations of a past life, similarly, due to the wholesome and unwholesome kammabhava performed and exerted in this present life, resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter will arise in a future life according to the four types of endowments. This very point is taught as "Bhava paccayā jāti = Due to kammabhava, the states of upapattibhava arise and become manifest." (This is the language of the Paramatthakathā = the pure nature of Abhidhamma).

Meaning of the verse: In the verse, for the sake of easy understanding by the general public, it is composed by mixing ultimate reality (paramattha) and conventional concepts (paññatti). The meaning is:

Due to the power and potential of the two types of kamma, namely wholesome kammabhava and unwholesome kammabhava, when all beings end their current present life, birth (jāti)—which is the arising (uppāda) of resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter at the moment of rebirth and during the course of life according to the natural law of kamma (kamma-niyāma)—appears in the appropriate realms where those two types of kamma cast their results: the Asaññasatta realm which has only one aggregate of matter, the four Immaterial realms which have only four mental aggregates, and the Sensual realms and Fine-material Brahma realms (excluding Asaññasatta) which have the full five aggregates.

From here onwards, to be concise, where "resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter" should be written, I will only write "upapattibhava". In the states of resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter called upapattibhava, there is the moment of arising (uppāda-khaṇa), the moment of presence (ṭhī-khaṇa),
730:
Bhaṅga-khaṇa = the moment of dissolution. There are three sub-moments in a brief duration: the moment of arising (uppāda-khaṇa) is called birth (jāti), the moment of presence (ṭhiti-khaṇa) is called aging (jarā), and the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khaṇa) is called death (maraṇa). Kamma-bhava (kamma-process) acts as a condition for the arising of the uppāda-khaṇa of upapatti-bhava (rebirth-process), which is jāti. This occurrence of jāti, the moment of arising in upapatti-bhava due to kamma-bhava, is described in the verse as: "Ever-occurring jāti, clinging to rebirth."

This jāti, the moment of arising in upapatti-bhava, does not occur only once in a lifetime; it occurs repeatedly, causing the body to grow and develop into a distinct form. Depending on their respective kamma-bhava, beings are born into various forms and classes, such as the warrior caste (khattiya), the brahmin caste (brāhmaṇa), etc.; beings of great power or small power; beings of low status or high status; beings of bad conduct or good conduct. This diversity is due to the power of the four types of birth (jāti): aṇḍaja-jāti (egg-born), jalābuja-jāti (womb-born), saṃsedaja-jāti (moisture-born, such as in moss or lotuses), and opapātika-jāti (spontaneous birth, where one appears fully formed, like a sixteen-year-old girl or a twenty-to-twenty-five-year-old man at the very moment of rebirth).

(In this regard: Even siblings born from the same womb—brothers and sisters—differ from one another in terms of being inferior or superior because the root cause, kamma-bhava, shapes them. Therefore,
731:
The Blessed One taught (in the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pāḷi, Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta, page 244): "Kammaṃ satte vibhajati yadidaṃ hīnapaṇītatāya = Kamma divides beings into the inferior and the superior." This distinction should also be noted.)

## (11) Jātipaccayā Jarāmaraṇaṃ

When rebirth-jāti clings again, and beings of the three realms in various forms—human and celestial—arise prominently in different places, there are, according to the tradition of the three stages of life (beginning, middle, and end), successive phases. From the start of rebirth, following the sequence of hours, there is a continuous and relentless process of maturing and decaying, day and night. The two fires of aging—momentary aging (khaṇa-jarā) and serial aging (santati-jarā)—burn intensely. Beings of all ages, young and old, move incessantly through various stages. Any of the four types of death, accompanied by many dangers and interconnected causes, strikes as one. Regardless of being great or small, young or old, when the time of death arrives, the dissolution of the aggregates (khandha) is inevitable. Such is the power of aging and death (jarā-maraṇa). (Memorize this meaning).

Kamma-bhava conditions the manifest arising (uppāda) of upapatti-bhava. This manifest arising of upapatti-bhava is called jāti. Once jāti, the moment of arising, appears, then jarā (the moment of presence/ṭhiti-khaṇa) and maraṇa (the moment of dissolution/bhaṅga-khaṇa) follow in sequence. (Kamma-bhava conditions upapatti-bhava in its moment of arising; it does not condition presence or dissolution directly. However, as soon as the phenomenon of jāti/arising appears, jarā/presence and maraṇa/dissolution follow immediately, just as
732:
they follow closely behind, like water following a boat). It is only when there is jāti that jarā and maraṇa can occur; if there is no jāti, jarā and maraṇa cannot occur. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ = With birth as condition, aging and death come to be."

(Reflecting on the aforementioned statements, one should specifically note: Jāti refers to the moment of arising (uppāda-khaṇa) of the aggregates that occur throughout various lives. Jarā refers to the moment of presence or decaying (ṭhiti-khaṇa) of those aggregates. Maraṇa refers to the moment of destruction or cessation (bhaṅga-khaṇa) of those aggregates. This is the discourse on ultimate reality (paramattha-kathā)).

Meaning of the Verse: When rebirth is established in a new life, the phenomenon of jāti occurs repeatedly and successively, causing the continuity of aggregates to grow, appearing as humans or devas in distinct forms. When this happens, for the duration of one lifetime (such as the current hundred-year lifespan), there are the three stages of life: the first stage (the first 33 years and 4 months), the middle stage (the middle 33 years and 4 months), and the last stage (the final 33 years and 4 months). According to this tradition, as the phenomenon of jāti—the moment of arising of the aggregates in those lives—occurs repeatedly every hour and every moment, the phenomenon of jarā—the maturing or presence (ṭhiti-khaṇa)—follows closely and incessantly, day and night. This maturing or jarā is called the "fire of aging."

This fire of aging is of two types: (1) Khaṇa-jarā = the maturing or aging during the moment of presence (ṭhiti-khaṇa) of the aggregates in various lives; (2) Santati-jarā = the maturing or aging through the continuity (santati) of physical processes, such as the sequence of cold-born matter or heat-born matter, from one moment to the next.
733:
These are the two types. This is what is meant in the verse: "Khaṇa, santati, the fire of aging, two fires burning intensely."

(In this context, a question may arise: "Since both khaṇa-jarā and santati-jarā exist and are manifest in both the young and the old, why is it that the characteristics of aging—such as grey hair, loss of teeth, and wrinkled skin—do not appear clearly in the young, but only in the old?"

The answer is: The characteristics of aging, such as grey hair, loss of teeth, and wrinkled skin, become clearly manifest only in the old because they have suffered the repeated blows of aging. To elaborate: starting from the moment of the initial embryonic stage (kalala), as beings reach the moment of presence (ṭhiti-khaṇa) or aging of preceding physical states, the succeeding physical states that arise anew do so in accordance with the nature of those preceding decayed states. They arise as matured, then more matured, and then even more matured. Therefore, at the moment of presence (ṭhiti-khaṇa), which is the time of extreme maturation of physical states—day by day, month by month, year by year, and stage by stage—the newly arising physical states manifest clearly with the characteristics of aging, such as grey hair, loss of teeth, and wrinkled skin. Thus, these signs are prominent only in the elderly.

These signs—grey hair, loss of teeth, and wrinkled skin—are objects of eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññeyya) that can be seen with the eyes; they are not the actual jarā itself. They are merely the marks or blows of jarā. The actual jarā is an object of mind-consciousness (mano-viññeyya) that can only be known through mental reflection.)
734:
To make it clearer: On a path eroded by a violent flood or a path where a great fire has raged, one sees the broken trees and plants or the remaining charcoal and ashes caused by the water or fire. The eroding water and the burning fire themselves are known only through mental reflection. Similarly, in the extremely matured physical states—the path where the violent water of jarā and the great fire of jarā have eroded and burned—the visible signs such as grey hair (or white hairs), loss of teeth (or broken teeth), and wrinkled skin (or wrinkled flesh) should be understood only as the marks or blows of the erosion and burning caused by the water and fire of jarā. By seeing these marks, the violent water and great fire of jarā are known through mental inference. (These words are very profound; one can only understand the deep meaning by reading and reflecting on them repeatedly. Please strive to read and contemplate them.)

Due to the incessant and intense burning of the aforementioned fires of khaṇa-jarā and santati-jarā, different stages of life occur, such as the young age, middle age, old age, the age of ten, twenty, thirty, and so on. Jarā drives beings toward these stages.

Immediately after the moment of presence called jarā, the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khaṇa) is reached. Every being is dying at every moment through momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa). (Since they have not yet reached conventional death (sammuti-maraṇa), they do not realize they are dying.)

To make it clearer: Death (maraṇa), the cessation and destruction, is of three types: (1) khaṇika-maraṇa, (2) samuccheda-maraṇa, and (3) sammuti-maraṇa.
735:
Among these three: (1) The cessation and destruction of mental and physical phenomena (nāma-rūpa dhamma saṅkhāra) upon reaching their own moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khaṇa) is called khaṇika-maraṇa (momentary death). Each group or unit of consciousness and mental factors (citta-cetasika) has a lifespan of three sub-moments: the moment of arising (uppāda-khaṇa), the moment of presence (ṭhiti-khaṇa), and the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khaṇa). This duration of three sub-moments is called one great mind-moment (cittakkhana). Within the brief duration of a finger snap or a flash of lightning, over a hundred thousand crores (one hundred trillion) of such mind-moments arise and cease. (Except for the four characteristics of matter (lakkhaṇa-rūpa) and the two types of intimation (viññatti-rūpa)), the remaining 22 types of matter have a lifespan of about 17 mind-moments. The two types of intimation matter are phenomena that follow the mind (cittānuparivatti-dhamma); they arise when the mind arises and cease when the mind ceases. Among the four characteristics of matter, the matter of arising (jāti-rūpa), namely upacaya and santati, constitutes the arising phase (uppāda-khaṇa) of matter and lasts for about one sub-moment. The matter of aging (jaratā-rūpa) constitutes the presence phase (ṭhiti-khaṇa) of matter and lasts for about 49 sub-moments. The matter of impermanence (aniccatā-rūpa) constitutes the dissolution phase (bhaṅga-khaṇa) of matter and lasts for about one sub-moment. (As stated in the Paramattha-saṅkhapa: "In a flash of lightning, the number of mind-moments is a hundred thousand crores.") Thus, every single being is dying through khaṇika-maraṇa more than a hundred thousand crore times within the duration of a finger snap or a flash of lightning.

(2) Samuccheda-maraṇa refers to the type of death that completely and utterly cuts off the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha) for Arahants. Indeed, for Arahants, after the decease-consciousness of final passing away (parinibbāna-cuti), new mind and matter and new lives no longer arise. Like a great flame that has been extinguished, the great suffering of the round of rebirths is completely uprooted. Therefore,
736:
The passing away or death of these Arahants is called Samuccheda-maraṇa, which means death that completely eradicates the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra).

(3) Sammuti-maraṇa refers to the cessation of the continuity of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) within a single existence for all beings other than the Buddha and Arahants. (Furthermore, the term 'death' used in conventional worldly language for inanimate objects, such as 'the tree is dead,' 'the iron is dead,' or 'the mercury is dead,' is also called sammuti-maraṇa. However, such types of death are not intended or referred to in this current chapter on death. In this chapter, sammuti-maraṇa specifically refers to the cessation or stopping of the continuity of the life-faculty for the duration of one lifetime of living beings).

This sammuti-maraṇa is of four types: (1) Āyukkhaya-maraṇa = death due to the exhaustion of the life-span, even though the kammic force for longevity still remains; (2) Kammakkhaya-maraṇa = death due to the exhaustion of the kammic force, even though the life-span still remains; (3) Ubhayakkhaya-maraṇa = death due to the exhaustion of both the life-span and the kammic force; and (4) Upacchedaka-maraṇa = death caused by the intervention of a destructive unwholesome kamma (upacchedaka-akusala-kamma) that cuts off life even though both the life-span and kammic force still remain. (As stated in the Paramattha-saṅkhitta: 'Death occurs through the end of life-span, the end of kamma, the end of both, or by the cutting off of bad kamma; these are the four types of death').

Among these four types of death, any one of them associates with many dangers that threaten life and, regardless of whether a being is great or small, young or old, when the time arrives, it oppresses them so that the aggregates of that existence fall away and they pass away. Among these four types of death associated with many dangers—
737:
—when any one of them oppresses, all beings, whether great or small, must inevitably pass away as their aggregates fall apart. With reference to this meaning, it is composed in the verse: 'Any one of the four types of death... (etc.)... is the power of aging and death (jarā-maraṇa).'

(Special Note: These three phenomena—birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa)—are like enemy assassins who wander about seeking an opportunity to oppress these beings.

To make it clearer: Suppose there is a man who has three enemies wandering about seeking an opportunity to oppress and kill him. Among those three, the first enemy says, 'Friends, I will speak of the benefits of such-and-such a forest and lead that man there; it will not be difficult for me to lead him there' (1). Then the second enemy says, 'Friend, once you have led that man to the forest, I will strike and beat him to make him weak; it will not be difficult for me to make him weak' (2). Then the third enemy says, 'Friend, once that man has been beaten and made weak, let it be my responsibility to cut off his head with a very sharp sword' (3). These three enemies, having spoken thus, act according to their plan.

In this analogy, the first enemy's act of speaking about the forest's benefits and leading the man there is like the function of birth (jāti), which pulls a being away from their beloved circle of relatives in this present life and causes them to arise in one of the five destinations (gati). The second enemy's act of beating the man to make him weak is like the function of aging (jarā), which causes the strength and vigor of the aggregates in whichever of the five destinations they have arisen to decline and diminish, leading to a state of frailty where one must depend on others and is confined to a bed of sickness.
738:
The act of making one reach such a state is the function of Jarā (old age). Like the cutting of a man's head with the sharp sword of a third enemy, the act of causing the cessation and termination of the life-continuity (jīvita-santāna) for one existence is the function of Maraṇa (death).

Alternatively, the suffering of Jāti (birth) should be understood as entering a very dangerous desert journey. The suffering of Jarā (old age) should be understood as the weakness of a man who lacks food and drink within that desert. The suffering of Maraṇa (death) should be understood as that weak man being unable to move, being oppressed by lions, leopards, and tigers, and perishing in ruin. This is a special note.

## (12) Soka, Parideva, Dukkha, Domanassupāyāsā
## Sambhavanti

If there is the Jāti of rebirth and the existence of aggregates, when one encounters and cannot avoid separation from relatives (ñāti), wealth (bhoga), etc., there arises the heat of soka (sorrow), the crying of parideva (lamentation), the burden of maintaining life, the suffering (dukkha) of heat and cold, and due to undesirable things, the mind becomes unclear, sobbing and gasping in distress. These five sufferings in brief, and infinite in detail, are encountered; this is the rate of the original Jāti. (Memorize the essence).

Meaning of the verse: Just as Jarā and Maraṇa exist if there is Jāti, if there are the aggregates of the four types of rebirth called Jāti, one will naturally encounter the five types of Byasana (misfortune/loss) according to the nature of existence (as per the verse: Ñā, Bho, Rogā, Sīlā, Diṭṭhi—these five exist, know them as Byasana): (1) Ñāti-byasana = ruin of relatives, (2) Bhoga-byasana = ruin of wealth, (3) Roga-byasana = oppression by diseases, (4) Sīla-byasana = ruin of morality, (5) Diṭṭhi-byasana = perversion of view. When encountering these,
739:
one may encounter the Dhamma of Soka, which is the burning of the heart with anxiety; the Dhamma of Parideva, which is crying and lamenting aloud; the Dhamma of Dukkha, which is bodily suffering; the Dhamma of Domanassa, which is mental suffering; and the Dhamma of Upāyāsa, which is intense burning of the heart. In brief, these five sufferings, and in detail, infinite and numerous miseries are encountered. The meaning is that the root cause of these occurrences is indeed the Dhamma of Jāti.

## (13) Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa
## Samudayo hoti

In the long round of Saṃsāra, all that occurs starting from 'you' and 'I' is not a 'being'; if the true elements are extracted, let the vision be clear that there are only the two groups of Mind and Matter. Branching out from the root of Avijjā and ending with Jarā and Maraṇa, these twelve factors of Dhamma are mistakenly thought of as 'this is a human' or 'this is a deva', and thus the round of rebirth continues to flourish. In all that is long and infinite, there is not even a speck of what is called happiness; it is purely suffering (dukkha) in succession. This is the true nature of how this body arises. (Memorize the essence).

(Since the meaning is already clear from the verse itself, the prose explanation for this verse is not written).

This is the Law of Paṭiccasamuppāda.
