## The Four Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa

As soon as the Blessed One attained Buddhahood, He also attained the Four Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa (Analytical Knowledges). These Four Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa, mentioned in the section on attaining Buddhahood below, are: (1) Attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa, (2) Dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa,
740:
(3) Nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa, and (4) Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa.

## (1) Attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa

Various distinctions and diverse types are called paṭisambhidā. The knowledge that sees and understands these various distinctions thoroughly and completely is called paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa. The knowledge that analytically understands various meanings and various results thoroughly and completely is called Attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa. In this Attha-paṭisambhidā, the term 'attha' (meaning/result) comprises five types: (a) the collection of all results produced by causes, (b) Nibbāna, (c) the meaning of the Pali texts, (d) the collection of resultant (vipāka) consciousness and mental factors, and (e) the collection of functional (kiriya) consciousness and mental factors.

As soon as the Buddha attained Enlightenment, He attained the knowledge (Attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) that analytically understands these five types of 'attha' thoroughly and completely. By the power of this Attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa, He Himself understands the various meanings and various results of each and every Dhamma in diverse ways, and He is able to teach them so that others can also understand them easily. Here, the wisdom associated with the four types of great functional consciousness (mahā-kiriya) associated with knowledge that takes these five 'attha' as objects, and the four Path-knowledges (magga-ñāṇa) and four Fruition-knowledges (phala-ñāṇa) that take Nibbāna as an object, are called the Buddha's Attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa. This refers to the Attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa of the Buddha. (For the Sekha Ariyas who have attained Analytical Insight, such as the Venerable Ānanda, the term Attha-paṭisambhidā refers to the wisdom associated with the four types of great wholesome consciousness (mahā-kusala) associated with knowledge that takes the five 'attha' as objects,
741:
and the lower Path-knowledges and lower Fruition-knowledges that take Nibbāna as an object).

## (2) Dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa

The knowledge that analytically understands various distinct teachings and various causes thoroughly and completely is called Dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa. In this Dhamma-paṭisambhidā, the term 'dhamma' (teaching/cause) comprises five types: (a) the collection of causes that produce results, (b) the four Noble Paths (ariya-magga), (c) the sequence of the Pali texts, (d) wholesome (kusala) consciousness and mental factors, and (e) unwholesome (akusala) consciousness and mental factors.

As soon as the Buddha attained Enlightenment, He attained the knowledge (Dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) that analytically understands these five types of 'dhamma' thoroughly and completely. By the power of this Dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa, He Himself understands the various aforementioned dhammas in diverse ways and is able to teach them so that others can also understand them easily. Here, for the Buddha's Dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa, one should take the great functional (mahā-kiriya) knowledge that takes the five 'dhamma' as objects; for the Sekha Ariyas who have attained Analytical Insight, such as the Venerable Ānanda, one should take the great wholesome (mahā-kusala) knowledge that takes the five 'dhamma' as objects. (The same method applies to the latter two knowledges).

## (3) Nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa

The knowledge that analytically understands the various sounds and words of the Māgadha language, the language of the Ariyas known as natural expression (sabhāva-nirutti), which is the means for expressing the aforementioned five types of 'attha' and five types of 'dhamma' naturally, is called Nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa. As soon as the Buddha attained Enlightenment, He understood the various sounds of the Māgadha language, the natural expression of the Ariyas—
742:
He had also already attained the Analytical Knowledge of Language (Nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa). Because He possessed this Analytical Knowledge of Language, He Himself understood the various grammatical forms of the natural language, the noble usage of the Magadhi tongue, and was able to teach others so that they could understand easily.

Indeed, among the five types of Attha (meaning/result) and the five types of Dhamma (cause/condition), there are various grammatical forms of the natural language, the noble usage of the Magadhi tongue, which naturally express each specific aspect. (For example) because He clearly and thoroughly understood the various grammatical forms of the natural language, the noble usage of the Magadhi tongue, regarding the single phenomenon of contact (phassa), He taught that single phenomenon of contact with a full range of natural linguistic terms such as "phassa, phusanā, samphusanā, samphusitattaṃ". He even taught the single phenomenon of craving and greed (taṇhā-lobha) using more than a hundred terms (refer to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pāḷi).

## (4) Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa

The knowledge that clearly and thoroughly understands the functions of the preceding Analytical Knowledge of Meaning (Attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), Analytical Knowledge of Dhamma (Dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), and Analytical Knowledge of Language (Nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), such as: "Attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa performs the task of clearly and thoroughly understanding the five types of Attha; Dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa performs the task of clearly and thoroughly understanding the five types of Dhamma; Nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa performs the task of clearly and thoroughly understanding the various grammatical forms of natural language," is called the Analytical Knowledge of Perspicacity (Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa). The Blessed One had already attained this Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa at the very moment He attained Buddhahood. (Regarding these three—Nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa...
743:
...and 4. Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa, it should be understood following the previous method that they arise as Mahā-kiriya and Mahā-kusala knowledges).

(Special Note: Among these four Analytical Knowledges, the fourth, Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa, although it knows the functions of the preceding three knowledges, it cannot itself perform the functions of those knowledges. This is like a learned (bahussuta) monk with a poor voice who cannot perform the task of a monk who is a preacher of Dhamma (dhammakathika) with a good voice but little learning (appassuta).

Suppose there are two monks: a bahussuta monk with a poor voice but great wisdom, and an appassuta monk with a good voice but little wisdom. After they have taught and preached the Dhamma together, the appassuta monk with the good voice, wherever he goes, preaches the Dhamma by stirring the entire audience with the quality of his beautiful voice. The audience, being very satisfied and joyful, speaks words of praise, saying, "Judging by the way this monk preaches the Dhamma now, he must be a Tipiṭakadhara (bearer of the Three Baskets)." Hearing this, the bahussuta monk with the poor voice becomes envious and says, "Listen to his preaching again next time, then you lay devotees will know whether this person is a Tipiṭakadhara or not." (By saying they would know next time, he meant: "Because he is an appassuta person, if he preaches again, he will preach the same thing; that venerable has nothing else to preach.") Although that bahussuta monk with the poor voice spoke thus out of envy, he himself was by no means capable of preaching the Dhamma in a way that would stir the entire audience.

Similarly, among the four Analytical Knowledges, Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa knows the functions of the preceding three knowledges, but it cannot itself perform the functions of those knowledges. This should be noted as a special point; this matter is explained on page 376 of the Vibhaṅga Commentary).

The section on the four Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) is finished.
744:
## Six Uncommon Knowledges (Asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa)

The six knowledges that are attainable only by the Blessed Buddhas and are not shared with Paccekabuddhas or Noble Disciples (Ariya-sāvaka) are called the "Six Uncommon Knowledges." These six are: (1) Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa, (2) Āsayānusaya-ñāṇa, (3) Yamaka-pāṭihīra-ñāṇa, (4) Mahākaruṇāsamāpatti-ñāṇa, (5) Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa, and (6) Anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa.

(1) Among these six, the knowledge that knows the maturity or immaturity of the faculties of beings is called Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa. With this knowledge, the Blessed One clearly perceives: "These beings have mature faculties; these beings have immature faculties. These beings are ready for liberation; these beings are not yet ready for liberation." (In this context, 'faculties' refers to these five qualities: faith (saddhā), energy (viriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā)).

(2) Āsayānusaya-ñāṇa is the knowledge that knows the inclinations (āsaya) and latent tendencies (anusaya) of beings. (The meaning of this Āsayānusaya-ñāṇa should be referred to and noted again in the section on the attribute 'Lokavidū' among the nine attributes of the Buddha on pages 597 and 598). The two Pāḷi terms 'Āsayānusaya' are called in Burmese "the inclination and the internal seed-element of beings." With this Āsayānusaya-ñāṇa, the Blessed One clearly perceives the inclinations and internal seed-elements of beings, knowing: "In such and such beings, such and such an inclination (āsaya) is strong, and such and such a latent defilement seed-element (anusaya) is predominant."
745:
Because the Blessed One is a master of these two knowledges—Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa and Āsayānusaya-ñāṇa—He can preach the Dhamma according to the temperaments of beings and easily lead them to liberation. Because he was not fully endowed with these two knowledges, even the great Elder Sāriputta could not know the maturity or immaturity of the faculties and the nature of the internal latent tendencies of beings. Therefore, at times, he would fail to preach the Dhamma suitable for certain beings; the Dhamma he presented would not match the disposition of the being, and thus he would be unable to preach in a way that led them to attain the higher Dhamma.

(3) The knowledge that can perform the Twin Miracle of water and fire is called Yamaka-pāṭihīra-ñāṇa. Using this Yamaka-pāṭihīra-ñāṇa, the Blessed One displayed the Twin Miracle of water and fire on four occasions: (a) once at the terrace of the Great Bodhi tree (Mahābodhi-maṇḍa) to dispel the doubts and pride of devas and brahmās; (b) once during His first visit to the city of Kapilavatthu to humble the pride of His Sakyan relatives; (c) once near the mango tree planted by the gardener Kaṇḍa at Sāvatthī, which grew, blossomed, and bore fruit all in one day, to humble the pride of the heretics; and (d) once at a gathering concerning Pāthikaputta. (The adoration of this Yamaka-pāṭihīra has already been written in the third volume of this Great Chronicle of Buddhas on pages 530, 531, 532, 533, and 534).

(4) Mahākaruṇāsamāpatti-ñāṇa: This means that the Blessed One, seeing the distressed beings who are overwhelmed and drifting in the great ocean of Saṃsāra with massive waves such as birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa), enters the Attainment of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) associated with great pity, thinking, "This world...
746:
...is burning brightly like a great prison on fire." The knowledge associated with that attainment is called Mahākaruṇāsamāpatti-ñāṇa. Every day, during the night and at dawn, the Blessed One enters these Attainments of Great Compassion two trillion four hundred billion (2,400,000,000,000) times.

(5) Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa is the noble knowledge that completely perceives all knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma) in their entirety. Because He possesses this Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa, the Blessed One is called the "Sabbaññū Buddha" (Omniscient Buddha). This Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa is also called Samantacakkhu (the All-Seeing Eye). The manner in which this Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa perceives all phenomena should be studied as extracted from the Burmese translation of the Paṭisambhidāmagga Piṭaka.

(6) Anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa: This is the same Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa, but it is called Anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa (Unobstructed Knowledge) according to the definition "Natthi āvaraṇaṃ etassāti anāvaraṇaṃ," because no phenomenon and no person can hinder or block it from perceiving. This is just as faith (saddhā), energy (viriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) are called 'faculties' (indriya) because they exercise control in their respective functions, and are called 'powers' (bala) because they can overwhelm and suppress the five opposing states: lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and delusion.

These are the Six Uncommon Knowledges.
747:
## Ten Powers (Dasabala-ñāṇa)

The Ten Powers are:
(1) Ṭhānāṭhāna-kosalla-ñāṇa: The knowledge that perceives according to reality what is possible and what is impossible.
(2) Vipāka-ñāṇa: The knowledge that perceives according to reality the results (vipāka) of actions (kamma) performed and undertaken in the three periods of time, along with their productive (janaka) and supportive (upatthambhaka) causes.
(3) Sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadā-ñāṇa: The knowledge that perceives according to reality the various practices leading to all realms of existence and the practice leading to Nibbāna.
(4) Anekadhātunānādhātu-ñāṇa: The knowledge that perceives according to reality the various natures of the aggregates (khandha), the various natures of the sense-bases (āyatana), and the various natures of the elements (dhātu) related to animate conditioned things (upādinnaka-saṅkhāra), as well as the various distinctions in the world of inanimate conditioned things (anupādinnaka-saṅkhāra).

(The Paccekabuddhas and the two Chief Disciples know only a portion of the distinctions in the world of animate (upādinnaka) conditioned things; they do not know the distinctions in the world of inanimate (anupādinnaka) conditioned things.

The Blessed One, however, knows: "Because such and such an element is predominant, the trunk of such and such a tree is white in color. The trunk of such and such a tree is black. The trunk of such and such a tree is smooth. The trunk of such and such a tree has thick bark. The trunk of such and such a tree has thin bark. Because such and such an element is predominant, the leaf of this tree has such a nature in terms of color and shape." Because such and such an element is predominant...
748:
Because of the predominance of such and such elements, the flowers of this particular tree are blue, yellow, red, white, fragrant, or foul-smelling. Because of the predominance of such and such elements, the fruits of this particular tree are small, large, long, short, round, well-shaped, ill-shaped, smooth, rough, fragrant, foul-smelling, sweet, bitter, sour, pungent, or astringent. Because of the predominance of such and such elements, the thorns of this tree are sharp, blunt, straight, curved, red, black, blue, or white.” In this manner, He distinguishes and understands the diverse nature of the inanimate world of non-clung-to formations (*anupādinnaka-saṅkhāra*). Indeed, the power of this *Anekadhātu-nānādhātu-ñāṇa* (Knowledge of Diverse Elements) belongs only to the Buddhas. It is not the knowledge of Paccekabuddhas or Noble Disciples. This distinction should be noted. (Abhi-A. 2, p. 438).

(5) *Nānādhimuttika-ñāṇa* = The knowledge that truly perceives the various inclinations, desires, and dispositions of beings.

(6) *Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa* = The knowledge that truly perceives the maturity or immaturity of the faculties of beings.

(7) *Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpatti-ñāṇa* = The knowledge that truly perceives the factors of defilement and decline, the factors of purification and progress, and the factors of emergence regarding the *jhānas*, deliverances (*vimokkha*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*).

(8) *Pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa* = The knowledge that truly perceives the sequence of past aggregates, lives, and existences.

(9) *Cutūpapāta-ñāṇa* (or) *Dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa* = The knowledge that truly perceives the passing away and rebirth of beings.
749:
(10) *Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa* = The Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship (*Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa*) which is the end of the taints (*āsavas*). These are the Ten Powers of Knowledge (*Dasabala-ñāṇa*).

## How the Ten Powers of Knowledge are Utilized
The Blessed One first uses the *Ṭhānāṭhāna-ñāṇa* (Knowledge of Possibility and Impossibility) to contemplate whether the beings to be guided (*veneyya*) possess the obstacles of defilement, such as fixed wrong view (*niyata-micchādiṭṭhi*), which would prevent them from attaining the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints (*Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*), i.e., the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship.

Next, with the *Kamma-vipāka-ñāṇa* (Knowledge of Kamma and Result), He contemplates whether those beings possess obstacles of result (*vipākantarāya*), such as being born with a rootless (*ahetu*) or double-rooted (*dvihetu*) rebirth-linking, which would hinder the attainment of *jhāna*, Path, and Fruit.

Next, with the *Sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadā-ñāṇa* (Knowledge of the Way Leading Everywhere), He contemplates whether those beings possess obstacles of action (*kammantarāya*), known as the five great heinous crimes (*pañcānantariya-kamma*).

After contemplating with these first three knowledges whether the beings to be guided possess the three great obstacles—obstacles of action, obstacles of defilement, and obstacles of result—which block *jhāna*, Path, and Fruit, He then uses the *Anekadhātu-nānādhātu-ñāṇa* to contemplate the diverse temperaments of those beings who are free from these three obstacles, in order to preach the Dhamma suitable to their nature.

Then, without regarding whether the beings' efforts and actions are pure or impure, but according to their inclinations and dispositions—

* The five great heinous crimes (*pañcānantariya-kamma*) are: (1) Matricide = *mātughātaka-kamma*, (2) Patricide = *pitughātaka-kamma*, (3) Killing an Arahant = *arahantaghātaka-kamma*, (4) Drawing the blood of a Buddha = *lohituppādaka-kamma*, (5) Causing a schism in the Saṅgha = *saṅghabheda-kamma*. These five will definitely result in rebirth in the lower realms in the very next life.
750:
—He contemplates the inclinations and dispositions of those beings with the *Nānādhimuttikatā-ñāṇa* (Knowledge of Diverse Dispositions) for the purpose of preaching the Dhamma. After clearly perceiving their inclinations and dispositions, He contemplates the maturity or immaturity of their faculties, such as faith (*saddhā*), with the *Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa* (Knowledge of the Maturity of Faculties) to preach according to their capacity.

Having contemplated thus and seeing that those beings possess the maturity of faculties sufficient to attain *jhāna*, Path, and Fruit, if those beings to be liberated are in a distant place, He quickly travels to them through special psychic power, as He has reached the pinnacle and mastery of *jhānas* and related states through the *Jhānādi-saṅkilesa-vodāna-vuṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*.

Upon arrival, He contemplates their past lives with the *Pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*, and their current state of mind with the *Cetopariya-ñāṇa* (Knowledge of Others' Minds) attained through the power of *Dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa*. Being free from confusion regarding the practice leading to the Path of Arahantship through the power of *Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*, He preaches the Dhamma to those beings so that they may attain the Path of Arahantship. Therefore, these Ten Powers of Knowledge are taught in this sequence. (From A.A. 3, p. 298).

These are the Ten Powers of Knowledge (*Dasabala-ñāṇa*).

## Cuddasa-buddha-ñāṇa = The 14 Buddha-knowledges
The 14 Buddha-knowledges are: the 4 Truth-knowledges (*Sacca-ñāṇa*), the 4 Analytical-knowledges (*Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*), and the 6 Uncommon-knowledges (*Asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa*). Among these 14, the 4 Truth-knowledges and the 4 Analytical-knowledges are shared with the disciples (*sāvakas*).
751:
The disciples also attain them; however, the 6 Uncommon-knowledges (*Asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa*) belong only to the Buddhas and are not shared with the disciples.

Just as the 6 Uncommon-knowledges are the unique knowledges of the Buddhas, there are also the 18 Uncommon Qualities (*Āveṇika-guṇa*) which are the exclusive property of the Buddhas. I shall now present the devotional verses of these 18 Uncommon Qualities as composed and arranged by the Venerable Ledi Sayadaw—

## The Pali and Meaning of the Āveṇika Qualities
*Jeyyatu. Buddhānaṃ jīvitassa na sakkā kenaci antarāyo kātuṃ. Buddhānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇassa na sakkā kenaci antarāyo kātuṃ.*

*Atītāṃse buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ. Anāgatāṃse buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ. Paccuppannāṃse buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ. (3)*

*Imehi tīhi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivattaṃ, sabbaṃ vacīkammaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivattaṃ, sabbaṃ manokammaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivattaṃ. (3)*

*Imehi chahi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato natthi chandassa hāni, natthi dhammadesanāya hāni, natthi vīriyassa hāni, natthi samādhissa hāni, natthi paññāya hāni, natthi vimuttiyā hāni. (6)*

*Imehi dvādasahi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato natthi davā, natthi ravā, natthi apphuṭaṃ,*
752:
*natthi vegāyitattaṃ, natthi abyāvaṭamano, natthi appaṭisaṅkhānupekkhā. (6)*

*Imehi aṭṭhārasahi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato na sakkā kenaci antarāyo kātuṃ.*

(The meaning is as follows):
*Jeyyatu* = May there be victory by repelling and overcoming the two kinds of dangers: internal and external, within and without.

*Buddhānaṃ* = Of the Omniscient Buddhas. *Jīvitassa* = Of the life, which is firmly established to last for the full duration of the life-span allotted for their appearance. *Antarāyo* = An obstacle that would intervene and destroy it before the full completion of that span. *Kenaci* = By anyone at all, such as Devadatta, Māra the celestial commander, the ogre Āḷavaka, and so forth. *Kātuṃ* = To plan, strive, or arrange for its destruction. *Na sakkā* = It is not possible.

*Buddhānaṃ* = Of the Omniscient Buddhas. *Sabbaññutaññāṇassa* = Of the golden Omniscient Knowledge, which can see and know everything in its entirety, without exception, within the infinite range of all things to be known (*ñeyya*). *Antarāyo* = An obstacle that would obscure or destroy the great Omniscience so it cannot manifest. *Kenaci* = By anyone at all among the great humans, Asuras, or even Baka the Brahmā. *Kātuṃ* = To plan, strive, or arrange for it to be obscured. *Na sakkā* = It is not possible.

*Bhagavato* = Of the Blessed One, endowed with the six and eight kinds of glory. *Buddhassa* = Of the Omniscient Buddha. *Ñāṇaṃ* = The golden Omniscient Knowledge. *Atītāṃse* = Regarding the vast collection of Truths and things to be known that have passed in the long front of the past saṃsāra, where no beginning can be seen. *Appaṭihataṃ* = Is free from any opposing factor that could block, hinder, or prevent the vision of even a single subtle atom (1).
753:
*Bhagavato* = Of the Blessed One, abundant in the six and eight kinds of glory. *Buddhassa* = Of the Omniscient Buddha. *Ñāṇaṃ* = The golden Omniscient Knowledge. *Anāgatāṃse* = Regarding the vast collection of Truths and things to be known that will come in the long future of saṃsāra, where no end can be seen. *Appaṭihataṃ* = Is free from any opposing factor that could block, hinder, or prevent the vision of even a single subtle atom (2).

*Bhagavato* = Of the Blessed One, radiant with the six and eight kinds of glory. *Buddhassa* = Of the Omniscient Buddha. *Ñāṇaṃ* = The golden Omniscient Knowledge. *Paccuppannāṃse* = Regarding the vast collection of Truths and things to be known that are currently occurring, arising and passing away incessantly within the thirty-one planes of existence and the infinite universes. *Appaṭihataṃ* = Is free from any opposing factor that could block, hinder, or prevent the vision of even a single subtle atom (3).

*Imehi tīhi dhammehi* = With these three expansive and uncommon qualities and virtues. *Samannāgatassa* = Who is perfectly endowed and complete. *Bhagavato* = Of the Blessed One, overflowing with the six and eight kinds of glory. *Buddhassa* = Of the Omniscient Buddha. *Sabbaṃ* = Every single one without exception. *Kāyakammaṃ* = All bodily actions, such as going, standing, sitting, lying down, moving forward or backward, advancing or retreating, stretching or bending, and all other various movements. *Ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ* = Has the four types of wisdom—clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*), clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāya-sampajañña*), clear comprehension of the resort (*gocara-sampajañña*), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*)—as the precursor and leader. *Ñāṇānuparivattaṃ* = Always follows exactly as directed by the wisdom of clear comprehension (4).

*Sabbaṃ* = Every single one without exception. *Vacīkammaṃ* = All verbal actions, including all that is spoken, uttered, and expressed. *Ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ* = Has the four types of wisdom—clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability,
754:
clear comprehension of the resort, and clear comprehension of non-delusion—as the precursor and leader. *Ñāṇānuparivattaṃ* = Always follows exactly as directed by the wisdom of clear comprehension (5).

*Sabbaṃ* = Every single one without exception. *Manokammaṃ* = All mental actions, including all that is thought. *Ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ* = Has the four types of wisdom—clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of the resort, and clear comprehension of non-delusion—as the precursor and leader. *Ñāṇānuparivattaṃ* = Always follows exactly as directed by the wisdom of clear comprehension (6).

*Imehi chahi dhammehi* = With these six expansive and uncommon qualities and virtues. *Samannāgatassa* = Who is perfectly endowed and complete. *Bhagavato* = Of the Blessed One, overflowing with the six and eight kinds of glory. *Buddhassa* = To the Omniscient Buddha. *Chandassa* = Regarding the two kinds of desire: *āgama-chanda* (the desire for the goal), which arose in the being of the Hermit Sumedha, the future Buddha, with the aspiration, "I will carry the many beings living in the ten thousand world-systems to the shore of peace (*khema*)"; and *adhigama-chanda* (the desire for attainment), which is the fulfillment of all wishes as part of the glory of *kāma*. *Hāni* = Any failure or deficiency in achieving as much as was intended. *Natthi* = Does not exist even in the slightest degree (7).

*Dhammadesanāya* = Regarding the noble teaching that analyzes and points out the way to achieve the true liberation (*nissaraṇa*) and the path out of the three cycles of existence (*vaṭṭa*). *Hāni* = Any failure or decrease in achieving the great fruit of liberation and escape. *Natthi* = Does not exist even in the slightest degree (8).

*Vīriyassa* = Regarding the energy [which is so great that even if] the ten thousand world-systems, measuring 1,203,450 yojanas in circumference, were filled with glowing coals and spear-points—
755:
755
If a person can reach the other shore, he will certainly become a Buddha; with such courage, he can cross over without a hair's breadth of hesitation. This is the Āgama-vīriya (Energy of Arrival), which is the courageous effort. The Āgama-vīriya is also capable of fulfilling the fourfold unique tasks and is proficient in the tasks of Sammappadhāna (Right Exertion). The Adhigama-vīriya (Energy of Attainment) is the perpetual renewal of strength to ensure that the five daily duties are never neglected. Of these three types of Vīriya, there is no Hāni (decline or deficiency). Not even an atom of it exists (9).

Regarding Samādhi (Concentration): There is the Pakati-samādhi (Natural Concentration) which remains unshaken and firm like Mount Meru, even when storms blow from the eight directions, remaining steady even when encountering the eight worldly conditions (Lokadhamma) simultaneously. There is also the Appanā-samādhi (Attainment Concentration), which is the foundation of the powers of Iddhividha-abhiññā (Supernormal Powers), Dibba-cakkhu (Divine Eye), Dibba-sota (Divine Ear), Cetopariya-abhiññā (Knowledge of Others' Minds), Pubbenivāsānussati-abhiññā (Recollection of Past Lives), Yathākammūpaga-abhiññā (Knowledge of Beings Passing Away According to Karma), and Anāgataṃsa-abhiññā (Knowledge of the Future), having reached the limit of the five masteries (Vasī). Of these two types of Samādhi, there is no Hāni (decline). Not even an atom of it exists (10).

Regarding Paññā (Wisdom): There is the noble Mahāvajira-ñāṇa (Great Diamond Knowledge), numbering two million four hundred thousand, which clearly sees the end of all conditioned things (Saṅkhāra-dhamma) in the three realms across the ten thousand world systems without exception, and which is practiced daily without ceasing. Of this Wisdom, there is no Hāni (decline). Not even an atom of it exists (11).

Regarding Vimutti (Deliverance): Like the destruction of a hundred thousand crores of worlds, that which is poured out and spread to cover all beings—Brahmas, humans, devas, and those in the four woeful states—without exception throughout the universe...
756:
756
...namely the four Ceto-vimutti (Deliverance of Mind) of the Brahma-vihāras: Mettā (Loving-kindness), Karuṇā (Compassion), Muditā (Appreciative Joy), and Upekkhā (Equanimity). Also, the noble Vimutti of the supreme bliss of the fourth jhāna of Arahattaphala, numbering about two million four hundred thousand, which is entered into day and night without ceasing, even during the moments of preaching to the assembly of Brahmas, humans, and devas. Of these five types of Vimutti, there is no Hāni (decline). Not even an atom of it exists (12).

In the Buddha, the Exalted One, who is fully endowed with these twelve unique and expansive qualities (Asādhāraṇa-dhamma), and who shines with the sixfold and eightfold glories: There is no bodily, verbal, or mental action performed, spoken, or thought that is devoid of mindfulness and clear comprehension (Sati-sampajañña), or that is frivolous, negligent, or jesting. Not even an atom of such exists (13).

There is no action that is done hastily, carelessly, or without due consideration, lacking mindfulness and clear comprehension, such that wise persons could speak of it as a flaw or a lapse. Not even an atom of such exists (14).

There is no matter where, even if acting with consideration, something is left incomplete or unpervaded because of a lack of wisdom or failure to see the full scope of the opportunity, such that wise persons could speak of it as a deficiency. Not even an atom of such exists (15).

There is no instance where, due to the influence of the mind, one acts out of fear or excessive playfulness, leading to transgressions in body or speech that are improper or erroneous, such that wise persons could speak of it as a fault. Not even an atom of such exists (16).
757:
757
Abyāvaṭamano: There is no occurrence of a thought-process (Javana-cittuppāda) that is occasionally devoid of the great exertion (Mahā-ussāha) and activity directed towards the two benefits: His own welfare (Attahita) and the welfare and happiness of the many beings living in the ten thousand world systems. Not even an atom of such exists (17).

Appaṭisaṅkhānupekkhā: There is no such thing as ignoring or being indifferent to any of the six objects—visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects—that appear at the six doors of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, without investigating them or knowing them clearly with mindfulness. Not even an atom of such exists (18).

In the Buddha, the Exalted One, who is fully endowed with these eighteen unique and expansive qualities (Asādhāraṇa-dhamma), and who shines with the sixfold and eightfold glories: No one is able to create any obstacle (Antarāya) to His life or the radiance of His wisdom, despite many efforts and schemes. It is not possible.

Tad-eva vacanaṃ saccaṃ, bhagavantaṃ namāmahaṃ.
Etena sacca-puññena, cintā mayhaṃ samijjhatu.

That very word, which describes and praises the eighteen unique qualities (Āveṇika-guṇa) of the Buddha with devotion, is indeed the truth, excellent and certain. I pay homage to the Exalted One, who is endowed with the glory and grace of the Āveṇika-dhamma, bowing my head with joined palms in reverence. By this merit of truth from praising the eighteen Buddha-dhammas...
758:
758
...and by the volition of the meritorious deed of paying respectful homage: May all my noble thoughts and intentions for the increase of both mundane and supramundane benefits, in the present and in the future, be fulfilled and accomplished without delay, just as I have planned.

Here ends the Eighteen Unique Qualities (Āveṇika-guṇa).

(Since the four Vesārajja-ñāṇa (Groundedness of Confidence) have already been written starting from page 649 of this fifth volume of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, they are not repeated here.

Note: The description of the Buddha's qualities such as Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa, Asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa, and Dasabala-ñāṇa is like taking a single drop of water from the ocean to taste its saltiness; it is merely a drop from the vast ocean of the Buddha's qualities. It should be specially noted that the qualities of the Buddha not yet mentioned in this text are more numerous than the volume of water in the great ocean.)

## Special Notes on the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta

I shall now present in order the "Special Notes for the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta and the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta" as directed on page 430 of the second volume of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas.

Before the Buddha appeared, there were prominent teachers known as recluses (samaṇas) throughout the Middle Country (Majjhima-desa). Among those many teachers, some practiced and taught Kāmasukhallikānuyoga (devotion to sensual pleasures) and others practiced and taught Attakilamathānuyoga (devotion to self-mortification) as the duty and practice of a recluse.
759:
759
While the world was covered in the great darkness of practicing and teaching these two low paths as the true Dhamma, the Buddha preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta on the full moon day of Āsāḷha in the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakarāj), just as the sun was about to set. (Keep the text and meaning of the Dhammacakka in mind.)

As soon as the Buddha began this Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta with the sentence, "Dveme bhikkhave antā pabbajitena na sevitabbā" (Monks, these two extremes should not be followed by one who has gone forth), the great echo produced by the Buddha's power reached down to Avīci and up to the highest heaven (Bhavagga), spreading throughout the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth (Jāti-khetta). At that very time, eighteen crores of Brahmas, who possessed mature roots of merit and the necessary supportive merit (adhikāra) to realize the Four Noble Truths, had already assembled in unity at the place in the Isipatana Deer Park where the first sermon was to be preached. The time the first sermon began was when the sun was about to set in the west and the moon was about to rise in the east.

The summary of the sequence of this Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is as follows: The Buddha first preached to the group of five monks (Pañcavaggī) about the two low paths to be avoided. Then, He preached the Middle Way (Majjhima-paṭipadā) consisting of the Eightfold Path to be followed. Then, He preached the Four Noble Truths in brief. Then, regarding the Four Noble Truths for Himself...
760:
760
...He preached that He only claimed Buddhahood when He was fully endowed with the three types of knowledge for each of the truths. Then, He preached that while this discourse was being delivered, the Venerable Koṇḍañña attained the stage of a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). After the Buddha had set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, the deities from the earth-dwelling devas (Bhumma-deva) up to the Brahmas shouted cries of praise. The great earth shook. A great radiance, produced by the mind and the seasonal conditions (cittappaccaya-utusamuṭṭhāna) through the power of Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), appeared, being a thousand times greater than the radiance of devas and Brahmas. At that time, the Buddha's disposition was one of great joy and delight, both at the beginning and the end of the sermon. Unable to contain the surge of rapture (pīti), He uttered the inspired exclamation (Udāna): "Aññāsi vata bho Koṇḍañño, aññāsi vata bho Koṇḍañño" (O, Koṇḍañña has indeed understood the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation! O, Koṇḍañña has indeed understood the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation!). (This sound of the inspired exclamation also spread throughout the ten thousand world systems). Then, at the request of Venerable Koṇḍañña to receive ordination as a monk, the Buddha called him with "Ehi Bhikkhu," and thus Venerable Koṇḍañña became an "Ehi Bhikkhu" monk. This is the summary of the sequence of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.

## Definition of Dhammacakka
(In this context, one might ask: What is called 'Dhammacakka'? The answer is: That which arises in the Buddha's continuum...)
761:
761
Penetrative Knowledge (the four Path Knowledges are called Penetrative Knowledge) and Teaching Knowledge—these two types of knowledge are called the Dhammacakka (Wheel of Dhamma).

To elaborate: The four Path Knowledges, which possess twelve aspects regarding the Four Noble Truths and arose within the continuum of the Buddha (the Bodhisatta who was about to become Buddha) while seated at the Throne of Great Enlightenment; and the Teaching Knowledge, which possesses twelve aspects and causes the teaching of the Truths to arise within the continuum of the Buddha while seated in the Isipatana Migadāya forest delivering the first sermon of the Dhammacakka—both are called Dhammacakka. Both these knowledges are called Dhammacakka (the Dhamma-wheel or Dhamma-weapon) because, like a wheel-weapon that can subdue and destroy enemies, they can subdue and destroy the enemies of defilements (kilesa).

Both these knowledges are indeed knowledges that arose within the heart of the Buddha. The Buddha, who clearly manifested both these knowledges through this first sermon, is said to have 'turned' or 'set in motion' the Dhammacakka. The Buddha is said to be 'still setting in motion' or 'still turning' this Dhammacakka until the moment the Venerable Koṇḍañña, along with eighteen crores of Brahmas, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). This is because the task of setting it in motion or turning it was not yet completed. From the moment the Venerable Koṇḍañña and the eighteen crores of Brahmas were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry, the Buddha is said to have 'turned' or 'set in motion' the Dhammacakka. This is because the task of setting in motion and turning these two types of Dhammacakka knowledge—which no one had set in motion or turned for such a long period from the disappearance of the Dispensation of Kassapa Buddha until the appearance of this Buddha—was completed. (From Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Vol. 3, page 181).

In this context, when the four Path Knowledges called Penetrative Knowledge (Paṭivedha) realize the four Truths, they realize the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha-sacca) or Nibbāna by taking it as an object. However, the other three Truths should be understood as being realized by the 'accomplishment of the task' (kicca-siddhi). Realization by the accomplishment of the task means:
762:
762
It means that because the Path Knowledge (Magga-ñāṇa) abandons and destroys the defilement of delusion (moha) or ignorance (avijjā) which covers and protects the Four Noble Truths, the task of realizing the Four Noble Truths is already completed at that very moment (the moment of the Path).

This concludes the special notes on the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.

## Special Notes on the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta
After the Buddha established the Venerable Koṇḍañña in the Fruit of Stream-entry, from the first day after the full moon of Āsāḷha, He no longer entered the town or village even for alms. He looked after those monks of the group of five (pañcavaggī) like children, residing only within the monastery and teaching and admonishing them. At that time, on the first and second days after the full moon, the Venerable Vappa and the Venerable Bhaddiya respectively were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry and received the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination.

Thereafter, the Buddha had only the three monks—Venerable Koṇḍañña, Venerable Vappa, and Venerable Bhaddiya—go for alms, while the Venerable Mahānāma and the Venerable Assaji were not sent for alms but remained in the monastery to be taught and admonished. The Buddha and all five members of the group of five—these six—subsisted on the alms food received by the three monks: Venerable Koṇḍañña, Venerable Vappa, and Venerable Bhaddiya. Then, on the third and fourth days after the full moon, the Venerable Mahānāma and the Venerable Assaji respectively were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry and received the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination.

After the five elders of the group of five were thus established in the Fruit of Stream-entry in succession, on the 5th day after the full moon of Āsāḷha, the Buddha reflected, "Now I shall preach the Dhamma to these five monks of the group of five so that they may reach the Path and Fruit of Arahantship."
763:
763
Having thus reflected, He preached this Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta on that day. (Keep in mind the Pali text and meaning of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta).

The summary of the sequence of this Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta teaching is as follows:
(a) First, the Buddha preached the nature of non-self (anattā) of the five aggregates, based on the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa), starting with: "Rūpaṃ bhikkhave anattā = Monks, form is not self."

(b) After that, He preached the nature of impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anattā) of the five aggregates by asking: "Taṃ kiṃ maññatha bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā = Monks, what do you think about this which I, the Buddha, am about to ask? Is form permanent or impermanent?" and so forth. This teaching, delivered by repeatedly asking about the nature of impermanence, suffering, and non-self of the five aggregates and having the listeners answer according to their understanding, is designated in the great Commentaries and Sub-commentaries as the Te-parivaṭṭa-dhamma-desanā = the Dhamma teaching delivered through three rounds of questioning. In this section also, the primary intention is to teach the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) by using the characteristics of impermanence and suffering as a basis.

To elaborate: In some suttas, the Buddha teaches the characteristic of non-self in connection with the characteristic of impermanence (one should see the Chachakka Sutta in the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pali). In some suttas, He teaches the characteristic of non-self clearly in connection with the characteristic of suffering (one should see the first part of this present Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta). In some suttas,
764:
764
He teaches the characteristic of non-self clearly in connection with both impermanence and suffering (one should see the Te-parivaṭṭa-dhamma-desanā section of this present Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, as well as the Arahanta Sutta in the Khandhavagga Saṃyutta Pali, pages 68-69 of Vol. 2, etc.). The reason for teaching the characteristic of non-self in connection with impermanence and suffering is that the nature of impermanence and the nature of suffering are obvious in the world, while the nature of non-self is not obvious in the world.

To make it clearer: When utensils such as pots and bowls are accidentally broken, many people say, "Oh, impermanence (anicca)!" but no one says, "Oh, non-self (anattā)!" When boils, wounds, or swellings appear on their bodies, or when they are pierced by thorns, many people say, "Oh, suffering (dukkha), suffering!" but no one says, "Oh, non-self (anattā)!" The reason they do not say "Oh, non-self" is that the characteristic of non-self is not clear, is difficult to see, and difficult to make known. Therefore, the Buddha teaches the characteristic of non-self in connection with the characteristic of impermanence, or in connection with the characteristic of suffering, or in connection with both. In this Te-parivaṭṭa-dhamma-desanā section of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, the characteristic of non-self is also taught in connection with both impermanence and suffering.

(c) Then, He taught: "Tasmā tiha bhikkhave yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ... sampappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ = Therefore, monks (because all five aggregates are impermanent and suffering, and thus should not be regarded as 'mine', 'I', or 'my self'), any form whatsoever—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—should be seen as 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'...
765:
765
...with right insight-wisdom and Path-wisdom according to how it truly is." In this way, He taught the method of contemplating the five aggregates with insight-wisdom, and the method of realizing them through the accomplishment of the task (kicca-siddhi) with Path-wisdom upon reaching the Path.

(Special note: In practicing insight, contemplating as impermanent (anicca) can abandon the attachment of conceit (māna). Contemplating as suffering (dukkha) can abandon the attachment of craving (taṇhā). Contemplating as non-self (anattā) can abandon the attachment of wrong view (diṭṭhi). In this section, contemplating as "This is not mine" is for abandoning the attachment of craving; it follows the same course as the contemplation of suffering. Contemplating as "This I am not" is for abandoning the attachment of conceit; it follows the same course as the contemplation of impermanence. Contemplating as "This is not my self" is for abandoning the attachment of wrong view; it is the contemplation of non-self itself—this should be specifically noted).

(d) Then, as the conclusion of the teaching, He taught how the stages of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā-ñāṇa), Path-knowledge, Fruit-knowledge, and Reviewing-knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) arise step by step up to the Fruit of Arahantship if one repeatedly contemplates the five aggregates according to point (c), starting with: "Evaṃ passaṃ bhikkhave sutavā ariyasāvako..."

(e) Then, He concluded the teaching by stating that while this Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta was being preached, the monks of the group of five reached the Fruit of Arahantship and became Arahants.

Based on this sutta, it is evident that the five elders of the group of five reached the Fruit of Arahantship through the meditation on the aggregates (khandha-kammaṭṭhāna), contemplating the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Therefore, for the sake of Burmese Buddhist devotees:

1. Known as the aggregate of Form (Rūpa), it does not last for a long time; arising for a moment, it vanishes in a moment. By the dual oppression of arising and vanishing, it is incessantly and greatly painful. It has no solid core or essence. When looking and contemplating with the eye of wisdom, its nature of impermanence is indeed suffering and non-self.

2. Known as the aggregate of Feeling (Vedanā), it also does not last for a long time; arising for a moment, it vanishes in a moment. By the dual oppression of arising and vanishing, it is incessantly and greatly painful. It has no solid core or essence. When looking and contemplating with the eye of wisdom, its nature of impermanence is indeed suffering and non-self.

3. Known as the aggregate of Perception (Saññā), it also does not last for a long time; arising for a moment, it vanishes in a moment. By the dual oppression of arising and vanishing, it is incessantly and greatly painful. It has no solid core or essence. When looking and contemplating with the eye of wisdom, its nature of impermanence is indeed suffering and non-self.

4. Known as the aggregate of Mental Formations (Saṅkhāra), it also does not last for a long time; arising for a moment, it vanishes in a moment. By the dual oppression of arising and vanishing, it is incessantly and greatly painful. It has no solid core or essence. When looking and contemplating with the eye of wisdom, its nature of impermanence is indeed suffering and non-self.

5. Known as the six types of Consciousness (Viññāṇa), this aggregate also does not last for a long time; arising for a moment, it vanishes in a moment. By the dual oppression of arising and vanishing, it is incessantly and greatly painful. It has no solid core or essence. When looking and contemplating with the eye of wisdom, its nature of impermanence is indeed suffering and non-self.

One should memorize, recite, and develop these verses of insight on the five aggregates, keeping them in mind. (These five verses are included here to make the meaning easier to perceive than contemplating in Pali.)

The special notes on the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta are finished.

## The Ratana Sutta: Pāḷi and Meaning
According to the instruction at the bottom of page 305 of the third volume of this Great Chronicle of Buddhas, which states, "The Pāḷi and meaning of this Ratana Sutta, which is worthy of listening and devotion, is presented in the section on Dhamma-ratana," I shall now present the meaning of the Ratana Sutta as written by the Ko-saung Sayadaw, who composed the Pāḷi and the meaning of the Buddha's attributes.

*Paṇidhānato paṭṭhāya tathāgatassa dasa pāramiyo, dasa upapāramiyo, dasa paramatthapāramiyo ti = samattiṃsa pāramiyo, pañca mahāpariccāge, lokatthacariyaṃ ñātatthacariyaṃ buddhatthacariyan ti = tisso cariyāyo, pacchimabhave gabbhavokkantiṃ, jātiṃ, abhinikkhamanaṃ, padhānacariyaṃ, bodhipallaṅke māravijayaṃ, sabbaññutañāṇappaṭivedhaṃ, dhammacakkappavattanaṃ, nava lokuttaradhamme ti sabbe pime buddhaguṇe āvajjitvā vesāliyā tīsu pākārantaresu tiyāmarattiṃ parittaṃ karonto āyasmā ānandatthero viya kāruññacittaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā—*

*Koṭīsatasahassesu, cakkavāḷesu devatā.*
*Yassāṇaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti, yañca vesāliyā pure.*
*Rogāmanussadubbhikkha-sambhūtaṃ tividhaṃ bhayaṃ.*
*Khippamantara-dhāpesi, parittaṃ taṃ bhaṇāma he.*

**Paṇidhānato** = From the time of the aspiration, when [the Bodhisatta] lay prostrate at the feet of the fourth Sovereign [Dīpaṅkara Buddha] in the Sāramanda kalpa, and having served with great strength and devotion, received the flower of the Definite Prophecy (Niyata-byākarana) and placed it upon his head. **Paṭṭhāya** = Starting from then. **Tathāgatassa** = Of the Inconceivable Noble Buddha, who came in the same manner as all the Kings of Dhamma who have passed away, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

(In this context, the method of counting the 108 Noble Persons is as follows: There are four Noble Ones established in the Path (maggatṭhāna) and four Noble Ones established in the Fruit (phalatṭhāna). (Setting aside the four Path-attainers for a moment), among the four established in the Fruit: 1. The Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer) is of three types: (a) Ekabījī Sotāpanna = one who has only one more life to be born; (b) Kolaṃkola Sotāpanna = one who has two to six more lives; (c) Sattakkhattuparama Sotāpanna = one who has at most seven more lives. When these three types are multiplied by the four modes of progress (paṭipadā), there are 12 types of Sotāpanna.

(The period from the start of meditation until the removal of hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is the 'Paṭipadā' stage. After the hindrances are removed, the period until reaching the Path-knowledge is the 'Abhiññā' (higher insight) stage. A person who can remove hindrances easily and without hardship during the Paṭipadā stage is called one with 'Sukha-paṭipadā' (pleasant progress). One who removes them with difficulty and hardship is called one with 'Dukkha-paṭipadā' (painful progress). In the Abhiññā stage, one who reaches the Path quickly after hindrances are removed is called a 'Khippābhiññā' person (one of quick intuition). One who reaches the Path slowly is called a 'Dandhābiññā' person (one of slow intuition). 1. One who removes hindrances easily and reaches Path-knowledge quickly...
778:
778

...is called a 'Sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā' person. 2. One who removes hindrances easily but reaches the Path slowly is called a 'Sukha-paṭipadā dandhābiññā' person. 3. One who removes hindrances with difficulty but reaches Path-knowledge quickly is called a 'Dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā' person. 4. One who removes hindrances with difficulty and reaches the Path slowly is called a 'Dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābiññā' person. Since each type of Sotāpanna is multiplied by these four modes of progress, there are 12 types of Sotāpanna.

The Sakadāgāmī (Once-returner) is also of three types: the Sensual-sphere Sakadāgāmī, the Fine-material-sphere Sakadāgāmī, and the Immaterial-sphere Sakadāgāmī. When these three are multiplied by the four modes of progress, there are 12 types of Sakadāgāmī. Referring to these 12 Sotāpanna and 12 Sakadāgāmī, the Nissaya uses the term 'dvāda, dvāda' (twelve, twelve).

The Anāgāmī (Non-returner) is of five types: 1. Antarā-parinibbāyī, 2. Upahacca-parinibbāyī, 3. Sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī, 4. Asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī, 5. Uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī. In the five Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) where Anāgāmī reside: 5 types in Avihā, 5 in Atappā, 5 in Sudassā, 5 in Sudassī, and 4 in Akaniṭṭha (excluding the Uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī who is already counted), making a total of 24 types of Anāgāmī.

The Arahant is of two types: 1. Sukkhavipassaka Arahant = one who has pure insight without jhāna or supernormal powers; 2. Samathayānika Arahant = one who has the vehicle of tranquility, possessing jhāna and supernormal powers. Referring to these 24 Anāgāmī and 2 Arahants, the Nissaya uses the term 'jovī, dva' (jovī = 24, dva = 2).

Adding the 12 Sotāpanna, 12 Sakadāgāmī, 24 Anāgāmī, 2 Arahants, and the 4 Path-attainers (maggatṭhāna), the total is 54. When these 54 are multiplied by the two-fold dominance of faith (saddhā-dhura) and wisdom (paññā-dhura), the total becomes 108.

## Aspiration Poem for the Conclusion of the Ratana Sutta
Yaṃkiñ, Khayaṃ, Yaṃbud, Yepug,
Yesup, Yathin, Yerī, Sahā.
Kiñcā, Vanap, Varo, Khīṇaṃ,
Vandāmi sirasāmahaṃ—
Recite the original 'Yānīdha' and the aspiration verses without fail. Just as the three calamities were averted in Vesālī at the beginning, they will be swiftly cleared away. Do not let the instructions of 'Kammavāso Pabbāso' be vague or confused. Even the Buddha—
793:
793
Those who believe in the sharpness and stability of the Dhamma-cakka (Wheel of Dhamma) issued from the golden mouth of the Buddha will have their virtues shine. Therefore, let all people, monks and layfolk alike, who wish to be purified of dangers, recite and listen to this Paritta called the Ratana Sutta—which displays a unique combination of virtues—with worship, love, faith, and refuge.

(This word-for-word translation and aspiration poem of the Ratana Sutta are extracted from the 'New Nissaya of the Great Paritta, Myingyan 9-Saung Version').
